names: The Joyful Beggar, novel by Louis de Wohl (1958)

suitability.note: There are battles and sword fights without gore, and Francis's blindness, stigmata and death are shown plainly but gently. The main obstacle for children is the slow pace and long speeches.

doctrine: Innocent III gave verbal approval to Francis's first rule; the definitive Rule was confirmed by Honorius III in the bull Solet annuere of 29 November 1223, and binds the friars to observe the Gospel in obedience, without property and in chastity. Clare's order followed the same poverty under its own rule. Francis was ordained deacon but, out of humility, never sought the priesthood. He received the stigmata on La Verna in September 1224, around the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross, and the Church keeps a commemoration of the Stigmata on 17 September. He was canonised on 16 July 1228 by Gregory IX, who as Cardinal Hugolino had been protector of the order, the role Cecil Kellaway plays. His feast is 4 October.
production: Twentieth Century-Fox made the film from Louis de Wohl's novel The Joyful Beggar (1958), with Plato A. Skouras producing and Michael Curtiz directing. Filming began in Italy on 28 October 1960 and took about five months, in Assisi, elsewhere in Umbria and in Rome; the papal apartment at the Basilica of San Francesco stood in for the Lateran. Reshoots followed at the Fox lot in Los Angeles in March 1961. Mario Nascimbene's score was reported as the first film soundtrack to use Gregorian chant. It premiered in San Francisco on 12 July 1961 and in Assisi on 4 October 1961. Reviews were cool: the New York Times called it serene and static and Variety complained of ponderous verbosity. It earned about $920,000 in North American rentals, and Skouras blamed weak support from the Church as well as the reviews. Dolores Hart, who played Clare, entered the Benedictine Abbey of Regina Laudis in 1963.

title: Monsieur Vincent
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review and Steve Vineberg's essay independently document an unsentimental portrait of priestly charity, with specific episodes (the plague village, the Ladies and Daughters of Charity, the foundlings) and a brief war-time assault image advised. AlloCiné settles identity.
summary: Pierre Fresnay's austere Vincent de Paul turns the organisation of charity into high drama in Maurice Cloche's understated, Oscar-honoured 1947 biography.
synopsis: Vincent, a young priest who has been comfortable as chaplain to a great family, takes the poor parish of Châtillon-les-Dombes. Plague has struck it, and the villagers stone him from their windows. He shames a lord who has barred his doors, finds an orphaned girl beside her dead mother, and persuades an overburdened neighbour to take her in. His first confraternity of charity grows from this. In Paris he enlists aristocratic Ladies of Charity, who soon send their maids instead of coming themselves. With Louise de Marillac he forms the Daughters of Charity from country girls. He serves as chaplain to the galley convicts, argues with Richelieu, and struggles over abandoned infants whom even the sisters at first refuse to touch. War ravages the provinces. Old and nearly blind, he charges a young sister with the hardest lesson of service to the poor.
inclusion: Fresnay won the Best Actor prize at Venice, and his Vincent is no plaster saint. He is dry, ironic, sometimes harsh, and always working. Jean Anouilh co-wrote the screenplay, and the dialogue has an edge; Claude Renoir's black-and-white images are sober and handsome. Steven Greydanus calls it a towering achievement. He praises its refusal to romanticise the poor or excuse the rich, and its sense of Vincent as an organiser who turned almsgiving into institutions. Steve Vineberg singles out the foundling sequence. The film is episodic, and some threads, the galleys and the foundlings, are left hanging; Greydanus calls it a fragment of a larger story. It received a special Academy Award as best foreign-language film in 1949.
themes: Charity here is a duty laid on the Christian, and it is uncomfortable. The poor are often ungrateful, dirty and rude, and Vincent insists they are owed help anyway. The rich are criticised not for having money but for wanting the satisfaction of giving without the labour. Vincent's priesthood is the source of his work: he prays, preaches and hears confessions, and the film never presents him as a social reformer who happens to wear a cassock. The Daughters of Charity appear as a new form of consecrated life lived in the streets. The final lesson, that the poor must be served humbly enough to forgive us our bread, is the film's moral centre.
history: Vincent de Paul (1581–1660) was parish priest at Châtillon-les-Dombes in 1617, where he founded the first Confraternity of Charity. He founded the Congregation of the Mission in 1625 and, with Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity in 1633. He was royal chaplain of the galleys and organised care for foundlings and relief for war-ravaged Lorraine. He was canonised in 1737.
liberties: The film omits Vincent's early life, including the disputed story of his capture by pirates. It compresses forty years into a series of episodes and leaves several outcomes unclear. One German plot summary says he takes a galley convict's place at the oar, a hagiographic legend historians reject; this is unconfirmed for the film.
advisories:
Brief violence (stoning); a fleeting war montage with a glimpse of rape, nothing explicit.

Plague, death, misery and abandoned babies.

Best for teenagers and adults.

suitability.note: A stoning, a brief war montage with a glimpse of rape, plague, death and abandoned babies, none shown graphically. It is slow and talky, and teenagers will follow it better than small children.

doctrine: Vincent's work is the corporal works of mercy as the Church has always taught them: feeding the hungry, tending the sick, ransoming captives and burying the dead. Christ says that what is done to the least of his brethren is done to him (Matthew 25:40). Vincent also served the Council of Trent's reform of the clergy: his Congregation of the Mission (founded 1625) gave missions to country people and trained priests, and the Council's decree on seminaries (Session 23, 1563) was in the same spirit. He founded the Daughters of Charity in 1633 with Louise de Marillac as women who lived in the world rather than in an enclosure. He was canonised by Clement XII in 1737, and Leo XIII named him patron of all charitable societies in 1885. His traditional feast is 19 July.
production: Maurice Cloche directed from a screenplay by Jean Anouilh and Jean Bernard-Luc. Pierre Fresnay played Vincent, and his performance won him the Volpi Cup for best actor at Venice in 1947. The film was released in France on 5 November 1947 and won the Grand Prix du Cinéma Français. It is a black-and-white picture of 114 minutes. In the United States it received an honorary Academy Award as the best foreign-language film released there in 1948, and it was nominated for the BAFTA for Best Film. Sight and Sound called Fresnay's performance 'one of the most perfect pieces of work' seen for many years. In 1995 the Vatican included it in its list of great films.

title: The Reluctant Saint
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog gives a detailed plot and production record, TCM's article documents the US–Italian co-production and its reception, and Greydanus's review recommends it for families. It is gentle, accurate in spirit, and has no content concerns beyond a brief exorcism scene.
summary: Maximilian Schell plays Joseph of Cupertino, the slow-witted friar who flew, in Edward Dmytryk's gentle, funny and finally moving Italian-shot comedy.
synopsis: In seventeenth-century Apulia, Giuseppe Desa is a clumsy, dim young man whom nobody in his village wants. His mother Francesca, tired of him, gets her brother to have the Franciscan friary take him. Giuseppe is put to work in the stables, where he is happy with the animals and humble before everyone. The kindly bishop sees something in him and lets him try for ordination, and against all expectation he passes the examination when he is asked the one text he knows. Father Raspi (Ricardo Montalban), a strict and learned friar, distrusts him and suspects the devil when strange things start to happen, even attempting an exorcism. Then Giuseppe, praying before a statue of the Madonna, rises into the air, and the whole friary has to reckon with a holiness it did not see coming.
inclusion: This is a modest film, and it knows it. Schell, fresh from his Oscar for Judgment at Nuremberg, plays Joseph without condescension: slow, sweet and stubborn. He later counted it among his best performances. Montalban's Raspi is a good foil, a clever man humbled by a simple one. Shot in Rome and Lazio with Nino Rota's score, it looks and sounds Italian. Steven Greydanus calls it fine family viewing and admires the way the film holds back the miracles for over an hour, so that we know Joseph as a person before we see him fly. The comedy is broad and the special effects are dated, and it failed at the box office; Dmytryk called it his biggest flop. It deserves better.
themes: The film is about humility and how God chooses the weak to confound the strong. Joseph is not clever, and the friars, especially Raspi, assume that holiness must look like learning. His obedience is total: he does whatever task he is given. Raspi's suspicion of the devil reflects the Church's real caution about extraordinary phenomena, and the film treats it fairly before showing the truth. Joseph's love of animals and his joy in prayer echo St. Francis. The ordination scene, where he passes by being asked the one thing he knows, is told as Providence. The levitations are a fruit of his love for Our Lady, not a show.
history: Giuseppe Desa (1603–1663) was born at Cupertino in Apulia, was accepted by the Conventual Franciscans after several rejections, and was ordained in 1628. His ecstasies and levitations, witnessed by many, led the Inquisition to examine him and move him from friary to friary; he died at Osimo. He was canonised in 1767 and is the patron of students taking examinations.
liberties: The film compresses his life to the years up to his first levitations and omits the Inquisition's investigations and his later confinement. Father Raspi is largely an invented composite. The exam story is told as a single scene. The plot puts much of the early action at the friary at Grottella, where the historical Joseph lived.
advisories:
Brief exorcism scene, played seriously but not frightening.

Mild comic slapstick; no violence or sexual content.

Suitable for all ages.

suitability.note: Light comedy with a short, serious exorcism scene that is not frightening. No violence or sexual content, and a plainly innocent hero, which makes it a good family saint film.

doctrine: Joseph of Cupertino (1603-1663) was refused by the Conventual Franciscans and later by the Capuchins, then admitted to the clerical state in 1625 and ordained priest in 1628. His ecstasies and levitations were reported by many witnesses; he was kept from public ministry and the Inquisition examined him. The Church teaches that such phenomena are gratuitous graces and are not themselves the measure of holiness, which is charity and humility, as Benedict XIV argued in his treatise on beatification. Priests are bound to test claims of the extraordinary, as Father Raspi does. Benedict XIV beatified him in 1753 and Clement XIII canonised him in 1767. His feast is 18 September. He is the patron of students facing examinations.
production: Edward Dmytryk directed this American-Italian comedy-drama, shot in Rome, from a script by John Fante and Joseph Petracca, with music by Nino Rota. It is in English and runs 105 minutes. Maximilian Schell played Joseph (called Giuseppe Desa in the film), Ricardo Montalbán played Father Raspi and Akim Tamiroff the bishop. A TV Guide review praised the light tone but found the direction lifeless. No Legion of Decency rating was found.

title: Heaven over the Marshes
decision: PUBLISH: Identity is established by the Museo Nazionale del Cinema and contemporary Italian criticism, and the treatment by the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico synopsis, Aristarco (1949) and Morandini. The record gives no running time, so the unresolved 111 v. 98 minute discrepancy between festival records and the 2010 Fox DVD does not affect anything published; it is noted for viewers.
summary: Augusto Genina's neorealist-style life of Maria Goretti, filmed in the Pontine marshes with peasant non-actors: the story of a twelve-year-old who resisted, died and forgave.
synopsis: Luigi Goretti, a farm labourer, brings his wife and six children to the malarial marshes near Nettuno, where the landowners lodge them in a farmhouse with the Serenellis, a father and son who resent them. Luigi works tirelessly, but malaria kills him, and the fatherless family is left at the Serenellis' mercy. The drunken old man pursues the widow, who rebuffs him. His son Alessandro becomes obsessed with Maria, the eldest daughter and still almost a child. He tries small gifts, then force; she escapes him, and he threatens her. On a July afternoon, with everyone in the fields, he drags her into the house and, enraged by her refusal, stabs her again and again. Taken to hospital, she suffers for a day, holds firm in her faith, and forgives her murderer before she dies.
inclusion: Genina shot on location in the marshes with non-professional actors, and Ines Orsini, a peasant girl, plays Maria with plain conviction. G. R. Aldo's photography of the flat, fevered landscape won admiration, and Genina won the Nastro d'Argento for direction. A 1955 survey of Italian cinema found it lacking in religious depth but called it sincerely moving and a faithful chronicle of events. Guido Aristarco, writing in Cinema in December 1949, faulted its pictorial calligraphy and sentimental touches with the children, yet judged it the best film Genina had made in Italy. Morandini called it neorealism in a Catholic key. It is a serious, restrained treatment of a martyrdom that could easily have been exploited.
themes: Maria's purity is presented as a choice of the will, not innocence alone: she knows what Alessandro wants and refuses it, even at the cost of her life. Her forgiveness of her murderer on her deathbed is the film's spiritual climax and the heart of her holiness. The poverty of the family, the fever of the marsh and the absence of the father show the conditions in which sin grows, without excusing it. The title sets heaven against the stagnant swamp. The film ends with Maria's death, before Alessandro's conversion, and so leaves the fruit of her forgiveness to the viewer's knowledge.
history: Maria Goretti was stabbed on 5 July 1902 at Le Ferriere di Conca, in the Pontine marshes, by Alessandro Serenelli, and died the next day at Nettuno after forgiving him. Serenelli later repented in prison and was reconciled with her mother. Pius XII beatified Maria in 1947 and canonised her on 24 June 1950, seven months after the film opened on 24 November 1949.
liberties: Genina compressed and shaped events, and his screenplay was more explicit in its symbolism than the finished film, according to the Torino retrospective essay. The film stops at Maria's death and omits Alessandro's later conversion. Andreotti recalled that Pius XII, at a screening, was troubled by one scene that showed more of the girl than he thought fitting.
advisories:
Attempted sexual assault of a child, implied and not explicit; a fatal stabbing; a long death scene.

Death of a father from malaria; drunkenness and threats.

For older teenagers and adults; discuss with younger viewers before watching.

The 2010 Italian DVD is listed at 98 minutes against the 111 minutes in festival records; it may be cut. No English-subtitled edition was found.

doctrine: Pius XII beatified Maria Goretti on 27 April 1947 and canonised her on 24 June 1950. The crowd was too large for St Peter's, so the rite was held in the square, with her mother and four of her surviving children present. Her feast is 6 July, and her body rests in the Passionist church of Our Lady of Graces at Nettuno. She is honoured as a martyr in defence of chastity: St Thomas teaches that any virtuous deed referred to God can be a cause of martyrdom, as with St John the Baptist, who died for rebuking adultery (Summa II-II, q. 124, a. 5). Her refusal ('it is a sin') rests on the old teaching, set out by St Augustine in The City of God (I, 16-18), that purity is a virtue of the will: violence suffered without consent is no sin in the victim, while consent is sin even where nothing is done.
production: Augusto Genina wrote the screenplay with Suso Cecchi d'Amico and Fausto Tozzi. Renato and Carlo Bassoli produced it. It was shot in the summer of 1949, with interiors at Cinecittà and exteriors around Nettuno, and Genina cast local peasants, Ines Orsini among them, beside a few professionals. G. R. Aldo photographed it and Antonio Veretti wrote the score. At the 10th Venice Film Festival in 1949 it won the prizes for best Italian film and best director and the award of the Catholic film office (OCIC). It opened in Italy on 24 November 1949, seven months before the canonisation. Genina won the Nastro d'Argento for direction in 1950. Catholic critics held it up as an alternative to secular neorealism; others found it decorous but on the surface. In 2008 it was named among the 100 Italian films to be saved.

title: Thérèse: The Story of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
originalTitle: Thérèse: The Story of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
decision: PUBLISH as a modest family film, with its weaknesses stated: the Austin Chronicle review confirms credits, PG rating and 2004 release; Greydanus's review (Decent Films/National Catholic Register) documents a reverent, faithful outline of Story of a Soul with an engaging lead, while noting thin treatment of the Little Way. Secular reviews (Austin Chronicle, Film Threat) and the Catholic News Service reviewer's 'hagiographic tableaus' confirm the craft is weak. No doctrinal or reverence concerns are recorded by any source.
summary: A sincere, low-budget American biopic of the Little Flower, reverent and family-safe, that walks through Story of a Soul without quite catching its depth.
synopsis: Thérèse Martin grows up the youngest of five sisters in a pious, loving household in Alençon and Lisieux. Her mother dies when she is four, and she becomes her father Louis's 'little queen'. One by one her sisters enter the Carmel, and Thérèse, still a girl, resolves to follow. Refused because of her age, she appeals to the bishop and then, on pilgrimage to Rome, to Pope Leo XIII himself. Admitted at fifteen, she learns to serve awkward, elderly sisters with patience and to make small sacrifices out of love. Her father declines into illness. Thérèse falls ill with tuberculosis and dies in the infirmary at twenty-four.
inclusion: This is a film to watch with children rather than one to admire for craft. It was made on a small budget, and it shows: the staging is stiff, much of the supporting cast is weak, and the script tells rather than shows. What it has is sincerity and an attractive lead. Lindsay Younce plays Thérèse as a normal, likeable young woman rather than a plaster figure, and Steven Greydanus finds her deathbed scenes genuinely affecting. Defilippis himself is good as Louis Martin. Passages from Thérèse's own writing are read in voiceover, which is the best thing about it.
themes: The film follows the main events of Story of a Soul: the devout family, the call to Carmel, the appeal to Leo XIII, the patient charity of convent life, the trial of illness. Prayer, the sacraments and religious life are shown with uncomplicated reverence. Its weakness is the teaching. Greydanus and Marjorie Baumgarten both note that the film gives little sense of the 'little way' of spiritual childhood that made Thérèse a Doctor of the Church, and her dark night of faith is reduced to a voiceover line.
history: Thérèse Martin (1873–1897) entered the Lisieux Carmel at fifteen and died of tuberculosis in 1897. Her autobiography, Story of a Soul, spread her Little Way worldwide, and Pius XI beatified her in 1923 and canonised her in 1925, naming her patroness of the missions in 1927.
liberties: The film omits Thérèse's scrupulosity and emotional struggles, the troubles of her sister Léonie, her work with the novices and much of her spiritual trial at the end. The Martin family is presented as almost flawless. Greydanus notes at least one small factual slip in the Christmas conversion scene.
advisories:
The death of a parent and a brief frightening image.

Thérèse's final illness and death are shown plainly.

Rated PG. Suitable for children with parents.

doctrine: Thérèse entered the Carmel of Lisieux at fifteen, by special leave of the Bishop of Bayeux and, after her pilgrimage, of Leo XIII. The film shows the Carmelite life: strict enclosure, the divine office, perpetual abstinence and the Rule of St Albert as reformed by St Teresa of Avila. Her Little Way is confidence in God and the offering of small acts out of love, which the Church teaches is a path to holiness open to all, since every state of life is called to perfection. Pius XI beatified her on 29 April 1923, canonised her on 17 May 1925 and named her, with Francis Xavier, patron of the missions in 1927. Her feast was 3 October.
production: Leonardo Defilippis of Saint Luke Productions directed and played Louis Martin, with the script credited to Patti Defilippis. It ran 96 minutes and is rated PG. It opened in United States cinemas in the autumn of 2004. The Austin Chronicle reviewer found it an inspirational story for believers but artless and poorly crafted.

title: Fray Escoba
decision: PUBLISH: José María Aresté's DeCine21 critique describes specific episodes (the food basket, clashes with the porter, the farewell to his mother) that place Martín's charity and humility at the centre; the ICAA record confirms identity, a Dominican religious adviser and an all-ages video rating. The film's whimsy and anecdotal structure are noted as weaknesses, not doctrinal problems.
summary: A modest Spanish biopic of Martín de Porres, the mixed-race Dominican lay brother of Lima whose broom became the emblem of his holiness.
synopsis: Martín, son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman, grows up in Lima between his father's world and his mother's poverty. He gives up the advantages his father could offer and asks to serve the Dominicans. Set to sweeping and menial work, he earns the nickname "Fray Escoba" (Brother Broom). Episodes follow his care for the sick and the poor, his friction with the convent porter, Padre Barragán, and a growing reputation for wonders he does not seek: in one scene a basket keeps yielding food for the hungry. The film closes its family story with Martín's emotional parting from his mother.
inclusion: Ramón Torrado made a plain, warm film for a broad audience, and its best quality is that it keeps Martín at floor level. Holiness here is measured by the broom, the infirmary and the begging round rather than by spectacle. René Muñoz gives Martín a gentle, unpushy presence, and the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos gave him a special prize for it in 1961. José María Aresté calls the farewell with his mother the film's strongest moment. The weaknesses are those of Spanish devotional cinema of the period: episodic construction, some sentimental comedy and miracle scenes staged with a fairy-tale touch that Aresté compares to Mary Poppins. As an introduction to the saint for a family, it does its job.
themes: The film's Catholic subject is humility made concrete. Martín chooses the lowest work in a religious house and treats it as service to Christ in the poor and the sick. Miracles are present, but they arise from works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, rather than replacing them. Martín's patience with a sharp-tongued superior shows obedience as a daily discipline, not a pious attitude. A Dominican priest, Fr. Antonio Sánchez, served as religious adviser on the production.
history: Martín de Porres (1579–1639) was born in Lima to the Spaniard Juan de Porres and Ana Velázquez, a freed woman of African descent. Barred by colonial rules from entering as a full religious at first, he joined the Dominican convent of the Holy Rosary as a donado (lay helper) and later professed as a lay brother. He was known for nursing the sick, caring for the poor and animals, and for reported miracles. He was beatified in 1837 and canonised by John XXIII on 6 May 1962, the year after this film was made.
liberties: The screenplay by Jaime G. Herranz is credited as "inspired by" the life of the then Blessed Martín, and it arranges traditional anecdotes into a loose sequence. Conversations, the porter's characterisation and the staging of individual miracles are dramatic inventions.
advisories:
Rated suitable for all audiences on its Spanish video releases (1988 and 2008).

Illness, poverty and an emotional parting between mother and son.

Suitable for children; younger viewers may need help with the period setting.

doctrine: Martín de Porres lived the Dominican life as a lay brother, which the Church honours as a true state of perfection through the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. His care of the sick and the poor is the corporal works of mercy. The Church teaches that all men are equal before God and redeemed by Christ: Paul III's bull Sublimis Deus (1537) declared the Indians of the New World to be rational men who could not lawfully be enslaved, and the principle governs the case of a mulatto boy who was kept from full profession. Martín was beatified by Gregory XVI in 1837 and canonised by John XXIII on 6 May 1962, before the Council opened in October of that year. He died on 3 November 1639.
production: Ramón Torrado directed this Spanish black-and-white film for Copercines in 1961, from a script by Jaime García-Herranz. René Muñoz played Martín, and Esther Zulema his mother. The film runs about 101 minutes. It was a success on release, and the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos gave García-Herranz its medal for best screenplay and Muñoz a special acting award in 1961. It appeared a year before Martín's canonisation, which made it timely. It was rated for all audiences on its Spanish video releases in 1988 and 2008. Few details of its shooting are recorded.

title: Un mulato llamado Martín
alternateTitles: La vida de San Martín de Porres
decision: GREY: Identity, credits and the main episodes are established (Sentido Fílmico, Spanish Wikipedia, a Lima devotional blog), but no critic has assessed how the film treats the saint, and its synopses frame his life as a 'fight against slavery' in a 1970s Peruvian production made under the Velasco-era film law. That framing is unexamined. Martín was canonised in 1962, so the post-1965 rule does not apply. Settled by a review or recorded viewing that addresses the miracles, the convent life and the slavery theme. Year: the SIC and INAH listings give 1974 (probably production); IMDb and Sentido Fílmico give the Lima premiere, 25 September 1975.

grey.question: The film is securely identified: Tito Davison directed it for Mexican and Peruvian producers, with René Muñoz as Martín, and it opened in Lima in 1975. What is missing is any critical review of how it treats the saint. Its published synopses present his life as a struggle against slavery and against the barriers between slaves, priests and nobles, and it was made under Peru's state film law of the early 1970s. A review or a recorded viewing showing whether this is the charity of the traditional lives or a social reading of the saint would settle it.

summary: Tito Davison's Mexican–Peruvian life of St Martin de Porres, with René Muñoz returning to the role he first played in Fray Escoba.
synopsis: Martín is the illegitimate son of a Spanish nobleman, Don Juan de Porres, and a woman of African descent. The film follows him from a devout childhood in colonial Lima to the Dominican convent of Santo Domingo, where his birth allows him only the place of a donado, a lay helper, and he takes the lowest work. Episodes described in published accounts include a trader at the port of Callao trying to sell him as a slave until a friar intervenes; his care for Balu, an enslaved man who has turned to violence and later gains his freedom; a temptation by the devil on the convent stairs; and his gift of his father's shirt to Tupac, an Indigenous man whose son is sick. Fray Barragán, the porter, is his companion and a comic foil.
inclusion: Few films about the Lima saint were made in Peru itself, and this one was shot partly in the real convent of Santo Domingo, where Martín lived and died, with a largely Peruvian supporting cast drawn from television. René Muñoz, the Cuban actor who first played Martín in the Spanish Fray Escoba (1961), took the part again here and in Mexican television serials. A Lima devotional writer says this film gives more room to Martín's works of mercy than the earlier Spanish one, which he calls sugary. No critic has described how well it is made or how it stages the saint's miracles. On present evidence it is of most interest to viewers who know Fray Escoba and want a Latin American treatment of the same saint.
themes: In the accounts available, Martín's holiness is shown through humility and charity: a donado who sweeps, serves and gives away what he has. The convent of Santo Domingo frames his religious life, and his temptation by the devil, a traditional element of his legend, is staged on its stairs. The film's synopses also present his life as a struggle against slavery and against the barriers between slaves, priests and nobility. That may be no more than the charity of the old lives of the saint, or it may be a 1970s social reading; no source yet says which. The same devotional writer notes that some episodes are not historically proven.
history: Martín de Porres (1579–1639) was born in Lima, the son of a Spanish nobleman, Juan de Porres, and Ana Velázquez, a freed woman of African descent. He entered the Dominican convent of the Holy Rosary (Santo Domingo) as a lay helper, later professed as a lay brother, and became known for his care of the sick and poor, his penances and reported miracles. He was beatified in 1837 and canonised by John XXIII on 6 May 1962.
liberties: The devotional account notes that not every episode in the film is historically proven. The enslaved man Balu and the Indigenous father Tupac are not figures of the standard biographies, and the attempted sale of Martín at Callao is not part of the usual record. The friendship with Fray Barragán is played partly for comedy.
advisories:
A violent enslaved character; an attempt to sell the young Martín as a slave.

A scene of diabolical temptation.

No source records sexual content or strong violence, but no detailed content review exists.

Its treatment of slavery and social class has not been assessed.

doctrine: Martin de Porres (1579–1639) was a lay brother of the Dominican convent of the Holy Rosary at Lima, known for his care of the sick, his penances and his devotion to the Rosary. He was beatified by Gregory XVI in 1837 and canonised by John XXIII on 6 May 1962, before the Second Vatican Council opened. His feast falls on 3 November. The Church's teaching on slavery is that Paul III in Sublimis Deus (1537) declared the Indians rational beings who may not be enslaved, and Gregory XVI in In supremo apostolatus (1839) condemned the slave trade. Martin served all alike, in the tradition of the corporal works of mercy, and his humility is the mark of the religious life, not a social programme.
production: Tito Davison directed this Mexican-Peruvian co-production for Clasa Films Mundiales and Filmadora Peruana, produced by Héctor López, with a screenplay by Fernando Almada, Edmundo Báez and Fernando Mariscal. It runs 94 minutes in Spanish and was released in 1975. René Muñoz plays the saint. The music is by Leopoldo de la Rosa. No critical review of its treatment of the saint has been found, and no Catholic rating from the period.

What has not been assessed is how it treats the saint and his institute. The reviews found judge its craft, not its faith or its history, and the fullest descriptions of its content come from the De La Salle Brothers, who sponsored its DVD release. summary: Luis César Amadori's Spanish biopic, with Mel Ferrer as the Reims canon who gave up rank and fortune to found the Brothers of the Christian Schools.
synopsis: Set in the France of Louis XIV, the film follows Jean-Baptiste de La Salle, a canon from a well-off family, as he turns to the education of poor children. Catalogue summaries and the Lasallian Brothers' own notice describe its arc: his first involvement with schools, the founding of the Brothers of the Christian Schools, and the hardship and obstacles he meets in trying to offer free schooling to all children. Mel Ferrer plays La Salle, with Fernando Rey, Mabel Karr, Manuel Alexandre and Antonio Ferrandis among the Spanish cast. No detailed scene-by-scene account of the film has been found.
inclusion: La Salle is one of the great figures of Catholic education, yet he has rarely been filmed, and this is the only feature about him. Spain put real resources into it: Amadori, a veteran of Argentine cinema then working in Spain, Mel Ferrer in the lead, and a strong supporting cast that includes Fernando Rey. The one detailed review found, by Paco Casado for Cine y Max, calls Amadori's direction diligent, the colour photography acceptable, Gregorio García Segura's score good and Ferrer well suited to the part. But he blames a weak script and a polished, Hollywood-style surface that leaves the saint himself thinly drawn. DeCine21 rates it 5/10. It reached the United States in 1976 as Who Are My Own and returned on DVD in 2010.
themes: The film's subject is the founding of a teaching institute: La Salle's renunciation of comfort and status, and his dedication of his life to free Christian schooling for poor children. DeCine21 presents him as a holy man whose service of others follows Christian teaching. No source describes how the film treats the Brothers' community life and prayer, the sacraments, or La Salle's conflicts with church authorities and the Paris schoolmasters. Its picture of Catholic reform in seventeenth-century France has not yet been assessed.
history: Jean-Baptiste de La Salle (1651–1719), a priest and canon of Reims, founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools in the early 1680s. He pioneered free elementary schools, teaching in French rather than Latin, and the training of teachers. He resigned his canonry and gave away his inheritance for the work, and faced lawsuits from the guilds of schoolmasters. He was canonised by Leo XIII in 1900, and Pius XII named him patron of teachers in 1950.

doctrine: La Salle's Brothers of the Christian Schools are lay religious: he refused to let them become priests, so that they would stay teachers. The aim of the schools was to teach poor boys the catechism and the faith along with reading and writing, in line with the Council of Trent's order that children be taught Christian doctrine (the Roman Catechism, 1566). The Institute was bound by simple vows, and its Rule gained papal approval from Benedict XIII in 1725, after his death in 1719. La Salle gave away his canonry and inheritance, an act of evangelical poverty. He was canonised by Leo XIII on 24 May 1900, and Pius XII proclaimed him heavenly patron of all teachers of youth in 1950.

title: Don Bosco
decision: GREY: identity is secure (ACMI, Box Office Mojo, Wikipedia credits) and one independent, scene-level review exists (Avellina Balestri, Catholic Insight, 2016), which is enthusiastic. Not PUBLISH because that is a single modern review that does not address liberties, the film was co-produced by Elle Di Ci (the Salesian publisher's film arm, an interested party), it adds an invented brothel subplot, and its weighting of Bosco's conflict with Archbishop Gastaldi is unexamined. Settles with a second independent review (e.g. the 1988 Italian press: Repubblica, Segnalazioni cinematografiche) or a documented viewing.

grey.question: The film's identity is secure, and one independent review, Avellina Balestri's in Catholic Insight, finds it devout and balanced. That is not yet enough. It was co-produced by the Salesians' own publishing house, it adds an invented subplot about a girl and a brothel, and nobody has examined how it presents Bosco's quarrel with Archbishop Gastaldi. A second independent review, or a documented viewing that checks the Lina subplot, the dreams and the Gastaldi conflict against the historical record, would settle it.

summary: Leandro Castellani's centenary-year biopic, co-produced by the Salesians' publishing house, with Ben Gazzara as the Turin priest who battles poverty, the state and his archbishop for his boys.
synopsis: In nineteenth-century Turin Don Giovanni Bosco, guided by a dream he has had since boyhood, gathers poor and abandoned boys into his oratory. Officials complain that he is harbouring misfits. During political unrest he is offered money to stop, and there are attempts on his life, among them poisoned wine; a large grey dog that he believes heaven sent turns away an assassin. A subplot follows Lina, a girl whose mother wants her to work in a brothel beside the oratory, and Giuseppe, one of Bosco's boys, who takes her side and is later arrested for robbery. A hostile bishop suspends Bosco's faculty to hear confessions. He goes to Rome, wins the support of Pius IX and founds the Salesians. The film ends with his last days.
inclusion: Ben Gazzara's Bosco is the film's main asset. Avellina Balestri, reviewing it for the Canadian magazine Catholic Insight, calls it his finest performance and praises its mixture of earthy realism and mysticism. She finds the production uneven, thinks Patsy Kensit miscast as Lina, and is irked by the English dubbing of some Italian actors. Released in the centenary year of Bosco's death, it was written by Ennio De Concini and scored by Stelvio Cipriani, with Laurent Terzieff as Archbishop Gastaldi, Raymond Pellegrin as Pius IX and Philippe Leroy as Leo XIII. Unusually for a saint's film, it puts on screen the opposition Bosco met from his own archbishop as well as from the state. It runs about 108 minutes.
themes: The Catholic content is Bosco's pastoral method and his supernatural life: the oratory as a place of work, prayer and play for boys nobody else wanted; his dreams, treated as genuine guidance, including visions of the Christ Child and Our Lady that he recounts before the Pope; and the grey dog that protects him. Balestri finds it balanced, showing good and bad churchmen without attacking the Church. How the conflict with Archbishop Gastaldi is weighted, and whether the invented Lina story serves the portrait of Bosco or distracts from it, has not been examined by any other reviewer.
history: John Bosco was born near Castelnuovo in Piedmont in 1815. As a young priest in Turin he began his oratory for poor boys on 8 December 1841; by 1868 the Salesian Society he founded had fifty priests and teachers. He met complaints from the authorities and even an attempt to have him confined in an asylum. He died in Turin on 31 January 1888 and was canonised by Pius XI in 1934. The film's account of his quarrel with Archbishop Gastaldi has not been checked against the record.
liberties: Lina, her mother and the brothel, and Giuseppe's romance and arrest, form a subplot that no source identifies as historical; it appears to be invented. Balestri does not discuss historical liberties. The order of events in the film, with the bishop's sanctions coming before the Roman journey and the founding of the Salesians, has not been checked against the record.
advisories:
A subplot involves a brothel and a mother pressing her daughter to work there; sources do not describe explicit content.

Assassination attempts, a poisoning and an arrest.

ACMI classifies it PG.

The English version dubs some Italian actors.

doctrine: Bosco's method was the preventive system, which the Catholic Encyclopedia describes as gaining love before inspiring fear, with teachers as father, adviser and friend, and the foundation of frequent Confession, frequent Communion and daily Mass. His oratory began on 8 December 1841, the feast of the Immaculate Conception defined by Pius IX in 1854. The church he built at Valdocco was consecrated on 9 June 1868 under the patronage of Our Lady, Help of Christians. The Salesian Society was approved by Pius IX provisionally in 1869 and finally in 1874. The film's dreams are Bosco's own; the Church does not require belief in private visions, and the grey dog Grigio is a popular tradition. Bosco was canonised by Pius XI on Easter Sunday 1934; his feast is 31 January.
production: Leandro Castellani directed this centenary-year film, marking 100 years since Bosco's death in 1888, from a script by Ennio De Concini. It was made by Elle Di Ci and Tiber Cinematografica. Ben Gazzara, an American, played Bosco in an English-language version, and some Italian actors are dubbed; the running time is 108 minutes. Columbia Tri-Star distributed it in Italy, where it was released on 30 September 1988. Avellina Balestri, reviewing it for Catholic Insight, gave it five stars and thought it uneven but Gazzara's finest performance, though she found Patsy Kensit miscast and the dubbing irksome.

title: Ignatius of Loyola
decision: PUBLISH: Ignatius was canonised in 1622, so rule (a) does not apply. Independent reviews (Oggs Cruz in Rappler; Rome Jorge and Rea Gierran in adobo Magazine) establish a straightforward conversion narrative that sets out the saint's virtues without reinterpreting him, and Brad Miner's detailed review (The Catholic Thing, used for content) confirms the penances, temptations and Inquisition trial are treated reverently. The producer, Jesuit Communications, is an interested party and is disclosed; no source reports post-conciliar framing in the film itself.
summary: Paolo Dy's Filipino-made, Spanish-cast biography follows Iñigo de Loyola from his wound at Pamplona through the cave at Manresa to his trial before the Inquisition.
synopsis: In 1521 Iñigo López de Loyola, a Basque nobleman, defends Pamplona against the French and has his leg shattered. It is set, broken again and reset, and he is left with a limp. Convalescing, he reads a life of Christ and lives of the saints and resolves to change his life. Taken to a brothel by his brother and cousin, he refuses the prostitute Ana and talks with her about Christ instead. He gives up his sword, nurses the sick in a hospital and withdraws to a cave, where he fasts, scourges himself and is tempted by a devil who wears his own face. From this struggle come the notes that become the Spiritual Exercises. When he begins to preach and gather followers without a degree or holy orders, he is brought before an inquisitor, examined and vindicated. The film ends before the founding of the Society of Jesus.
inclusion: It is the first English-language feature about Ignatius, made with unusual ambition for a low-budget Filipino production: shot in the Basque Country and Navarre, with Lee Meily's photography and a score by Ryan Cayabyab. Andreas Muñoz, a Spanish stage actor, carries it; Rina Jimenez-David in the Inquirer praised the intensity of his performance, and Miner thought it the best Catholic film he had seen in years. Oggs Cruz in Rappler was cooler. The battles borrow from The Lord of the Rings, the Spanish-accented English grates, and the story lacks a central conflict and circles a point made early. He still found it affecting in its quieter scenes, especially Iñigo's conversation with the prostitute. The adobo reviewers fault thin sound and visible CGI. It is earnest rather than subtle, and suits viewers who want a plain account of a conversion.
themes: The film is a conversion story told in traditional terms. Iñigo's change begins with reading the life of Christ and the saints, passes through renunciation, works of mercy and harsh penance, and is tested by a devil who tempts him with his former self. The penances are shown frankly; the adobo reviewers note that sceptics may read them as madness, while Miner reads them, as the film intends, as the road to sanity and holiness. The Spiritual Exercises appear as the fruit of that struggle. The Inquisition scenes make churchmen the antagonists, but Ignatius submits to examination and is cleared, which is close to what happened. Cruz observes that it seeks only to set out the saint's virtues. Although Jesuit Communications produced it, none of the reviews reports a modern reframing of Ignatius or his mission.
history: Iñigo López de Loyola (1491–1556) was wounded by a cannonball at the siege of Pamplona on 20 May 1521. Recovering at Loyola, he read lives of Christ and the saints. In 1522 he left his sword at Our Lady's altar at Montserrat and spent months in penance at Manresa, where the Spiritual Exercises took shape. Preaching without theological training led to imprisonment and examination at Alcalá and Salamanca. He studied in Paris, and the Society of Jesus was approved in 1540. He was beatified in 1609 and canonised in 1622.
liberties: The inquisitor is named Frías, apparently after Alonso de Salazar Frías, who was born after Ignatius died; Miner notes the anachronism. The separate inquiries at Alcalá and Salamanca are compressed into one trial, and the threat of burning is stated rather than shown. The brothel scene and the devil in Iñigo's likeness are dramatic inventions. The film stops before Paris and the founding of the Society.
advisories:
Battle violence and a painful leg-setting.

Self-flagellation and severe penances, the main reason for its PG-13 rating according to Miner.

A brothel scene with a prostitute; nothing sexual is shown.

Scenes of diabolical temptation.

The Inquisition episode is compressed and partly anachronistic.

title: Claret
decision: GREY: Identity, credits and outline are established (Cine con Ñ interview, DeCine21, Crux), and Claret was beatified in 1934 and canonised in 1950, so rule (a) does not apply. Every substantive review found comes from a Catholic outlet (DeCine21, El Debate, Filasiete, Cinemanet, Catholic Review) and the Claretians co-produced the film, so there is no independent assessment of its treatment; the makers' human-dignity framing of the Cuban years is unexamined. Year: 2020 is the production year given by DeCine21; first release was 24 September 2021 in Spain. Settled by a secular review or a check of the dialogue.

grey.question: Claret is securely identified: Pablo Moreno's Spanish feature, released in 2021, with Antonio Reyes as the archbishop and the writer Azorín's 1930s inquiry as its frame. What is missing is an independent review of how it treats him. The reviews so far all come from Catholic outlets, and his own congregation, the Claretians, co-produced it. Its publicity stresses his defence of enslaved people in Cuba and calls him a man for our time. A secular review, or a check of the dialogue, showing that his preaching and priestly work stay at the centre would settle it.

summary: Pablo Moreno's low-budget Spanish biography of St Anthony Mary Claret, framed by the writer Azorín's 1930s inquiry into the slanders that pursued the archbishop.
synopsis: In the 1930s the writer Azorín, who had once repeated the hostile legend about Archbishop Claret, discovers that the sources behind it were falsified and sets out to establish the truth, consulting Pío Baroja along the way. His inquiry frames the story of Claret's life. The son of a Catalan textile family, Claret chooses the priesthood, becomes a missionary preacher and founds a congregation. Sent to Cuba as Archbishop of Santiago, he defends enslaved people, makes powerful enemies and survives attempts on his life. Recalled to Madrid as confessor to Queen Isabel II, he is drawn into palace intrigue and the quarrels of the Carlist era while longing to return to the missions; a papal representative tells him to stay. The two timelines run in parallel, and Azorín's own exile is set beside Claret's.
inclusion: Claret is one of the most important Spanish saints of the nineteenth century, and this is the first feature film about him. Moreno's framing device is its best idea: the inquiry of Azorín, an anticlerical writer who came to defend the archbishop, gives the story an argument about how reputations are made and unmade. José María Aresté of DeCine21 found the device effective and praised Antonio Reyes as a Claret both spiritual and approachable, while noting a stock voice-over and abrupt jumps. John Mulderig of the Catholic Review found it informative but stiff, with awkward dialogue made worse by the English dub. Alba Recondo's Isabel II has been singled out by Spanish reviewers. The budget is visibly small. It is most useful for viewers who know little of Claret and want the outline of his life.
themes: On the evidence of the reviews, the film presents Claret's holiness as uncompromising zeal. He preaches, founds a congregation, governs his diocese and refuses to soften the demands of the faith, and this earns him enemies. His defence of the enslaved in Cuba is prominent; the director describes him treating slaves and the queen with the same human dignity. Whether the film keeps that charity rooted in his missionary preaching and sacramental work, or reads him chiefly as a social reformer, no independent review says. Azorín and Pío Baroja, neither of them practising Catholics, are shown treating his memory with intellectual honesty. His years as royal confessor are shown as a trial of obedience: he wants to go back to the missions and is told to stay.
history: Antonio María Claret (1807–1870), born at Sallent near Barcelona, the son of a small woollen manufacturer, worked as a weaver before entering the seminary at Vic. Ordained in 1835, he became a popular missionary preacher, and in 1849 founded the Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary. As Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba from 1851 he reformed the clergy and survived many attempts on his life; at Holguín an assassin cut his face open. From 1857 he was confessor to Isabel II. He attended the Vatican Council and died at Fontfroide in 1870.
liberties: The 1930s frame rests on a real episode, Azorín's public change of mind about Claret, but its staging, including the conversations with Baroja and the parallel with Azorín's own exile, is the film's construction. No review lists specific inventions in Claret's life, and how far the film compresses or rearranges events has not been checked.
advisories:
Brief violence with slight gore: an assassination attempt and the aftermath of a lynching and a battle.

Adultery and illegitimacy are part of the court intrigue; a couple of mild oaths.

Suitable for teenagers.

Co-produced by the Claretians, Claret's own congregation; its emphasis on his anti-slavery work has not been independently assessed.

title: A Man for All Seasons
decision: PUBLISH: The 'autonomous conscience' objection (Duffy; echoed by Weigel) is aimed chiefly at Bolt's preface and at the historical More's omitted record, while the film itself has More defend papal primacy at his trial, refuse a heretic son-in-law and die 'God's first' (Wilson, Weigel, plot record). The omission of More's actions against heretics is disclosed as a historical liberty rather than treated as a doctrinal defect.
summary: Zinnemann's film of Robert Bolt's play follows Thomas More from royal favour to the scaffold as he refuses to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church.
synopsis: Sir Thomas More, a lawyer and devout family man, is admired across England when Henry VIII wants his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled. Cardinal Wolsey asks for More's help; More will not give it. After Wolsey's fall More becomes Lord Chancellor, then resigns when the clergy submit to the King. He keeps silent on the marriage and the new oath, trusting that the law protects a man who says nothing. Thomas Cromwell works patiently to break that silence. More is imprisoned in the Tower, separated from his wife Alice and daughter Meg, and finally convicted on the perjured evidence of Richard Rich, a young man he once refused to promote. Only after the verdict does he say plainly what he believes.
inclusion: This is a film made almost entirely of conversations, and it is gripping. Bolt's dialogue is sharp and often funny, and Paul Scofield plays More as a man of wit and warmth who would much rather live than die. The supporting cast is excellent: Orson Welles as a bloated, worldly Wolsey, Leo McKern as Cromwell, Robert Shaw as a boisterous and dangerous Henry, Wendy Hiller as Alice, John Hurt as the weak, ambitious Rich. Ted Moore's photography and Georges Delerue's score keep it handsome without fuss. The Catholic case is clear: More's quarrel is not over a divorce as such but over whether a king can make himself head of the Church. The film lets his conviction emerge slowly, under pressure, through legal caution, family love and finally open witness.
themes: The film turns on papal primacy and the indissolubility of marriage. More refuses to take an oath that would deny the Pope's authority, and at his trial he argues that no temporal ruler may claim the government of the Church, citing Christ's commission to St Peter. He forbids his daughter to marry Will Roper while Roper holds Lutheran views, and his last words are that he dies the King's good servant, but God's first. Critics such as Eamon Duffy argue that Bolt made More a modern hero of personal integrity; Bolt's own preface encourages that reading. Joe Wilson and George Weigel reply that on screen More rarely talks about conscience at all and grounds himself in God. The more convincing reading is theirs, though the film's emphasis on keeping one's 'self' is real and worth noticing.
history: More resigned as Lord Chancellor in 1532, refused the oath attached to the Act of Succession in 1534, and was tried for treason on 1 July 1535. Accounts of the trial record that, at its close, he declared the Act on which he was indicted contrary to the laws of God and his holy Church. He was beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535 and canonised in 1935.
liberties: The film leaves out More's writings against Protestants and his part, as Chancellor, in prosecuting heretics; the biographer Richard Marius thought this produced a More who would barely be recognised in his own time. Rich's long acquaintance with More is expanded for dramatic shape. Several private conversations, including those with Norfolk and Cromwell, are invented, though the main events follow the record.
advisories:
More is beheaded at the end; the blow is not lingered on.

No sexual content or strong language. Long dialogue scenes and legal argument suit teenagers and adults more than young children.

The film omits More's role in the prosecution of heretics, so it should not be taken as a complete biography.

sources.title: Blessed Thomas More
sources.claims: Act of Succession oath, supremacy statutes, resignation 1532, trial 1 July 1535, beheading 6 July 1535, beatification 1886

names: A Man for All Seasons, play by Robert Bolt (1960)

suitability.note: There is a beheading, handled without lingering, and no sex or bad language. The film is made of long dialogue scenes about oaths and law, which suit teenagers better than young children.

doctrine: More died for the primacy of the Roman Pontiff. The Act of Succession (1534) required an oath that rejected the Pope's authority, and the Act of Supremacy named Henry Supreme Head of the Church in England. The Church holds that Christ gave Peter the keys (Matthew 16:18-19), and the Vatican Council defined the Pope's universal jurisdiction in 1870. More's refusal is therefore obedience to a divine law above the King's. It is not the modern claim that each man's private conscience is final. He was beatified by Leo XIII in 1886 and canonised, with John Fisher, by Pius XI on 19 May 1935. His silence rests on the legal maxim that silence gives consent, and he did not risk perjury or a lie to save himself.
production: Robert Bolt wrote the play in 1960 and the film keeps its form. Fred Zinnemann produced and directed, and insisted on Paul Scofield, who had played More in London and on Broadway, even though the producers doubted his box-office value. The actors took salary cuts to keep the budget under $2 million. John Hurt had his first major film role as Rich, and Vanessa Redgrave appears briefly as Anne Boleyn. The picture was released by Columbia in 1966 and earned about $28.4 million. It won six Academy Awards, among them Best Picture, Director, Actor, Adapted Screenplay, Colour Cinematography and Colour Costume Design, and also the BAFTA for Best Film. The film leaves out More's part in the prosecution of heretics.

title: Becket
decision: PUBLISH (teens and up): AFI Catalog identity and synopsis; Greydanus's Decent Films review (+3) judges it reverent, with sincere faith and carefully staged liturgy. The serious historical liberties, above all the invented libertine past and mistress, which the Catholic Encyclopedia flatly contradicts, and the unfair portrait of Alexander III, are stated plainly; they shape the drama but do not turn the martyrdom against the faith.
summary: Richard Burton's Becket and Peter O'Toole's Henry II, drinking companions turned archbishop and king, in a lavish film of Anouilh's play about friendship broken by the honour of God.
synopsis: Henry II spends his days hunting and carousing with his clever friend Thomas Becket and makes him Chancellor, where Becket bleeds the Church for the Crown. When Henry demands Becket's mistress for himself, Becket gives her up and she kills herself. On the death of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Henry forces Becket into the see, expecting a compliant ally. Becket warns him he cannot serve both God and the king, resigns the chancellorship and defends the Church's rights. Henry turns on him with false charges; Becket flees to France and the Pope. A last meeting on horseback produces a hollow peace. Becket returns to Canterbury, Henry cries out to be rid of him, and four barons kill him at the altar.
inclusion: The two performances carry it. O'Toole's Henry is needy, funny, petulant and frightening, and Burton plays Becket with a cool reserve that slowly becomes something like holiness. Greydanus calls the film a reverent masterpiece, though less incisive than A Man for All Seasons, and finds Burton harder to warm to than Scofield's More, which is fair. Geoffrey Unsworth's colour photography and the huge Canterbury set are handsome, and the ceremonies, the consecration, an excommunication, the chant, are staged with real care. It is long and theatrical, and Anouilh's dialogue is more epigrammatic than devout. But the moment when Becket, having found a cause worthy of his honour, chooses God over his friend is genuinely stirring.
themes: The question is the freedom of the Church from the Crown. Once consecrated, Becket gives his goods to the poor, takes up prayer and penance, and refuses to let the king control ecclesiastical courts or appointments. Greydanus judges that he genuinely loves God, though Anouilh frames his conversion as the discovery of an honour worth serving, the honour of God. Liturgy and the sacramental office of a bishop are treated with dignity. The papacy fares worse: Alexander III and his court are shown as calculating politicians, which Greydanus thinks unfair. The ending, Henry submitting to a flogging by monks and proclaiming Becket a saint, honours the martyr.
history: Thomas Becket was born in London of Norman parents, served Henry II as Chancellor, and was consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162. He resisted the Constitutions of Clarendon, spent six years in exile, returned in 1170 and was killed in his cathedral by four knights on 29 December. Alexander III canonised him in 1173, and Henry did public penance at his tomb in 1174.
liberties: Anouilh made Becket a Saxon to set him against the Norman king; he was Norman. The film gives him a mistress and a life of drinking and womanising with Henry; the Catholic Encyclopedia records that no word was ever said against his purity. Gwendolen is invented. The Pope is made a cynic. Gilbert Foliot's role is simplified, and Becket's exile is compressed.
advisories:
Implied sexual immorality and womanising in the early scenes; Henry takes Becket's mistress, who then kills herself.

The murder in the cathedral is violent but brief. Some coarse language and demeaning treatment of women.

Greydanus rates it for teens and up.

The saint's pre-ordination life is invented and should not be taken as history.

sources.title: Becket (1964 film)
sources.claims: Cast, screenplay, source play, crew, locations, budget, release, gross, awards

names: Becket, or The Honour of God, play by Jean Anouilh (1959)

suitability.note: Early scenes of drinking and womanising, a woman who kills herself, and a brief, bloody murder in the cathedral. Long (148 minutes) and wordy, so it suits teenagers and adults.

doctrine: Becket defended the liberty of the Church against Henry II's Constitutions of Clarendon (1164), above all the claim to try clergy in royal courts. The Church holds that clerics are tried by their own courts (the privilege of the forum). Becket's motto in the play is 'the honour of God'. He was killed at the altar steps on 29 December 1170 and was canonised by Alexander III on 21 February 1173; the pilgrimage to Canterbury lasted until Henry VIII destroyed the shrine in 1538. Anouilh's Becket is a Saxon who is converted by the weight of his office, which is dramatic invention: the real Becket was of Norman parents, and was only a deacon until ordained priest on the eve of his consecration. A martyr who dies for the Church's liberty gains the crown of martyrdom.
production: Hal Wallis produced for Paramount from Anouilh's 1959 play, with Edward Anhalt writing the script and Peter Glenville directing. It was shot at Shepperton Studios and on location at Alnwick and Bamburgh castles in Northumberland. The budget was about $3 million. It opened as a roadshow on 11 March 1964 and ran 148 minutes. It took about $9.2 million in the box office and won the Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay among twelve nominations, including Best Picture, Burton and O'Toole. It won Golden Globes for Best Drama and for O'Toole. A restored print was shown again in 2007.

title: The Carmelites
decision: PUBLISH: Identity confirmed by AlloCiné and the Gaumont catalogue; James Travers's detailed review and the Aleteia appreciation establish a faithful adaptation of Bernanos centred on fear, grace and martyrdom, and the film won the OCIC Grand Prix hors-festival in 1960. The fictional Blanche and the dramatised convent are disclosed; Time Out's dissent concerns style, not doctrine.
summary: A Dominican priest and Bresson's former cameraman film Bernanos's play about the Carmelites of Compiègne and a frightened novice who finds her courage at the scaffold.
synopsis: In 1789 two young women enter the Carmel of Compiègne. Sister Constance is cheerful and ready for the life; Blanche de la Force is crippled by fear of death and doubts her vocation. The dying prioress asks that Blanche be watched over. As the Revolution turns against religious houses, the community shelters Blanche's brother, attends a clandestine Mass said by a hunted priest, and is ordered to disperse. The sisters keep their common life in secret, are arrested and condemned. Blanche has already fled. On the day of the execution she watches her sisters climb to the guillotine, and joins them.
inclusion: Most of Bernanos's dialogue survives, and it is the reason to see the film: hard, plain exchanges about fear, pride and what it costs to give one's life. The cast is remarkable for a religious picture of its day. Jeanne Moreau plays Mother Marie de l'Incarnation, the nun most eager for martyrdom; Madeleine Renaud is the old prioress; Alida Valli the new one; Pascale Audret is Blanche. The style is more conventional and more lavish than Bresson's, and Time Out found it static and pallid. James Travers thought the opposite, judging that it does justice to the play and that the final scaffold sequence is overwhelming. The real strength is the subject: a community of contemplatives who choose to die together rather than abandon their vows.
themes: The film is about fear and grace. Blanche does not overcome her terror by willpower; the story suggests she is carried by the prayer and sacrifice of others, and Bernanos's line that fear is a fantasy of the devil sums up its view. Religious vows, the cloister, the Mass and the Divine Office are treated as realities worth dying for, not as picturesque background. The revolutionary officials are shown as persecutors of the Church, but the film's interest is less in politics than in the different temperaments of the nuns: Constance's simplicity, Marie's zeal, the prioresses' humility. Bernanos was a Catholic novelist and Bruckberger a Dominican, and the treatment of martyrdom is orthodox.
history: Sixteen Discalced Carmelites of Compiègne were guillotined in Paris on 17 July 1794 after offering their lives for peace and for the Church in France. They sang the Salve Regina and the Veni Creator on the way to the scaffold. Pius X beatified them in 1906.
liberties: Blanche de la Force is fictional, invented by Gertrud von Le Fort for her 1931 novella and kept by Bernanos. Conversations inside the convent, Blanche's family and her flight are imagined. Jean-Louis Barrault has an odd cameo as a mime. The martyrs' real vow and community life are compressed into a few scenes.
advisories:
The final sequence shows the nuns going one by one to the guillotine; it is grim rather than graphic.

Revolutionary menace and the execution sequence may disturb younger viewers. No sexual content is reported. Suitable for older children with an adult, and for teenagers and adults.

sources.title: Martyrs of Compiègne
sources.claims: Execution 17 July 1794; sixteen Carmelites; prioress Madeleine Lidoine; offering made at Easter 1792; beatified 27 May 1906 by Pius X; Bernanos commissioned in 1947 by Bruckberger and Agostini; play premiered in Zurich 1951

names: Dialogues des Carmélites, play by Georges Bernanos (1951), from Die Letzte am Schafott, novella by Gertrud von Le Fort (1931)

suitability.note: The nuns go one by one to the guillotine in the closing scene, grim but not graphic. The film is black and white, French, slow and talky, and about fear of death, so it will hold teenagers better than small children.

doctrine: The Martyrs of Compiègne were sixteen Discalced Carmelites guillotined in Paris on 17 July 1794. Their prioress, Mother Teresa of St Augustine (Madeleine Lidoine), had proposed at Easter 1792 that the community offer itself as a sacrifice for France and for the French Church. Pius X beatified them on 27 May 1906, the first martyrs of the Revolution recognised by the Holy See. Their story shows the Church's teaching on martyrdom for the faith, here for fidelity to religious vows and the cloister, which the Revolution had outlawed. Blanche de la Force is an invention of Le Fort, not one of the sixteen; Bernanos's play makes her fear and her return the heart of the story. The Salve Regina and Veni Creator they sang are the traditional prayers of the Church.
production: In 1947 Raymond-Léopold Bruckberger, a Dominican, and the director Philippe Agostini were preparing a film from Gertrud von Le Fort's novella and asked Georges Bernanos to write the dialogue. The film was not made then. Bernanos died in 1948 and his text was first staged in Zurich in 1951; it was later the basis of Poulenc's opera. Bruckberger and Agostini finally made the film in 1960, in black and white, for Champs-Élysées Productions, with Italian participation from Titanus, and Lux as French distributor. It was released in France on 10 June 1960 and runs about 113 minutes. Jean Françaix wrote the music. It won the OCIC Grand Prix hors-festival in 1960. Critics were divided: Films de France thought it faithful and the last scene affecting, Time Out thought it static and pallid.

title: Vaincre ou mourir
decision: GREY: Independent treatment exists, so the film is not 'unverified'. Press critics (Le Monde, Télérama, L'Obs, François Huzar) judge the craft poor; historians (Jean-Clément Martin, Paul Chopelin and François Huzar, Guillaume Lancereau) find few factual errors but a narrow, partisan frame. The subtitle file shows more religious substance than the historians allowed: refractory priests hunted and Mass said in hiding, a sworn priest rejected, Sacred Heart badges, the rising fought for God and king and for souls, a treaty valued for freedom of Catholic worship, a Latin Mass, and absolution before the execution. The chaplain refuses Charette's reprisals as a priest. The word genocide is not used in the opening interviews. The reservation is the partisan historical frame.

grey.question: The reservation is historical. The film was made by the Puy du Fou, and its opening interviews include Reynald Secher, whose description of the 1794 repression as genocide is widely disputed, though the word is not used in the film. Historians found few factual errors but a narrow and partisan frame: the Republic's massacres are shown and the Vendéen killings at Machecoul are not. The religious side is sound and more present than critics allowed, with Mass in hiding, a chaplain who refuses reprisals and absolution before death. Viewers sympathetic to the Vendéens should weigh that one-sidedness against the history.

summary: The Puy du Fou's first feature tells the Vendée war through Charette, the reluctant former naval officer who led the rising and was shot at Nantes in 1796.
synopsis: In 1793 François-Athanase Charette de La Contrie, a former naval officer living quietly at Fonteclose, is pressed by angry peasants to lead their rising against the Republic. He proves a skilful and charismatic guerrilla leader, fighting with an army of peasants, women and young men, among them the fighter Céleste Bulkeley and his companion Hervouët de La Robrie, with the abbé Remaud at his side. Victories give way to losses and to the reprisals of the Republic's infernal columns. In 1795 he makes peace at La Jaunaye, but the peace breaks down. Betrayed and hunted, he is captured by General Travot and shot at Nantes in March 1796, after receiving absolution. Short interviews with historians open the film, and Charette's voice-over carries it.
inclusion: It is the only recent French feature on the Vendée war, a subject French cinema has largely avoided, and it drew nearly 300,000 spectators in France despite a hostile press. Hugo Becker's Charette is the performance reviewers single out. Most notices are poor: Le Monde called it a historical dud, Télérama said it was bad enough to put off royalists, L'Obs found it inert and preachy, and François Huzar, judging it purely as cinema, found the dialogue false, the voice-over constant and the battles illegible. DeCine21 is kinder, praising the costumes and photography and noting the small budget. Jean-Clément Martin found its women fighters, émigré links and infernal columns broadly credible while faulting the narrow focus on Charette. It is worth seeing as a sincere but clumsy attempt at a neglected chapter of Catholic France.
themes: The Vendéens fight for God and the king, and the film shows why: refractory priests are hunted and Mass is said in hiding, a sworn priest is rejected, the rebels wear the Sacred Heart, and the 1795 treaty is valued for restoring freedom of Catholic worship. A Latin Mass is celebrated in the field, and Charette receives absolution before he is shot; Aleteia's critic reads the execution as a deliberate echo of Calvary. The abbé Remaud refuses, as a priest, Charette's call for reprisals in kind. Paul Chopelin and François Huzar still find the religious crisis thinly explained. The film does not make Charette a saint; he says he is no saint but will not go to hell.
history: In March 1793 the Convention's levy of 300,000 men set the west of France ablaze, and the peasants of the Vendée, who had resented the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1790) and the persecution of their priests, took up arms. Pius VI had condemned the Civil Constitution in Quod aliquantum and Charitas in 1791. François-Athanase de Charette de La Contrie (1763-1796), a former naval officer, became a leader of the rising and fought the Republican columns in the marshes of Poitou. He agreed the peace of La Jaunaye in February 1795 with the Republic, though the peace broke down. He was captured by General Travot in March 1796 and shot at Nantes on 29 March. The Republic's 'infernal columns' of 1794 devastated the region. Historians still dispute the death toll and the use of the word 'genocide'.
liberties: Jean-Clément Martin points to one clear error: the film shows Charette signing the 1795 peace of La Jaunaye, which, he says, only the Republican side signed. He adds that the Republicans were more numerous and better armed than the film suggests, and Vendéen society more varied and organised. The massacre of Republicans at Machecoul in March 1793 is left out, and rival leaders such as Stofflet are pushed aside by the focus on Charette.
advisories:
Battle scenes, executions, and reprisals against civilians by Republican troops.

Charette is shot by a firing squad.

Rated for all audiences in French cinemas; not recommended under 10 on French television.

Historically one-sided: the opening interviews include Reynald Secher, whose genocide thesis is widely disputed, though the word is not used in the film.

doctrine: The Vendéens fought for their priests and their altars, and the Church had already condemned the Civil Constitution, which put the clergy under the State, as schismatic and heretical in its principles (Pius VI, 1791). The film's last scene, in which Charette receives absolution before the firing squad, shows the Church's teaching that a man in danger of death should receive the sacrament of Penance, and that a priest may absolve anyone in extremis. Whether the Vendée war was a just war is a separate question: the Church teaches that insurrection against an unjust authority is lawful only when tyranny is manifest, prolonged and without remedy, and that the means must be just, so the reprisals on both sides are not excused by the cause.

Mottez wrote the script from the park's show Le Dernier Panache, and filming began in March 2022 in and around the park. The historian Jean-Clément Martin was consulted during development but later asked for his involvement to be withdrawn. It ran 100 minutes, had previews on 8 December 2022 and opened in France on 25 January 2023, drawing about 287,600 admissions. The press was mostly negative; Le Monde called it a historical nonsense, while the traditionalist Catholic monthly La Nef praised it. Two La France insoumise deputies attacked it as anti-republican.
