title: The War of the Vendée
decision: GREY: identity, outline, cast and the director's own account of his liberties are documented by several sources, so it is not HOLD; but no independent critic has assessed its history. The only full review by an outsider, Joseph Pearce's (2013), is appreciative, sets historical accuracy aside and has an indirect tie to the DVD's distributor (Ignatius Press). Settles with an independent review, or a scene log checked against academic histories of 1793-94 (Huchet 1988; Jean-Clément Martin), covering Robespierre, the devil figure, Fr Bernier and the morality of the rising.

grey.question: No independent critic has assessed how this film handles its history. What has been written comes from the director, from Catholic outlets that promoted it and from family-viewing guides. Joseph Pearce's appreciative essay concedes that it gives up historical nuance and shows Robespierre as demonically possessed. Morlino drew mainly on Reynald Secher's disputed genocide thesis and combined people and events. A review or documented viewing that checks the Revolutionaries, the devil figure, the priest Fr Bernier and the rising itself against academic histories of 1793–94 would settle it.

summary: Jim Morlino's low-budget drama of the 1793 Catholic rising in western France, played entirely by a cast of some 250 children and teenagers.
synopsis: In 1793 the Revolutionary government has outlawed priests who refuse the constitutional oath and orders a mass levy of conscripts. In a village of the Vendée, peasants and local nobles decide to take up arms for their priests and their king. The film follows the villagers and their families through secret meetings, a Latin Mass celebrated before battle, early victories, losses and reprisals. A boy, Remy, is turned away from the men's council and longs to fight; the village women push the hesitant men to act. In Paris, Robespierre appears as the sinister face of the Revolution. A priest, Fr Bernier, ministers to the rising, and the devil appears as a hooded figure. Every role, the adults included, is played by young performers, more than 250 of them.
inclusion: It is one of very few English-language films about the Vendée, and it keeps the religious cause of the rising at the centre: the persecution of priests who refused the oath, and Mass said in Latin before battle. Morlino made it through his Navis Pictures as a children's cinema project, with a cast all under 21 and a tiny budget. Fr John Zuhlsdorf, writing from a DVD supplied for review, found the acting uneven but praised Kevin Kaska's score. Joseph Pearce, an editor for Ignatius Press, which distributes the DVD, expected a bad film and was charmed, while admitting that it trades historical nuance for plain good against plain evil. Catholic festivals gave it prizes for young audiences. It is made for families and older children.
themes: The film's Catholic content is the defence of the sacraments and of faithful priests. The rising is presented as a response to the persecution of clergy who refused the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and the Mass before battle is its central religious image. The devil appears as a hooded figure, and Pearce reads Robespierre as shown possessed. What has not been established is how the film handles the morality of armed rebellion, the Republican atrocities it chose to omit, and its priest character, Fr Bernier.
history: The Vendée rising began in March 1793, when conscription for the levy of 300,000 men set off armed revolt across parts of Maine-et-Loire, Vendée, Deux-Sèvres and Loire-Inférieure. Françoise Huchet's study traces its first days in Maine-et-Loire between 2 and 22 March 1793. Hostility to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the persecution of priests who refused the oath were central grievances. The Catholic and Royal Army won early victories before defeat at Cholet and Savenay in late 1793, followed by severe Republican repression in 1794. Historians still argue over death tolls and over Secher's description of the repression as genocide.
liberties: Morlino says he combined characters and events and put historical figures together in one village "for convenience", though several never met. He also says he left out many atrocities because the film was made for young people. His main research source was Reynald Secher's A French Genocide, whose central term he acknowledges is hotly contested by historians. Pearce notes that the film removes the nuance that historical accuracy demands.
advisories:
Battle scenes with swords, muskets and cannon; parent reviews report no blood.

Persecution of priests, deaths and bereavement.

The devil appears as a hooded figure.

All adult roles are played by children and teenagers; the acting is uneven.

The film presents the conflict as plain good against plain evil and follows Secher's disputed genocide framing.

doctrine: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy, passed on 12 July 1790, made bishops and parish priests elected state officials. From 27 November 1790 every priest had to swear to it; seven of 135 bishops did. Pius VI condemned it in Charitas (13 April 1791). He declared the elections of the new constitutional bishops null, suspended the clergy who had sworn unless they retracted within forty days, and told the faithful to shun the intruded pastors and hold to their lawful ones. This is why Vendéan peasants walked to hidden Masses said by priests who had refused the oath. On armed resistance, St Thomas teaches that a government directed to the ruler's private good rather than the common good is tyrannical, and that overthrowing it is not sedition, unless the disorder causes the people greater harm than the tyranny (Summa II-II, q. 42, a. 2, ad 3).
production: Jim Morlino, a Connecticut actor turned film-maker, made The War of the Vendée as the second film of his company Navis Pictures, after St. Bernadette of Lourdes (2009). He wanted an action story for boys that showed courage and sacrifice; a friend pointed him to the Vendée. He drew on Reynald Secher's A French Genocide, Michael Davies's For Altar and Throne, Warren Carroll's The Guillotine and the Cross, Simon Schama's Citizens and William Bush's To Quell the Terror. More than 250 children and teenagers, all unpaid amateurs, play every role. Morlino wrote, lit, shot, edited and produced it himself, and put out-of-pocket costs at about $30,000. The one large expense was Kevin Kaska's score, recorded by an orchestra of about 80 at Warner Bros. The DVD came out on 24 February 2012, the 219th anniversary of the 1793 levy decree, and was entered in the Mirabile Dictu festival that summer.

title: The Scarlet and the Black
decision: PUBLISH: Television Academy records confirm the 1983 CBS film; Greydanus's Decent Films review gives a scene-aware positive assessment (priestly charity, accurate closing coda) and flags the invented Pius XII Concordat scene; CNA/Catholic World Report confirms the history of O'Flaherty's escape line and Kappler's 1959 baptism. Dramatic liberties are ordinary for the genre and do not distort the religious meaning.
summary: Gregory Peck plays Mgr Hugh O'Flaherty, the Irish Vatican priest who hid thousands of escaped prisoners and Jews under the nose of the SS in occupied Rome.
synopsis: Rome, 1943. German troops occupy the city, and SS chief Herbert Kappler paints a white line across the edge of St Peter's Square: if Monsignor O'Flaherty steps over it, he will be shot. O'Flaherty, an Irish official of the Holy Office, has already started hiding escaped Allied prisoners and Jews in flats, convents and monasteries, with help from priests, diplomats and Roman families. He slips past the line in disguises, outwits raids and survives an attempt on his life inside the Vatican. As the Allies approach, Kappler, fearing for his own family, asks his enemy for help. A closing coda follows the two men after the war.
inclusion: This is a well-made, old-fashioned television thriller with a priest as its hero, and it never lets you forget he is a priest. Peck plays O'Flaherty as blunt, funny and fearless, a man who boxes and plays golf but treats every life he hides as a charge from God. Christopher Plummer's Kappler is cold and intelligent rather than a cartoon villain, and their duel gives the film its spine. The best scenes turn on mercy: O'Flaherty's choice when Kappler pleads for his wife and children, and the true postscript about what the priest did for Kappler in prison. Steven Greydanus calls it riveting and edifying. Rome locations and an Ennio Morricone score help; the pacing sags in the middle.
themes: The film's Catholic heart is the priest's refusal to divide people into those who deserve help and those who do not. O'Flaherty hides Jews, Communists and Allied soldiers alike, and finally extends the same charity to the man who tried to have him killed. The Vatican appears as a place of real moral tension: O'Flaherty's superiors worry that his work threatens the Holy See's neutrality, and John Gielgud's Pius XII is sympathetic. Greydanus notes one scene in which the Pope has second thoughts about the Concordat with Germany, which is a filmmakers' invention.
history: Hugh O'Flaherty was born at Kiskeam, County Cork, on 28 February 1898 and ordained in Rome on 20 December 1925. He served in the Vatican diplomatic service in Egypt, Haiti, Santo Domingo and Czechoslovakia and was made a monsignor in 1934. During the German occupation of Rome, from September 1943 to June 1944, he ran what became known as the Rome Escape Line, sheltering escaped Allied prisoners, Jews and others. Estimates of those saved run to about 6,500. Herbert Kappler, head of the SS in Rome, was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1948. O'Flaherty visited him every month and baptised him in 1959. After the war Pius XII made O'Flaherty a domestic prelate and notary of the Holy Office, and he received the CBE and the American Medal of Freedom. He died at Cahersiveen, County Kerry, on 30 October 1963.
liberties: The film is based on J. P. Gallagher's book The Scarlet Pimpernel of the Vatican and compresses events into a cat-and-mouse plot. The SS general Max Helm is a fictionalised stand-in for Karl Wolff, who was still alive. The scene of Pius XII doubting the Concordat is invented. Kappler's appeal to O'Flaherty over his family is dramatised for the climax.
advisories:
Wartime violence, including executions, a raid and the murder of a priest; no graphic gore by modern standards.

No sexual content of note. Suitable for teenagers and up; younger children may find the menace and killings upsetting.

The Vatican scenes are dramatised and should not be taken as a record of Pius XII's words.

suitability.note: There are executions, a raid and the shooting of a priest, shown without graphic gore, and constant menace from the SS. There is no sexual content. The running time (about 2 hours 25 minutes) will try younger children.

doctrine: O'Flaherty's work is a list of the corporal works of mercy as St Thomas gives them: to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, harbour the harbourless and ransom the captive (Summa II-II, q. 32, a. 2). His treatment of Kappler follows St Thomas's teaching on enemies. Charity must not shut an enemy out of the love owed to all men, and we must be ready to help an enemy in urgent need; going further and overcoming evil with good belongs to the perfection of charity (q. 25, aa. 8-9). The Vatican's caution in the film has a real basis. Under the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929 the Holy See pledged itself to perpetual neutrality in international disputes, so a priest using Vatican property for the Allies put it at risk.
production: The film was adapted from J. P. Gallagher's 1967 book The Scarlet Pimpernel of the Vatican. It was produced for CBS by Bill McCutchen, with Jerry London directing. It was shot in Rome and the Vatican, photographed by Giuseppe Rotunno, with music by Ennio Morricone. Some characters were renamed: General Max Helm stands for Karl Wolff, who was still alive, and Hirsch for Erich Priebke. CBS first broadcast it on 2 February 1983, at 143 minutes, and sent more than 500,000 scripts to schools to be read aloud in class. It won the Emmy for sound mixing and was nominated for editing and title design.

title: The Assisi Underground
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a bishop, a Franciscan priest and enclosed nuns are the rescuers) and securely identified (Box Office Mojo, Wikipedia, Winnert). The reservation is historical and can be stated: the film follows Ramati's book, built on Niccacci's recollections, which Don Aldo Brunacci, the actual organiser, called a novel, and which Michele Sarfatti shows to contain inventions such as Bartali's courier runs. Not PUBLISH because no substantive independent review addresses its treatment of the faith and it is unchecked whether the film carries the anti-Pius XII charge of the book's British title. It would move to PUBLISH if the dialogue shows no such charge, since this record discloses the history.

grey.question: The Assisi Underground honours a real rescue, but tells it through Alexander Ramati's book, built on Padre Rufino Niccacci's own recollections. Don Aldo Brunacci, who actually ran the network for the bishop, called that book a novel and said many details were invented or distorted, including Niccacci's arrest and the cyclist Gino Bartali's courier runs, for which historians have found no documents. Ramati's British edition was titled While the Pope Kept Silent, and whether the film repeats that charge against Pius XII has not been checked. It is a dramatisation of the Church's rescue work, not a record of it.

summary: Alexander Ramati's Cannon-produced drama of the Franciscan Padre Rufino Niccacci and the Assisi clergy who hid Jews from the Germans in 1943–44.
synopsis: In 1943, after the Germans occupy northern Italy, the Bishop of Assisi, Giuseppe Placido Nicolini, charges the Franciscan Padre Rufino Niccacci with saving Jewish refugees. Rufino hides them in the town's monasteries and convents, one of them under the formidable Mother Giuseppina, dresses some as friars and nuns and teaches them enough Latin prayers to pass. False identity papers are printed in the town, and the cyclist Gino Bartali is among the characters. Rufino guides refugees towards the Allied lines, makes promises to compromised fascists and befriends the German commandant, Colonel Müller, a medical officer who quietly supplies medicines to the town. The SS grow suspicious, arrest Rufino and put him before a firing squad, and Müller uses his influence to save him. Closing titles describe what became of the real people.
inclusion: The rescue is real: Yad Vashem has honoured Niccacci, Don Aldo Brunacci and others among the Assisi clergy and townspeople, and about three hundred Jews survived the occupation there. The film puts the Church's work at the centre, with a bishop, a friar and enclosed nuns risking their lives for strangers. It has assets: Giuseppe Rotunno's photography of Assisi, James Mason's last screen role as the bishop, Irene Papas and Maximilian Schell. Critics found it dull. Derek Winnert calls it well-meaning but ineptly told and Ben Cross uninspiring, and the theatrical version, cut to 115 minutes from a television version of about three hours, shows its seams. It is worth knowing as a rare popular film about Catholic rescuers, provided the history is kept apart from Ramati's version of it.
themes: The clergy act on their bishop's orders, so the rescue is shown as the work of the Church and not of rebels within it, and its subject is charity. Enclosure is opened and habits are lent to save lives, and the Jewish refugees are sheltered without pressure to convert; historically the Assisi nuns even prepared the meal that ended Yom Kippur in 1943. Rufino is a clever, sometimes devious priest who lies to the occupiers and bargains with fascists, and the film treats this as justified by necessity. The good German colonel is a believing Catholic. What no review settles is how the film treats Pius XII. Accounts of the rescue say the bishop acted on the Pope's wishes, but Ramati's book was published in Britain as While the Pope Kept Silent.
history: After the German occupation of northern and central Italy in September 1943, Assisi became a refuge for Jews. Bishop Giuseppe Placido Nicolini, with the Franciscan Fr Rufino Niccacci and the priest Aldo Brunacci, sheltered several hundred Jewish refugees in convents and monasteries, and local printers made false papers. Yad Vashem named Niccacci one of the Righteous Among the Nations in April 1974. The cyclist Gino Bartali carried documents for the wider Florence-Assisi network, as Yad Vashem recognised in 2013. The film rests on Alexander Ramati's 1978 book, whose account of the rescue historians have not accepted in every detail.
liberties: Brunacci, who ran the operation, called Ramati's book nothing but a novel and said many details were invented or distorted. The film makes Niccacci the organiser; Brunacci says it was he, not Niccacci, who was arrested in May 1944. Gino Bartali's role as a courier, taken from the book, has no documentary support, according to the historian Michele Sarfatti. The plan that protected Assisi as a hospital town also happened differently.
advisories:
Wartime menace, arrests, a threatened execution and some violence.

No sexual content reported.

Suitable for older children and adults; slow in places.

Its history follows a contested account that exaggerates Niccacci's role, and its treatment of Pius XII is unchecked.

names: The Assisi Underground: The Priest Who Rescued Jews, book by Alexander Ramati (1978)

suitability.note: Arrests, the threat of execution and some wartime violence, with no sexual content reported. It is slow in places, and the history it tells is contested.

doctrine: Sheltering the persecuted is a work of mercy, and Pius XII had taught in Mystici Corporis (1943) that the Church embraces all men. The Church's moral theology allows a man to withhold the truth from those with no right to it, by silence or mental reservation, but not to lie; the film's friars and nuns, who teach refugees Latin prayers so as to pass as religious, are working within that distinction. Pius XII's own part in the rescue is a matter of dispute that the film does not settle.
production: Alexander Ramati wrote the screenplay from his own 1978 book, which in turn rests on Fr Rufino Niccacci's account, and directed the film. Menahem Golan and Yoram Globus produced it through Golan-Globus Productions as a US-Italian co-production. Giuseppe Rotunno photographed it and Dov Seltzer wrote the music. It ran 115 minutes and opened in the United States in September 1985. Critics gave it a poor reception. The cast included Ben Cross, James Mason and Maximilian Schell.

title: The Ninth Day
decision: PUBLISH: the Film Fund Luxembourg catalogue confirms identity; Greydanus's detailed review and Thomas Wolter's essay in forum (Luxembourg, 2004) establish both the film's moral seriousness and exactly what is invented. The interrogation is openly a dramatisation of nine days Bernard's diary barely describes. The Pius XII material is a character's doubt answered by his bishop's account of reprisals, not the film's verdict; its one chronological slip (the Dutch reprisals of summer 1942) is noted. A Luxembourg critic's complaint that the film is pro-Church propaganda is recorded.
summary: A starved priest is let out of Dachau for nine days and given a choice by a Gestapo officer: win over his bishop for the Reich, or go back to the camp.
synopsis: Dachau, early 1942. Abbé Henri Kremer, a Luxembourg priest, survives in the priests' block amid hunger, beatings and executions. Suddenly he is released and sent home, apparently for his mother's funeral. In Luxembourg he must report each day to Untersturmführer Gebhardt, a young Gestapo officer who once studied for the priesthood. Gebhardt wants Kremer to persuade the Bishop of Luxembourg, who has shut himself away in protest, to accept the occupation; then a signed declaration will do. If Kremer refuses or runs, the priests in Dachau will pay. Over nine days the two men argue about faith, obedience and the Church's silence while Kremer's family urges him to save himself.
inclusion: Schlöndorff turns a small episode into a tight moral drama, and the film's achievement is that the arguments are real arguments. Ulrich Matthes, gaunt and hollow-eyed, plays Kremer as a man with no heroism left, only conscience. August Diehl's Gebhardt is clever, polite and a theologian of sorts, which makes him more dangerous than a thug. The Dachau scenes are brief and restrained but unforgettable. Steven Greydanus gives it his top grade, noting that it shows several kinds of resistance and their costs rather than offering a simple defence or accusation. It is short, grey and austere.
themes: Kremer's choice is the classic one between apostasy dressed as prudence and fidelity that may cost his life. The film is sharp on how temptation works: Gebhardt does not ask him to deny Christ, only to compromise a little for the good of others. The priests in Dachau pray, say Mass in secret and share bread; some of them are shown collaborating or bitter. The Church's public silence is debated openly. Kremer says he never doubts the Church but sometimes doubts the Holy Father, and his bishop answers that protests have brought reprisals on the very people they were meant to help.
history: Jean Bernard (1907–1994), a Luxembourg priest, was arrested in 1941 and sent to Dachau, where he was among the many priests held in the clergy block. In February 1942 he was released for nine days, apparently to win over Luxembourg's clergy, refused, and returned. He was freed in August 1942, later edited the Luxemburger Wort and led the international Catholic film office (OCIC). His memoir is Pfarrerblock 25487.
liberties: The hero is renamed Kremer. Bernard's diary says almost nothing about the nine days, so the daily interrogations and Gebhardt are invented; Thomas Wolter notes none of the conversations happened as staged. A detail from Primo Levi's memoirs is borrowed. The bishop's reference to reprisals after the Dutch bishops' protest is anachronistic: that protest and the arrests that followed, including Edith Stein's, came in July and August 1942, after the story's February setting.
advisories:
Concentration-camp brutality: beatings, starvation and deaths, shown briefly and without lingering.

Some crude language. No sexual content.

Suitable for older teenagers and adults.

The film raises the question of Pius XII's public silence through its characters; it is a drama, not a historical verdict.

doctrine: Gebhardt's offer is a temptation that tries to pass a compromise off as prudence. The Church teaches that one may never do evil that good may come of it (Romans 3:8), and that obedience to civil power ends where it commands what God forbids (Acts 5:29). Priests owe obedience to their bishop, and the bishop's silence, or protest, is for him to judge. Pius XI condemned Nazi racial and religious policy in Mit brennender Sorge (14 March 1937). Priests in Dachau said Mass in secret; the Church recognises the dignity of those who suffer for the Faith, and the Mass was celebrated there under severe restriction.

Ulrich Matthes plays Kremer and August Diehl the Gestapo officer Gebhardt. In the film the priest is arrested in February 1941, sent to Dachau, and released for nine days in January 1942 under pressure to persuade his bishop to collaborate. title: Network of Freedom
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established (SensaCine, eCartelera, ACI Prensa interview, Almudi). Hélène Studler is not beatified, so rule (a) does not apply. The film was commissioned by the Vincentian Family for its 400th anniversary, and the only independent review found (Miguel Ángel Pizarro, eCartelera) addresses the performance and production but gives one line to the faith. Not PUBLISH because the treatment of her religious life is unassessed; the old 'martyrs' collection is dropped, since she died of illness. Settled by a fuller independent review or a check of the dialogue in the convent scenes.

grey.question: The film's identity and subject are clear: Pablo Moreno's 2017 Spanish feature about Sister Hélène Studler, the Daughter of Charity whose network in occupied Metz smuggled some two thousand prisoners to safety. It was commissioned by the Vincentian Family, and the director says they wanted a figure close to people of today rather than a saint's life. The one secular review found praises Assumpta Serna but says little about how religious life is shown. A fuller review, or a check of the dialogue, showing that her vocation and prayer stay at the centre would settle it.

summary: Assumpta Serna plays Sister Hélène Studler, a Daughter of Charity in occupied Metz whose escape network smuggled some two thousand prisoners of war to safety.
synopsis: Metz, 1940. Sister Hélène Studler, a Daughter of Charity who cares for orphans and the destitute at a city hospice, sees Lorraine annexed and a camp for French prisoners of war built near the city. Under Red Cross protection she and her sisters, with volunteers from the town, bring the prisoners food and water. Relief turns into rescue. The sisters begin smuggling men out of the camp and across the new frontier into unoccupied France, and a clandestine network, linked to the Resistance, grows around them. The work puts her community and her helpers in danger. Among those the network helps, in the film as in history, are the future president François Mitterrand and General Henri Giraud. St Louise de Marillac, co-foundress of her congregation, appears as a figure in the story.
inclusion: Hélène Studler's story is little known outside Lorraine, and no French film has told it. Moreno made this one on a budget of roughly half a million euros, commissioned by the Vincentian Family for the 400th anniversary of its charism, with Burgos standing in for Lorraine and Spanish actors playing French and Germans. Miguel Ángel Pizarro of eCartelera, the only secular critic found, called Assumpta Serna's performance one of her strongest in years and said she carries the film over its weak early production design, which he compared unfavourably with Spanish television drama. He found the faith shown as the heroine's inner strength rather than as propaganda. The press average on SensaCine is low. It is a modest, sincere film whose main interest is the true story and Serna.
themes: Sister Hélène acts as a Daughter of Charity: the film roots her rescue work in the Vincentian tradition of serving the poor, Catholic accounts describe her as sustained by prayer, and St Louise de Marillac appears. The director calls his approach Christian humanism and says the Vincentians wanted a figure close to people of today rather than a saint's biography; the anniversary campaign the film served took the text 'I was a stranger and you welcomed me'. Pizarro reads the faith as her inner strength. How much the film shows of her religious life, prayer, community and obedience, as against the humanitarian adventure, no independent review says.
history: Marie Joséphine Studler (1891–1944), born at Amiens to an Alsatian family, joined the Daughters of Charity in 1912 and worked at the Saint-Nicolas hospice in Metz from 1918. From 1940 to early 1942 she ran an escape network for prisoners of war, draft evaders and Allied airmen, credited with helping over 2,000 people. She was arrested in 1941 and released for ill health. Her network helped Mitterrand escape in December 1941, and from Lyon she found the guide for Giraud's escape in 1942. She died of cancer at Clermont-Ferrand on 3 December 1944.
advisories:
Wartime setting with arrests, danger and some violence; no source details its extent.

No sexual content reported.

Rated not recommended for under-12s in Spain.

Commissioned by the Vincentian Family, her own religious family; no independent review addresses its treatment of religious life.

doctrine: The Daughters of Charity were founded in 1633 by St Vincent de Paul and St Louise de Marillac, to serve the poor in the world rather than behind a cloister. Their members take simple vows renewed each year. Vincent was canonised by Clement XII in 1737 and Louise by Pius XI in 1934. The work shown in the film belongs to the corporal works of mercy, 'I was in prison and you came to me' (Matthew 25:36), and to the Church's teaching that the duty of charity extends to enemies. The real Sister Hélène Studler (1891-1944) was a Daughter of Charity who ran a network that helped prisoners of war and other fugitives escape from the Germans; she was awarded the Légion d'honneur and the Croix de guerre in November 1944.
production: Pablo Moreno directed and wrote this Spanish feature, released in Spain on 20 October 2017. Assumpta Serna plays Sister Hélène and Gladys Balaguer plays St Louise de Marillac. title: Quo Vadis
decision: PUBLISH: Re-checked against the AFI Catalog's full synopsis. The joint suicide is real but belongs to the pagan Petronius and his slave Eunice, while the Christians die by martyrdom and Nero's own suicide is shown as cowardice; the coercive start of the romance is Nero's act, which Lygia escapes and refuses until Vinicius turns towards Christ. Neither is endorsed by the film. Liz Gloyn and the Dickinson College essay give substantive treatment. Both elements are flagged in advisories.
summary: MGM's Technicolor epic of Nero's Rome sets a Roman commander's pursuit of a Christian girl against the Great Fire, the first persecution and the deaths of St Peter and St Paul.
synopsis: In AD 64 the commander Marcus Vinicius returns to Rome and falls for Lygia, a Christian hostage raised by a retired general. When she rebuffs him, his uncle Petronius gets Nero to hand her to Marcus as a gift; her giant servant Ursus rescues her. Marcus tracks her to a secret gathering where St Peter tells of his time with Christ. Lygia will not marry him at the price of her faith. Nero burns Rome to inspire a poem and, to save himself, blames the Christians. On the Appian Way Peter meets his Lord and turns back to Rome. Christians are thrown to the lions, Peter is crucified, Petronius takes his own life, and Lygia is tied in the arena before a bull, with Ursus her only defender.
inclusion: This is the film that started the 1950s epic cycle, and it has the virtues and faults of the type. The sets, crowds and Robert Surtees's colour photography are lavish; the burning of Rome is spectacular. Peter Ustinov's Nero, vain, petulant and murderous, steals the picture, and Leo Genn's ironic Petronius runs him close. Robert Taylor and Deborah Kerr are stiff, and the romance is the weakest part. What surprises modern viewers, as the classicist Liz Gloyn found, is how central the Church is: Peter and Paul appear in person, the catacomb liturgy and Peter's preaching are given time, and the martyrs go to the lions singing. The Christian community is idealised but attractive.
themes: The film's subject is the Church's first persecution and the witness of the martyrs. Peter recounts the miraculous catch and the Resurrection, the Domine, quo vadis legend sends him back to Rome to die, and he is crucified head downward, as tradition reports. Paul preaches that Christ conquers by love. Lygia prays for Marcus's conversion and refuses to buy his love with her faith; Peter marries them in prison. Against this the film sets Roman decadence and Nero's claim to divinity. Petronius dies as a cultivated pagan; the contrast with the Christians who 'know how to die' is the point.
history: Rome burned in July 64, and Nero blamed the Christians, whom Tacitus records were killed in his gardens. Early tradition, reported by Origen through Eusebius, says Peter was crucified head downward at his own wish; the date of his death is uncertain within 64 to 68. The Quo vadis encounter on the Appian Way is an ancient legend, not a scriptural event. Petronius's forced suicide is recorded by Tacitus.
liberties: Lygia, Vinicius and Ursus are fictional, from Henryk Sienkiewicz's 1896 novel. The joint suicide with a slave is borrowed from Seneca and Paulina, who survived. There is no evidence that Poppaea proposed blaming the Christians. Nero's death and Galba's arrival are compressed into the aftermath of the persecution. The flowering staff is a pious legend.
advisories:
A long scene shows Petronius and his slave Eunice opening their veins and dying at table; it is calm and bloodless but sympathetic to them.

Christians are killed by lions and burned at the stake, mostly offscreen; Nero strangles Poppaea and is helped to stab himself; sword fights and a man's neck broken.

Nero orders Lygia given to Marcus as a slave at the start; scantily dressed dancers and Roman revels.

Younger children may find the arena scenes frightening.

names: Quo Vadis, novel by Henryk Sienkiewicz (1896)

suitability.note: Christians are killed by lions and burned alive, though mostly out of sight, and a long suicide scene is calm and bloodless. There are scantily dressed dancers at Nero's feasts. Younger children may find the arena frightening and the three hours long.

doctrine: The Church teaches that the Apostle Peter was the first bishop of Rome and the head of the Apostles, a primacy later defined at the First Vatican Council (1870); the film's Peter is its pastor and martyr, crucified head downward at his own wish, as Origen reports. The martyrs are those who die for the faith: the Church counts martyrdom as the baptism of blood. Lygia refuses to marry a pagan, and rightly: under the 1917 Code (canon 1070) the difference in religion between a baptised and an unbaptised person is a diriment impediment to marriage that only dispensation could remove. The 'Domine, quo vadis?' scene is not Scripture: it comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter, c. AD 180, and it is a legend.
production: MGM's first attempt in 1949, with Gregory Peck and Elizabeth Taylor, was postponed; Mervyn LeRoy took over the next year with Robert Taylor and Deborah Kerr. Shooting began on 22 May 1950 at Cinecittà, Rome, and the film cost about $7 million, then the most expensive ever made. Sam Zimbalist produced it. Peter Ustinov's Nero and Leo Genn's Petronius were nominated for Oscars, with six other nominations, and none won. MGM released it on 2 November 1951 at 171 minutes. It earned about $21 million and was the highest-grossing film of 1951. The National Legion of Decency classified it A-I. The dancers at Nero's feasts and the joint suicide of Petronius and Eunice are the passages parents will notice.

title: Fabiola
decision: GREY: The reservation is documented by contemporary pre-conciliar Catholic evidence: Paola Palma's archival study (Schermi, 2017) shows the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico classified the Italian release 'adulti con riserva', and Vittorino Veronese of Catholic Action found it 'molto discutibile' for its thesis and sensual material. The English subtitle file shows what that thesis is: not indifferentism, since the Christians say Rome must become Christian and the martyrs confess Christ, but non-violence and human brotherhood. The film is dedicated to the victims of all violence, its Christians speak of a world without masters or slaves, and Rhual's refusal to kill rests on the claim that a Christian never kills. No baptism occurs. Not REJECT; the rating and the sensual material keep it GREY.

grey.question: Fabiola was sold as a Catholic epic, but the Italian Catholic film office of its day classified it 'adults with reservations', and Catholic Action's Vittorino Veronese found its thesis questionable and its sensual scenes gratuitous. The dialogue shows a thesis of non-violence and human brotherhood, dedicated to the victims of all violence, with an absolute refusal to kill that goes beyond Catholic teaching on just defence. Yet the martyrs confess Christ plainly, and Fabiola declares herself a Christian in the arena. The question is whether that witness outweighs a gladiator romance, the sensual scenes and the loose use of Wiseman's novel.

summary: Blasetti's huge postwar epic, very loosely from Cardinal Wiseman's novel, turns the Church of the catacombs into a gladiator romance and murder plot that ends in the arena.
synopsis: In Rome around 312, Fabiola, a senator's daughter, falls for Rhual, a Gaulish gladiator who is secretly an agent of Constantine. Her father, Senator Fabius, who favours tolerance and the freeing of slaves, is murdered, and the Christians are blamed and put on trial. Rhual is condemned with them to the arena. Fabiola at first suspects him, then takes her stand with the Christians in the arena. Rhual refuses to kill his opponents and the other gladiators follow him. Constantine's army reaches Rome, the city rises, and the film ends under the Christian standards of the new emperor.
inclusion: Fabiola opened the postwar wave of religious epics, as the Treccani film encyclopedia notes, and it was the biggest Italian spectacle since the war: Michèle Morgan, Henri Vidal and Michel Simon, enormous sets, and the top box office of its Italian season. French critics in 1949, as Paola Palma's archival study shows, admired Blasetti's handling of crowds while finding the film too long. Time Out's reviewer finds it dull until the violent climax in the arena; Manny Farber, seeing the shortened American version, called it a chaos of disconnected sequences. Its interest now is largely historical: an ambitious Catholic spectacle in postwar Italy, made by a company widely taken for a Vatican enterprise, whose Catholic credentials the Catholic film bodies then publicly disowned.
themes: Wiseman's 1854 novel is a Catholic apologetic for the Church of the catacombs, ending in Fabiola's baptism. The film keeps the persecution, the arena and names such as Sebastiano, Cecilia and Sira, but builds its story on an invented gladiator who serves Constantine, a murder mystery and a love affair. A French critic in 1949 complained that Fabiola reaches Christianity by way of profane passion, and Veronese judged the thesis questionable. The dialogue shows what he meant: the film is dedicated to the victims of all violence, and its Christians preach brotherhood, a world without masters or slaves and an absolute refusal to kill, which goes beyond the Church's teaching on just defence. Yet the faith is not diluted: the martyrs confess Christ, and Fabiola declares herself a Christian in the arena.
history: The novel and the film are set in Rome at the start of the last great persecution. In 302 Diocletian and his Caesar Galerius agreed at Nicomedia to suppress Christianity. The first edict of February 303 ordered churches destroyed and Scriptures burned, and stripped Christians of rank of their status. Further edicts imprisoned the clergy, then compelled them to sacrifice under torture, and finally extended the order to the laity. Diocletian abdicated on 1 May 305, and the persecution went on in the East under his successors until the toleration granted in 311 and the Edict of Milan of 313. Fabiola herself is Wiseman's invention.
liberties: Rhual, the gladiator-agent of Constantine, the murder of Fabiola's father and the love story are invented. The novel's martyrdoms of Agnes, Pancratius and Tarcisius do not appear in the cast lists consulted. The film sets its action around 312, on the eve of Constantine's victory, rather than in the Diocletian persecution where Wiseman places most of the story, and it ends with Constantine's army entering Rome. The baptism of Fabiola and her household that the novel narrates does not occur in the dialogue.
advisories:
Prolonged kisses and love scenes, a banquet dance and semi-nude courtesans: the material a 1949 Catholic critic asked to have cut.

Arena martyrdoms and mass violence at the climax.

Classified 'adults with reservations' by the Italian Catholic film office in 1949. Adults and older teenagers.

Versions vary widely, from the Italian release of about 164 minutes to an American dubbed cut of about 97, and the French release differed again. Check which version a copy is.

names: Fabiola, or the Church of the Catacombs, novel by Cardinal Nicholas Wiseman (1854)

suitability.note: The full version has long love scenes, a banquet with semi-nude courtesans and mass killings in the arena, and the Italian Catholic film office rated it for adults with reservations in 1949. The shorter dubbed versions cut much of this but keep the martyrdoms.

doctrine: Wiseman wrote the novel as the first of a series of tales on periods of Church history, and it shows the early Church's practice: the catechumenate, baptism of adults after instruction, burial of the martyrs in the catacombs and veneration of their tombs. Several of its figures are real martyrs. St Sebastian was buried on the Via Appia, as the Depositio martyrum of 354 records, and his feast is 20 January; the Catholic Encyclopedia judges the later Acts of his martyrdom unhistorical. St Cecilia's feast is 22 November, and the date of her martyrdom is uncertain. The Church teaches that martyrdom, the free acceptance of death for the faith, justifies even the unbaptised as baptism of blood.
production: Salvo D'Angelo's Universalia Film produced Fabiola with French stars and money through Franco-London Films. At least ten writers worked on a long and troubled script, eight of them credited, among them Cesare Zavattini, Diego Fabbri and Vitaliano Brancati. It was shot almost entirely at Cinecittà, with the arena combat and martyrdoms filmed in the Arena di Verona. It opened in Italy on 3 March 1949, distributed by Warner Bros., and was the highest-grossing Italian film of the 1948–49 season. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico classified it 'adults with reservations', and the Dominican Félix Morlion's praise in the OCIC review was later corrected to accept that rating. Critics faulted its history and some bold scenes. Shortened dubbed versions reached Britain, as The Fighting Gladiator, and the United States in 1951. A restoration was shown in Rome in 2001; the surviving copy runs about 164 minutes.

title: Diary of a Country Priest
alternateTitles: Le Journal d'un curé de campagne
decision: PUBLISH: Steven Greydanus's detailed review and the critical tradition around the film establish a portrait of priestly perseverance and grace in apparent failure, drawn faithfully from Bernanos. Adult material (an affair, a threatened suicide) is part of the moral drama and is disclosed.
summary: Bresson's spare adaptation of Bernanos follows a sickly young curé whose parish rejects him, and finds holiness in apparent failure.
synopsis: A young priest arrives in Ambricourt, a village in northern France. He is poor, ill, inexperienced and awkward, and his parishioners respond with indifference or mockery. He records everything in a diary. The older curé of Torcy gives him blunt advice about running a parish. At the château, the count is having an affair with the governess, and the count's daughter Chantal hates them both and threatens to kill herself. The priest confronts the countess, who has been bitter towards God since the death of her son. In a long exchange she yields and makes her peace, and she dies that night. Gossip about the encounter turns the village further against him. Diagnosed with stomach cancer, he travels to Lille and dies in the lodgings of a former seminary friend who has left the priesthood.
inclusion: This is one of the essential films about the priesthood. Bresson strips away everything decorative: Claude Laydu's still face, the diary voice-over, Léonce-Henry Burel's grey images of the Artois countryside. What remains is a man trying to do his duty with almost no visible success. The scene with the countess is the dramatic peak; Greydanus compares it to the great dialogues in The Brothers Karamazov. André Bazin's 1951 essay on the film helped make it a landmark of modern cinema. It won the Prix Louis Delluc and the International Award and OCIC (Catholic) prize at Venice. The pace is slow and the tone severe, and some viewers find it opaque. It rewards patience.
themes: The film's subject is the priesthood stripped of consolation. The curé suffers spiritual dryness, physical weakness and the contempt of his flock. He feels unable even to pray, yet keeps saying Mass, visiting and hearing confessions. Greydanus notes how he accepts failure, dryness and persecution and turns them into a kind of victory. The countess scene shows the cure of souls in action: he refuses to accept her despair and leads her to surrender her grief to God. The end gives Bernanos's last words to the priest: "All is grace." The film treats a priest's life as fruitful in ways he cannot see.
liberties: Bresson follows the novel closely but cuts heavily, especially the long reflective passages and several conversations with the curé of Torcy. He invents almost nothing; his changes are mainly omissions and a sharper focus on the priest's isolation.
advisories:
An adulterous affair (implied, not shown).

A girl threatens suicide; a death; terminal illness.

Slow and austere; best for older teenagers and adults.

names: Journal d'un curé de campagne, novel by Georges Bernanos (1936)

suitability.note: An implied affair, a girl's threat of suicide, a sudden death and a slow death from cancer. Nothing is shown, but the film is long, silent in manner and austere, and the Legion of Decency rated it A-II; it rewards serious teenagers more than children.

doctrine: The priest's last words, 'All is grace', are those of St Thérèse of Lisieux in her last conversations; Bernanos borrowed them knowingly. The countess scene turns on despair, which the theologians count among the sins against the Holy Ghost because it refuses God's mercy, and on resignation to His will as its remedy. The curé's own state is the dryness the spiritual writers describe, after St John of the Cross, as a purifying night in which the soul feels abandoned while it is being drawn closer. His priesthood does not depend on his feelings: the Council of Trent (Session XXIII) teaches that ordination imprints an indelible character, and Trent (Session VII) that the sacraments act by the rite performed, not by the minister's holiness. Final perseverance, which he receives without a priest at hand, is a special gift of God (Trent, Session VI, canon 22).
production: Georges Bernanos published the novel in 1936, and it won the Grand Prix du roman of the Académie française. Jean Aurenche and Pierre Bost wrote an earlier adaptation that Bernanos rejected. Bresson wrote his own screenplay after Bernanos died in 1948, cutting heavily but inventing almost nothing. He cast mostly non-professionals, whom he called 'models', with Claude Laydu, in his first film, as the curé, and had them repeat takes until their movements became automatic. It was his first use of a voice-over drawn from a diary. Léonce-Henri Burel photographed it in northern France. Released on 7 February 1951, it was a financial success in France. At Venice it won the prize for photography, the International Award and the OCIC Catholic award, and it also took the Prix Louis-Delluc. André Bazin called it a masterpiece. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II on its American release. Tarkovsky called it his favourite film, and it is regularly named in Sight and Sound polls.

title: I Confess
decision: PUBLISH: America's Catholic Movie Club essay, TCM and the AFI Catalog establish the seal of confession as the film's governing moral fact; the priest keeps it at the risk of his life. Mature material (murder, blackmail, a past romance) is disclosed.
summary: Hitchcock's most Catholic film: a Quebec priest hears a murderer's confession and then, bound by the seal, cannot clear himself when suspicion falls on him.
synopsis: In Quebec City, Otto Keller, a German refugee who works at the parish, confesses to Father Michael Logan that he has killed a lawyer named Villette during a robbery, wearing a cassock as a disguise. Witnesses saw a priest leaving the house. Inspector Larrue learns that Villette had been blackmailing Ruth Grandfort, a married woman who had loved Logan before his ordination, and Logan becomes the chief suspect. He will not say what he knows. Keller, increasingly afraid, plants evidence against him. Logan is tried, acquitted for want of proof and jeered by a hostile crowd outside the courthouse, before the truth comes out in a confrontation at the Château Frontenac.
inclusion: Hitchcock, raised a Catholic and taught by Jesuits, built a thriller around a rule most of his audience did not understand, and the film's power comes from treating that rule as absolute. Montgomery Clift plays Logan almost entirely through silence and posture. Robert Burks's location photography makes Quebec's steep streets and churches part of the drama. The flaws are real: Hitchcock himself thought it heavy-handed and humourless, and the Ruth flashbacks are stiff. But few Hollywood films show a priest paying so high a price for keeping the seal, and none does it with more conviction.
themes: The seal of confession is the hinge of the plot. Logan may not reveal what Keller told him, even to save himself from the gallows, and he never considers doing so. Hitchcock blamed the film's weak box office on audiences who did not grasp why a priest would stay silent. John Dougherty, writing in America, calls it a uniquely Catholic moral conundrum. The film also draws the contrast between the penitent's duty and the priest's: Keller confesses but does not make amends, and his fear drives him to frame the man bound to protect his secret.
liberties: This is fiction, not a reconstructed case. The investigation and trial are simplified for suspense. The play's darker ending, in which the innocent priest dies, was replaced at the studio's insistence, and the play's illegitimate child was cut.
advisories:
A murder, blackmail and a police shooting.

Flashbacks to the priest's pre-ordination romance with a woman who had married another man; restrained.

Suitable for teenagers and adults.

sources.title: I Confess (film)
sources.claims: Cast and roles

names: Nos deux consciences, play by Paul Anthelme (1902)

suitability.note: A murder, blackmail and a police shooting, with a restrained flashback to the priest's romance before ordination. Nothing is graphic, but the plot turns on adult guilt and suspicion and will mean little to younger children.

doctrine: The seal of confession binds the priest absolutely. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215, canon 21) ordered that the priest must not betray the sinner 'by word or sign or by any manner whatever', on pain of deposition and perpetual penance in a monastery. The canon makes no exception. The 1917 Code (canon 889) restates that the seal is inviolable: the confessor must not betray the sinner in the slightest, by word, sign or any other way, for any reason. Logan's silence before the police and the court is therefore not heroism of his own choosing but plain obedience to the law of the sacrament.
production: Paul Anthelme's play Nos deux consciences was published in 1902. His nephew inherited the rights in 1947 and sold them to the writer and agent Louis Verneuil, who passed them to Hitchcock. In 1951 Hitchcock developed it alongside another property, The Bramble Bush, and chose it. Jack Warner rejected the original ending, in which the priest is hanged before his innocence is proved, and the pre-ordination child was cut, for fear of offending Catholics. Anne Baxter replaced the Swedish actress Anita Björk. The film was shot from 21 August to 22 October 1952, almost entirely on location in Quebec City, including the Château Frontenac, the Lévis ferry and the church of Saint-Zéphirin-de-Stadacona, with Father Paul LaCouline as technical adviser. Montgomery Clift spent a week at a Quebec monastery to prepare. It premiered in Quebec City on 12 February 1953. Contemporary reviews found it slow, and Hitchcock later called it heavy-handed and said non-Catholics could not accept the priest's silence. America's Catholic Movie Club has since treated it as Catholic noir.

title: Angels of Sin
decision: PUBLISH: Doug Cummings's detailed essay and the BFI record establish a drama of zeal, pride, humility and repentance inside a Dominican congregation that receives women from prison; the ending joins the religious and the legal acceptance of guilt. Murder and emotional cruelty are disclosed.
summary: Bresson's first feature: a novice in a convent for former prisoners sets out to save a hardened young woman, and has to be saved from her own pride first.
synopsis: Anne-Marie, a well-off young woman with a fervent vocation, enters the Dominican Sisters of Bethany, a congregation that welcomes women released from prison. Accompanying the sisters to collect a released inmate, she fixes on another prisoner, Thérèse, who insists she was framed by her former lover. On release, Thérèse shoots him, then takes refuge in the convent as a novice. Anne-Marie's possessive zeal to convert her irritates the community and leads to her own humiliation and expulsion. She keeps vigil by the grave of the congregation's founder and falls gravely ill. Readmitted and dying, she is nursed by Thérèse, who is finally moved by her. As Anne-Marie dies, the police arrive, and Thérèse holds out her wrists.
inclusion: Made under the Occupation by a director just back from a German prison camp, this is a remarkable debut. The style is not yet the bare Bresson of later films. There are professional actresses, a score and Jean Giraudoux's polished dialogue. But the concentration is already there in the white habits, the closed spaces and the faces of Renée Faure and Jany Holt. Doug Cummings shows how carefully the film weighs Anne-Marie's humility against her pride, and the convent's rivalries against its charity. It is not a sentimental convent picture. The community is petty at times, and the heroine is often wrong. That honesty makes the final act of grace convincing.
themes: The film is about the purification of zeal. Anne-Marie genuinely wants to save a soul, but her charity becomes possessive and proud, and the community's discipline, including penance and obedience, exposes this. Her suffering and death become the means of Thérèse's conversion. The film insists that repentance includes accepting earthly justice: Thérèse's surrender to the police completes her change of heart rather than contradicting it. The religious community is shown with its faults, but its vocation and rule are taken seriously.
history: The Dominican Sisters of Bethany were founded in 1866 by the Dominican Jean-Joseph Lataste, who had preached in women's prisons and wanted a community in which former prisoners and women without a criminal past lived as equals. The characters of the film are fictional, but the congregation is real.
liberties: Anne-Marie, Thérèse and the crime are fictional. The congregation is real, but the film condenses its life into a few dramatic months, sharpens its internal rivalries, and gives Giraudoux's literary dialogue to its sisters. It is not a documentary of Bethany houses.
advisories:
A deliberate killing (shown in preparation, act brief).

Humiliation, emotional cruelty, illness and death.

Mature teenagers and adults.

sources.title: Blessed Jean-Joseph Lataste (1832-1866)
sources.claims: Lataste founded the House of Bethany on 14 August 1866 for women who had been in prison

suitability.note: A woman shoots her former lover, and the novices suffer humiliation, illness and death. There is no sex or gore, but the story is austere, adult in its psychology and in French; it will mean little to younger children.

doctrine: The Dominican Sisters of Bethany (the Congregation of Bethany) were founded in 1866 by Fr Jean-Joseph Lataste, O.P., to receive women released from prison alongside women of no criminal past. They live under the Dominican rule with choir, silence and penance. The film's drama depends on the traditional teaching that zeal for souls must be founded on humility. Anne-Marie's expulsion for pride is the community's discipline in action, and her vigil at the founder's grave and her death are offered as expiation for another. That one soul may offer sufferings for another rests on the communion of saints and on the teaching that works of satisfaction have their value only in union with Christ (Council of Trent, Session XIV, chapters 8 and 9). Thérèse's surrender to the police reflects the teaching that repentance does not cancel the temporal punishment due to a crime.
production: The Dominican priest Raymond-Léopold Bruckberger proposed a film about the Sisters of Bethany and worked on the script with Bresson and Jean Giraudoux. Roger Richebé is credited as producer. Bresson, then known only as a stills photographer and an assistant, made his first feature during the German occupation of France with professional actors, unlike his later work. Working titles included Bethany and The Exchange, the latter Bresson's preferred title. Giraudoux's name stood above Bresson's on the posters. It was released in France on 23 June 1943 and runs about 80 minutes. It is usually seen as his most conventional film, though critics find in it the ellipses, close-ups of hands and prison setting of his later work.

title: I Was a Parish Priest
decision: PUBLISH: the Italian Catholic Cinematografo record gives a full narrative and a 1955 Segnalazioni cinematografiche notice; together they establish a priest who sides with exploited miners and is then sent back to them by his bishop. The 2019 diocesan capsule is retained only for production context; its synopsis echoes the DVD blurb and is not independent criticism.
summary: Rafael Gil's prize-winning drama of a young priest who takes the miners' side in a bitter strike and pays for it with his superiors and his own body.
synopsis: In 1930, Father Andrés Mendoza, just out of the seminary, is sent to Aldemoz, a poor mining village full of resentment. The mine owner, Don César, tries to win him over, while the miners, led by the embittered Martín, distrust him. When a worker is unjustly dismissed, the men strike and occupy the mine. Andrés tries to mediate, fails, and then openly backs the strikers. Don César has to give way but complains to the bishop. Later, the owner's son and Martín's small daughter wander into an abandoned, unstable gallery and have to be rescued. Then a cave-in traps several men, among them Martín, Don César and the priest, until their comrades dig them out. Martín will not reconcile with Don César even underground, but does so at his injured daughter's bedside. The bishop summons Andrés and lets him return to his miners.
inclusion: This is one of the more interesting Spanish religious films of the 1950s because it takes sides. Rafael Gil and the writers Vicente Escrivá and Ramón D. Faraldo give the young priest a real fight, on the side of the workers, against the man who owns the mine. Claude Laydu, two years after Diary of a Country Priest, plays another young curé, dubbed into Spanish. Francisco Rabal won best-actor prizes as Martín. The 1955 Italian Catholic notice found the opening slow and somewhat naive but called the mine sequence intense and convincing and praised the photography. It won the top prize at the first San Sebastián festival and was also shown at Venice.
themes: The film puts the Church's social teaching into the mouth of a parish priest. Andrés defends a just wage and fair treatment, which he sees as part of caring for souls, and he refuses to be the owner's chaplain. The script also checks him. His siding with the strike costs him the trust of his superiors, and the decisive reconciliation comes through suffering and charity in the mine rather than through victory. The bishop's decision to send him back makes the point that the priest's place is with his poor parishioners, under obedience. The approach fits Rerum novarum and Quadragesimo anno rather than any revolutionary programme.
history: Released on 30 September 1953, the film was declared "of national interest" by the Franco regime's film authorities, which brought official support. The Colegio de Médicos reportedly objected to its portrayal of a doctor and sought to have it banned. It won the Gran Premio at the first San Sebastián International Film Festival in 1953. Music is by Joaquín Rodrigo.
liberties: Aldemoz and its strike are fictional. The film should not be taken as a portrait of Spanish labour relations in 1930. The concentration of rescue and reconciliation into a few days is dramatic shorthand.
advisories:
Mining accidents, trapped men and children in danger; a child is injured.

Class hostility and threats.

Best for older children with an adult, teenagers and adults.

sources.title: Rerum novarum
sources.claims: Just wage and the victim of force in necessity (nn. 43-45); workers' associations a natural right (nn. 49-58); duties of employers and workers (n. 20)

sources.title: Quadragesimo anno
sources.claims: Family wage and the three considerations (nn. 71-74); condemnation of class struggle (n. 112); Catholic workers' associations (nn. 31-36)

suitability.note: A cave-in traps men underground and two children stray into a collapsing gallery, one of them hurt. The strike, the class hatred and the long scenes of argument suit teenagers better than small children.

doctrine: Leo XIII's Rerum novarum (15 May 1891) taught that a wage must be enough to support a thrifty worker, that necessity does not make a harsh bargain just, and that workers have a natural right to form associations; it urges Christian workers to form their own where others are hostile. Pius XI's Quadragesimo anno (15 May 1931) added that a just wage must keep the worker and his family, and also weighs the state of the business and the common good. Both condemn class hatred and treat the Church as the reconciler of employer and worker, which is the part Andrés plays at the bedside.
production: Rafael Gil's film was written by Vicente Escrivá and Ramón D. Faraldo and produced by Manuel J. Goyanes for Aspa Producciones, with CIFESA as distributor. It is set in the early 1930s, shot in black and white, and runs 96 minutes. The French actor Claude Laydu, who had played the priest in Bresson's Diary of a Country Priest two years earlier, took the lead; Joaquín Rodrigo wrote the music. It was released in Spain on 30 September 1953. It won the Golden Shell at the first San Sebastián festival in 1953 and the Bronze Lion at Venice. Rabal won a Fotogramas de Plata for his part. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico's review, quoted in the record, found the opening slow but the mine sequence strong.

title: Balarrasa
decision: PUBLISH: Independent treatment is now substantial: DeCine21's review, Rubén Higueras Flores's close textual analysis (ZER, 2017), Matt Losada's article (Romance Notes, 2011) and Fernán Gómez's own recollection (via Joan Ripollès, Centro Virtual Cervantes). Higueras finds undercurrents linking religion with coercion and renunciation, but concludes they do not overturn the plain reading: a sinner's conversion, a priestly vocation and the restoration of a family to the faith. That reading is sound, and the adult material serves it. Year 1951 (Cannes competition 1951; scholars date the production 1950).
summary: Nieves Conde's postwar melodrama about a reckless Legion officer whose comrade dies in his place, and who becomes a priest and sets out to save his own family.
synopsis: A Spanish missionary is lost in an Alaskan blizzard, and as he faces death he remembers his life. During the Civil War, Lieutenant Javier Mendoza, known as Balarrasa, is a hard-drinking Legion officer. He gambles away his guard duty to a comrade, Joaquín, who is shot on the watch that should have been Javier's. Shaken, he leaves the army for the seminary in Salamanca. Back home as a seminarian, he finds his family in moral ruin: his widowed father gambles, his brother Fernando trades in black-market currency, his sister Lina is the mistress of the crook their father owes money to, and his youngest sister Mayte drifts between suitors. Javier sets about putting them right. Lina dies in a car crash while fleeing with her lover, and the shock brings the family back to the faith. Javier is ordained and leaves for the missions.
inclusion: Balarrasa was one of the most successful Spanish religious films of its time. It was chosen for the Cannes competition in 1951, and it made Fernando Fernán Gómez a leading man; he and Nieves Conde won the Spanish film writers' medals for actor and director. Vicente Escrivá's script is a moral fable, but Nieves Conde gives it a hard edge. The family scenes have the shadows and night-time look of film noir, and the picture of a prosperous postwar family rotting from within anticipates his social drama Surcos. DeCine21 praises the realism, the humour that leavens the drama and Fernán Gómez's performance, and notes that priests advised the production. Fernán Gómez himself later found the family's sins mild stand-ins for the real problems of the time.
themes: This is a vocation story built on guilt and reparation. Javier reads his comrade's death as a debt: the life left to him is not his own, so he gives it to God. The film shows seminary study, Latin and Thomist philosophy, ordination with the kissing of the new priest's hands, and the missions. At home his work is the cure of souls: grace at table, a Gospel warning about empty hands, steady pressure on each sinner. Lina's death, with her empty hands raised and Javier, not yet a priest, unable to absolve her, is a stark lesson about dying unprepared. Higueras Flores argues that the film quietly ties religion to renunciation and coercion, but he concludes that this does not overturn its plain religious meaning.
history: Balarrasa is fiction. Its writer, Vicente Escrivá, co-founded the production company Aspa Films with the director Rafael Gil in 1950 and became a leading maker of Catholic films in 1950s Spain. The story of a Legion officer who exchanges his uniform for a cassock reflects the early Franco years, when the regime increasingly presented itself through the Church rather than the army; Matt Losada and Higueras Flores both read the film in that light.
advisories:
A soldier is shot dead; a fatal car crash; a young woman's deathbed.

An officers' drinking party in a brothel (not explicit); an illicit affair, gambling and black-market dealing.

Javier urges a shy suitor to punch a rival, a scene played for comedy.

DeCine21 recommends it for adults; Spanish television rates it for all audiences.

suitability.note: A mistress, an officers' party in a brothel, gambling and a fatal car crash are all in the story, though nothing is shown. It is in Spanish with subtitles and quite talky, so it suits teenagers better than young children.

doctrine: The story turns on a vocation that follows a bad conscience. The Council of Trent taught that a priest is called by God and tested in a seminary (Session 23, chapter 18, which founded the diocesan seminaries), and the film's Salamanca seminary reflects this. Javier's guilt over a comrade's death and his return to the Faith show the sacrament of Penance: contrition, confession and satisfaction. His family's rescue by a death, and the shock that follows, recall that grace can work through suffering, though the Church does not teach that a particular misfortune is sent as a punishment for a particular sin. Pius XI's Rerum Ecclesiae (28 February 1926) urged the whole Church to support foreign missions.
production: José Antonio Nieves Conde directed from a script by Vicente Escrivá, with Fernando Fernán Gómez in the lead. It was shot in Madrid (Centro, Retiro, Salamanca and Ciudad Lineal districts) and in Salamanca province. The film was shown at the 1951 Cannes Film Festival. At the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos medals for 1951, Nieves Conde won Best Director and Fernán Gómez Best Actor.

title: The Fugitive
decision: PUBLISH: AFI and TCM establish the film and its changes to Greene; Greydanus (A-, +3) and the 1948 Venice International Award (reported as the first OCIC prize) support a reverent treatment of a hunted priest who baptises, seeks to say Mass and dies rather than apostatise. The reservation about the altered protagonist dissolves: the changes remove the novel's sacrilegious and sexual sins rather than add doctrinal error, at the cost of Greene's complexity. Legion of Decency rating not found; verify.
summary: John Ford's stark, stylised version of Greene's The Power and the Glory: Henry Fonda's hunted priest, the last in a state where religion is outlawed, walks back towards martyrdom.
synopsis: In an unnamed Latin American state the government has outlawed religion and hunts its priests. One nameless priest remains. He returns to his abandoned village church, where María Dolores, an unmarried mother whose child was fathered by the police lieutenant, finds him, and he baptises the village children in secret. The lieutenant takes hostages to force him into the open. The priest flees towards the port, shadowed by an informer and crossing paths with an American wanted for murder. Unable to say Mass without wine, he is arrested, unrecognised, with a bottle of brandy. Safe over the border, he goes back when a beggar brings a note, supposedly from the dying American, asking for confession. Captured, he refuses to renounce his faith and is shot. At the end another priest comes to the church to pray with the faithful.
inclusion: This is the most openly religious film John Ford made, and Steven Greydanus notes that Ford himself thought it his best. Gabriel Figueroa's black-and-white photography, shot on location in Taxco, Cholula and Cuernavaca, is its great strength. Henry Fonda plays the priest as a frightened man whose courage comes late, with Pedro Armendáriz as the lieutenant and J. Carrol Naish as the informer. Greydanus grades it A- and says that, though it softens Greene, it still packs spiritual punch; the debate between priest and lieutenant remains a high point. Its faults are real: Dennis Schwartz found it turgid and its religious symbols simplistic, and Bret Wood suggests the images are so striking that they distract from the priest's plight. It shared the International Award at Venice in 1948. As a parable of the persecuted Church and of a people's need for priests, it is direct rather than subtle.
themes: The film's subject is the sacramental priesthood under persecution. The priest baptises children who have had no priest for years. The plot turns on the Mass: without altar wine he cannot celebrate, and his search for it leads to his arrest. An informer betrays him, and he goes back across the border because a dying man may need a priest. Offered his life for apostasy, he refuses. His flaw in the film is pride in his office and fear, not the novel's drunkenness and fathered child. That makes him more conventionally edifying: Greydanus calls the result a softened, conventionalised Greene, and Schwartz thinks it loses the novel's moral urgency. The closing image of another priest arriving to pray states plainly that the Church outlasts its persecutors.
history: Mexico's 1917 constitution restricted the Church, and in 1926 President Calles enforced it. The bishops suspended public worship at the end of July 1926, foreign priests were expelled, and several states limited the number of priests to a handful or none. In Tabasco, under Governor Tomás Garrido Canabal, churches were closed and priests driven out or forced to marry. The Cristero rising (1926–29) ended in a settlement, but persecution flared again in the 1930s. Graham Greene travelled in Mexico in 1938, when churches in several states were still closed and priests were in hiding, and drew on that for his novel.
liberties: Greene's 'whisky priest' is an alcoholic who has fathered a child with María; the film makes the lieutenant the father and gives the priest only pride and fear. Greene's lieutenant is an idealist who wants to help the poor; Ford's is a harder tyrant. The setting is left unnamed rather than Mexico, and a spoken prologue presents the story as true.
advisories:
Hostages are taken and threatened; a gunfight in a cornfield; the priest is executed (not shown graphically).

An unmarried mother and the officer who fathered her child; she dances in a cantina to distract the police.

Drinking and a jail sequence.

Steady tension and menace; best for teenagers and adults.

names: The Power and the Glory, novel by Graham Greene (1940)

suitability.note: Hostages are threatened, there is a gunfight and the priest is shot off screen; an unmarried mother and a cantina dance are part of the plot. Nothing is graphic, and the Legion of Decency classified the film A-I, but the steady menace suits older children.

doctrine: Two points of sacramental law drive the plot. The Mass requires wine of the grape: the 1917 Code (canon 815) and the long tradition behind it make true wine necessary matter, so brandy will not serve and the priest must hunt for it. And the duty of a priest to the dying is grave: where a soul may be lost without absolution, the pastor is bound to go even at risk to his life, which is why the priest crosses back over the border. Pius XI protested against the Mexican persecution in Iniquis afflictisque (18 November 1926), listing the limits placed on the number of priests, the expulsion of foreign clergy and the closing of seminaries and convents, and returned to it in Acerba animi (1932) and Firmissimam constantiam (1937). Baptism of children, shown in the village, is necessary for salvation (Trent, Session VII).
production: Ford and Merian C. Cooper made it as the first of three Argosy Pictures films for RKO, which shared costs and profits while Argosy kept creative control. Dudley Nichols wrote the screenplay, but Ford departed from much of it on location. The film was shot in Taxco, Cholula and Cuernavaca and at Churubusco Studios in Mexico City, with a crew that was Mexican apart from two assistant directors and an editor. Emilio Fernández, the associate producer, brought in Dolores del Río, Pedro Armendáriz and the cameraman Gabriel Figueroa. It cost about $1.5 million, opened on 3 November 1947 and lost money. At Venice in 1948 it won the OCIC (Catholic film office) prize. Ford defended it; Bret Wood has called it perhaps his last great 'art film'. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: Going My Way
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog gives a full synopsis and production record; John Clark (NCRegister), Anthony Esolen and Joe Wilson give detailed Catholic readings of its portrait of parish priesthood. The Criteria critique and David E. White's scholarly chapter (the film nearly omits the supernatural and sacramental) are real limits and are stated in the record, but they describe an emphasis, not a teaching that contradicts the faith.
summary: Bing Crosby's easygoing young curate quietly takes over a debt-ridden New York parish from its stubborn old pastor, played to perfection by Barry Fitzgerald.
synopsis: St Dominic's, a poor New York parish, is about to lose its church to the mortgage holder. The bishop sends Father Chuck O'Malley, a former songwriter who wears a sweatshirt and plays golf, ostensibly as curate to the elderly Father Fitzgibbon, in fact to take charge without humiliating him. O'Malley turns a gang of street boys into a choir, helps a runaway girl, marries her to the landlord's son, and sells a song to pay the debt. Fitzgibbon learns the truth and runs away into the rain, then comes round. When the church burns, the parish starts again, and O'Malley moves on to the next troubled parish.
inclusion: McCarey made a comedy about two priests, and the comedy is real. Barry Fitzgerald's Fitzgibbon, crotchety, vain, devoted and finally touching, is one of the great character performances of the period, and his scenes with Crosby have an easy rhythm that holds the film together. Crosby underplays O'Malley's tact: he takes over without ever saying so. The film is long and loosely plotted, the opera interlude with Risë Stevens stops it dead, and the delinquents reform suspiciously fast. But its picture of a parish as a place where a priest knows the landlady, the policeman and the boys stealing turkeys has warmth and observation. The final scene, with Fitzgibbon's mother, is famous for good reason.
themes: The film's subject is the parish priest as a father to his people: patience with an older priest, care for the poor and the young, refusal to humiliate anyone. Esolen calls its governing virtue tact, a form of charity. John Clark draws out its respect for ordinary priestly service and a line affirming the indissolubility of a valid marriage. What it hardly shows is the supernatural centre of the priesthood. The scholar David E. White notes that it leaves out nearly all supernatural, sacramental and theological reference, and Thomas Mirus and James Majewski argue that O'Malley is admired for singing and charm rather than anything spiritual. That criticism is fair. Watch it as a portrait of priestly kindness, not of the priest at the altar.
liberties: Fiction; no historical persons. The parish is idealised and the plot runs on coincidence and a hit song.
advisories:
No violence beyond a church fire. A runaway girl lives in an apartment paid for by a young man before they marry; nothing is shown.

Suitable for all ages, though younger children may find it slow.

The priesthood is presented almost entirely through pastoral kindness; sacramental life is largely absent.
