sources.title: Going My Way
sources.claims: Cast and roles; credits (screenplay Butler and Cavett, story McCarey, music Dolan, cinematography Lindon); locations incl. St Monica's, Santa Monica; 3 May 1944 premiere; highest grossing film of 1944; seven Oscars; presentation of a copy to Pius XII

suitability.note: Nothing frightening beyond a church fire, and no coarse language. It runs over two hours and is gentle and episodic, so younger children may drift; the boys' choir and Fitzgerald's comedy keep many of them with it.

doctrine: The film shows the pastor's office as the Council of Trent described it: to know his flock, preach, teach children and relieve the poor (Session 24 and Session 5, decrees on reform). Pius XI's encyclical Ad Catholici Sacerdotii (1935) states the weightier doctrine the film leaves aside: the priest is another Christ, ordained to offer the Mass and forgive sins, and is bound to holiness of life. The O'Malley-Fitzgibbon dialogue on a marriage that lasts "till death" reflects Christ's teaching (Matthew 19:6), which Pius XI restated in Casti Connubii (1930): a valid, consummated Christian marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power. A priest's easy sociability is no fault, but the 1917 Code (canon 124 ff.) expects clerics to live in a manner befitting their state.
production: Leo McCarey, who had a Catholic upbringing, wrote the story, produced and directed it for Paramount. He had Bing Crosby play a young curate and Barry Fitzgerald an old pastor, and Frank Butler and Frank Cavett wrote the screenplay. Interiors were made at Paramount; St Monica's Church in Santa Monica stood in for St Dominic's, and the Robert Mitchell Boychoir sang. Risë Stevens, then at the Metropolitan Opera, appears in the opera scene. The film opened in New York on 3 May 1944 and was the highest-grossing film of 1944. It won seven Academy Awards, including Best Picture, Director, Actor (Crosby) and Supporting Actor (Fitzgerald), and Fitzgerald was nominated for the same role as lead and supporting actor. Crosby and McCarey later presented a print to Pope Pius XII at the Vatican. Crosby played O'Malley again in The Bells of St Mary's (1945).

title: The Bells of St. Mary's
decision: PUBLISH: AFI Catalog record plus Stephen B. Earley's 1945 America review, which judged it 'tremendously spiritual' and among the best screen portraits of a sister's life, and Joe Wilson's detailed reading. The 'personable priest' critique (Criteria; White) applies more weakly here than to Going My Way because the sisters' vocation and prayer are central; it is noted in the record.
summary: Father O'Malley meets his match in Ingrid Bergman's Sister Benedict as a parish school fights to survive, in McCarey's warmer, more prayerful sequel to Going My Way.
synopsis: Father O'Malley becomes pastor of St Mary's, whose sisters run a crumbling parish school. The superior, Sister Mary Benedict, disagrees with him about almost everything, from school holidays to whether a struggling girl should pass her exams. She prays that the businessman Horace Bogardus will give the school the new building he is putting up next door; Bogardus wants the school site for a car park. O'Malley helps a deserted mother and her daughter Patsy, and nudges Bogardus towards charity. Bogardus gives the building. Then Sister Benedict is found to have early tuberculosis, and the doctor wants her transferred without being told why. She believes O'Malley has had her removed.
inclusion: This is the better of McCarey's two priest pictures, and the reason is Ingrid Bergman. Her Sister Benedict is strict, competitive, funny and devout, and she plays the part without condescension: Earley, writing in America in 1945, said sisters at an advance screening recognised themselves in her. The rivalry with Crosby's O'Malley is gentle comedy between two people who respect each other. Some scenes are pure McCarey: the infants' Nativity play, the nun teaching a bullied boy to box. It is sentimental and long, and the Bogardus subplot is contrived. But the last scene, in which Sister Benedict goes to the chapel to pray for guidance before leaving, and O'Malley finally tells her the truth, is beautifully done.
themes: The film takes religious life seriously. Sister Benedict's vocation is the teaching of children, and she holds to standards because she believes they serve the child. She prays for the school and the prayer is answered, though through a cranky businessman rather than a wonder. Her final trial is obedience: she accepts a transfer she does not understand and takes it to prayer before she knows the reason. O'Malley is still more pastoral counsellor than sacramental minister, and critics such as Thomas Mirus find the faith shallow; but here the sisters' prayer and obedience give it more spiritual weight than Going My Way.
liberties: Fiction. McCarey based Sister Benedict on his aunt, a sister of the Immaculate Heart community in Hollywood; Bergman's habit is a composite of two orders.
advisories:
A deserted mother says she has relied on 'the generosity of men', and her daughter mistakes her father for one of her mother's clients; this is handled discreetly.

A nun is diagnosed with tuberculosis. A schoolyard fight and a boxing lesson.

Suitable for all ages.

suitability.note: There is a schoolyard fight, a nun's illness and a discreet subplot about a deserted mother, none of it shown in a way that troubles young children. Children may not follow the adult story, but the school scenes and the sisters will hold them.

doctrine: The film's setting is the American parish school, which the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore (1884) required every parish to build and maintain, and which teaching sisters largely staffed. Pius XI's encyclical Divini Illius Magistri (31 December 1929) taught that the school must be Catholic in its teachers, syllabus and textbooks, with religion as the foundation and crown of all training, and that Catholic children may not attend neutral or non-Catholic schools except as tolerated by the Ordinary (canon 1374 of the 1917 Code). Sister Benedict's acceptance of her transfer is the vow of obedience in practice: a religious obeys a lawful superior without being told the reason. The pastor's authority over the parish school, and his deference to the sisters' rule within their community, are shown accurately for the period.
production: Leo McCarey wrote the story and produced the film for his own Rainbow Productions, with RKO distributing. Bing Crosby returned as Father O'Malley from Going My Way (1944), and Crosby's nomination made him the first actor nominated twice for the same role. Dudley Nichols wrote the screenplay. It opened in New York on 6 December 1945 and was the highest-grossing US film of 1945, earning a profit of about $3.7 million, the most profitable in RKO's history. It received eight Academy Award nominations, including Best Picture, Actor, Actress and Director, and won for Sound Recording. The New York Times found it too close to Going My Way and lacking its charm, while Variety praised its simple scenes that tug at the heart. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: Boys Town
decision: GREY: Identity and content are settled by AFI, the Legion of Decency's A-I (the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment), the 1938 Photoplay Studies guide and Simcha Fisher's review. The transcript shows two points the Founder should weigh: the film presents as an ideal a community where each boy worships as he pleases and a boy with no religion can stay that way, and it builds its message on the motto that there is no bad boy. It is not REJECT, because a priest acting under obedience is the centre and the lines describe the real institution's practice. It would be PUBLISH if the Founder judges this a charity's policy rather than indifferentism.
summary: Spencer Tracy won an Oscar as Fr Edward Flanagan, the Omaha priest whose town for homeless boys rests on his belief that there is no bad boy.
synopsis: Father Edward Flanagan visits a condemned man who blames the institutions that failed him as a boy, and resolves to reach boys before they go wrong. With his bishop's permission and a loan from a pawnbroker friend, he opens a home in Omaha, then builds a self-governing town for boys outside the city, kept afloat by appeals and debts. Whitey Marsh, a cocky young tough sent by his gangster brother Joe, sneers at the place, runs a cynical campaign for mayor and loses. He walks out, and the little boy Pee Wee, following him, is hit by a car. Whitey then stumbles into Joe's bank robbery and is wounded, and Flanagan shields him from the sheriff. In the end Whitey leads the boys to the gang's hideout, the robbers are captured, the publicity rescues Boys Town, and Whitey is elected mayor.
inclusion: Tracy's performance is the reason the film lasts: brisk, humorous and quietly obstinate. It won him his second Oscar in a row. Mickey Rooney, as Whitey, is energetic and often hammy, and Simcha Fisher, reviewing it recently, finds that the second half slides into melodrama. Norman Taurog shot parts of it at the real Boys Town with Flanagan as technical adviser, and it was one of the biggest hits of 1938. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I. It remains the best-known film portrait of an American priest at work among the poor. The opening, in which Flanagan sits with a man about to be executed, sets a pastoral tone the rest of the film mostly keeps.
themes: Flanagan is shown as a priest acting under obedience. He asks his bishop's permission, gives up the offer of a parish, and says he has nothing for the fight but faith. Prayer appears at meals and in Whitey's plea, in a church, for Pee Wee's life. Two things need weighing. The film's motto, that there is no such thing as a bad boy, leans towards blaming circumstance for sin, though Flanagan's insistence on discipline and responsibility qualifies it. And the boys explain that at Boys Town everyone worships as he pleases and a boy who is nothing can stay nothing. The film presents this as part of the ideal, and its dedication speaks of boys of every creed.
history: Edward Joseph Flanagan (1886–1948), an Irish-born priest of the Omaha diocese, opened a home for boys in Omaha in 1917 and later moved it to farmland west of the city, where it became the incorporated village of Boys Town. He took in boys of any race or religion. The 1938 study guide notes that the home had cared for over 4,400 boys by then. Flanagan is a Servant of God; his cause for canonisation has been opened.
liberties: Whitey, his brother Joe, the bank robbery and the condemned man Dan Farrow are invented. The film compresses twenty years into a short span. AFI records that its ending, which suggested the town's money troubles were over, was later blamed for a drop in donations, one reason MGM made a sequel.
advisories:
A condemned man's last hour; a bank robbery and shooting; a small boy is hit by a car.

A boy is pranked in blackface, a period joke.

Suitable for most ages.

The film presents Boys Town's open policy on religion, including for boys with none, as an ideal.

grey.question: Boys Town is a warm portrait of a real priest, and the Legion of Decency rated it A-I in 1938. Two things deserve weighing. It presents as an ideal a community where each boy worships as he pleases and a boy with no religion can stay that way, and its famous motto, that there is no bad boy, leans towards treating sin as the product of circumstance. Readers can judge whether these describe a charity's practical policy or a quiet religious indifferentism.

sources.title: The Syllabus of Errors (1864)
sources.claims: Condemned propositions 15 and 16 on religious indifferentism

names: Original story by Dore Schary and Eleanore Griffin

suitability.note: The opening has a condemned man's last hour, and later there is a bank robbery with a shooting and a small boy hit by a car, which may upset young children. Otherwise it is a clean family picture about a priest who will not give up on boys others have written off.

doctrine: Flanagan's work is the corporal and spiritual works of mercy carried out by a parish priest under his bishop: feeding and sheltering the homeless, instructing the ignorant, admonishing the sinner. The Baltimore Catechism lists both sets of works, and the film shows them in practice. The film's praise of a home where each boy worships as he pleases needs to be set beside the Church's teaching against religious indifferentism. Pius IX's Syllabus of Errors (1864) condemned the propositions that every man is free to profess whatever religion his reason judges true, and that salvation can be found in the observance of any religion. Flanagan admitted boys of every creed out of charity; that is a different thing from holding that creed does not matter, and the film blurs the two.
production: MGM made Boys Town from an original story by Dore Schary and Eleanore Griffin, scripted by John Meehan and Schary. Father Flanagan was credited as technical adviser, and the film opens with a dedication to him and his work. Filming ran from 6 June to 8 August 1938, partly on location at the real Boys Town near Omaha, Nebraska. Edward Norris replaced Donald Barry as Joe Marsh several weeks into the shoot. It opened in September 1938 and was one of the highest-grossing pictures of the year. Spencer Tracy won the Academy Award for Best Actor and dedicated it to Flanagan; Schary and Griffin won for Original Story, and the film was nominated for Best Picture and Best Director. Tracy kept his statuette, and the Academy changed the inscription on the one Boys Town received to name Father Flanagan. MGM followed it with Men of Boys Town (1941).

title: Come to the Stable
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review, TCM and the AFI Catalog establish a gentle comedy in which two French nuns' trust in providence and works of mercy drive the plot, with a sympathetic bishop. The sentimentality noted by Greydanus is disclosed.
summary: Two French nuns arrive in a Connecticut village determined to build a children's hospital with no money, in a gentle Fox comedy loosely based on the founding of Regina Laudis.
synopsis: Sister Margaret and Sister Scholastica arrive in Bethlehem, New England, on a snowy night, with a promise to keep: a children's hospital. They take shelter with Amelia Potts, an eccentric painter of religious pictures. They set their hearts on a hilltop owned by a gambler, Luigi Rossi, and on land next to a songwriter, Robert Mason, who wants peace and quiet. With prayer, persistence and some cheerful bending of the rules, they work on the bishop, the gambler and their reluctant neighbour. Not every scheme works, and the bishop worries about their judgment, but the hospital begins to take shape.
inclusion: Henry Koster's film is a well-made studio comedy with real affection for religious life. Loretta Young and Celeste Holm play the nuns with conviction rather than winks, and Elsa Lanchester is a delight as their painter friend. All three were Oscar-nominated, and the film received seven nominations in total. Steven Greydanus calls it sweet and uplifting, and also more conventional and sentimental than Lilies of the Field. The sisters sometimes get their miracle and sometimes look credulous and silly. That is about right. It is a warm Christmas-season film for the whole family rather than a serious study of a vocation.
themes: The sisters' faith is simple and direct. They pray for what they need and expect an answer, and the film plays this both as comedy and as sincere trust in providence. Their hospital is a concrete work of mercy. The bishop is portrayed sympathetically: he supports their mission but doubts their practical sense. Greydanus suggests the film leaves open whether God is testing their faith or teaching them prudence, and perhaps both. The Bethlehem setting and the Nativity imagery tie the story to Christmas.
history: In 1947 two French Benedictine nuns, Mother Benedict Duss and Mother Mary Aline (Trilles de Warren), came from the Abbey of Jouarre to Bethlehem, Connecticut, and began a contemplative community on a farm there, which became the Abbey of Regina Laudis. A neighbour, the painter Lauren Ford, helped them. Clare Boothe Luce, a convert, wrote a story about them. The nuns were enclosed Benedictines who prayed the Divine Office, not an active order, and they did not build a hospital.
liberties: The real foundation was a contemplative Benedictine monastery. The film turns it into an active order building a children's hospital, invents the gambler, the songwriter and other neighbours, and adds the comic set pieces. TCM notes the plot was changed partly to avoid needing the real nuns' rights.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable; suitable for children.

Some mild comic deception by the sisters.

names: Original story by Clare Boothe Luce

suitability.note: Gentle comedy with nothing to object to; the sisters bend the truth a little in good causes. Children should enjoy the nuns' schemes and the Christmas ending.

doctrine: The sisters are shown as religious who have taken the three vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, as in the 1917 Code. The Church distinguishes the active life from the contemplative: the Benedictines on whom the film is loosely based live under the Rule of St Benedict, in enclosure, with the Divine Office sung in choir, and "ora et labora" as their motto. The film's hospital project, and the gambler who is persuaded to give land, touch the corporal works of mercy and the Church's teaching that alms and sacrifice made for love of God are meritorious (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 16).  Their comic deceptions are not an example to follow: a lie is never lawful, even in a good cause.
production: Twentieth Century-Fox made the film under producer Samuel G. Engel and director Henry Koster. Clare Boothe Luce's story was turned into a screenplay by Oscar Millard and Sally Benson. The characters of Sister Margaret, Sister Scholastica and Amelia Potts were based on Mother Benedict, Mother Mary Aline and Lauren Ford, but the film made the sisters an active order with a children's hospital. It premiered at the Rivoli Theatre in New York on 27 July 1949 and grossed about $3 million. It was nominated for seven Academy Awards, including Best Actress (Loretta Young) and Supporting Actress (Celeste Holm and Elsa Lanchester), Best Story, Cinematography and Original Song, but won none. Loretta Young played the lead.

title: Heaven Knows, Mr. Allison
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency rated it A-I (1956–57), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Steven Greydanus (A−) and Dennis Schwartz (B+) describe its treatment. The earlier doubt about the novice's commitment is settled by the English subtitle track: she refuses Allison's proposal because her heart is 'given to Christ', explains that vows bind under pain of losing one's soul and can be lifted only by papal dispensation, and the film ends with her vocation intact.
summary: John Huston strands a Marine corporal and a young nun on a Japanese-held Pacific island; he falls in love with her, and she keeps her vocation.
synopsis: In 1944 Corporal Allison, a Marine cut off from his unit, drifts on a raft to a small South Pacific island. Its sole inhabitant is Sister Angela, an Irish nun not yet in final vows, stranded since the old priest she came with died. They fish, catch turtles and plan to sail for Fiji on his raft, until Japanese troops occupy the island and the pair hide in a cave. Allison raids the enemy camp for food and kills a soldier who finds him. He tells Angela he loves her and asks her not to take her vows; she answers that her heart already belongs to Christ. Later, drunk on Japanese sake, he frightens her into running out into the rain, and she falls ill. When the Americans attack, Allison disables the Japanese guns and is wounded. She walks beside his stretcher as the Marines carry him away.
inclusion: This is Huston working in the vein of The African Queen: two people, one setting, and a patient study of how they come to respect each other. Robert Mitchum gives one of his best performances as an orphaned, unschooled Marine, and Deborah Kerr, nominated for an Oscar, plays the nun with humour and backbone rather than sweetness. Oswald Morris's CinemaScope colour photography of Tobago, standing in for the Pacific, is handsome, and the raid on the Japanese camp is tense. The middle stretch is slow and the outcome predictable; Dennis Schwartz calls it lightweight but a small gem. Steven Greydanus notes that the film understands the Marine Corps better than the convent. It never cheats: the love is real, and so is her refusal.
themes: The drama is a vocation tested and kept. Sister Angela first appears praying the Hail Mary. She explains that final vows come only after years of probation, that breaking them would cost a religious her soul, and that only the Pope can grant a dispensation. When Allison proposes, she calls her profession a betrothal to Christ and shows him the ring she will exchange for a gold one at her vows. She wavers once, under the strain of the siege, wondering whether God means her to take them, and she asks him whether he is obeying God or his own wish to fight. Her prayer for him, a good man outside the Church, is simple and orthodox. The film sets her vows beside his loyalty to the Marines, which makes them look more alike than they are.
advisories:
War violence: Allison kills a Japanese soldier with a knife, and there is a battle at the end.

A drunken scene in which Allison frightens the nun.

Suitable for older children and up.

The film treats religious vows respectfully, but often compares them with a Marine's loyalty to his corps.

sources.title: Heaven Knows, Mr. Allison
sources.claims: Cast, crew, filming in Tobago from August 1956, Legion of Decency monitoring, Mahin on Frenke, budget, nominations, reviews

names: Heaven Knows, Mr. Allison, novel by Charles Shaw (1952)

suitability.note: A Marine kills a Japanese soldier with a knife and there is a battle at the end. A drunken scene frightens the nun. There is no sexual content, and older children can watch it.

doctrine: Sister Angela is a novice who has not yet made her final vows. The Church teaches that the state of consecrated virginity is higher than marriage, and the Council of Trent (Session 24, canon 10) condemns anyone who says otherwise. A novice is not bound by vows and may leave. A professed religious makes vows of poverty, chastity and obedience to God, and they are not broken by the claims of any lesser love. Angela refuses Allison's plea not to take her vows, saying her heart already belongs to Christ. The film often likens vows to a Marine's loyalty to his corps. The comparison is imperfect: vows are made to God, and a soldier's oath is made to a human institution.
production: The film comes from Charles Shaw's 1952 novel, in which the heroine is already a nun. An earlier treatment, in which a laywoman disguised herself as a nun and loved the Marine, was rejected by Church advisers, and a revised story was approved in May 1954. Twentieth Century-Fox bought the rights that year. Filming began in August 1956 in Tobago, and the National Legion of Decency monitored the shoot. Huston and John Lee Mahin wrote the script, and Mahin said that the producer Eugene Frenke pressed for more sex. The film was shot in CinemaScope and DeLuxe Color, ran 106 minutes and cost about $2.9 million. Deborah Kerr was nominated for the Academy Award for best actress, and Huston and Mahin for the screenplay. Contemporary reviews were generally favourable.

title: Lilies of the Field
decision: GREY: It is Catholic-centred: the nuns, their trust in Providence and a chapel for the Mass drive the plot. It won the OCIC (Catholic) award at Berlin in 1963 (AFI), a pre-conciliar Catholic film-office judgment, and Greydanus (+3) and Esolen establish its content. But the transcript confirms the point the earlier HOLD raised: the Baptist hero is presented at Mass as sent by 'the God of all faiths', the sisters learn and sing his spiritual, and the offer to teach him their Latin chant goes nowhere. Given the Founder's position on interreligious framing, that is a real question for the reader rather than grounds for PUBLISH. It is not REJECT: the film presents personal charity, not the post-conciliar Church or dialogue as a programme. The Legion of Decency rating was not found.
summary: Sidney Poitier won an Oscar as a Baptist handyman who builds a desert chapel for a group of refugee German nuns in Arizona.
synopsis: Homer Smith, a Black ex-serviceman drifting through Arizona, stops at a remote farm for water. It belongs to five nuns, refugees from East Germany, led by the formidable Mother Maria, who decides at once that God has sent him. She talks him into mending her roof, then into building a chapel for the local Mexican-American Catholics, who have only an outdoor Mass said by a travelling priest. Homer, a Baptist, works without pay, teaches the sisters English and takes a paid job to buy their food. He wants to build the chapel alone and clashes with Mother Maria's stubbornness; he leaves, comes back, and finally lets the townspeople help. The chapel is finished on the eve of its dedication. Homer drives off in the night as the sisters sing the spiritual he taught them.
inclusion: It is a small film, shot in two weeks around Tucson on a tiny budget, and it works through its two lead performances. Poitier is funny, proud and touchy, and he became the first Black actor to win the Oscar for best actor. Lilia Skala's Mother Maria is the richer part: an iron-willed refugee who trusts Providence completely and bargains like a peasant. Their battle of wills, fought in broken English and in duelling Bible verses, is the heart of it. Anthony Esolen stresses that it is not a sentimental film, and Steven Greydanus finds nothing objectionable in it. Jerry Goldsmith's score and the spiritual 'Amen' stay in the memory. The Mexican townspeople are thinly drawn, and the hard-drinking travelling priest is a stock joke.
themes: The Catholic side is solid. The sisters live by prayer and poverty, Mother Maria trusts God for every brick, and the whole plot exists to give a poor parish a place to celebrate Mass. The difficulty is how the film handles religion between Homer and the nuns. He skips Mass for what he calls a Baptist breakfast; the sisters learn his spiritual and sing it; Greydanus notes that Homer's suggestion that they teach him their Latin chant, the Tantum ergo, goes nowhere. At the outdoor Mass he is introduced to the congregation as sent by 'the God of all faiths'. The film treats the difference between Catholic and Protestant as a matter of temperament and breakfast.
advisories:
No violence, sexual content or bad language.

Suitable for all ages.

The film presents a warm religious exchange between a Baptist and Catholic nuns, and one line calls God 'the God of all faiths'.

grey.question: Lilies of the Field is plainly Catholic in its nuns, its Mass and its chapel, and it won a Catholic award at Berlin in 1963. The question is its religious friendship. The Baptist handyman is introduced at Mass as sent by 'the God of all faiths', the sisters learn and sing his spiritual, and the exchange never runs the other way. Readers can decide whether this is ordinary charity between neighbours or a gentle indifferentism that treats the creeds as interchangeable.

sources.title: Mortalium animos
sources.claims: One visible Church under one head; doctrinal differences cannot be set aside; unity by return of separated Christians

names: The Lilies of the Field, novel by William E. Barrett (1962)

suitability.note: No violence, sex or bad language, and the story is gentle and funny. A child may need help with the nuns' accents and with the idea that Homer, a Baptist, is not bound by their Catholic rules.

doctrine: The title comes from the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:28), on trusting Providence. The film sets a Baptist beside Catholic nuns as though their religions were two roads to one place; the Church's teaching is different. Pius XI's encyclical Mortalium animos (6 January 1928) taught that Christ founded one visible Church under one head, that doctrinal differences cannot be set aside for the sake of fellowship, and that unity comes by the return of separated Christians to it. The line at the outdoor Mass that he is sent by 'the God of all faiths' is the film's, not the Church's. The nuns' life of poverty, prayer and enclosure is traditional religious life, and a chapel for a poor parish is a proper work of charity.
production: William E. Barrett's novel appeared in 1962. James Poe adapted it, and Ralph Nelson produced and directed for Rainbow Productions, with United Artists as distributor. Filming took about fifteen days on a ranch near Tucson, Arizona, with a budget of roughly $250,000; the church doors came from the chapel in Sasabe, Arizona. Jerry Goldsmith wrote the score and Jester Hairston arranged the spiritual 'Amen' and sang Poitier's part. It was shown at Berlin in June 1963, winning the INTERFILM jury prize and the Silver Bear for Poitier, and opened in New York on 3 October 1963. Poitier won the Academy Award for Best Actor, the first Black man to win in a leading role, and Skala was nominated for Best Supporting Actress. The Catholic organisation OCIC gave it a special award,. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 2020.

title: Fighting Father Dunne
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency rated it A-I (1947–48), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Variety's review (12 May 1948) and The Exhibitor give independent contemporary accounts, and Bonnie Stepenoff's Missouri Encyclopedia entry settles the history. Its liberties (an invented condemned boy, a borrowing from Boys Town) are disclosed. The priest acts under his archbishop's authority, and the climax is the conversion of a condemned boy, so no doctrinal reservation arises.
summary: Pat O'Brien plays the St Louis priest who opened a home for homeless newsboys in 1906, in an affectionate RKO tribute that ends in a condemned cell.
synopsis: St Louis, 1905. Father Peter Dunne finds newsboys sleeping in packing cases and freezing on the streets, and resolves to house them. Archbishop Glennon gives his blessing but no money, so Dunne begs, borrows and bargains: a rented house, donated food, a pony and cart from a reluctant merchant. His boys fight rival newsboys for street corners, and a circulation manager's thugs harass them. Matt Davis, a hostile boy whose father is in prison, joins the home, quarrels with the others and leaves. Later, on the run after a break-in, he panics and shoots a policeman who wanted to help him. He is sentenced to hang. Dunne pleads with the governor and fails, but stays with Matt, who turns to God before his execution. Dunne goes back to his boys and carries on.
inclusion: It is a modest studio picture, and it borrows heavily from Boys Town, but it has a real subject and a lead who believes in it. Pat O'Brien, Hollywood's most familiar screen priest, plays Dunne as patient and practical rather than pious; Variety praised him in 1948 for making the priest warm and human. Much of the pleasure lies in the small tricks by which Dunne coaxes beds, food and transport out of the city. Charles Kemper, Una O'Connor and Arthur Shields supply the comedy. The pace is leisurely, the newsboys' feuds are routine, and the condemned-boy finale is melodrama. But the closing scenes give a priest's duty to a dying sinner its full weight, and the film keeps its sentiment in check.
themes: Dunne's charity is shown as a priest's work done under obedience. He asks the archbishop's permission, accepts that the diocese cannot pay, and keeps the home going by begging. The film's Catholicism is practical rather than theological, and for most of its length it shows little of the sacraments. Its heart is the ministry to the condemned boy at the end. Dunne fights for a reprieve, fails, and then prepares Matt to die reconciled to God. Variety's reviewer describes the boy turning to God on the eve of his hanging. The film does not pretend that love always spares a boy the consequences of his crime, which gives it more moral weight than many films of its kind.
history: Peter Joseph Dunne (1870–1939) was orphaned as a child and ordained in 1903 by Archbishop John Glennon of St Louis. In February 1906 he opened a shelter for homeless boys, and in 1907 it moved into a purpose-built home on Washington Avenue. Glennon gave him a lifelong commission to care for homeless boys, and he was made a papal chamberlain in 1927. The home ran until 2006, when it merged into Catholic Services for Children and Youth.
liberties: The historian Bonnie Stepenoff calls the film an affectionate tribute rather than a factual account, and notes how much it borrows from Boys Town. Matt's crime and execution are invented. A real former resident, Matthew Davis, sued RKO in 1950 for damage to his reputation and lost. The film dates the founding to 1905; the home opened in 1906.
advisories:
A boy shoots a policeman, and a condemned boy's last hours are the climax.

Street fights between newsboys; a horse is killed and a boy's leg is crushed.

Suitable for children of about ten and up, with the ending in mind.

sources.claims: Fighting Father Dunne (RKO) A-I, 1947-48

suitability.note: A boy shoots a policeman and is hanged off screen, and there are street fights and a crushed leg. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I, and children old enough to take the ending will find a lively story of boys helped by a priest.

doctrine: The film's religion is the corporal works of mercy, here the care of orphaned and homeless boys, with the priest acting under his bishop. A secular priest cannot found a work of this kind without the leave of his ordinary, which is why Dunne must ask Archbishop Glennon. The last scenes touch the Church's teaching on the dying: a condemned man who repents may receive absolution, Viaticum and Extreme Unction, and the Church has always held that a death-sentence does not bar him from the sacraments. The pardon Dunne begs from the governor reflects the older Catholic view that clemency is a duty of a ruler, while the civil power retains its right to punish.
production: RKO made the film from an original story by William Rankin, scripted by Martin Rackin and Frank Davis, as a successor to MGM's Boys Town (1938). Ted Tetzlaff directed and Pat O'Brien took the lead. RKO announced trade screenings for 11 May 1948 and the US release followed on 19 June 1948. In May 1948 the real Matthew L. Davis sued RKO for $300,000, claiming the portrayal of the film's Matt Davis damaged his reputation. The Legion of Decency classed it A-I. Reviews were divided: Harrison's Reports called it a fine drama, Thomas Pryor of the New York Times thought it too sentimental, and the New Yorker said Dunne's work was commendable but not very exciting.

title: Father Brown
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency rated it A-I (released in the US as The Detective; 1953–54 list), which is the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Movie Nation's review and the contemporary notices quoted by Wikipedia give an independent account of its treatment. The English subtitle track confirms the sermon on grace, the Friday clue, the priest staking the cross on Flambeau's soul, and the prodigal-son ending. No doctrinal problem was found.
summary: Alec Guinness plays Chesterton's mild London priest, who loses a precious relic to a master thief and then pursues the thief's soul across France.
synopsis: Father Brown, a small and untidy London parish priest, is caught one night by the police at an open safe: he is putting back money a parishioner stole. His bishop then sends him to Rome with the ancient cross of St Augustine, which the famous thief Flambeau has sworn to steal. Brown guesses that a fellow priest on the journey is an impostor, because he orders a ham sandwich on a Friday, but in the Paris catacombs the man knocks him down and takes the cross. In disgrace, Brown tells his superiors that he gambled the cross for Flambeau's soul. With the help of the widowed Lady Warren, he sets a trap at an auction and traces the thief to a ruined château in Burgundy, full of stolen art. The film ends in Brown's church, as he reads the parable of the prodigal son.
inclusion: Robert Hamer, who made Kind Hearts and Coronets, brings the same dry wit to a gentler story. Guinness is the reason to watch. His Brown is absent-minded, polite and immovable, and the film never makes fun of his faith. The comedy is good, especially the auction and a chase in which priest and thief empty a milk van together. Peter Finch makes Flambeau vain and likeable, and Joan Greenwood adds warmth. The plot is thin and the middle sags. Roger Moore of Movie Nation ranks it below Guinness's best comedies, and Variety thought the casting its main distinction. It is still one of the few films in which a priest's detective work exists to save a sinner rather than to punish him.
themes: The film's Catholic ideas are stated plainly. Brown's first sermon says that nobody is made simply good or bad, that God's grace is offered to everyone, and that it must not be presumed on. He spots the false priest because a priest would not eat meat on a Friday. Rebuked for losing the relic, he says he staked it on the thief's soul, and he tells Flambeau he wants both back. His method is patience and mercy, not arrest: he refuses to help the police jail a man whose sickness is in his soul. A fable about a woman lost for clutching her onion makes the point about possessions, and the closing reading of the prodigal son marks Flambeau's return.
history: G. K. Chesterton published 'The Blue Cross', the first Father Brown story, in 1910, and collected it in The Innocence of Father Brown (1911). Chesterton became a Catholic in 1922. Guinness was received into the Catholic Church in 1956, two years after the film, and Movie Nation notes that the role is said to have affected his spiritual life.
liberties: Only the opening idea comes from 'The Blue Cross'. In the story, Valentin of the Paris police trails Flambeau across London, Brown keeps the real cross safe by switching parcels, and he unmasks the thief because Flambeau, disguised as a priest, attacks reason, which Brown calls bad theology. The film lets Flambeau steal the cross and invents Lady Warren, the auction, the Burgundy château, the art collection and Flambeau's repentance. In Chesterton, Flambeau reforms only in later stories.
advisories:
A thief knocks the priest down; otherwise only comic theft and mild peril.

No sexual content or bad language.

Suitable for all ages, though younger children may find it slow.

names: 'The Blue Cross', short story by G. K. Chesterton (1910)

suitability.note: Comic theft and a brief knock-down, with no bad language or sexual content. Younger children may find the talk slow, but the chase and the priest's gentle humour carry it.

doctrine: Chesterton's priest solves crimes by understanding sin from the confessional rather than by clues, and tells Flambeau that he knows the human heart because he has heard so many confessions. The film touches the Church's teaching that the priest hears confession as judge and physician, and that the sacramental seal is inviolable (Fourth Lateran, 1215, canon 21; 1917 Code, canon 889). It also shows the distinction between material theft and the thief's state of soul: Father Brown seeks the thief's conversion, not his punishment, and Flambeau's reform is a picture of contrition and amendment of life. The Blue Cross itself is a silver cross set with sapphires, a sacred object that a thief may not lawfully take; theft of a sacred thing is sacrilege.
production: Robert Hamer directed this British comedy for Facet Productions, from a screenplay credited to Thelma Schnee, Maurice Rapf and Hamer. Rapf was blacklisted in Hollywood and is thought to have written much of it. It was made at Riverside Studios in London on a budget of about £122,000, and Guinness was announced for the title role in May 1953. The producer Paul Finder Moss died in June 1954, soon after the film was finished. It opened in Britain on 8 June 1954 through Columbia and in the United States as The Detective. It ran 91 minutes and was shown at Venice in 1954. Sight and Sound called it a little classic of its kind.

title: El padrecito
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and well documented, now including a full Spanish subtitle transcript: a young priest's ministry, with Mass, confession, baptism and papal social teaching at its centre. Not PUBLISH because several comic beats treat sacramental discipline lightly (a refused baptism, a boy told he need not confess because 'no one knows yet what sin is', indulgences offered in a bet, the Last Supper retold in Cantinflas's patter), and no contemporary Catholic rating or independent critical assessment of its treatment was found. Not REJECT: its social teaching is quoted from Leo XIII, Pius XI and John XXIII, and the film itself mocks the liturgical novelties the priest pretends to propose. A Mexican Legion of Decency or Spanish Catholic rating from 1964–65 would settle it.
summary: Cantinflas plays a young priest sent to help an old parish priest in a Mexican town, winning it over with dice, a bullfight and papal social teaching.
synopsis: Father Sebastián arrives in the small town of San Jerónimo el Alto to assist the elderly parish priest, Father Damián. Damián's sister Sara takes him for a usurper, and most of the town agrees. He refuses to baptise a baby under a name he finds ridiculous, plays dice for school supplies, dances in the bell tower and preaches a sermon that the municipal president takes as an insult. The local strongman, Don Silvestre, a professed atheist, tries to drive him out and sabotages a bullfight meant to pay for a clinic; Sebastián fights the bull himself. Accused of teaching Communism, he quotes the popes' encyclicals. He opens a school, wins the clinic's land from Don Silvestre at cards and helps Damián's niece with the strongman's son. When a visiting prelate comes to replace Damián, Sebastián poses as a wild innovator so that the old man can stay.
inclusion: This was Cantinflas's first priest role and one of his biggest late hits in Mexico and Spain, directed by his regular collaborator Miguel M. Delgado. The pleasure is his patter: the cantinflesque double-talk that turns a sermon or a confession into a comic routine. Ángel Garasa's gentle old Damián is a good foil, and the farewell has real warmth. Critics at the time found it moralising and unoriginal, typical of Cantinflas's later films, and at two hours it is long. The social argument is pointed for 1964: the priest opens a school, raises money for a clinic, and quotes papal encyclicals when he is accused of Communism. John Mraz reads the film as anti-political rather than revolutionary, and the ending is a private bargain, not a programme.
themes: Sebastián's faith is never in doubt. He says Mass, hears confessions, visits the dying and preaches, and when Sara calls his talk of fair wages Communism he answers with Leo XIII, Pius XI and John XXIII. The trouble is in the jokes. He refuses a baptism over a silly name, though Damián rightly says a sacrament is never refused. He tells a boy who dislikes confession that he need not go, since no one knows yet what sin is. He offers indulgences in a bet, and his Last Supper sermon, in Cantinflas's patter, calls Christ a revolutionary of goodness. The film does not endorse liturgical novelty: his promise of mariachis instead of bells is a ruse, and the prelate dismisses it.
advisories:
A fist fight and a bullfight.

The priest gambles and drinks rum and brandy, played for laughs.

Jokes at the expense of confession, baptism and indulgences; a comic retelling of the Last Supper.

Long (about two hours). Suitable for older children with some explanation of the jokes about the sacraments.

grey.question: El padrecito admires its priest, but several of its jokes are at the sacraments' expense. Sebastián refuses a baptism over a silly name, tells a boy he need not confess because no one knows yet what sin is, offers indulgences in a bet, and retells the Last Supper as comic patter that calls Christ a revolutionary. Against this, his social teaching is quoted from Leo XIII, Pius XI and John XXIII, and the film mocks liturgical novelty. No Catholic rating from 1964 has been found; one would settle whether the comedy was judged irreverent.

suitability.note: A fist fight, a bullfight and a priest who gambles, drinks and jokes about confession and indulgences. Nothing is violent or sexual, but children need a parent to explain which jokes are wrong. Long at two hours.

doctrine: The film's social teaching rests on the encyclicals: Leo XIII's Rerum novarum (1891) on just wages and the rights of workers, and Pius XI's Quadragesimo anno (1931), which condemned both unregulated capitalism and socialism. Pius XI also condemned Communism as 'intrinsically wrong' in Divini Redemptoris (1937). Where the film is shaky is on the sacraments. A priest may not refuse Baptism, and the Code of 1917 required a Christian name for the child. Children are bound to confession from the age of reason, about seven, as Pius X taught in Quam singulari (1910), and to say no one knows what sin is contradicts the Church's moral teaching. Indulgences may not be offered as stakes in a bet: the Council of Trent (session 25) condemned all trade in them. The film itself rejects liturgical gimmicks, which is to its credit.
production: Miguel M. Delgado directed this Cantinflas vehicle, produced by Jacques Gelman and distributed by Columbia, from a script by Mario Amendola and Renée Asseo. Raúl Lavista wrote the music. It opened in Mexico on 3 September 1964 and runs 124 minutes. Some critics accused Cantinflas of mocking the priesthood; he replied that his message would be positive and Christian. Reviewers have called it a moralising film short on originality. Scholars including John Mraz read political overtones in it. No 1964 Catholic rating found.

title: The Little World of Don Camillo
alternateTitles: Le Petit Monde de don Camillo
Il piccolo mondo di don Camillo
decision: PUBLISH: Jacques Lourcelles (Cinema Ritrovato programme note), contemporary reviews (Valobra in Rassegna del Film, Crowther in The New York Times, Offord in the Socialist Standard) and Cathopedia's scene list together document a comedy built on a priest's rivalry with a Communist mayor, the crucified Christ's rebukes, the sacraments and reconciliation. Edition differences (French version longer, including the attempted suicide) are disclosed.
summary: Fernandel's hot-tempered parish priest and Gino Cervi's Communist mayor feud, brawl and make peace in a Po Valley village, while Christ on the altar crucifix keeps the priest in line.
synopsis: In a small town on the Po plain after the war, the Communists win the local elections and Peppone becomes mayor. His rival is the parish priest, Don Camillo, a big man with big fists, who takes his grievances to the crucifix above the altar, and Christ answers him, usually with a rebuke. The two men clash over a new Casa del Popolo, a strike, a football match, a procession and the baptism of Peppone's son, whom the mayor wants to name after Lenin. Between quarrels they cooperate when the village needs them. Two young lovers from feuding families try to drown themselves, which forces both men to help. After a final brawl the bishop transfers Don Camillo to a mountain parish. Peppone forbids the town to see him off, but waits for him at the next station.
inclusion: Julien Duvivier and René Barjavel turned Giovannino Guareschi's newspaper stories into one of the most popular European films of the 1950s. Fernandel's elastic face and Gino Cervi's slow-burning mayor make an ideal comic pair. Jacques Lourcelles called Fernandel's mix of serenity and mischief superb, and Bosley Crowther praised its vigorous and amiable conflict. The film is episodic. Fabrizio Valobra, reviewing in 1952, found it fragmentary and sketch-like, with only the procession and the closing walk to the station showing Duvivier's real style. That is fair, but the episodes are well built, and the conversations with the crucifix give the comedy a moral centre.
themes: The crucifix is the film's conscience. Christ, voiced by Ruggero Ruggeri in the Italian version and Jean Debucourt in the French, regularly checks the priest's temper and vanity; in one scene he tells him to throw away the stick he means to use. Don Camillo submits, grumbling. The sacraments are taken seriously beneath the jokes. He insists on a proper Christian name at the baptism, but he baptises the child. He also blesses the Communists' new building. The film's argument is that a priest may oppose Communism with all his strength and still owe its members love and pastoral care. Its anti-Communism is comic, not hateful.
history: Guareschi, editor of the satirical weekly Candido, began the stories in 1946 and collected them as Mondo piccolo: Don Camillo (1948). They grew out of the bitter 1948 election campaign between the Christian Democrats and the Communist–Socialist Popular Front. Guareschi presented the Christ of the stories as the voice of his own conscience. The film was shot in Brescello, Emilia, and released in Italy in March 1952 and in France in June 1952.
liberties: The screenplay selects and links separate Guareschi stories into a loose chronicle. The Italian and French versions differ. The French cut is longer, extending the attempted suicide, the brawl, the football match and Signora Cristina's funeral, and adding a short exchange with a statue of Our Lady. The US version adds an English narration by Orson Welles.
advisories:
Fist fights and comic brawling, including by the priest.

Two young lovers attempt suicide by drowning (longer in the French version).

Political insults and threats played for comedy.

Suitable for families with older children.

sources.claims: Cast, writers, producers, music, cinematography, dual-language shooting, admissions, 2008 list

names: Mondo piccolo: Don Camillo, stories by Giovannino Guareschi (1948)

suitability.note: Fist fights and comic brawling, political threats played for laughs, and a lovers' suicide attempt by drowning that ends safely. Children will enjoy the talking Crucifix and the slapstick, though the political jokes are lost on them.

doctrine: The talking Crucifix presents a priest in daily conversation with Christ, and Christ rebukes the priest's anger and pride. The film touches several Catholic points. A priest may not use violence to settle quarrels, and Don Camillo's temper is a fault he is made to confess. The Church condemned Communism: Pius XI's Divini Redemptoris (1937) called it intrinsically perverse and forbade Catholics to help it, and the Holy Office decree of 1 July 1949 excommunicated Catholics who knowingly profess and spread its doctrine. Yet the stories also show that Communists are baptised souls who still honour the sacraments, and the Church asks for charity to the person while refusing the error. The bishop's removal of a priest to another parish is within a bishop's ordinary power.
production: Julien Duvivier directed this Franco-Italian co-production, made by Francinex and Rizzoli Amato. The actors spoke their own languages on set and the other language was dubbed. It opened in Italy on 18 March 1952. It was the highest-grossing film of all time in both Italy and France by admissions, about 13.2 million and 12.8 million. It made Fernandel an international star and led to four sequels, among them Monsignor and the final round already on this list. In 2008 the Italian ministry placed it on its list of 100 Italian films to be saved.

title: The Return of Don Camillo
decision: PUBLISH: Roberto Chiesi's Cinema Ritrovato programme note and the Cinematografo record document the exiled priest's grief at the silence of the crucifix, his return and the Po flood as the film's core, and identify the French version as the fuller one (Italian censors cut scenes, including the crucifix carried through the snow). Contemporary and later criticism (Zannino 1953; Bertarelli 2001) is recorded; comic pranks and a joke 'sale' of a soul are disclosed.
summary: Duvivier's sadder sequel sends Don Camillo into mountain exile, brings him home to his feud with Peppone, and ends with the Po in flood.
synopsis: Exiled to Montenara, a poor village in the mountains, Don Camillo finds a half-ruined church, an empty rectory and parishioners who ignore him. He misses his town, his people and the crucifix that used to talk to him. Back home, Peppone needs him: a stubborn landowner refuses to allow flood defences on his land, and only the priest can move him. The mayor asks the bishop to bring Don Camillo back. The feud resumes at once with a boxing match, a race between the town-hall clock and the church bells, a forged party letter and a castor-oil toast. Don Camillo also visits Peppone's unhappy son at boarding school. Then the Po bursts its banks. The villagers are evacuated to the main embankment while Don Camillo stays alone in his church.
inclusion: Roberto Chiesi calls this the more melancholy and bitter of the first two films, and its exile scenes the best in either. Duvivier lets the fog, the cold rectory and the silent crucifix register without milking them. Fernandel is again excellent, and Gino Cervi's Peppone is more vulnerable. The comic middle section is looser. Contemporary critic F. Zannino found the conflicts superficial and resolved as soon as they appear, while Massimo Bertarelli later praised its warmth and called it tender and very funny. Both are right. Use the French version where possible. Italian censors cut several scenes, including the most beautiful religious sequence.
themes: The heart of the film is a priest's loneliness without his Lord. In exile the crucifix of the mountain church is silent. In the French version Don Camillo carries his old crucifix up to the rectory, stumbles under its weight in falling snow, and rejoices when it speaks to him again. The flood shows the priest as shepherd: he stays in his church when everyone else leaves. Duvivier wanted the priest to drown and wake in a paradise like his own town. Guareschi and the producer refused, so the film keeps only a dream of heaven, from which he wakes to Peppone's face. The comic subplot in which an old man buys a young militant's "soul" is a joke, not a theology.
history: Giovannino Guareschi (1908-1968), a Catholic and anti-communist journalist, published his first Don Camillo story in 1946, in the Po valley of Emilia, where Communists and the Church were rivals after the war. The mayor, Peppone, and the priest, Don Camillo, are friends and enemies, and the priest's talks with the crucifix over the altar are a device of the stories. The setting is real: the 1948 Italian election pitted the Christian Democrats against the Communist-Socialist front, and Pius XII's Holy Office in 1949 forbade Catholics to join or support Communist parties.
liberties: Guareschi objected strongly to Duvivier's changes, and the ending is a compromise between them. The French and Italian versions differ substantially: besides the crucifix scene, the Italian cut softens a harsh episode with a draft-dodger that shows Don Camillo's petty side and trims a scene with Peppone's son. Running times range from about 100 minutes (Italian) to 115 (French).
advisories:
Fist fights, a boxing match and cruel practical jokes, including dosing a man with castor oil and a forged letter.

A flood with danger to life; a dream of death.

A comic subplot about selling one's soul.

Suitable for families with older children.

sources.claims: Cast and roles; screenplay Barjavel, Duvivier, Amato; Guareschi credited; producer Amato; music Cicognini; cinematography Brizzi; released 5 June 1953; 115 minutes; second most popular film in France in 1953; second of five Fernandel films

names: Don Camillo stories by Giovannino Guareschi

suitability.note: Fist fights, a boxing match and cruel practical jokes are played for laughs. The flood and a dream of death are the only frightening parts, and the dubbed or subtitled comedy suits families with children of eight or older.

doctrine: The talking crucifix is a literary device. The Church has never required belief in a dialogue with a crucifix, but she has always taught that images of Christ may be honoured because the honour passes to the prototype (Council of Trent, Session 25; II Nicaea, 787). The film's priest has faults, namely pride, a temper and mischief, and the stories turn on how a priest's character does not alter the validity of his sacraments (Trent, Session 7, canon 12). The politics behind it are real: Pius XI condemned communism in Divini Redemptoris (1937), and the Holy Office decree of 1 July 1949 declared that Catholics who knowingly profess and spread its materialistic and anti-Christian doctrine incur excommunication. Don Camillo and Peppone, who still baptise their children and go to Mass, show the Italian peasant's loyalty to the Church under a party label.
production: Julien Duvivier directed this second Don Camillo film for Giuseppe Amato, as a French-Italian co-production, with Fernandel and Gino Cervi returning from the first film (1952). It was released on 5 June 1953. The French cut runs about 115 minutes. It was the second most popular film of 1953 at the French box office. Five Fernandel Don Camillo films were made in all.

title: Don Camillo's Last Round
alternateTitles: La Grande Bagarre de Don Camillo
decision: PUBLISH: The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico's Segnalazioni cinematografiche (vol. 38, 1955) reviewed the film favourably as a small world ruled by good sense and human understanding, and the Cinema Ritrovato note (quoting Ojetti, Cinema, 1955) and Cinematografo record give independent criticism. A French subtitle transcript confirms the Catholic substance: the crucifix rebukes the priest for blasphemy, he keeps the seal of confession and he defends Peppone's marriage. Electoral tricks and brawls are comic and disclosed.
summary: Carmine Gallone's third Don Camillo film sets priest and mayor against each other in the 1953 election, with Peppone's marriage and a seat in Parliament at stake.
synopsis: Peppone, still mayor of the little town on the Po, stands for Parliament on the Popular Front list in the 1953 general election. Don Camillo campaigns against him with every trick he knows, but the rivalry has limits. The priest coaches the mayor through the primary-school leaving exam he never passed, and takes his price: a signed permit for a new chapel. The party sends a striking young activist, Clotilde, to run the campaign, and Peppone's wife Maria packs her bags to go back to her mother; Don Camillo steps in to save the marriage. A German tank, hidden on a farm since the war, threatens to land Peppone's men in prison. At the closing rally the priest turns the mayor's speech into a patriotic occasion. Peppone is elected, resigns as mayor and boards the train for Rome, but gets off and rides home with the priest.
inclusion: Duvivier had gone and Fernandel needed persuading, so Rizzoli made this third film alone, with Carmine Gallone directing and Guareschi writing the script himself. It is looser and more repetitive than the first two. The Catholic film office's reviewer said in 1955 that it repeats familiar situations but has some happy ideas, and praised the direction and acting; Pasquale Ojetti, in Cinema, found the commercial intent obvious but credited Guareschi's writing. The best scenes are domestic rather than political: the giant priest drilling the mayor in arithmetic, Maria's threatened departure and the ending at the station, which answers the farewell of the first film. Fernandel and Gino Cervi are as good as ever, and the film was a big hit in Italy and France.
themes: The crucifix still keeps the priest honest. When Peppone is elected, Don Camillo jokes that Stalin could burn a one-ton candle and become pope; Christ tells him his anger has made him blaspheme, and he asks pardon. A wartime story shows a priest crossing gunfire to hear a dying man's confession and refusing afterwards to repeat a word of it. Marriage is defended plainly: the priest's intervention keeps Peppone's family together against the party's distractions. The anti-Communism is open, as it was in Italian Catholic life in 1953, including a Vatican Radio voice telling voters that God sees them in the booth. The electoral tricks are comedy, not a model of conduct.
history: Giovannino Guareschi (1908–1968) founded the satirical weekly Candido in 1945 and began writing the Don Camillo stories in the late 1940s, out of the bitter contest between the Church and the Communists after the war. This film moves them to the general election of 7 June 1953. Christian Democracy won 40.1 per cent of the vote for the Chamber, the Communists 22.6 and the Socialists 12.7; the centre coalition fell just short of the majority needed to trigger the new seat bonus. In 1954 Guareschi was tried for libel over two wartime letters he had published and attributed to the Christian Democrat leader Alcide De Gasperi; convicted, he refused to appeal and served 409 days in prison in Parma.
liberties: The story is assembled from Guareschi's own stories, with Leo Benvenuti, Age and Scarpelli reportedly helping uncredited. Unlike the first two films, it was an Italian production without a French partner, and Fernandel is dubbed in the Italian version. The exam, tank and rally episodes are independent comic sketches strung on the election.
advisories:
Fist fights, a boxing-style brawl and political insults, played for comedy.

A marriage in crisis over a young woman's attentions to the husband; nothing sexual is shown.

A wartime story with a dying man; a hidden tank and talk of explosives.

The priest uses tricks and pressure in an election campaign, presented as comedy.

Suitable for families with older children.

sources.claims: Held 7 June 1953; DC 40.1%, PCI 22.6%, PSI 12.7% (Chamber); majority bonus not triggered, coalition at 49.9%

names: Giovannino Guareschi (with Leo Benvenuti, Age and Scarpelli, uncredited)
The Mondo piccolo (Don Camillo) stories by Giovannino Guareschi

suitability.note: Brawls, insults and election tricks are all played for comedy, and a marriage under strain is handled without anything sexual on screen. The politics of 1953 Italy will pass over younger heads, but the priest's talks with the crucifix and the friendship between two enemies are easy to follow.

doctrine: The wartime confession story rests on the seal of confession. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215, canon 21) bound every priest not to betray a penitent 'by word or sign', on pain of deposition and perpetual penance in a monastery; the Church has always treated it as admitting no exception. Christ's rebuke after the election also has a basis: the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) calls blasphemy in its general nature a mortal sin, 'the gravest that may be committed against religion'. In defending Peppone's marriage the priest stands on the unity and fidelity of marriage taught by Pius XI in Casti Connubii (31 December 1930). The campaign itself reflects the Holy Office decree of 1 July 1949, approved by Pius XII: Catholics might not join or favour Communist parties, those who knowingly did so could not receive the sacraments, and those who professed materialist Communism incurred excommunication as apostates.
production: Rizzoli had difficulty continuing the series. Julien Duvivier, who directed the first two films, withdrew, and Fernandel at first refused to put on the cassock again for fear of being identified with the part. After long negotiations Rizzoli made the third film alone, without a French co-producer, with Carmine Gallone directing and Guareschi writing the script from his own stories; Leo Benvenuti, Age and Scarpelli are reported to have helped without credit. Anchise Brizzi photographed it and Alessandro Cicognini wrote the music. It premiered in Rome on 25 October 1955 and was released in France as La Grande Bagarre de Don Camillo, where it was among the leading Paris grosses of the year. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico's review found it repetitive but praised the direction and acting; Pasquale Ojetti in Cinema saw its commercial purpose but credited Guareschi's writing.

title: Don Camillo: Monsignor
originalTitle: Don Camillo monsignore... ma non troppo
decision: PUBLISH: Segnalazioni cinematografiche (Centro Cattolico Cinematografico, vol. 50, 1961) reviewed it as a weaker but sound instalment showing men of good will and sense working for the common good; Cinema Ritrovato and Image et Son supply independent criticism. The disputed 'Christ was born a proletarian' speech was checked in an English subtitle transcript and on Wikiquote: it is a debating trick in which the priest steals the Communists' language to give church land to the poor, and Peppone protests that he is cheating. It states nothing contrary to Catholic teaching on Christ's poverty. Don Camillo is a monsignor, not a bishop.
summary: Promoted to monsignor in Rome, Don Camillo is sent home with Senator Peppone to settle a fight over a wayside chapel, a church wedding and a pools win.
synopsis: Some years on, Don Camillo works in Rome as a monsignor and Peppone sits in the Senate for the Communists. Both miss their town. When the council's plan for new public housing threatens a small chapel of Our Lady that the people venerate, the Vatican and the Party each send their man home to settle it, and the two find themselves sharing a sleeping car. At a public meeting by the chapel Don Camillo outflanks the Communists, offering church land for the houses on condition that they serve all the poor alike. Peppone's son Walter is to marry; his father wants a civil ceremony to spite the priests, his mother refuses to let the boy live in sin, and the wedding takes place in church. Peppone secretly wins the football pools and needs the priest to collect the money. The quarrels done, both men return to Rome.
inclusion: This is the series running on habit. Gallone said the two leads had become commedia dell'arte masks who could live apart from politics, and the film proves both the charm and the limits of that. The Catholic film office's reviewer in 1961 found less freshness and invention but some lively, colourful scenes, and credited Gallone's precise direction and the actors' proven skill. J. Grob, in Image et Son, was bored stiff. At nearly two hours it is the longest and slackest of the five. Still, Fernandel's monsignor, embarrassed by his promotion and itching to be a country priest again, is a good comic idea, and the wedding quarrel has real bite. It was one of the biggest Italian hits of the 1961–62 season.
themes: The crucifix speaks again after three years of silence in Rome; Christ tells him God is no nearer here, he is simply nearer to himself. Christ also refuses to name a thief, asking whether the priest wants him to be a spy. The clearest Catholic statement is the wedding: Maria defends sacramental marriage against her husband and the party. The disputed speech says that Christ chose to be born not a bourgeois but a proletarian, to know the suffering of those who work. It is Don Camillo stealing Peppone's vocabulary, and Peppone says so. Christ's poverty and labour are old Catholic teaching; Leo XIII made the same point about the carpenter's son. The chapel of Our Lady, which a workman refuses to knock down, shows popular devotion treated with respect.
history: By 1961 the Don Camillo films had become a reliable Rizzoli franchise. This fourth film was shot in Brescello and nearby Boretto; photographs from the shoot are held at the Museo Peppone e Don Camillo in Brescello. It was released in Italy on 7 October 1961 and earned more than 1.1 billion lire in the 1961–62 season. Comrade Don Camillo (1965), the fifth film, is set earlier in the story.
liberties: Leo Benvenuti, Piero De Bernardi and Gallone wrote the screenplay from Guareschi's characters and stories, adding the Roman framing. Some English-language sources call Don Camillo a bishop; the Italian credits and dialogue make him a monsignor. Running times vary between about 100 and 117 minutes in different prints.
advisories:
Comic quarrels and political insults.

The death and funeral of a young Communist activist.

A priest's bargaining and blackmail, and a pools win hidden from the party, all played for comedy.

Suitable for families with older children.

sources.claims: Cast roles, screenplay, producer, music, cinematography

names: Don Camillo stories by Giovannino Guareschi

suitability.note: Comic quarrels, political insults and the funeral of a young Communist, with no violence to speak of. The jokes about Italian politics will pass children by, but the slapstick and the talking Crucifix hold them.

doctrine: Don Camillo is made a monsignor, a prelate with the title and dress of a domestic prelate of the Holy Father, and finds that the honour sits ill with the work of a parish priest. The film shows that a priest's dignity lies in the care of souls and in living among his flock. It also shows the Church's refusal to let parish property be taken for party ends, in the dispute over the chapel of the Madonnina. The Church condemned Communism (Pius XI, Divini Redemptoris, 1937; Holy Office decree, 1 July 1949), while the stories keep showing that Communists are baptised souls whom the Church asks the priest to treat with charity while refusing their error.
production: Carmine Gallone directed the fourth Don Camillo film for Angelo Rizzoli's Cineriz. Shooting began on 22 May 1961 and ended in July, mostly at Brescello, with other scenes at Godezza, Boretto, Castelnovo di Sotto and Rome. Some episodes were written for the film and others come from Guareschi stories such as Il pittore, Il muraglione and Il campanone. The script alludes to the Reggio Emilia deaths of 7 July 1960. It opened in Italy on 7 October 1961, ran 117 minutes in black and white, and drew about 6.6 million spectators, earning around 1.1 billion lire. It was the sixth-highest grosser of the year in Italy. Though fourth to be made, it is set last in the story. The series continued with Comrade Don Camillo (1965).

title: Don Camillo in Moscow
decision: PUBLISH: Segnalazioni cinematografiche (Centro Cattolico Cinematografico, vol. 58, 1965) reviewed it as continuing the series' moral pattern and showing both men's honest humanity; Jean A. Gili's Cinema Ritrovato note and the Cinematografo record give independent criticism. An English subtitle transcript settles the doubtful points: the Soviet church is shown as a 'church of silence' turned granary, Don Camillo says Mass in secret and brings Viaticum to a dying woman, and he does not share rites with the Orthodox priest but shames him into ministering to his own parishioner. Comic deceptions (false identity, a layman in clerical disguise) are disclosed.
summary: Comencini's last Fernandel–Cervi film smuggles Don Camillo into the Soviet Union on forged papers, where he finds a church turned granary and a dying woman waiting for a priest.
synopsis: A Soviet collective farm sends Brescello a tractor that will not start until the priest blesses it, and Peppone announces a twinning with a Russian village. Don Camillo fights the plan with a hunger strike, then blackmails the mayor into taking him along as Comrade Tarocci, on forged papers, with a prayer book disguised as the thoughts of Lenin. In the Soviet Union he says Mass in a hotel room full of microphones, finds the village church used as a grain store, and answers an anonymous note in Latin asking for a priest for the kolkhoz chairman's dying mother. Unable to understand her confession, he forces the frightened local Orthodox priest to do his duty. A young comrade falls for the interpreter and stays. Back home the bishop sends Don Camillo to escort a party of priests to America, and Peppone turns up among them in clerical disguise.
inclusion: Comencini made it to pay off a debt to Rizzoli, and disliked it. Jean A. Gili finds weariness and a lack of invention, but also rhythm, some funny moments and a certain authority. The Catholic film office's reviewer in 1965 said it repeats the moral pattern of the earlier films and fairly shows the honest humanity of both men; D. Biondi, in Il Resto del Carlino, praised the stars and Comencini's lively camera. The Italian opening drags. The Russian half is better than its reputation: the hotel-room Mass, the secret visit to the dying woman during a vodka contest staged to keep her son away, and above all the scene in the ruined church, the best religious sequence of the later films.
themes: The film takes the persecuted Church seriously beneath the jokes. In the village church, now a granary, Christ speaks from the cross: grain is the bread of man, he says, and he is that bread, so even those who come for grain must think of him. It is, he says, the church of silence, the phrase Pius XII's generation used for the Church behind the Iron Curtain. Don Camillo smuggles hosts, says Mass in secret and risks arrest to bring the sacraments to a woman whose son kept her from confession for twenty years. He does not take over the Orthodox priest's role but sends him in. Some moral corners are cut for comedy: a lie of identity, and an oath dismissed as 'only a word' to save two supposed refugees.
history: Giovannino Guareschi (1908-1968) wrote the Don Camillo stories from the late 1940s, out of the Church's contest with the Communists in post-war Italy. In the Soviet Union the churches were closed or put to other uses, and the Church behind the Iron Curtain was called the Church of silence. Pius XI condemned atheistic Communism in Divini Redemptoris (19 March 1937), and a Holy Office decree of 1 July 1949, approved by Pius XII, forbade Catholics to join or favour Communist parties. The story is set in the time of Khrushchev's thaw and the exchange of delegations between Italy and the USSR.
liberties: The film changes the novel's blackmail plot, makes the delegation mainly Brescello's, makes the Soviets friendlier in keeping with the détente of 1965, and reverses the young militant Scamoggia's ending. The novel ends with the bishop promoting Don Camillo; the film replaces this with the American trip for continuity with Don Camillo: Monsignor.
advisories:
Comic fist fights and a drinking contest with vodka.

A dying woman; secret sacraments under threat of arrest.

Peppone's flirtation with a fairground woman is used for blackmail; a young couple's romance.

The priest travels under a false name with forged papers, and Peppone disguises himself as a priest at the end; both are played for comedy.

Suitable for families with older children.

names: Il compagno don Camillo, novel by Giovannino Guareschi (1963)

suitability.note: Fist fights, a vodka-drinking contest and a priest travelling on forged papers are all played for comedy. A dying woman is anxious for a priest, which is the one sober scene. Fernandel's face and the talks with the crucifix keep it easy to follow for children.

doctrine: In the film the Church of silence is the Church that cannot speak or build behind the Iron Curtain. Pius XI's Divini Redemptoris (19 March 1937) calls atheistic Communism intrinsically wrong and tells Catholics not to collaborate with it, citing the persecutions in Russia, Mexico and Spain. The Holy Office decree of 1 July 1949 applied this to membership and the sacraments. Don Camillo's cheerful lie of identity, and an oath dismissed as 'only a word', do not follow the older moral teaching, which does not permit a lie even for a good end, though it allows a person to keep silent. The Church recognises the orders of the Orthodox, and in danger of death any priest absolves validly (1917 Code, canon 882).
production: Luigi Comencini directed the fifth and last Fernandel-Cervi film, and also produced it, from a screenplay by Piero De Bernardi and a story by Leo Benvenuti. Rizzoli, Francoriz and Omnia made it as an Italian, French and West German co-production. Shooting ran from 15 April to 8 July 1965, mostly at Brescello, with a church at Monterosi, Trastevere station and Rome's Urbe airport standing for Russia. It premiered in Rome on 18 September 1965 and runs about 104 to 109 minutes. Comencini disliked it, made it to cancel a debt to Rizzoli, and the note by Jean A. Gili calls the film tired but amusing. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico's Segnalazioni said it repeated the moralising approach of the earlier films and showed the honest humanity of both men. Armando Nannuzzi photographed it.
