title: Angels with Dirty Faces
decision: GREY: The contemporary Catholic judgment was negative. The Legion of Decency classed it B, morally objectionable in part (Motion Picture Daily's 1938 report of the Legion list; the Legion's 1959 cumulative list), so it cannot be PUBLISH. The transcript confirms the disputed ending: the priest asks Rocky to feign cowardice and then confirms the story to the boys, and Rocky refuses religious ministrations. It is not REJECT, because the priest's pastoral struggle is the moral centre and the questions can be stated plainly. It would move only if the Legion's stated objection were found to be minor and the Founder accepted the ending.
summary: Curtiz's Warner Bros. gangster classic sets James Cagney's killer against Pat O'Brien's slum priest, in a fight for the street boys who idolise the gangster.
synopsis: Two New York slum boys are caught robbing a freight car. Jerry Connolly gets away; Rocky Sullivan is caught and goes from reform school into crime. Years later Rocky returns from prison to find Jerry the parish priest, running a gym for the local boys. The boys idolise Rocky, and his money and swagger undo Jerry's work. Rocky forces his share out of the crooked lawyer Frazier and the boss Keefer and gives Jerry money for the gym, while Jerry starts a public campaign against the city's rackets. When Rocky learns that the two men plan to kill Jerry, he shoots them, is captured after a siege and is sentenced to the electric chair. Jerry asks him to die as a coward so the boys will stop admiring him. Rocky refuses, then goes to his death screaming for mercy. Jerry tells the boys it is true.
inclusion: This is one of the best Warner Bros. crime films: fast, hard and handsomely shot by Sol Polito, with a Max Steiner score and Michael Curtiz's sure pacing. Cagney, nominated for an Oscar, makes Rocky charming and lethal, and Pat O'Brien's Jerry is a believable parish priest, coach and reformer. The famous ending refuses to say whether Rocky broke or chose to break for the boys' sake, and that ambiguity is the film's strongest idea. Motion Picture Daily called it one of the finest pictures of the 1938 season. The Dead End Kids are loud and the middle plotting is routine. Alexander McGregor, in his study of the Church and Hollywood, treats Jerry as the model of the two-fisted screen priest of the 1930s.
themes: The film is a contest between a priest and a gangster for the same boys. Jerry admits that the boys learn the quickest way is a racket or a gun, says that only the grace of God separates him from Rocky, and asks his friend for one thing: to settle his account with God. At the end he walks with Rocky to the chair. But Rocky tells the guards to keep out the incense and holy water, and the film shows no confession and no sacraments; he dies begging not to be sent to hell. Jerry's request asks a dying man to deceive the public, and Jerry then confirms the story to the boys. The film presents this as a last act of charity. It also gives its gangster most of the glamour.
advisories:
Frequent gun violence and several killings, including a long siege and shoot-out.

An execution scene in which the condemned man screams for mercy; reviewers describe it as staged largely in shadow.

Crime is made glamorous for much of the film.

Best for teenagers and adults.

The Legion of Decency rated it B, morally objectionable in part; its published list gives no reason.

grey.question: The Legion of Decency classed Angels with Dirty Faces B, objectionable in part, in 1938, without publishing its reason; the glamour given to Cagney's killer is the likeliest ground. The ending raises a second question. Father Connolly asks a condemned man to pretend to be a coward so that boys will despise him, then confirms the story to them, and Rocky goes to his death having refused the priest's ministry. Readers can weigh whether a pious deception, and a death with no repentance shown, make an acceptable Catholic ending.

sources.claims: Cast, crew, production history, release, gross, awards

suitability.note: Gunfights, killings and a death-row walk in which the condemned man screams, shown mostly in shadow. Crime looks attractive for much of the film, so younger children need a parent to explain the priest's last request.

doctrine: The film turns on a priest's pastoral duty to a criminal friend and to the boys who look up to him. The Church holds that no one is beyond mercy while he lives and that the priest must urge a condemned man to repent and be reconciled to God. It also teaches that bad example corrupts the young, and that the State may lawfully take the life of a convicted criminal, as St Thomas Aquinas teaches (Summa II-II, q. 64, a. 2). Rocky's last-minute behaviour is ambiguous: the audience cannot tell whether he repents or acts out cowardice for the boys' sake. Only God knows the state of his soul.
production: Rowland Brown wrote the original story in August 1937. Cagney, who had left Warner Bros. for Grand National, returned to Warner with the story after that deal collapsed. Michael Curtiz directed. Shooting began in June 1938 at Warner's Burbank studios, and the execution scenes were shot at Sing Sing. The film opened in late November 1938 and took about $1.7 million. It received Academy Award nominations for Curtiz, Cagney and Brown, and Cagney won the New York Film Critics' best actor award. The Legion of Decency rated it B, objectionable in part. The film entered the US National Film Registry in 2024.

title: The Miracle of the Bells
decision: GREY: The English subtitle file confirms the earlier reading and corrects one detail. Father Paul tells Bill there was no miracle, that the Church accepts none without careful inquiry, and that it is his duty to tell the people; in his sermon he declines to say what turned the statues, leaving that to others, and speaks instead of the miracle of people like Olga. A broadcast says the bishop is sending a representative and that the decision belongs to Church authorities. He never affirms divine intervention. The closing exchange is with the studio head Marcus Harris, not Bill: Harris says that when something makes the world better God had something to do with it and he asks no questions, and the reply, apparently Father Paul's, is 'In my religion, too.' A pious evasion, not a false miracle endorsed: a real but weighable reservation, not REJECT.
summary: A press agent brings a dead actress home to a mining town, pays every church to ring its bells, and sets off a 'miracle' the priest knows is not one.
synopsis: Bill Dunnigan, a press agent, escorts the body of Olga Treskovna to Coaltown, the mining town where she grew up poor. Olga, a struggling actress, had been cast as Joan of Arc and finished the film knowing she was dying of tuberculosis caught from the coal dust of her childhood. The producer now refuses to release it. Bill asks Father Paul of the poor Polish parish of St Michael's to bury her, then pays every church in town, with cheques he cannot cover, to ring its bells for three days. Crowds and reporters arrive. At the funeral the statues of St Michael and Our Lady turn on their pillars to face her coffin. Father Paul finds the natural cause; Bill begs him not to take the miracle from the people. The story spreads, and the studio releases the film.
inclusion: There is real Catholic texture here. James Day, in the National Catholic Register, notes that Father Paul says Mass in Latin, explains the Angelus to Bill, and keeps his parish devoted to St Michael, and he calls the film a near masterpiece. Frank Sinatra, cast only after the producer had sought the Church's approval, plays the priest, and Day praises his sincerity; Fred MacMurray plays the press agent and Alida Valli plays Olga. Michael De Sapio grants that the film is often dismissed as saccharine but argues it is a sombre post-war document with noir touches. Most critics disagreed. Time and James Agee mocked its piety, the Golden Turkey Awards later ridiculed Sinatra, and it lost about $640,000.
themes: The devotion to St Michael, the Latin Mass and the life of a poor parish are specific and sincere. The problem is the climax. Father Paul finds the natural cause at once and tells Bill plainly that there was no miracle, that the Church accepts none without careful inquiry, and that it is his duty to tell the people. At Bill's urging he does not. His sermon leaves the cause to others and speaks of the miracle of Olga's goodness. The film ends with the studio head saying he asks no questions when God makes the world better, and Father Paul seems to agree. Trent (Session XXV) reserves new miracles to the bishop and orders superstition removed; the priest claims nothing, but he lets a misunderstanding stand.
history: Jesse L. Lasky produced the film for RKO from Russell Janney's 1946 bestseller, with a script by Ben Hecht and Quentin Reynolds. It opened in New York on 16 March 1948 and nationally on 27 March. It was poorly reviewed and lost about $640,000.
liberties: Fiction. The film condenses Janney's long novel, drops many subplots, and makes Olga's film a life of Joan of Arc rather than an unnamed religious picture. A Pennsylvania man sued RKO, claiming he was caricatured as the undertaker Nick Orloff.
advisories:
An actress dies of tuberculosis; long deathbed and funeral scenes.

No sexual content of note.

Suitable for older children and up.

The ending turns on a priest who knows the natural cause of an apparent miracle and does not tell his parish, though he claims no miracle himself.

grey.question: During the funeral two statues turn to face the coffin. The priest quickly finds the cause: the crowd's weight has shifted their pillars. He tells the press agent there was no miracle and that the Church accepts none without inquiry, and the bishop is said to be investigating. But he does not tell his people. His sermon leaves the cause to others and speaks only of the dead girl's goodness, and the film ends satisfied that the town's renewed faith matters more than the truth. No false miracle is claimed; the question is whether a priest's silence, letting a misunderstanding stand for a good end, is acceptable.

sources.claims: Legion of Decency classification of the film

names: The Miracle of the Bells, novel by Russell Janney (1946)

suitability.note: A young actress dies of tuberculosis and the deathbed and funeral take a long time. There is no violence or sexual content, though the slow, sentimental drama will bore small children.

doctrine: Father Paul's position is the Church's own: the Council of Trent (Session XXV, 1563) ordered that no new miracle be acknowledged until the bishop has examined and approved it, and that superstition be removed from devotion to the saints and their images. A priest therefore has no right to proclaim a miracle, and the film's ending sits uneasily with that rule, since he is persuaded not to say what he knows of the natural cause. Truthfulness is no small matter in Catholic moral teaching, though a pastor may choose what to preach. The St Michael devotion is traditional: he is named in the Mass at the Confiteor and, from 1886 by order of Leo XIII, in the prayer said after low Mass. Olga's film role, Joan of Arc, was canonised in 1920.
production: Russell Janney's novel appeared in 1946 and was a bestseller. Jesse L. Lasky Jr. and Walter MacEwen produced the film for RKO, with a script by Ben Hecht and Quentin Reynolds, and Irving Pichel directed. Exteriors were shot in Glen Lyon, Pennsylvania, the mining town behind Coaltown. It opened in New York on 16 March 1948 and nationally on 27 March, running 120 minutes. Critics were hostile: Time said 'St. Michael ought to sue' and James Agee declared himself founder of a 'Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to God'. It lost about $640,000 and was repossessed by Bank of America. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: The Keys of the Kingdom
decision: GREY: The subtitle file confirms the Legion's likely targets and adds one more. As a student Chisholm asks whether God sets value on creed, an accident of birth, and his rector says that He does. In China Chisholm says heathen priests are often good and noble men, tells the mandarin that the Methodist newcomers serve the same true God, and says no one is a Christian who is not tolerant. At Willie's death he prays the De profundis, tells him his salvation is his own doing and is thanked for not bullying him into heaven. Nothing denies the Church's claim outright, so it stays a weighable reservation rather than REJECT, but the drift towards indifferentism is now documented in the dialogue.
summary: Gregory Peck plays a Scottish priest whose fifty years, most of them as a missionary in China, are read from his diary in Fox's handsome adaptation of Cronin's bestseller.
synopsis: In 1938 a monsignor arrives at a Scottish parish to retire its elderly priest, Francis Chisholm, whose unorthodox preaching has drawn complaints, and reads his journal overnight. Francis's parents died after an anti-Catholic mob attacked his father; the girl he loved bore a child out of wedlock and died; at seminary he was rebuked for questioning what he was taught. Sent to China, he finds his mission church destroyed by flood, turns away converts who come only for rice, cures a mandarin's son but refuses the father's offer to convert out of gratitude, and rebuilds with the land the mandarin gives. An aristocratic nun, Mother Maria Veronica, despises him until his humility wins her over. Civil war reaches the mission, and his unbelieving friend Dr Willie Tulloch is killed. Methodist missionaries arrive and are welcomed. Chisholm goes home, and the monsignor lets him stay.
inclusion: Peck carries the film across half a century of one man's life, and the role brought him an Oscar nomination for best actor; Bosley Crowther praised his quiet force. The film drew four nominations in all, among them Arthur C. Miller's black-and-white photography and the art direction of its Chinese village. The portrait of a poor, stubborn missionary who will not buy converts with rice or favours is attractive, and Steven Greydanus calls the film an edifying celebration of Christian virtue in an imperfect hero. It is also long and vague in its piety. James Agee came to find its sincerity and ethics bland, Crowther thought it a surface shadow of Cronin's novel, and the Church that sent Chisholm barely appears. It is worth seeing for Peck and for its picture of missionary patience, with the doctrinal question below kept in mind.
themes: The film admires Chisholm's charity, humility and refusal to coerce belief. The Church itself is thin: he is never shown saying Mass or administering a sacrament, and the nearest is a joke about confession. Cronin's novel was openly sceptical of the Church's unique claim, and the film tones this down without removing it. As a student Chisholm asks whether God sets an exclusive value on creed, an accident of birth. In China he speaks well of heathen priests, tells the mandarin that the Methodist newcomers serve the same true God, and says no one is a Christian who is not tolerant. At Willie's deathbed he prays the De profundis but does not press him to believe, and Willie thanks him for it. Taken together, these lean towards the indifferentism Pius XI condemned in Mortalium animos.
history: Francis Chisholm is fictional. A. J. Cronin (1896-1981) was the son of a Catholic father and a Presbyterian mother and was schooled at St Aloysius' College, Glasgow, before becoming a doctor. He lost his faith as a medical student and later came back to belief in a Creator. The Keys of the Kingdom (1941) is his most openly religious novel: the life of a Scottish priest who spends most of it trying to build a mission in a China torn by civil war, told from a frame set in Scotland in 1938.
liberties: Fiction, from Cronin's novel. The script was shaped with Breen's office and two Jesuit advisers, Albert O'Hara and Wilfrid Parsons, to meet the Code's objections to the novel's worldly priests and false-stigmata episode. The novel's line comparing Christ and Confucius became a remark about Christians and Confucians. The Chinese village was made orderly and clean after the Chinese consul objected.
advisories:
War scenes with shelling and shooting; a main character is shot dead.

An anti-Catholic mob attacks the boy's father, and both parents drown.

An illegitimate birth and the young mother's death are referred to.

Long (about 137 minutes) and slow in places; suitable for older children and up.

The Legion of Decency noted statements by the priest open to a meaning contrary to Catholic doctrine.

grey.question: The Legion of Decency passed this film for all audiences but flagged statements by the priest open to a meaning not in accordance with Catholic doctrine. The dialogue shows what they are. As a student Chisholm asks whether God values creed, which he calls an accident of birth. In China he praises heathen priests, tells a mandarin that Methodist missionaries serve the same true God, and says no one is a Christian who is not tolerant. He lets his unbelieving friend die unpersuaded and is thanked for it. Nothing denies the Church outright, but the drift is towards indifferentism.

names: The Keys of the Kingdom, novel by A. J. Cronin (1941)

suitability.note: There is war fighting in which a main character is shot dead, an anti-Catholic mob and the drowning of the boy's parents, and a reference to a birth out of wedlock. At about 137 minutes it is long and slow for younger children, and several of the priest's remarks about other religions need an adult to explain what the Church actually teaches.

doctrine: The film's key lines touch the dogma that there is no salvation outside the Church. Pius IX restated it in Quanto conficiamur moerore (10 August 1863): it is well known Catholic teaching that no one can be saved outside the Catholic Church. In the same letter he allowed that those in invincible ignorance of the true religion who keep the natural law are not punished for that ignorance. That is the narrow ground on which Chisholm's charity towards Willie can be read in a Catholic sense; it does not make creed indifferent. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) defines indifferentism as the denial of a duty to worship God by the one true religion, and calls the view that all religions are equally good a form of it. Refusing 'rice Christians' is sound: the Church has always required that an adult come to baptism freely and with faith, not for material gain.
production: David O. Selznick bought the screen rights to Cronin's novel, planning to produce it for United Artists; when Selznick International closed in 1943, Twentieth Century-Fox acquired them. Nunnally Johnson wrote the first script, and Joseph L. Mankiewicz, who became producer, substantially rewrote it. Alfred Hitchcock was interested in directing but made Lifeboat instead. Gregory Peck, then relatively unknown, took the lead. The film premiered on 15 December 1944, runs 136 minutes and cost about $3 million. It had four Oscar nominations, including Peck's first for Best Actor. Reviews were mixed. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: God Needs Men
decision: GREY: The English subtitle file, a rough translation, sharpens the reservation. Thomas pronounces absolution over a woman who believes she is dying and gives the full formula to Joseph as he dies after hanging himself. With hosts he has baked, and prompted by an islander, he recites the Mass as far as the words of consecration; only the gendarmes' arrival stops him, after which he says he will not say Mass. The curé tells him he does not know what sacrilege is and later calls the islanders pagans and savages. The ending is the burial at sea, not a return to Mass. REJECT is arguable, since the film presents simulated sacraments with sympathy; kept at GREY for the editor because Thomas knows he is not a priest, submits, and the film never claims his acts are valid.
summary: On a priestless Breton island, a fisherman-sacristan is pushed by his parish into the priest's role, and the film watches him go too far.
synopsis: Île de Sein, off Brittany, in the mid-19th century. The islanders fish and loot wrecks, and their discouraged rector leaves. They will not do without the sacraments, so they turn to the sacristan, Thomas Gourvennec (Pierre Fresnay), a fisherman who can barely write. He agrees to lead prayers and preach on Sundays, insisting that he is not a priest. The pressure grows. He pronounces absolution over a woman who thinks she is dying, hears the confession of the young Joseph Le Berre (Daniel Gélin), who admits to a crime, and, with hosts he has baked, recites the Mass as far as the consecration. Gendarmes arrive escorting a priest from the mainland. Joseph hangs himself, and Thomas absolves him as he dies. The islanders defy the curé over the burial, and Thomas leads them out to give the body to the sea.
inclusion: Few films put the question so bluntly: what is a priest for, and what happens to people who lose one? Jean Aurenche and Pierre Bost adapted Henri Queffélec's novel, and Delannoy stages it with care. Robert Lefebvre's photography gives strong high-angle views of the island and of Thomas hemmed in by his parishioners, and the choral music is used heavily. Fresnay dominates as a decent, unlettered man frightened by what is being asked of him. The International Catholic Film Office (OCIC) gave it its prize at Venice in 1950, and the Canadian Catholic film review Séquences called it frankly religious. It also has real faults. Séquences found the acting theatrical, Fresnay's gestures included, and the island's poverty too polished and picturesque; Fr Beirnaert of the Jesuit review Études, quoted there, missed the novel's sea and wind. It is worth seeing for its subject and for Fresnay's committed central performance.
themes: The islanders' faith is crude but real: they want sacraments, not ideas, and they fear damnation. Thomas knows he is not a priest and says so, yet he pronounces absolution twice, and with hosts he has baked he recites the Mass as far as the consecration before the gendarmes interrupt him. The film treats him with great sympathy. The curé who comes with gendarmes is cold and authoritarian; he tells Thomas he does not know what sacrilege is and later calls the islanders pagans and savages. Séquences noted that the film sets a 'democratic' lay leader against an odious cleric, which is why Protestants and anticlericals liked it. Against that, Thomas refuses to say Mass and accepts that a parish must obey its priest, and the story rests on the need for an ordained priest.
history: Queffélec based his novel, Un recteur de l'île de Sein, loosely on events on Sein in 1641. When two Jesuit missionaries landed, they found that a fisherman, François Le Su, had acted as catechist and preacher since the rector's death. They sent him to study on the mainland; he was ordained and returned as the island's priest. Queffélec's sacristan oversteps his lay powers, but the novel still ends with him entering the seminary.
liberties: The film moves the story from the 17th century to the mid-19th century and drops the ending of both the history and the novel, in which the sacristan becomes a priest. It enlarges the two confession scenes and creates an open conflict between Thomas and an authoritarian curé, which is not in the novel. Bretons objected that the real Church had welcomed the fisherman rather than opposing him.
advisories:
A suicide, and the crime confessed by Joseph, are central to the plot.

The islanders loot shipwrecks; there are scenes of anger and confrontation with gendarmes.

No sexual content of note. Suitable for older children with an adult; the story's questions are for adults.

A layman pronounces absolution and recites the Mass over hosts as far as the consecration, and the film is more sympathetic to him than to the lawful priest; no layman can validly absolve or consecrate.

grey.question: A fisherman acting as sacristan pronounces absolution over two people he believes are dying, and with hosts he has baked recites the Mass as far as the consecration before gendarmes arrive. The film is plainly on his side. The lawful curé is cold, calls the islanders pagans and savages, and is defied when they bury a suicide at sea. Thomas does refuse to say Mass and accepts that a parish must obey its priest, and the International Catholic Film Office gave the film a prize. Whether it defends the priesthood by showing what is lost without it, or admires a layman's simulated sacraments, is the question.

names: Un recteur de l'Île de Sein, novel by Henri Queffélec (1944)

suitability.note: A suicide and a confessed crime are central, and the islanders loot wrecks and confront gendarmes. Nothing is graphic, but the film asks adult questions and sympathises with a layman who simulates sacraments, so it needs explanation.

doctrine: Only a priest can validly absolve and consecrate. Trent teaches that the priest alone has the power to forgive sins in the sacrament of penance (Session XIV, chapter 6 and canon 9) and that the power to consecrate belongs to those ordained (Session XXIII). A layman who pronounces the words of absolution or of consecration confers and effects nothing. In danger of death, the Church allows anyone to baptise, but not to absolve. A suicide who dies impenitent was refused ecclesiastical burial under the 1917 Code (canon 1240); this is the point on which Thomas and the curé clash. The rule is a discipline, not a judgement on the soul. The Church allows that God may be merciful to one who repents at the last. The film's Thomas is unsure of his powers and stops short of the consecration. The viewer should not take his example as approved.
production: Jean Delannoy filmed Henri Queffélec's 1944 novel Un recteur de l'Île de Sein, scripted by Jean Aurenche and Pierre Bost. It was produced by Paul Graetz's Transcontinental Films. Location work began on the Île de Sein, but the islanders' distrust of the unit led the crew to shoot the exteriors at Plouguerneau and to build a model of the village at Pantin, outside Paris, with interiors at the Billancourt studios. It was released on 4 October 1950 and runs 100 minutes. The French delegation first withdrew it from the 1950 Venice Festival for fear of offending the Church, then accepted it for screening because of its popularity, including among Catholics. It won a special prize at Berlin in 1951.

title: The Unfrocked One
decision: GREY: The film's thesis is plainly orthodox: holy orders leave an indelible mark, so the apostate's mock consecration is valid and therefore sacrilegious, the young priest consumes the wine to stop its profanation, and the ending gives the dying priest's absolution and the apostate's contrition. The sacrilege is shown as horror, not approved, so REJECT does not apply. It is grey because a valid-in-the-fiction consecration is staged in a cabaret for shock, and because no contemporary Catholic review (Centrale Catholique cote, Radio-Cinéma, La Croix) has been found; present treatment evidence is a ciné-club note, a traditionalist recommendation, a hostile blog and viewer reviews. Finding the 1954 Centrale Catholique cote would settle it.
summary: Pierre Fresnay plays an apostate priest who mocks the Church, and Pierre Trabaud the young convert who becomes a priest to win him back, in Joannon's blunt, provocative drama.
synopsis: In a German officers' camp in 1945, Maurice Morand reveals that he is a priest when he gives the last rites to the dying chaplain. Morand has left the Church and despises it, but the young Gérard Lacassagne is moved and decides to become a priest himself, against his family and his fiancée. After the war Morand, back at the Sorbonne, publishes an attack on religion, while Gérard, in the seminary, keeps trying to bring him back. In a cabaret Morand mockingly says the words of consecration over white wine; since he is still a priest, Gérard takes it for the Blood of Christ and drinks it rather than leave it to be profaned. After his ordination Gérard visits Morand once more. They quarrel and Morand strikes him, reopening an old wound. Dying, Gérard absolves him, and Morand is left in tears and prayer.
inclusion: Fresnay, who had played St Vincent de Paul in Monsieur Vincent and a lay 'rector' in Dieu a besoin des hommes, gives the film its force; even the hostile blogger Narkissos admires his conviction, though some viewers find him overemphatic. The opening, with a sick chaplain collapsing at Mass and Morand forced to reveal himself, is the passage even detractors praise. The ciné-club de Montereau calls the film incisive and violent, the dialogue often brilliant, and praises Trabaud and Nicole Stéphane; it won a Bronze Bear at Berlin in 1954. It is a thesis film in the old French Catholic manner, built on the sacramental character of the priesthood, and it argues its case with melodrama: its detractors find the later scenes close to grand guignol, and Narkissos, comparing it with Bresson and Melville, dismisses it. A traditionalist reviewer, by contrast, praises its classical theology and calls the craft exceptional.
themes: Everything rests on the doctrine that ordination imprints an indelible character. Because Morand is still a priest, his cabaret consecration is real, and his blasphemy is a sacrilege rather than a joke; Gérard treats the wine as the Blood of Christ and consumes it to stop its profanation. The film also shows the last rites and the slow growth of a vocation against family opposition. The ending turns on sacramental absolution given by a dying priest to the man who has killed him. Its detractors' complaint, that it relies on shock where Bresson worked by restraint, has force.
advisories:
A sacrilege against the Eucharist is shown on screen: an apostate priest mockingly consecrates wine in a cabaret, and a seminarian drinks it to prevent its profanation.

A newly ordained priest is fatally struck by the man he is trying to save; a death in a wartime prison camp.

Adult themes of apostasy and self-hatred. Older teenagers and adults.

French with subtitles.

grey.question: The film's theology is traditional: an ordained man stays a priest, so his mock consecration in a cabaret is real and sacrilegious, and the young priest drinks the wine rather than leave it to profanation. The sacrilege is shown as horror and the ending turns on absolution and contrition. The question is one of taste and reverence: whether staging a valid consecration for shock, with the drunkenness and vomiting viewers describe, serves the argument or cheapens the Sacrament. A 1954 Catholic film-office rating has not been found and would settle how it was judged at the time.

sources.title: Holy Orders
sources.claims: Indelible character of Orders; validity independent of minister's holiness

suitability.note: A blasphemous mock consecration in a cabaret, a drinking scene, suicidal despair and the violent death of a young priest. The ideas are heavy and the staging is melodramatic; older teenagers who know what the Mass is can handle it, younger children cannot.

doctrine: Holy Orders imprints an indelible character. The Council of Trent (session 23, canon 4, 1563) anathematised anyone who denies that the sacrament of Order imprints a character or that a man once a priest can become a layman again. A priest who has apostatised therefore keeps the power to consecrate, and if he says the words with the intention of doing what the Church does, the consecration is valid, though the act is a grave sacrilege. Trent also teaches that the validity of a sacrament does not depend on the minister's state of grace. In danger of death any priest, even one suspended or excommunicated, absolves validly (Trent, session 14, chapter 7), which explains why the film's absolutions hold. The film's assumption that a mock consecration in jest would still be valid is disputed by theologians: validity needs the intention to do what the Church does.
production: Joannon wrote the screenplay with Roland Laudenbach and Denys de La Patellière, for Gaumont and the Société Française de Cinématographie, from his own idea; no source novel is listed. It was shot in late 1953 at La Celle-Saint-Cloud and Joinville and released in France on 26 February 1954. Running 107 minutes, it won the Bronze Bear at the 4th Berlin International Film Festival. Pierre Fresnay had already played St Vincent de Paul in Monsieur Vincent. Nicole Stéphane played Catherine Grandpré. Reviews since have split: a ciné-club called it incisive and violent, while a hostile blogger compared it unfavourably with Bresson. No Centrale Catholique rating or La Croix review has been found.

title: The Secret Conclave
originalTitle: Gli uomini non guardano il cielo
alternateTitles: Men Do Not Look at Heaven
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified The Secret Conclave A-I (1952–53 season), a contemporary Catholic judgment, and Variety's review (Hift, May 1953) gives an independent, substantive assessment: a moving lead performance and a fine conclave sequence in a cheaply made, static film. The Exhibitor's 1953 review and the Diocese of Treviso production history establish the content. Pius X was beatified in 1951 and canonised in 1954, so rule (a) does not apply. Invented elements (the final Mass, a fictional countess) are disclosed.
summary: Umberto Scarpelli's biography of St Pius X frames the Pope's last weeks in 1914, as war approaches, around flashbacks to his country priesthood, Venice and the 1903 conclave.
synopsis: Summer 1914. The Archduke has been murdered, and Pius X, old and ill, does what he can to stop the coming war. When the Austrian ambassador asks him to bless his country's troops, he refuses to bless a war. His nephew, a young priest, comes to Rome to help him, and in a night of prayer the Pope's life is recalled in flashback: a poor boyhood, a scholarship to the seminary, years as a country priest caring for the poor and for families struck by cholera, charitable work as bishop of Mantua and patriarch of Venice. The 1903 conclave is staged at length: Austria's veto against Cardinal Rampolla, rejected by the cardinals, and the ballots that elect Cardinal Sarto against his own pleas. The film ends with the Pope going to say Mass for the last time, offering his life with the sacrifice of the altar.
inclusion: This is the only feature film about Pius X, made within months of his beatification by a Venetian company with a historian and a priest as advisers. Its strength is Henry Vidon, a Vatican Radio employee cast for his likeness to Sarto. Variety's reviewer called his performance moving and thoroughly expert, and praised the conclave in the Sistine Chapel, staged with a documentary sobriety. The same review found the script static, the treatment sometimes amateurish, the photography and editing weak and the English dubbing spotty. The acting, largely by stage actors, is slow and the style old-fashioned for 1952. It suits viewers who want the history of a modern saint told plainly. Prints are scarce: the Cineteca Nazionale and the Vatican Film Library hold copies.
themes: The film is about a priest who never stopped being a parish priest. Sarto's motto, to restore all things in Christ, frames the story, and his nephew lists the work of the pontificate: the fight against Modernism, the reform of sacred music, the clergy and canon law, the abolition of the veto, and the admission of children to Holy Communion. The conclave shows the Church refusing a secular power's interference. The Pope's counsel to the countess, to bear her cross rather than leave her marriage, is traditional spiritual direction. The ending presents the Mass as sacrifice, and the Pope's death as an offering for peace.
history: Giuseppe Sarto (1835–1914), born at Riese near Treviso, was a curate and parish priest in the Veneto, then bishop of Mantua (1884) and patriarch of Venice (1893). He was elected Pope on 4 August 1903 after Austria-Hungary's veto against Cardinal Rampolla was announced in the conclave; he abolished the veto in 1904. He condemned Modernism in 1907 and in 1910 allowed young children to receive Communion. He died on 20 August 1914, weeks into the war. Pius XII beatified him in 1951 and canonised him in 1954.
liberties: Pius X died in bed, not at Mass; the closing Mass is a dramatic compression. The scene with the Austrian ambassador dramatises a story told after his death that historians treat with caution. The countess played by Isa Miranda is a composite, and the nephew's night of remembrance is the film's framing device. Shooting began in 1951, before canonisation, and the film was released in the second half of 1952.
advisories:
Deaths from cholera; the Pope's illness and death.

Talk of the coming war; a woman betrayed by her husband.

Slow and old-fashioned; the English-dubbed version is uneven.

Suitable for all ages.

suitability.note: Rated A-I by the Legion of Decency. Cholera deaths and the Pope's own death are treated quietly. It is slow and old-fashioned, and the English dub is uneven, but a child who likes saints' lives will follow it.

doctrine: Pius X took as his motto 'to restore all things in Christ'. In 1903 he confirmed in the Motu proprio Tra le sollecitudini the use of Gregorian chant. He condemned Modernism in the decree Lamentabili (3 July 1907) and the encyclical Pascendi (8 September 1907). By the decree Sacra Tridentina (20 December 1905) he urged frequent, even daily, Communion, and by Quam singulari (8 August 1910) he lowered the age of first Communion to the age of discretion, about seven. The conclave sequence concerns the 'veto' of Austria, which Pius X abolished in 1904 under penalty of excommunication for any cardinal who conveyed such a veto. He was beatified by Pius XII in 1951 and canonised on 29 May 1954. The Pope's counsel to the countess to bear her cross matches the indissolubility of marriage as the Church has always taught it.
production: Cinelia Film of Venice produced it in 1951–52, with the Diocese of Treviso supplying historical advice, shortly after Pius X's beatification. Umberto Scarpelli directed from a screenplay by five writers. Henri Vidon, a Vatican Radio employee, was cast for his resemblance to Sarto. The film was about 94 minutes in black and white and was released in Italy as Gli uomini non guardano il cielo, and in English as The Secret Conclave. The National Legion of Decency rated it A-I. Variety's reviewer in 1953 praised Vidon and the conclave but found the script static and the dubbing poor. Copies are in the Cineteca Nazionale and the Vatican Film Library.

title: Teresa de Jesús
decision: PUBLISH: Gil de Muro's Carmelite survey, Alonso Franch's production study and the decine21 review give accessible, specific evidence of fidelity to Teresa's life and writings and of how the series stages prayer, the Inquisition and opposition to the reform; RTVE and the Universidad de Navarra fix identity. RTVE's 'modernity' framing and the medical aside in Alonso Franch are disclosed; neither is shown to be the series' own account of Teresa's mysticism.
summary: Josefina Molina's eight-hour TVE series, carried by Concha Velasco, follows Teresa of Ávila from the Encarnación to her death through illness, prayer, reform and opposition.
synopsis: The series picks Teresa up at twenty-three, a nun in the large, sociable Carmelite convent of the Encarnación in Ávila. Years of sickness and half-hearted prayer give way to a deeper conversion. Against the hostility of the town council and of many in her own order she founds San José, a small, poor, enclosed house, and then takes to the roads to found more. Her autobiography attracts the attention of the Inquisition; the friars opposed to the reform imprison John of the Cross. Each episode takes its title from one of her books. The eighth, 'Hija de la Iglesia', covers her last hours and her death as, in her own words, a daughter of the Church.
inclusion: This is the most ambitious attempt Spanish film or television has made at Teresa. Carmen Martín Gaite wrote the dialogue, the Teresian scholar Víctor García de la Concha advised on the scripts, and the Encarnación was rebuilt in the studio down to the colour of the habits and the refectory bowls. It was shot on 35mm, like a cinema feature. Concha Velasco spent days studying Discalced Carmelite life before filming; her Teresa is shrewd, funny, stubborn and often ill, and both the Carmelite writer Eduardo Gil de Muro and decine21 call it the performance of her career. The length is the point: the series has time for what most saints' films skip, from convent politics, money and letters to long dry stretches of prayer and the slow cost of a vocation.
themes: Mental prayer is the centre: Teresa's struggle to pray, her visions and raptures, and a reform built so that nuns can pray in poverty and enclosure. Molina, an agnostic, set out to show a woman walking towards holiness rather than the finished saint, and the ecstasies are played physically; Velasco arches and cries out. Alonso Franch writes that Molina filmed them without violating their mystery, and the series does not offer a medical explanation. RTVE's catalogue blurb sells Teresa as a pioneer of 'liberation of the spirit' and European modernity, a framing the series' own ending, on her dying profession of loyalty to the Church, does not bear out. Alonso Franch's article also repeats, as an aside, a modern claim that she was neurotic and epileptic; that is his remark, not the drama's thesis.
history: Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada (1515–1582) entered the Encarnación in 1535 and founded San José in 1562, the first of her reformed Carmels. The Inquisition held her autobiography for years but never condemned it. She was canonised in 1622 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970. The series was filmed in 1983, premiered in Ávila and broadcast on TVE in 1984.
liberties: Dialogue is newly written to sound natural rather than quoted from her books, and events years apart are brought together in single scenes. The physical staging of rapture and levitation is an interpretation. Eight hours still leave out a good deal of her life, and Gil de Muro records that the Teresian scholar Tomás Álvarez had reservations he does not spell out. Shorter versions exist: a feature-length condensation and a four-episode cut.
advisories:
Prolonged illness, convulsive ecstatic states, a death-bed scene and the imprisonment of John of the Cross.

Slow and dialogue-heavy over about eight hours; best for teenagers and adults.

Spanish with subtitles. The Ignatius Press DVD carries the full series rather than a condensed version.

suitability.note: Teresa's long illness, convulsive raptures, a deathbed and the imprisonment of John of the Cross are the hard parts, none of them graphic. At about eight hours of slow dialogue about prayer, it suits teenagers better than children.

doctrine: Teresa entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation at Ávila in November 1535 and professed there in 1536 (Catholic Encyclopedia). She founded the reformed convent of St Joseph on 24 August 1562, the first of the discalced Carmels. Her teaching is that mental prayer, the conversation of the soul with God, is open to all who persevere, and that visions and locutions are to be tested by learned confessors, as she did with Dominicans and Jesuits. The reform, begun with St John of the Cross among the friars in 1568, met opposition before the discalced province was set up on 22 June 1580 with the support of Philip II. She died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582, a day reckoned as 15 October because of the calendar reform, and her feast is 15 October. She was beatified in 1614 and canonised by Gregory XV in 1622.
production: Josefina Molina directed this Spanish television series of eight episodes of about 60 minutes. Concha Velasco plays Teresa; Carmen Martín Gaite wrote the script of the film version and José Nieto wrote the music. It ran on TVE-1 from 12 March to 30 April 1984, and a 222-minute film version was also made. Spanish Wikipedia describes it as based on Juan de Orduña's 1961 film. Velasco won an Antena de Oro and a Fotogramas de Plata, and the series won two TP de Oro awards.

title: Clare and Francis
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review and the reported reaction of the Assisi friars document a reverent, Church-loyal portrait with no invented romance; the producer's catalogue confirms Clare's vows are shown. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Here the inventions are dramatic connective tissue, and the friars' objections concern depth and craftsmanship, not distortion of either vocation.
summary: A two-part Rai drama that tells the conversions of Francis and Clare side by side; its Clare is convincing, its young Francis less so.
synopsis: Assisi, 1198: the merchant families storm the towers of the nobility. Francesco, the cloth merchant Bernardone's son, is throwing stones; Chiara, a girl of the noble Offreduccio household, is trapped inside her besieged home. Years later the two meet again across a family table. Francesco renounces his father's wealth, rebuilds a ruined chapel with his own hands and attracts companions to a life of poverty. Chiara watches, and on the night of Palm Sunday she slips out of her house. In the little church Francesco has restored she lays aside her shoes and fine clothes, he cuts her hair, and she vows poverty, chastity and obedience. The rest of the drama follows the two communities, and the two friends, as they grow.
inclusion: Most films about Francis treat Clare as a footnote; this one gives her equal weight, and Mary Petruolo plays her as calm and self-possessed from the start. Steven Greydanus judged it a 'pick' and found the converted Francis 'joyful in humility' and devoted to the Church, though he thought the drama much less successful with Francis's worldly youth. It is a conventional Lux Vide production of the kind Rai made often in the 2000s, and some Assisi friars complained about its sets and images. Its best quality is restraint about the relationship at its centre. Father Vincenzo Coli of the Sacro Convento praised it for avoiding the cliché of the 'two little sweethearts', a romance for which there is no historical evidence.
themes: The vows are shown explicitly and treated as the climax: Clare's flight, tonsure and profession are staged as a consecration rather than an elopement. Poverty is a choice for Christ, not a social programme, and Francis's submission to the Church is part of his character. The friendship between the two saints is presented as love of each other in Christ. Some friars at Assisi, quoted in La Repubblica, felt that Francis's theological and human depth was thinned for television, a fair criticism of a drama that is stronger on gesture than on prayer.
history: Clare (1194–1253) left her family on Palm Sunday night 1212 and was received by Francis at the Porziuncola. She led the Poor Ladies at San Damiano for over forty years and outlived Francis by twenty-seven. Her rule was the first written by a woman to receive papal approval.
liberties: The early meetings between the two, their families' dinner and much of the dialogue are invented. The siege that opens the film draws on Assisi's civil conflict of 1198–1200 but is shaped for drama. Greydanus thought the portrait of Francis before his conversion weak and unconvincing. The film calls the church of Clare's profession simply one Francis restored; tradition places it at the Porziuncola.
advisories:
Mild violence in the street fighting that opens the film.

A few unpleasant images of leprosy.

Two long episodes (about 200 minutes); younger viewers may need it in parts. The US DVD offers Italian or an English dub.

suitability.note: The street fighting at the start and a few images of leprosy are the only rough moments, and there is no romance between the saints. At about 200 minutes in two parts it is long; children of eight or nine will follow it best an episode at a time.

doctrine: The Catholic Encyclopedia records that Clare left home on the night of Palm Sunday 1212 and that at the Porziuncola Francis cut her hair and clothed her in a rough tunic and veil. Gregory IX granted the Poor Ladies the Privilege of Poverty in 1228, securing their right to own nothing. Innocent IV confirmed Clare's own rule, keeping absolute poverty, on 9 August 1253, two days before her death. Alexander IV canonised her in 1255; her feast is 12 August. Gregory IX canonised Francis on 16 July 1228; his feast is 4 October, and the Impression of his Stigmata is kept on 17 September. Innocent III gave verbal approval to Francis's first rule; Honorius III approved the final rule in 1223. Pius XII named Clare patroness of television in 1958.
production: Lux Vide made the two-part drama with Rai Fiction and Rai Trade, produced by Luca Bernabei. Francesco Arlanch wrote the story and screenplay; Giovanni Galasso photographed it and Marco Frisina wrote the score. Fabrizio Costa directed, with Ettore Bassi as Francis and Mary Petruolo as Clare, and a supporting cast including Lando Buzzanca and the Spanish actress Ángela Molina as Francis's parents. Rai 1 broadcast it on 7 and 8 October 2007, around the feast of St Francis, to 6.7 and 7.8 million viewers. The friars of the Sacro Convento at Assisi were divided: some called it dignified and free of invented romance, others found it technically weak and thin on Francis's spirituality. Ignatius Press issued it in the United States with Italian and English soundtracks.

title: Saint Rita
decision: GREY: identity secure (FilmTV, Wikipedia, Ignatius); Rita was canonised in 1900, so neither hard rule applies, and nothing reported suggests post-conciliar framing. The only independent assessment is Greydanus's one-paragraph 'Pick' (NCR, 2007), which praises it but gives no account of its treatment beyond calling the arranged marriage a liberty (it is in fact traditional). Settles with a detailed review or a documented viewing of the Ignatius DVD covering Paolo's conversion and murder, Rita's prayer about her sons, her admission to the convent, the thorn wound and the presentation of her obedience in marriage.

grey.question: The only independent assessment is Steven Greydanus's one-paragraph recommendation of the DVD. It praises the film but says little about how it treats Rita's faith, and the one liberty it names, her arranged marriage, is in fact the traditional account. As a modern Italian television production it cannot be assumed sound. A detailed review or documented viewing covering Paolo's conversion and murder, Rita's prayer about her sons, her admission to the convent and the wound of the thorn would settle it.

summary: Lux Vide's two-part Italian television life of Rita of Cascia: unwilling bride, peacemaking wife and widow, and finally Augustinian nun, amid the blood feuds of fourteenth-century Umbria.
synopsis: Rita Lotti, the only child of elderly parents in the hills above Cascia, wants to become a nun, but her parents arrange her marriage to Paolo Mancini, a hot-tempered young man from a family caught up in local feuds. Through patience and prayer she draws him away from violence, and they raise two sons. The feud does not end with his change of heart. After she loses her husband and her sons, Rita seeks admission to the Augustinian convent in Cascia, where she must first make peace between the families before she can begin her life as a religious.
inclusion: It is the fullest screen life of Rita of Cascia, one of the most popular saints of Italian devotion. It was made in 2004 by Lux Vide, a company that specialised in television lives of saints, and broadcast on Canale 5 in two parts. Vittoria Belvedere plays Rita from girlhood to old age, opposite Martin Crewes as her husband Paolo, and Mgr Marco Frisina, the Roman priest-composer, wrote the score. Steven Greydanus gave the Ignatius Press DVD a short 'Pick' in the National Catholic Register, calling it engaging and edifying, with a crisp screenplay, solid performances and good production values, and comparing its feud plot to The Godfather. He recommended the Italian soundtrack with subtitles over the English dub.
themes: The film's subject is forgiveness in a culture of vendetta: a wife who draws her husband away from violence, a mother who wants her sons to forgive rather than avenge their father, and a widow who enters religious life only after reconciling the feuding families. Marriage, motherhood and the convent appear as stages of one vocation, which is the traditional shape of Rita's life. What has not been checked is the framing, for instance whether her obedience in marriage is shown as a virtue or as an injustice, and how the miraculous elements are handled; Greydanus raises no doctrinal problem.
history: Rita (c. 1381–1457; the 1912 Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1386–1456) married at twelve in obedience to her parents, lived eighteen years as a wife and mother, saw her husband murdered and prayed that her sons would not avenge him; both died reconciled to God. Refused at first by the Augustinians of Cascia, she was admitted after persistent pleading. She was canonised in 1900.
liberties: Greydanus says the film takes licence with the few known facts and singles out the arranged marriage against her wish for the convent; that marriage is in fact the traditional account given by the Catholic Encyclopedia. Other inventions of incident and dialogue have not been documented.
advisories:
Restrained menace and violence, including killings in a feud and a possible threat of rape.

Suitable for older children and up with parents; not rated.

Italian with English subtitles, or an English dub.

title: Saint Philip Neri: I Prefer Heaven
decision: PUBLISH: Edoardo Aldo Cerrato of the Oratorian Confederation's procura, the best-qualified critic available, judges the portrait of Philip's priesthood, confession and obedience 'sostanzialmente positiva' while listing the historical errors, which are disclosed here. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Unlike Bakhita and Moscati, the inventions here alter chronology and the Oratory's social make-up, not Philip's own vocational choices or his obedience.
summary: Gigi Proietti makes a warm, mischievous Philip Neri in Campiotti's two-part Rai drama, which is generous with invention but true to the saint's spirit.
synopsis: Filippo, already a priest, arrives in sixteenth-century Rome meaning to join Ignatius of Loyola's missionaries bound for the Indies. Instead he finds his mission in the streets around him: gangs of half-starved boys, families in debt, young men drifting. He gathers the boys, feeds them, teaches them to pray and plays with them, and his house becomes the Oratory. Opposition comes from the powerful and from Church authority, which at one point suspects him, and he bears it without breaking with the Church. In the second part the Oratory opens to adults, and young men formed there, among them a fictionalised Cesare Baronio, become priests of a new congregation.
inclusion: Gigi Proietti, a great Roman comic actor, was a natural Philip: shrewd, playful, quick to deflate pride, and plainly a man of prayer. Cerrato praised both him and the sets, and the drama mixes comedy with child poverty and illness. Its spiritual instincts are good. Cerrato, who saw it before broadcast at the producer's invitation, singled out a priest who goes to confession as well as hears it, who stays humbly faithful to the Church under trial, and who joins work and contemplation without setting them against each other. Several of the saint's own short prayers are woven into the dialogue. As history it is unreliable; as a picture of what a joyful priest looks like, it works.
themes: Confession is central. Philip hears the confessions of the boys and of Rome, and the film also shows him going to confession himself. Obedience under pressure is the other thread: when Church authority doubts him, he submits rather than rebels. His humour serves holiness. The recurring line 'State buoni, se potete' ('Be good, if you can') is invented, as Cerrato notes, but it fits the saint's gentle realism. The Oratory's prayer, music and charity are shown as means of bringing young people to the sacraments, not as social work alone.
history: Philip Neri (1515–1595) came to Rome as a young layman, lived there for years as a lay catechist and hermit in the city, and was ordained only in 1551. The Oratory grew from informal gatherings for prayer and spiritual conversation open to men of every class; the Congregation of the Oratory was approved in 1575. He was canonised in 1622.
liberties: Large. Philip arrives as a middle-aged priest, not the young layman he was; his meeting with Persiano Rosa is rearranged; the Oratory becomes chiefly a refuge for street boys rather than a gathering of young men and adults of all classes; Baronio is heavily fictionalised; and many episodes are invented outright. Cerrato lists these 'incongruenze storiche' while defending the film's spirit.
advisories:
Child poverty, hunger, illness and death, including the deaths of children.

Some menace from street gangs and from powerful enemies; no graphic violence is described in the sources.

Suitable for families with older children; the history needs correcting with a biography.

Italian with English or Spanish subtitles on the Ignatius DVD.

title: Saint Anthony: The Miracle Worker of Padua
decision: GREY: Identity and broad content are established (Italian and English Wikipedia, AlloCiné, the Città Nuova preview, the Messenger of Saint Anthony), but every account of the film's treatment comes from interested Catholic sources, and the March 2002 La Repubblica and Corriere della Sera notices cited for its historical failings could not be read. Not HOLD, because the film is clearly identified. An independent review or a transcript checking the invented early life, Teresa's role and the 'human rights' framing would move it to PUBLISH or to reservations.
summary: A Lux Vide television life of the Portuguese Franciscan, told in flashback by the sick friar, with Daniele Liotti as Anthony and an invented companion friar.
synopsis: In 1221 a ship bringing two friars back from Africa is wrecked off Sicily. Antonio is gravely ill; his companion, Giulietto, is a cheerful, simple brother. Sheltered by a community of friars, Antonio tells them his life. Born into the Portuguese nobility, he turns down the knighthood and the war his father intends for him and enters religion instead. He joins the Franciscans, goes as a missionary to Morocco and is driven back by illness. In Italy he meets Francis of Assisi and is sent out to preach and teach. His sermons attack pride and usury, he takes the side of the poor, and the healings attributed to him make him famous. He insists that God, not he, works the miracles.
inclusion: This was the first substantial screen life of Anthony since Pietro Francisci's little-known film of 1949, and Italian television treated it as an event: the Canale 5 premiere on 1 April 2002 drew about seven million viewers. Lux Vide made it with the cooperation of the friars of the Basilica in Padua, shot it in Spain in five weeks, and gave it a Marco Frisina score. The makers say little is documented of Anthony's early years, so those were largely invented, with historians and the Basilica's friars consulted. Daniele Liotti plays Anthony as a learned, ascetic preacher, set against Enrico Brignano's Giulietto, an invented friar who stands for Franciscan simplicity. The friars' own Messenger praised the casting and the staging of the miracles; no independent critic's review could be read. It is widely available with English subtitles on DVD and Catholic streaming services.
themes: The Catholic content is plain: a vocation chosen against a father's ambitions, the Franciscan ideal of poverty, preaching against sin and usury, and miracles worked through prayer. The Messenger of Saint Anthony points to Anthony's line that he does not work miracles, God does, which keeps the wonders tied to grace rather than to the saint's own power. The publicity leans towards a modern reading: the Città Nuova preview calls Anthony a forerunner of human-rights defenders, and the stress on his campaign for the poor may tilt the story towards social reform. How far the film itself carries that framing, and how it handles his doctrinal preaching and the sacraments, has not been checked against any independent account.
history: Fernando de Bulhões was born at Lisbon about 1195 and joined the Canons Regular of St Augustine. In 1220 the bodies of five Franciscans killed in Morocco were brought to Coimbra, and he left to join the Friars Minor, taking the name Anthony. He sailed for Morocco but fell ill, and the ship was driven to Sicily in 1221. He attended the Franciscan chapter at Assisi that year, was sent to a hermitage, and his gift for preaching was discovered by chance at an ordination. St Francis made him the order's first lector in theology. He preached in northern Italy and southern France against heresy, usury and injustice, and settled at Padua, where he died on 13 June 1231 at Arcella, aged about thirty-six. Gregory IX canonised him at Spoleto on 30 May 1232, within a year, and Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church on 16 January 1946.
liberties: The makers acknowledge that the early life is largely invented, including the clash with his father over knighthood and war. Giulietto is an invented character. Teresa, played by Vittoria Puccini, is not a known historical figure, and her role in the story could not be established. According to Wikipedia, La Repubblica and Corriere della Sera faulted the film's historical fidelity at its premiere; those reviews could not be read.
advisories:
A shipwreck, serious illness and scenes of miraculous healing.

No sexual content or strong language is reported; the role of a young woman in Anthony's early life is unverified.

Suitable for families; distributed unrated.

The early life is largely invented and is not a reliable guide to the saint's biography.

grey.question: This Lux Vide television film is a devout life of St Anthony, made with the cooperation of the friars of Padua, but no independent review of its treatment could be found: the detailed accounts come from the friars' own Messenger and from the producers. The makers admit the early life is largely invented, Italian critics reportedly faulted its history, and its publicity presents Anthony as a forerunner of human rights. An independent review, or a transcript showing how it handles his preaching, miracles and invented characters, would settle it.

doctrine: Anthony is the Doctor Evangelicus, so named by Pius XII, who proclaimed him a Doctor of the Church on 16 January 1946, for his sermons on Scripture. Canonisation is the Church's infallible declaration that a servant of God is in heaven, and the process took under a year for Anthony. The film shows him insisting that God, not he, works the miracles: the Church teaches that miracles are works of God and that a saint intercedes (Council of Trent, Session 25, on the invocation of saints). The devotion to St Anthony as the finder of lost things, and the 'Anthony's bread' for the poor, grew from the later Middle Ages; the Church allows but does not require them. His feast is 13 June.
production: Umberto Marino directed this Italian television film for Canale 5, from a script by Marino, Alessandra Caneva and Fernando Muraca. Luca Bernabei produced it and Marco Frisina wrote the music. It ran 102 minutes and was broadcast in 2002 on Canale 5, where more than seven million viewers watched the premiere. Critics faulted its lack of historical adherence.

title: Saint John Bosco: Mission to Love
decision: PUBLISH: A detailed Salesian review (interested but specific and critical) documents catechesis, Dominic Savio, Bosco's own words on holiness and his obedience to the Pope in the conflict with his archbishop, and lists the compressions and renamed characters disclosed here. Rai Teche and RaiPlay fix identity. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Here inventions are composites and telescoping that do not alter Bosco's vocation or obedience.
summary: Flavio Insinna plays Don Bosco in a brisk, compressed Rai/Lux Vide life of the Turin priest who built schools and a religious family for abandoned boys.
synopsis: A Piedmontese farm boy who lost his father young, Giovanni Bosco follows his mentor into the seminary and arrives in Turin as a young priest. The city is full of hungry, exploited and violent boys, some in prison. He gathers them on Sundays, feeds them, teaches them catechism and a trade, and is chased from site to site by suspicious neighbours, officials and clergy. A wealthy noblewoman, the Marchesa Barolo, helps and then drops him. His mother Margherita comes to cook for the boys. Dominic Savio arrives. A liberal official, played by Charles Dance, schemes against him, and his friendship with the archbishop turns to conflict, which Bosco ends by submitting at the Pope's request. The Salesian congregation is founded to carry the work on.
inclusion: Flavio Insinna, later a popular television host, plays Bosco, with Lina Sastri as Mamma Margherita and Charles Dance as the liberal official who opposes him. The film does what the best Bosco lives do: it shows a priest whose kindness to delinquent boys always aims at their souls. It quotes Bosco's own sayings on holiness, gives time to the catechism lessons, and introduces Dominic Savio, the pupil he raised to sanctity. The Salesian reviewer FrMike judges that it presents Don Bosco's mission and personality well, while poking at details: the repeated 'Father Bosco' of the dub, an Oratory placed miles out in the country, and needless name changes. He also found the Italian-origin lines well dubbed into English for the US DVD.
themes: The Preventive System is shown as religion, reason and kindness, with the sacraments and catechism at its heart, not as a secular method. Bosco's priesthood is active and pastoral, and his holiness is ordinary hard work and trust in Providence. The best scene, by the Salesian reviewer's account, is his conflict with the archbishop: the film shows an early friendship, the archbishop's zeal for training priests, his view of Bosco as proud, and Bosco's eventual humbling of himself in obedience to the Pope to end the dispute. Anticlerical politics of the Risorgimento form the background.
history: John Bosco (1815–1888) opened his Oratory at Valdocco in 1846, founded the Salesians in 1859 and the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians in 1872. His long dispute with Archbishop Lorenzo Gastaldi of Turin in the 1870s–80s was settled under Leo XIII. Dominic Savio died in 1857 aged fourteen. Bosco was canonised in 1934.
liberties: Events from 1844 to 1882 are telescoped, so Mamma Margherita (d. 1856) and Joseph Cafasso (d. 1860) are present at a finale set decades after their deaths. Opponents are renamed: the Salesian reviewer notes that the vicar Cavour becomes the 'Prefect Clementi', who later absorbs Urbano Rattazzi, and that in the version he saw Archbishop Gastaldi becomes 'Cardinal Fassati'. The Oratory is placed in open country rather than on Turin's edge.
advisories:
Neglected and abused children, prison scenes, illness and death.

Scuffles and street violence of a mild, television kind.

Good for families with children over ten, with an adult on hand to correct the compressed history.

Shot partly in English with British supporting actors; Italian and English tracks exist, and the English-subtitled Italian version condenses the dialogue.

suitability.note: Neglected and abused boys, prison scenes, illness and a boy's death are shown with the mildness of television. Street scuffles are brief, and the long length (196 minutes) and compressed history are the main difficulties for younger children.

doctrine: Bosco's preventive system rests on frequent Confession and Communion, daily Mass and a cheerful, watchful kindness, in which the teacher is father, adviser and friend. He opened his oratory in Turin in 1841 and the Salesian Society, approved by Pius IX provisionally in 1869 and finally in 1874. The church of Mary Help of Christians at Valdocco was consecrated on 9 June 1868. Domenico Savio, who died in 1857 aged fourteen, was one of his boys. The film shows Bosco submitting to the Pope's wish to end his dispute with the archbishop, which is the Catholic rule of obedience to lawful ecclesiastical authority. Pius XI canonised him in 1934; his feast is 31 January.
production: Lux Vide produced this two-part Rai Fiction drama, directed by Lodovico Gasparini from a script by Graziano Diana, with Luca Bernabei as producer. Flavio Insinna played Bosco and a British cast, including Charles Dance, took the supporting parts, so a good part was spoken in English. Marco Frisina wrote the music. It was shown on Rai 1 on 22 and 23 September 2004 and runs 196 minutes. The Salesian reviewer on the record found the history telescoped, with Cavour renamed Clementi and then merged with Rattazzi, and Gastaldi renamed Cardinal Fassati, but praised the scene in which Bosco humbles himself to the Pope. Ignatius Press issued it on DVD in the United States.

title: Maria Goretti
decision: GREY: The English subtitles settle what the earlier record left open. Maria refuses Alessandro by naming the sin and warning him of hell, the assault is brief and not lingered on, and on her deathbed she forgives him and asks to have him with her in heaven; his repentance follows. On the saint the film is sound. The reservation (editor ruling, 2026-10-11) is liturgical: Mass and Communion in 1902 are given in post-conciliar vernacular form ("The Body of Christ. Amen"; "Go, the Mass is over"), which places the reformed rite in a pre-conciliar saint's life as if it were the Church's worship of her day.
summary: Giulio Base's Rai film of the Goretti story, told in flashback from a hospital bed, with Martina Pinto as the devout farm girl killed in 1902.
synopsis: July 1902, the Pontine Marshes. Maria Goretti, not yet twelve, is rushed to hospital with stab wounds while carabinieri protect twenty-year-old Alessandro Serenelli from a lynch mob. As her mother Assunta waits and the Passionist Padre Basilio prays at her bedside, the film goes back. The Gorettis and the Serenellis share a farmhouse as illiterate labourers on a landowner's estate, in a district ravaged by malaria. Maria is cheerful, generous and preparing for her First Communion. Alessandro, raised by a drunken, irreligious father who resents Luigi Goretti's help, clings to his friendship with the girl. Illness and death strike the Goretti family, poverty deepens, and Alessandro's attention turns to menace. When Maria resists his assault, he stabs her. Dying, she forgives him.
inclusion: Rai broadcast the film in February 2003 for the centenary of Maria's death, and nearly ten million Italians watched it. Lux Vide made it with the patronage of the Passionist Congregation, which had promoted her cause, and with a score by Ennio and Andrea Morricone. Steven Greydanus, in the National Catholic Register, judged it dramatically effective, devout and responsible with the historical facts. The independent notices found are cooler: the most-read FilmTV.it review calls it conventional television drama, slow, didactic and peopled with one-dimensional characters, though it credits Martina Pinto and Fabrizio Bucci, and ranks it below Genina's 1949 Heaven over the Marshes. It is the more literal of the two films, framed through the memories of a Passionist priest, and keeps close to the familiar account of the martyrdom and the forgiveness.
themes: The film is about purity and forgiveness. Maria's piety is shown through prayer and her preparation for First Communion, which she receives; her father calls hatred a disease whose only cure is Jesus. When Alessandro attacks her she refuses by naming the sin and warning him of hell, and dying she forgives him and asks to have him with her in heaven: the traditional reading of her death. Alessandro is given a background of neglect and an irreligious, drinking father, which explains him without excusing him; his repentance is shown at her bedside and in a closing title. Padre Basilio, who cites Rerum novarum against the landowners, recovers from a crisis over his vocation through her example.
history: Maria Goretti was born at Corinaldo in 1890. Her family, ruined by poverty, settled in 1899 at Le Ferriere near Nettuno, sharing a house with the Serenellis; her father died of malaria soon after. On 5 July 1902 Alessandro Serenelli tried to rape her and, when she refused, stabbed her fourteen times. She forgave him and died the next day. He repented in prison, was released after twenty-seven years, asked her mother's pardon and became a Capuchin lay brother. Pius XII beatified her in 1947 and canonised her in 1950.
liberties: No detailed comparison with the historical record has been published; Greydanus found the film responsible with the facts. The framing through Padre Basilio's memories is a dramatic device, and his crisis over leaving the priesthood and the Countess Mazzoleni (Claudia Koll) appear to be inventions. Alessandro's plea for forgiveness at Maria's hospital bedside is invented; historically his repentance came in prison years later. The Communion and dismissal formulas, as subtitled, are those of the modern rite, an anachronism for 1902.
advisories:
Restrained but frank sexual menace and an attempted rape; a fatal stabbing (Greydanus). The dialogue of the assault is brief.

Death of a parent from illness; poverty and a drunken, abusive father.

Teens and up.

sources.claims: Art. 5: faith is not the only cause of martyrdom; all virtuous deeds referred to God are professions of faith

grey.question: On St Maria Goretti herself the film is sound: she refuses Alessandro by calling the act a sin, the assault is handled briefly, and she dies forgiving him and wanting him with her in heaven. The reservation is the liturgy. Mass and Communion in 1902 are shown with the vernacular formulas of the post-conciliar rite, an anachronism that presents the reformed Mass as the worship of her time. Viewers who accept that liberty will find an otherwise faithful account.

suitability.note: The attempted rape is brief and not shown in detail, but the sexual menace is plain and the fatal stabbing and her death in hospital are hard to watch. Older children who know the story will find a clear example of purity and forgiveness; a parent should watch with them.

doctrine: Pius XII beatified Maria Goretti on 27 April 1947, with her mother present, and canonised her on 24 June 1950 in St Peter's Square before a crowd of about half a million. She is venerated as a martyr. St Thomas Aquinas teaches that faith is not the only cause of martyrdom: any virtuous act referred to God is a profession of faith, so a death suffered in defence of chastity can be martyrdom (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 124, a. 5). The Passionists guided her spiritual formation and promoted her cause, and her remains rest in their basilica at Nettuno. Her feast is 6 July, the day she died. Her deathbed forgiveness of Alessandro follows Our Lord's prayer for His executioners (Luke 23:34).
production: Lux Vide and Rai Fiction made the film in 2002 for the centenary of Maria's death, with the patronage of the Passionist Congregation. Francesco Contaldo wrote the story and screenplay; Luca and Matilde Bernabei produced; Fabrizio Lucci photographed it; Ennio Morricone and his son Andrea wrote the score. Giulio Base, who directed, also plays the hospital doctor. Rai 1 broadcast it on 23 February 2003 to about 9.9 million viewers, a 35 per cent share, and TV2000 and Rai Premium have repeated it.
