title: Joseph of Nazareth
alternateTitles: Gli amici di Gesù – Giuseppe di Nazareth
Joseph of Nazareth: The Man Closest to Christ
decision: GREY: The subtitle file corrects the record and sharpens the question. Joseph is not a widower: his betrothed was killed at Bethlehem years before and he has never married, and the brethren are his nephews Joses, Simon and Judas, so Mary's perpetual virginity is kept on St Jerome's reading. The virginal conception is plain, and at his death Joseph addresses Jesus as Lord and God. The weak point is the annunciation to Joseph: he asks whether Mary was forced, suspects a village youth and says he trusts his eyes, and a rabbi advises marrying her and repudiating her quietly. That suspicion, allowed by some Fathers but rejected by Jerome and St Thomas, is for the reader to weigh. Not REJECT; not PUBLISH while the only assessment is one present-day Catholic critic.
summary: Lux Vide's television life of St Joseph, with Tobias Moretti as a carpenter who works on Herod's Temple, accepts Mary's child, and raises Jesus in Nazareth.
synopsis: Joseph, a carpenter of David's line who has mourned for ten years a betrothed killed in Bethlehem, works on Herod's rebuilding of the Temple, where the king learns his name and praises his skill. He lives with his nephews Joses, Simon and Judas; Judas dies after a clash with Roman soldiers. Joseph is betrothed to the young Mary. When he learns she is pregnant he asks whether she was forced or unfaithful and will not believe her, and a rabbi advises him to marry her and put her away quietly. An angel in a dream tells him the child is conceived by the Holy Spirit. After the birth in Bethlehem, Herod identifies the child through the craftsman he knows, and the family flees into Egypt. Back in Nazareth, Simon joins the Zealots and kills Joses as a traitor. Joseph dies with Jesus beside him, and Simon repents.
inclusion: Joseph rarely gets a film of his own, and this one, the first of Lux Vide's Friends of Jesus films and first shown on Canale 5 in January 2000, takes him seriously as a man with a trade, a family and a conscience. Tobias Moretti plays him as a vigorous craftsman rather than an old man, and Steven Greydanus found the result an attractive picture of Joseph as head of the Holy Family. There are good ideas: Joseph's distaste for the state of Herod's Temple foreshadows Christ's cleansing of it, and his resistance to early zealots anticipates Christ's refusal of armed means. The weaknesses are invention and contrivance. Greydanus finds Herod's acquaintance with Joseph unconvincing and the plotting round Mary's silence frustrating. Marco Frisina wrote the score. It suits families who know the Gospel accounts well enough to tell the inventions from the text.
themes: The centre is Joseph's obedience: a just man who accepts the angel's word and the care of the incarnate Son. The virginal conception is stated plainly, and Mary's perpetual virginity is kept: Joseph has never married, and the brethren of the Lord are his nephews, as St Jerome held. Joseph's first reaction is the weak point. He asks whether Mary was forced or unfaithful and trusts his eyes over her word, while she offers to accept punishment and calls him a just man. Some Fathers allowed that Joseph suspected Mary; St Jerome and St Thomas held that he did not, but was perplexed before a mystery. At his death Joseph addresses Jesus as the Lord's anointed, his Lord and his God.
history: The Gospels say little of Joseph: a just man of David's line, a craftsman of Nazareth, betrothed to Mary, who took her as his wife after an angel's message, went to Bethlehem, fled into Egypt and returned to Nazareth. He last appears when Jesus is twelve. That he was an older widower with children from an earlier marriage comes from the second-century Protoevangelium of James; St Jerome held instead that he was a virgin and that the brethren were cousins. The film follows Jerome.
liberties: Joseph's earlier betrothed, Herod's acquaintance with him through the Temple works, and the king's identification of the child through him are invented. The plan to marry Mary and repudiate her quietly is a speculative reading of Matthew. The Lord's brethren become Joseph's nephews Joses, Simon and Judas; James is left out, Judas dies young, and Joses is killed by his brother Simon, a Zealot, who repents at Joseph's deathbed. This sits awkwardly with the tradition linking Simon and Jude to the apostles of those names.
advisories:
Herod's threat to the child and the flight into Egypt; a clash with Roman soldiers; one nephew is killed by his brother.

Joseph suspects Mary of infidelity and confronts her angrily.

Suitable for older children and families.

Several episodes in the Holy Family's life are invented, and Joseph's suspicion of Mary goes beyond the reading of St Jerome and St Thomas.

grey.question: This Lux Vide film keeps the doctrine intact: the virginal conception is plain, Joseph has never married, and the Lord's brethren are his nephews, as St Jerome held. The question is its portrait of Joseph's first reaction. Before the angel speaks he asks whether Mary was forced, suspects a village youth and says he trusts his eyes over her word, and a rabbi advises him to marry her and repudiate her quietly. Some Fathers allowed such a suspicion, but Jerome and St Thomas held that Joseph never doubted her. The film also invents Herod's acquaintance with Joseph and has one nephew killed by his brother.

title: Saint Peter
decision: PUBLISH: The English subtitle file supplies the transcript the earlier question asked for. Peter's primacy is explicit: Christ's promise at Caesarea Philippi, on this rock I will build my church, is given in full; Peter is called first among the apostles; and at the Council of Jerusalem he closes the debate on his own authority and rules that Gentiles are to be baptised and saved by the grace of the Lord. The Last Supper presents Christ's body given in sacrifice and the new and eternal covenant. Quo Vadis and the inverted crucifixion follow tradition. Talk of embracing everyone refers to the Gentiles' admission, not to modern dialogue. Identity: Italian Wikipedia; content: Dove, CatholicMom and the dialogue check.
summary: Omar Sharif plays Peter from the days after the Crucifixion to his own death in Nero's Rome, in Lux Vide's two-part drama drawn from Acts and tradition.
synopsis: After the Crucifixion Peter is crushed by his denial and doubts he can lead the apostles. The risen Christ appears and forgives him, and at Pentecost the apostles receive the Holy Spirit and preach openly. Stephen is stoned, Saul persecutes the Church and is converted on the road to Damascus, Peter baptises the centurion Cornelius, and the apostles meet in Jerusalem to settle the admission of Gentiles before dispersing. In the second part an aged Peter reaches Rome in 64, on the day Paul is arrested. He works among the poor while invented subplots follow a gladiator and his family and a pair of young lovers. After the great fire Nero blames the Christians. Peter leaves the city, meets Christ on the road, turns back, gives himself up so that others may go free, and is crucified upside down at his own request.
inclusion: Omar Sharif's Peter is the reason to watch. Reviewers of different stripes single him out: the Dove Foundation's Edwin Carpenter calls the performance compassionate and strong, and Stuart Dunn at CatholicMom finds Sharif the highlight. The first part follows the Acts of the Apostles closely, and Dunn notes how much of the dialogue comes straight from Scripture. The second is looser, padding the Roman years with invented melodrama about a gladiator and two young lovers. It is a long, earnest television production, made for Rai by Lux Vide with San Paolo Film and scored by Marco Frisina, and about eight million Italians watched each night in October 2005. Its interest is that it keeps the Church, not the arena, at the centre: Peter as a weak man made strong, and the first community growing under persecution.
themes: The drama turns on Peter's repentance: the forgiven denier becomes the rock who leads the others. His primacy is explicit. Christ's promise at Caesarea Philippi is given in full, Peter is called the first of the apostles, and at the Council of Jerusalem he ends the debate on his own authority and rules that the Gentiles are to be baptised and saved by grace. Pentecost, the conversion of Saul and the baptism of Cornelius are decisive steps in the mission. At the Last Supper the Eucharist is Christ's body given in sacrifice and the new and eternal covenant. The Quo Vadis episode and the inverted crucifixion follow the ancient tradition of Peter's martyrdom in Rome.
history: Simon Peter, a fisherman of Bethsaida and Capernaum, was called by Christ and named Cephas, the Rock (John 1:42; Matthew 16:18). He denied his Master three times and was restored after the Resurrection (John 21). After Pentecost he led the Church in Jerusalem, baptised the centurion Cornelius, the first Gentile convert (Acts 10), and spoke the decisive word at the Council of Jerusalem about AD 49-50 (Acts 15). Tradition places him at Rome, and he died there in the persecution of Nero, probably between 64 and 67, crucified head downwards, as Origen reports. He was buried on the Vatican hill, where Constantine built the basilica over his tomb. Paul was beheaded at Rome in the same persecution.
liberties: The gladiator Davide, his wife Anna, and the young lovers Claudio and Silvia are invented. Dunn calls a market scene in which Jesus appears to Peter fictitious and unnecessary, and the subplot about Cornelius's family padding. Chronology is compressed: Peter reaches Rome on the day of Paul's arrest, and Paul is executed before the fire, although tradition places his death after it.
advisories:
Frequent violence: the stoning of Stephen, gladiator fights, an off-screen throat-cutting, a man set on fire, and Peter's crucifixion with brief blood (Dove).

Prostitutes approach Peter; brief romantic embraces; some cleavage.

Ages 12 and up.

Invented subplots fill much of the Roman half.

doctrine: Peter holds the primacy among the Apostles. The Church reads Matthew 16:18-19 and John 21:15-17 as Christ's grant to Peter of the keys and the care of the whole flock, and the First Vatican Council defined in 1870 (Pastor aeternus) that the Roman Pontiff succeeds him in this primacy and teaches infallibly ex cathedra on faith and morals. Peter's death at Rome is held by the Catholic Encyclopedia as established, and tradition places his tomb on the Vatican hill. The film's meeting with Christ on the Appian Way, 'Quo vadis?', comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter (late second century), not Scripture. The film's Council of Jerusalem presents the Church's teaching that the Gentiles are not bound by the Mosaic law.

title: Pius XII: Under the Roman Sky
decision: GREY: Independent coverage (Angela Cinicolo's Movieplayer.it review, Il Post's report, Donatella Di Cesare's essay in the Rome Jewish community's Moked dossier, Corrado Augias via Wikipedia) establishes the content and documented historical distortions, and Lux Vide itself conceded inaccuracies. The English subtitle file adds detail: the Pope orders enclosed convents opened and offers gold towards the ransom; a priest's appeal to General Stahel is shown halting the arrests; and the Pope explains his public silence by the Dutch bishops' protest, citing an unsupported figure of forty thousand deported. There is no doctrinal problem, and Pius XII is only Venerable, so rule (a) does not apply. The reservation is historical.
summary: James Cromwell plays Pius XII in Lux Vide's two-part drama of the German occupation of Rome, a sympathetic account of papal caution that Rome's Jewish community attacked as apologetic.
synopsis: September 1943: after the armistice, German troops occupy Rome, and Pius XII stays in the city. The Germans extort fifty kilograms of gold from the Jewish community under threat of deporting two hundred people. The Pope deals with the German commander, General Stahel, has Jews sheltered in convents and seminaries, and weighs whether to protest publicly, while Berlin considers abducting him. On 16 October about a thousand Jews are rounded up, among them the father of Miriam, a young Jewish woman. She escapes and is hidden in a convent with help from Davide, a black-market charmer who loves her, and Marco, a student who has joined the partisans. Stahel is replaced by the SS general Karl Wolff. Marco dies after the Via Rasella attack. Rome is liberated in June 1944, and Miriam finds her brother and marries Davide.
inclusion: This is the most substantial screen defence of Pius XII's conduct in occupied Rome, and part of its interest is the argument it provoked. Duguay stages the occupation well: Movieplayer.it's Angela Cinicolo praised the depiction of the German encirclement and the mounting fear in the ghetto, while finding the papal scenes almost didactic and the young people's romance sentimental. Cromwell plays Pius as reserved, prudent and troubled, a man who opens convents and churches but will not denounce the deportations publicly. The makers drew on testimony gathered for his beatification cause, and the distributor says so. Its critics, from Rome's chief rabbi Riccardo Di Segni to the philosopher Donatella Di Cesare, called it apologetic. Viewers who want the case for Pius told as drama will find it here, as long as they know where it bends the record.
themes: The Catholic subject is the Pope as shepherd under occupation: prayer before the crucifix, the duty to protect his flock, and charity to the Jews through religious houses. The film presents his public silence as prudence, not indifference: Pacelli says he cannot take one people's side against another, and fears that open protest would cost more lives. A German general keeps a rosary in his desk, and the ending points towards reconciliation. Di Cesare objected that the film casts Pius as carrying the cross, and that scenes of hidden Jews dressed as priests and nuns hint at conversion. Nothing here departs from Catholic teaching; the question is historical, not doctrinal.
history: German troops occupied Rome on 10 September 1943. On 26 September the SS demanded fifty kilograms of gold from the Jewish community in exchange for the Jews not being deported, and the gold was collected, with the Vatican reportedly offering to lend part of it. On 16 October the Germans arrested over a thousand Jews in the old ghetto and deported them to Auschwitz; only a handful returned. Many others were hidden in convents, monasteries and Vatican properties. On 23 March 1944 partisans attacked a German column in the Via Rasella, and on 24 March the Germans shot 335 men at the Ardeatine Caves. Rome was liberated on 4 June 1944. Pius XII (Eugenio Pacelli, pope 1939-1958) made no explicit public protest naming the Jews; historians still dispute whether more could have been done. The Vatican opened its archives for his pontificate in March 2020.
liberties: Miriam, Davide and Marco are invented. Critics identified concrete distortions: the film shows a priest's appeal to General Stahel cutting short the ghetto round-up, which Di Segni and many historians deny; the Italian Fascists all but vanish; Via Rasella and the Fosse Ardeatine get only passing notice; and, according to Corrado Augias, it credits Vatican pressure with a peaceful German withdrawal and omits the La Storta massacre. The Pope justifies his silence by the Dutch bishops' protest, with an unsupported figure of forty thousand deported. The kidnap plot rests on disputed sources.
advisories:
Round-ups, deportations and shootings; the Via Rasella attack and its aftermath.

A wartime romance between young adults; no explicit sexual content is reported.

Teens and up.

A one-sided treatment of a disputed history, with documented distortions.

grey.question: The film defends Pius XII's wartime conduct: he opens enclosed convents to Jews, offers gold for the ransom, and explains his public silence by the deportations that followed the Dutch bishops' protest. That is a legitimate view, but the film reaches it partly by altering the record. It shows a priest's appeal to the German commander cutting short the October 1943 round-up, nearly erases the Italian Fascists, and passes quickly over the Fosse Ardeatine. Rome's chief rabbi called it propaganda, and its producer admitted inaccuracies. Treat it as advocacy drama and read a serious history alongside it.

doctrine: In Mystici Corporis (1943) Pius XII taught that the Church is the Mystical Body of Christ and that Christ's charity extends to every person, and in Summi Pontificatus (1939) he affirmed the unity of the human race. The film leans on the Church's teaching on works of mercy: shelter for the hunted and fugitive. It also touches the difficult prudential question the Pope faced, whether public condemnation of a persecutor would save those in danger or provoke greater reprisals. The Church teaches that a pope's governance and prudential judgments are not infallible; infallibility is limited to definitions of faith and morals ex cathedra (Vatican I, 1870), so the debate about his silence is a question of historical judgment, not doctrine.
production: Christian Duguay directed this Italian-German television film, shown on Rai 1 in 2010. Luca Bernabei and Martin Choroba produced it. James Cromwell plays the Pope. Rome's Chief Rabbi, Riccardo Di Segni, called it propaganda and apologetics full of errors. Corrado Augias criticised it as a work meant to shape Pius XII's image for sainthood and listed historical falsehoods, among them the claim that the Pope personally stopped the raid on the Roman ghetto. The producer Bernabei admitted some inaccuracies but said it was not a documentary, and the writers said they aimed at storytelling, not historical judgment.

title: God's Mighty Servant
alternateTitles: God's Mighty Servant: Sister Pascalina Lehnert
God's Mighty Servant: Sister Pascalina Lehnert, Secretary of Pius XII
decision: GREY: Dating settled: Ziegler Film gives production year 2009; first broadcast on Das Erste on 22 and 23 April 2011 (Good Friday and Holy Saturday, per the Abendzeitung review of 20 April 2011); repeated 13 June 2012. Two independent reviews (Abendzeitung, evangelisch.de) establish the content and its historical liberties. The reservations are historical and concern the picture of convent life; neither hard rule applies (Pius XII is Venerable only; Pascalina has no cause). A Founder ruling that the convent portrayal is fair would move it to PUBLISH.
summary: A two-part German drama of Sister Pascalina Lehnert, the Bavarian nun who ran Eugenio Pacelli's household for forty years, with Christine Neubauer and Remo Girone as Pius XII.
synopsis: Josefine Lehnert, a Bavarian farmer's daughter whose father opposes her schooling, enters a convent as Sister Pascalina. She is sent to keep house for the papal nuncio in Munich, Eugenio Pacelli, and becomes his secretary. After her father dies unreconciled, her superiors and fellow sisters turn against her; she is accused of an improper relationship with Pacelli, confined, and sent away to recover from asthma. She returns to him when he becomes Cardinal Secretary of State and slips into the Vatican. In the second part she helps with the Reich Concordat and the encyclical Mit brennender Sorge, sees Pacelli elected Pius XII, and runs his war relief. The Pope weighs whether to protest the persecution of the Jews, opens church buildings to refugees and is warned of a plan to abduct him. He dies in 1958, still doubting his choices.
inclusion: The film is a rare view of the Vatican from inside the papal household, and of a woman who held real influence there without any office. Ziegler Film made it for ARD from Martha Schad's biography: three hours, period settings in Munich and Rome, and a Hitler putsch staged on the Odeonsplatz with hundreds of extras. The evangelisch.de reviewer found it gripping and free of religious kitsch, and thought Neubauer, a much-mocked star, right for the stubborn, practical nun. Robert Braunmüller in the Abendzeitung was scathing: dull, repetitive, sentimental at the end, and a whitewash of Pius XII. The Lexikon des internationalen Films called it sprawling. Remo Girone was nominated as supporting actor at Monte Carlo. It is worth seeing for its household view of a pontificate, provided the history is checked against better sources.
themes: The religious substance is Pascalina's vocation: obedience to superiors who mistreat her, fidelity to the priest she serves, and practical charity in the papal relief work. The convent scenes are unflattering. The evangelisch.de reviewer found the order's ways medieval and unworldly, and the drama of jealous sisters and a false charge of impropriety turns religious life into an obstacle course. Pius XII is devout, anxious and burdened by his silence, which Braunmüller reads as Catholic apologetics. The film does not mock the faith, but it treats Church institutions mainly as power and politics, with the heroine's common sense as the corrective.
history: Josefine Lehnert (1894–1983) joined the Holy Cross Sisters of Menzingen and from 1917 kept house for Pacelli as nuncio in Munich, and from 1925 in Berlin. She followed him to Rome, stayed throughout his pontificate and directed his private charity office from 1944 to 1958. Her memoir, written in 1959, was not allowed to appear until 1982. John XXIII gave her the Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice medal. She died in Vienna in 1983.
liberties: Braunmüller notes that the film brings Pascalina into Pacelli's household earlier than in fact, likens the Allied bombing of Rome to the deportation of its Jews, idealises King Ludwig III, and gives the Pope a line about his silence that predates knowledge of the Holocaust. The evangelisch.de reviewer adds that the second part makes Pascalina rescue Rome's Jews almost single-handedly. The house arrest and the accusations against her are dramatised from Schad's account.
advisories:
Wartime violence: revolutionary fighting in Munich, the 1923 putsch, the bombing of Rome and the deportations.

An accusation of an improper relationship between a nun and a prelate; no sexual content is reported.

Teens and up.

Historical compressions, and a heroine whose role is enlarged.

grey.question: This German two-parter is sympathetic to Sister Pascalina and to Pius XII, but its history is loose. Critics note that it enlarges her role until she seems to rescue Rome's Jews almost alone, shifts dates, and handles the Holocaust question sentimentally. Its picture of convent life is harsh: jealous sisters, a false charge of impropriety, superiors who block her at every turn. Viewers should weigh whether that picture of religious life is fair, and treat the wartime episodes as drama rather than history.

title: The Miracle of Father Kapaun
decision: GREY: Identity: a Wichita Eagle documentary by Travis Heying made with Roy Wenzl's December 2009 series (Newman University notice, 17 December 2009), distributed by Ignatius Press from 1 August 2010 (45 minutes). The subject's history is verified by the US Army's Medal of Honor page. Kapaun is Venerable (2025), so rule (a) does not apply. No independent assessment of the film's treatment, and the healings in its title are unapproved claims: unverified.
summary: Wichita Eagle journalists tell the story of Fr Emil Kapaun, the Kansas army chaplain who served fellow prisoners in a Korean War camp until his death in 1951.
synopsis: Emil Kapaun, the son of Czech immigrant farmers in Kansas, becomes a priest of the Diocese of Wichita and an army chaplain. In Korea in November 1950, at Unsan, he crosses open ground under fire to reach the wounded, refuses chances to escape, and is captured when he stays behind with injured men. In the camps at Sambukol and Pyoktong he forages for food, nurses the sick and leads prayers and services in defiance of the guards. He dies at Pyoktong in May 1951, aged 35. Men who were imprisoned with him, military historians and church officials tell the story. The last part follows his cause for canonisation and a Kansas family who believe his intercession saved their son's life, among recoveries that were then under Church investigation.
inclusion: The film began as journalism. Travis Heying, a Wichita Eagle videographer, made it alongside Roy Wenzl's eight-part series for the paper in December 2009; the Diocese of Wichita then screened it and Ignatius Press took it on. Its strength is testimony: men who were in the camps with Kapaun, filmed while some were still alive to speak. Kapaun's courage is beyond dispute: the Army awarded him the Distinguished Service Cross in 1951 and the Medal of Honor in 2013. At about 45 minutes, it is a television-length portrait rather than a full biography, and Heying and Wenzl later returned to the subject. It suits older children as well as adults, and is a good introduction to a pre-conciliar priest whose service was practical, physical and sacramental.
themes: Kapaun is presented above all as a priest: he leads prayers and services in the camp at the risk of punishment, cares for the sick and keeps faith among starving men under captors hostile to religion. That is a strong picture of the priesthood as sacrifice. The title is the problem. The miracle refers to recoveries that families attribute to his intercession, which the Church has not approved. Rome declared him Venerable in 2025 under the "offering of life" category introduced in 2017, not on the strength of a miracle. The film presents claims, not verdicts.
history: Emil Kapaun was captured at Unsan on 2 November 1950 after volunteering to stay with the wounded, and was held at Sambukol and Pyoktong, where he died on 23 May 1951. He received the Distinguished Service Cross in August 1951, while still listed as missing, and the Medal of Honor, presented by President Obama, on 11 April 2013. He was declared a Servant of God in 1993 and Venerable in February 2025.
advisories:

doctrine: A priest's first duty is the care of souls, and the film's account of Kapaun saying prayers and giving the sacraments to starving prisoners shows that duty at its limit. A priest may absolve a man in danger of death, and in grave necessity the sacraments are given as circumstances allow. The film's title refers to healings that families attribute to his intercession. Under the traditional procedure (Urban VIII, Benedict XIV), the Church examines a cause for proof of heroic virtue and then for miracles after death; a reported cure is not a miracle until the Church has examined and approved it. The claims of healing in the film are therefore those of the families and the film-makers, not of the Church. The Medal of Honor awarded to Kapaun in 2013 is a military decoration, not a judgment on his sanctity.
production: The Miracle of Father Kapaun is a 45-minute documentary with interviews of former prisoners who were in the camp with him, church officials, military historians and the Kansas family who credit his intercession for their son's recovery. Ignatius Press lists the DVD with a publication date of 1 August 2010, with a prayer card. Our record dates the film to 2009. Kapaun received the Medal of Honor on 11 April 2013. No independent review of the film has been found, and no Catholic rating.

title: The Blood & the Rose
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Renegade Productions press releases of 2011 and 2012; benefit premiere at the Warner Theatre, Washington, 24 January 2013, reported by the Catholic Review). Content is documented by Alberto González's detailed review for Aleteia and by CNA's interview with the director, both present-day Catholic outlets, so there is no independent assessment. Reservations: disputed claims about the tilma presented as findings, historical errors in the Spanish survey, and New Evangelization framing. Would move only with an independent review.
summary: Tim Watkins's documentary sets Our Lady of Guadalupe against Aztec sacrifice and the Marian history of Spain, then examines the tilma with claims that outrun the evidence.
synopsis: Narrated by Eduardo Verástegui and shot in Spain and Mexico over four years, the film is built in three parts. The first is history: Constantine, the Marian shrines and victories of Christian Spain from Covadonga to the Guadalupe of Extremadura, and the Aztec cult of human sacrifice as Bernal Díaz described it. The second tells the apparitions of December 1531 on Tepeyac: Juan Diego's errands to Bishop Zumárraga, the request for a church, the roses and the image found on his cloak. The third turns to the tilma itself, presenting claims about figures reflected in the Virgin's eyes and stars on her mantle said to match the sky of 1531. It ends by linking Guadalupe to the Marian apparitions of the twentieth century and by calling Catholics to follow Juan Diego as messengers of the faith today.
inclusion: The film's strength is its first half. Rather than starting at Tepeyac, Watkins starts in Spain, and argues that the Guadalupe story only makes sense against two backgrounds: a Spanish Catholicism shaped by centuries of war under Marian patronage, and an Aztec religion that fed its gods with human hearts. That contrast, which Alberto González's review for Aleteia follows closely, makes the scale of the conversions after 1531 intelligible. The apparition narrative is told straightforwardly and keeps the details of the traditional account. Watkins, a Baltimore businessman and documentary maker, made it as a catechetical film and toured it through parishes with study materials, so it is pitched at Catholics who know the image but not the history behind it. Nothing published assesses its craft independently.
themes: The film reads Guadalupe as a chapter in the enmity between the woman and the serpent of Genesis 3:15 and Revelation 12, and as the means by which Mary brought a people to her Son. That reading is traditional, and the image is treated as a sign pointing to Christ: Watkins stresses the bowed head and folded hands. Two things need caution. The scientific section presents disputed claims about the eyes and the stars as findings, though no Church authority has endorsed them. And the closing section frames the story in John Paul II's language of the New Evangelization, with Juan Diego, beatified in 1990 and canonised in 2002, held up as the model evangelist.
history: The 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia gives the traditional account. On 9 December 1531 the Virgin appeared to Juan Diego, a recent convert, on Tepeyac and asked for a church. Bishop Zumárraga asked for a sign. On 12 December she cured Juan's dying uncle and sent Juan with roses in his cloak, which, opened before the bishop, bore the image. Benedict XIV made Our Lady of Guadalupe national patron with a proper Mass and Office, and Leo XIII had the image crowned in his name.
liberties: The historical survey is triumphal and sometimes wrong. As González summarises it, Alfonso XI's victory at the Río Salado is said to have ended the Moorish presence in Europe, though Granada did not fall until 1492; Covadonga is told as a Marian victory without qualification. The claims about the tilma are presented as settled discoveries rather than contested interpretations.
advisories:
Descriptions and reconstructions of Aztec human sacrifice.

No sexual content reported. Suitable for older children with an adult.

The scientific claims about the image are presented as findings; they are disputed and have no Church endorsement.

grey.question: The Blood & the Rose tells the Guadalupe story in its traditional form and sets it against Aztec sacrifice and the Marian history of Spain. Its weaker parts are presented with the same confidence: claims that figures appear in the Virgin's eyes and that the stars on her mantle map the sky of December 1531, and a survey of Spanish history with plain errors. It also closes in the post-conciliar language of the New Evangelization. No independent review of the film exists; one would show how much weight the scientific section can bear.

doctrine: Apparitions are private revelation: the Church does not oblige belief in them, but approves devotion where she finds nothing contrary to faith. Benedict XIV declared Our Lady of Guadalupe patroness of New Spain in 1754 and approved a proper Mass and Office for 12 December. Leo XIII had the image crowned in 1895. The film reads the story through Genesis 3:15 and Apocalypse 12, passages the Church has long applied to Our Lady; Pius IX appeals to Genesis 3:15 in Ineffabilis Deus (1854). title: The Day the Sun Danced: The True Story of Fátima
originalTitle: The Day the Sun Danced: The True Story of Fatima
decision: GREY: Identity is established by TheTVDB (CCC of America's Saints and Heroes series; 30 minutes; United States), retailer and Formed listings, and the Dove Foundation's series review (based on a text by Fr Robert J. Fox). Content is known only in outline from these interested or series-level sources, and no independent assessment of its treatment exists. The year is disputed (1988 TheTVDB, 1989 fan wiki, ©1991 VHS in WorldCat per earlier research, 2005 DVD in TMDB); 1988 used provisionally. Would move with a transcript or a review.
summary: An animated retelling of the Fátima apparitions for young children, made by CCC of America and based on a text by Fr Robert J. Fox.
synopsis: In Portugal in 1916, during the First World War, an angel appears to three shepherd children, Lúcia, aged ten, and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta, aged nine and seven. He teaches them a prayer of adoration and tells them that the Hearts of Jesus and Mary are listening. In 1917 the Lady appears to them while they are minding their sheep near Fátima, again and again, asks them to pray the Rosary, since she can end the war, and entrusts them with secrets meant for the whole world. Few believe them, and they suffer for their testimony. Finally, before a great crowd in the rain, the sun appears to dance in the sky, and the children are accepted as the messengers of Our Lady of Fátima.
inclusion: This is one of the few versions of Fátima made for young children, and it has stayed in circulation for over three decades: first on video from CCC of America, which produced animated lives of saints for the home market in the late 1980s, and now on DVD from Catholic school suppliers and on the Formed streaming service. It runs under half an hour, which suits a classroom, and Seton's catalogue places it at third grade. It is part of a Saints and Heroes series that also includes Bernadette and Juan Diego, and is sold in a Marian set. Its story follows a text by Fr Robert J. Fox, a priest known for his books on Fátima. No critic has assessed its animation or its fidelity in print.
themes: From the available descriptions, the film keeps the core of the message for a young audience: the Angel's prayer of adoration, the Hearts of Jesus and Mary, the Rosary, prayer for peace and for sinners, and the Lady's secrets, with the Miracle of the Sun as their vindication. The Dove Foundation's notes for the series mention the Virgin described as sinless and people kneeling before her image. What the film does with the harder parts, the vision of hell and the request for the consecration of Russia, is not documented. One unverified viewer complaint says the Russia request is left out; if so, the story is simplified rather than falsified.
advisories:
No violence, sexual content or bad language reported for this episode; made for young children.

The Dove Foundation's content notes and its 12+ seal cover the whole Saints and Heroes series, not this episode alone.

Whether the vision of hell and the request for the consecration of Russia are included has not been verified.

grey.question: The Day the Sun Danced is a short animated version of the Fátima story for young children, from CCC of America and based on a text by Fr Robert J. Fox. Catalogue descriptions and the Dove Foundation's notes show the Angel, the Rosary, the secrets and the Miracle of the Sun. No published review checks how closely it follows Lúcia's memoirs, or whether it includes the vision of hell and the request for the consecration of Russia. A transcript or an independent review would settle it.

sources.title: Our Lady of Fátima
sources.claims: Angel 1916; apparitions 13 May-13 October 1917; custody 13 August and Valinhos 19 August; crowd estimate; deaths of Francisco 1919 and Jacinta 1920; Lúcia memoirs 1935-41; Bishop of Leiria approval 13 October 1930; Pius XII consecrations 1942 and 1952; coronation 1946; basilica 1954

suitability.note: A half-hour cartoon made for young children, with no violence or frightening content reported; Seton places it at third grade. The children's persecution by unbelieving adults and the secrets may need a word of explanation for the youngest.

doctrine: The Bishop of Leiria, José Alves Correia da Silva, declared the apparitions worthy of belief on 13 October 1930 and authorised the cult of Our Lady of Fátima. Pius XII consecrated the human race to the Immaculate Heart of Mary on 31 October 1942, naming the peoples of Russia, and consecrated Russia itself in the apostolic letter Sacro vergente anno of 7 July 1952. He had the Fátima statue crowned by a papal legate on 13 May 1946 and raised the sanctuary to a basilica in 1954. The Lady's requests, daily Rosary, reparation and prayer for sinners, rest on long-standing devotion; the Angel's prayer is one of adoration of the Holy Trinity. Private revelations, however approved, are not part of the deposit of faith.
history: In 1916 Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, shepherd children of Aljustrel near Fátima, reported three visits from an angel. From 13 May to 13 October 1917 they reported monthly apparitions of the Virgin at the Cova da Iria. On 13 August the district administrator, Artur Santos, took them into custody, and the August apparition came on the 19th at Valinhos. On 13 October a crowd estimated at 30,000 to 100,000 saw the Miracle of the Sun. Francisco died in the influenza pandemic on 4 April 1919 and Jacinta in Lisbon on 20 February 1920. Lúcia became a religious and wrote down the secrets in her memoirs of 1935 to 1941.
production: CCC of America made the film as part of its animated Saints and Heroes series for the home and school market; the series also covers Bernadette and Juan Diego. The story follows an original text by Fr Robert J. Fox, a priest known for his books on Fátima. Dates are uncertain: TheTVDB gives 1988, other listings 1989, a VHS copyright of 1991 is recorded, and a DVD followed in 2005. It runs about thirty minutes. It is still sold on DVD by Catholic school suppliers and streamed on Formed. The Dove Foundation approved the series as a whole for ages twelve and up. No director is credited in the sources found, and no independent review has been traced.

title: Thérèse
decision: GREY: The subtitle file settles part of what Greydanus described. The dream of a man dragging someone into the woods is told in a letter from Thérèse's sister Céline, not dreamt by Thérèse. Lucie's fixation is spoken plainly; Thérèse rebuffs her, the two are kept apart and Lucie later leaves the order. An old nun asks Thérèse for a kiss. Thérèse's trial of faith in her last illness is given in words close to her own writings. The host scene has no dialogue, so the subtitles cannot settle it. Nothing in the dialogue sexualises her love of Christ, so not REJECT; the surrounding material keeps it GREY.
summary: Cavalier's austere portrait of Thérèse Martin, from her girlhood longing for Carmel to her death at twenty-four, told in spare vignettes against a bare backdrop.
synopsis: Thérèse Martin, the youngest daughter of a devout Normandy family, wants to follow two of her sisters into the Carmel at Lisieux, though she is only fifteen. She presses her case as far as Pope Leo XIII. Admitted, she lives the enclosed life of work, silence and prayer among sisters who are sometimes petty, sometimes eccentric, and one of whom, Lucie, becomes fixated on her. Thérèse speaks of her vocation as a love affair with Jesus and prays for sinners, among them the condemned murderer Pranzini. At Christmas the nuns celebrate the birthday of the Child they call their husband. After her father's death, the hardships of the convent wear her down; she suffers physically, is shaken by doubt, and dies of tuberculosis.
inclusion: On artistic grounds it is among the most honoured saint films: it won the Jury Prize at Cannes and five Césars, including best film. Catherine Mouchet plays Thérèse as a determined teenager whose love for Christ is concrete and urgent, and the scholar Mary Bryant called the film the most effective and challenging screen version of her story in its decade. Cavalier strips everything away: sets and props are pared to a minimum against a neutral backdrop. Vincent Canby noted that there are no heavenly choirs and no visions bathed in light, and that the beauty of the images is not ornament. Greydanus compares the restraint to Bresson, as Marina Warner did. The film follows Thérèse's own conviction that love, not suffering for its own sake, is the point of sacrifice. Its weakness is that it observes her without explaining her: Greydanus calls it a reverie rather than a meditation, leaving her a riddle.
themes: The film is built on Story of a Soul: Thérèse's vocation, her small sacrifices, her prayer for Pranzini, the daily life of the Carmel and her last illness. Her love for Jesus is the centre of her life and is spoken in the romantic language she herself used. The film passes no judgment on her, and some critics have read it through Freud; Greydanus answers that psychoanalysis cannot account for her selflessness. The trouble lies around her rather than in her: an invented sister's declared attachment, which Thérèse rebuffs; an old nun's request for a kiss; a dream, told in a letter from her sister Céline, that mixes martyrdom with sexual violence; and an accidental desecration of a host. Her trial of faith at the end is taken from her own writings.
history: Thérèse Martin (1873–1897) entered the Lisieux Carmel at fifteen, after asking Leo XIII in person for permission, and died of tuberculosis at twenty-four. Pius XI beatified her in 1923 and canonised her in 1925. Her spiritual memoir, Story of a Soul, made her and her 'little way' known worldwide after her death.
liberties: Sister Lucie is a fictional character, and the film has her leave the order. The film works in elliptical vignettes and omits large parts of the life, including much of the family background. The dream imagery, given to a letter from Céline, is Cavalier's invention.
advisories:
Several sexual allusions; a dream, recounted in a letter from her sister, that mixes martyrdom with sexual violence imagery; a nun's declared attachment to Thérèse, which she rebuffs.

An accidental desecration of a consecrated host.

Illness and death from tuberculosis. Adults and older teenagers.

French with subtitles.

The film presents a canonised saint without passing judgment on her, and leaves room for the Freudian reading some critics have taken.

grey.question: Cavalier's Thérèse is restrained and largely reverent, and her own love of Christ is not sexualised. The difficulty is the material around her. An invented nun, Lucie, declares her love for Thérèse, is rebuffed and later leaves the convent; an old nun asks her for a kiss; a letter from her sister Céline recounts a dream of being dragged into the woods that blends martyrdom with sexual violence; and a host is accidentally desecrated. The film passes no judgment, and some critics read it through Freud. Viewers should judge whether this is honest observation of a convent or a slight on the saint.

names: Histoire d'une âme (Story of a Soul), autobiography of Thérèse of Lisieux (1898)

suitability.note: Sexual allusions, a dream mixing martyrdom with sexual violence, a nun's attachment to Thérèse, a desecrated host and a long death from tuberculosis. It is slow, in French with subtitles, and best for adults and older teenagers.

doctrine: Thérèse entered the Carmel at Lisieux on 9 April 1888, at fifteen, after asking Leo XIII for leave. The Carmelite life is enclosed prayer and penance offered for sinners and for priests, as she offered hers for the murderer Pranzini, executed in 1887. Her 'little way' of spiritual childhood is trust, humility and love in small duties. In her day the sisters received Holy Communion only a few times a week. Pius X's decree Sacra Tridentina (1905) encouraged frequent and daily Communion, and his decree Quam singulari (1910) lowered the age of First Communion to the age of reason. The Church teaches the Real Presence in the Eucharist (Council of Trent, Session 13, 1551), which is why the dropped host in the film matters. She was beatified in 1923 and canonised by Pius XI on 17 May 1925, and he declared her patroness of the missions in 1927.
production: Alain Cavalier directed and wrote the film with Camille de Casabianca, from Thérèse's autobiography. Catherine Mouchet played her. Cavalier visited the Lisieux Carmel and spoke with its sisters but did not film there. It was shown at Cannes in 1986, where it won the Jury Prize. At the 1987 César Awards it won best film, screenplay, cinematography and editing, and Mouchet won for most promising actress. Pauline Kael wrote that the viewer was 'trapped inside his glass bubble'.

title: The Mission
decision: GREY: The subtitle file confirms the reservation and corrects one point. Altamirano threatens the priests with excommunication if they stay; Mendoza renounces his vow of obedience to fight; Gabriel refuses him a blessing, telling him that dying with blood on his hands betrays everything and that if might is right love has no place. The film does state its verdict, through Altamirano, whose closing reflections say that he and men like him made the world as it is and that he is the one who is dead while the slain live. Its sympathy for disobedience is therefore explicit, but Gabriel's refusal is non-violent and the Catholic substance is strong (Greydanus, A−): a weighable reservation, not REJECT.
summary: Bolt and Joffé's epic of the Jesuit missions of Paraguay, destroyed after a 1750 treaty, with Jeremy Irons as a peaceful priest and Robert De Niro as a penitent slaver.
synopsis: In the 1750s Father Gabriel climbs the cliffs beside the Iguazú Falls, above which the Guaraní have sent a missionary to his death, and wins their trust by playing the oboe. Rodrigo Mendoza, a mercenary who captures Guaraní for slavers, kills his brother in a fit of anger. Gabriel sets him a penance: to haul his armour up the falls. He reaches the Guaraní he once hunted, is received among them and becomes a Jesuit. Then the Treaty of Madrid hands the territory to Portugal. A papal envoy, Cardinal Altamirano, tours the missions and must decide their fate, knowing that defending them could bring the Society of Jesus down in Europe; he orders them abandoned. Gabriel and Mendoza refuse to leave. Mendoza breaks his vows and trains the Guaraní to fight; Gabriel leads a procession with the Blessed Sacrament. Colonial troops destroy the mission and both priests are killed.
inclusion: The craft is not in doubt. Chris Menges's photography of the falls and the forest won an Oscar, Ennio Morricone's score is widely praised, and the film won the Palme d'Or. Its finest passages are thoroughly Catholic: Mendoza dragging his armour up the cliff as penance is a strong image of contrition, and the closing procession of the Blessed Sacrament through gunfire, the monstrance taken up by a Guaraní when Gabriel falls, is the film's most striking scene. The drama is weaker than the images. Greydanus finds the structure diffuse and Altamirano, the narrator, underwritten, and the film never quite settles whose story it is. Roger Ebert was harsher: every moment is watchable, he wrote, but the moments never add up to a story, and the final battle dissolves into chaos.
themes: Penance and forgiveness drive the first half, and the missions are shown as an attempt at a Christian society in which the Guaraní can live in peace. The second half turns on obedience. Gabriel defies his superiors but refuses violence and dies carrying the monstrance. Mendoza renounces his vow of obedience and takes up the sword, and Gabriel refuses to bless him. The film prefers Gabriel, but it treats both men's disobedience as nobler than the Church's compliance, and it closes on the envoy admitting that he made the world as it is and that he, not the slain, is the one who is dead. Greydanus argues that grave danger to souls could justify Gabriel's refusal and that a priest may not take up arms; the film does not weigh obedience itself.
history: The 1750 Treaty of Madrid transferred seven Jesuit missions east of the Uruguay River from Spain to Portugal. The Jesuits petitioned the king against it, but their General, Ignazio Visconti, ordered compliance and sent Fr Lope Luis Altamirano to enforce it. The Guaraní refused to move against the orders of both governor and missionaries, and fought under their own leaders, Sepé Tiaraju and Nicolás Ñeenguirú. They were crushed at Caaybaté in 1756. Madrid and Lisbon blamed Jesuit intrigue. The treaty was annulled in 1761.
liberties: The real Altamirano was a Jesuit sent by his own General, not a cardinal sent by the Pope. The film turns the official record on obedience round: the Society's General ordered compliance. Some individual Jesuits were accused of helping the rebels, but the Guaraní fought under their own leaders, whom the film leaves out, and historians now credit them with organising their own resistance. Gabriel and Mendoza are invented.
advisories:
Bloody battle violence and killings, including the shooting of priests and villagers in a procession.

Non-sexual ethnographic nudity among the Guaraní.

A man kills his brother in a fit of anger. Rated PG in the United States but better for teenagers and adults.

The film presents disobedience to religious superiors, and a Jesuit's armed resistance, as admirable, and it inverts the Society's official obedience.

grey.question: The Mission ends by honouring two Jesuits who disobey an order to abandon their missions despite a threat of excommunication. Mendoza renounces his vow of obedience and leads an armed defence; Gabriel refuses him a blessing, rejects violence and dies carrying the Blessed Sacrament. The film's verdict is spoken by the envoy himself, who concludes that he and men like him made the world as it is, and that he is dead while the slain live. It also turns history round: the real Altamirano was a Jesuit sent by his own General, and the Society ordered the missions surrendered. Viewers must weigh the film's view of obedience.

doctrine: The film sets Mendoza's penance, in which he drags his armour up the falls and is absolved, beside the Church's teaching on sacramental confession: sorrow, confession, absolution and satisfaction (Council of Trent, session XIV, 1551). Mendoza's slaying of his brother in a duel is mortal sin. Father Gabriel refuses to bless the sword; yet Catholic teaching allows a just war and the defence of the innocent (St Thomas, Summa II-II, q. 40), and the film leaves the question open. The Jesuit vow of obedience, which makes the superior's command as that of Christ, is central to the Society (Ignatius's Constitutions), and Father Fielding's armed resistance goes against it. Clement XIV suppressed the Society in 1773; Pius VII restored it in 1814.
production: Robert Bolt wrote the script for the producer Fernando Ghia. David Puttnam championed the project, recommended Roland Joffé as director and joined as co-producer; Goldcrest came in and Warner Bros. supplied $5 million. Filming began in April 1985, chiefly in Colombia, with Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay also named. Robert De Niro had bodyguards after the cartel led by Pablo Escobar threatened Americans in Colombia. The Jesuit C. J. McNaspy, whose book The Lost Cities of Paraguay lies behind the story, consulted. It premiered in competition at Cannes on 16 May 1986 and won the Palme d'Or. It won the Academy Award for cinematography and BAFTAs for Ray McAnally, editing and score. At $17.2 million against a budget of £16.5 million it was a commercial disappointment, and Goldcrest's losses contributed to that company's end.

title: The Innocents
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a Benedictine community, its vows and its Office) and well documented: Danish Film Institute and Wikipedia for identity, Kevin Jagernauth (The Playlist) and A. G. Harmon (Image) as independent treatments, Brad Miner (The Catholic Thing) for content. The Portuguese subtitle file confirms the reservation without turning it into a thesis. The abbess says she entrusted the baby to God and calls it Providence, then admits she damned herself to save the community and is called a murderer. One sister keeps her son and means to live her vocation differently; another gives up her child. The novice mistress defends faith through long doubt, and the closing letter credits God with sending the doctor. Not REJECT; not PUBLISH while the affair, an attempted assault and the departures need stating.

grey.question: The Innocents treats the nuns' faith and vows seriously and gives their prayer real weight. The reservation lies in where it places blame and how it ends. The abbess, fearing scandal, abandons a newborn and calls it Providence, later admitting she damned herself to save the community; a young nun kills herself; the way out is found by an unbelieving doctor, and some sisters leave religious life with the film's sympathy. The doctor's affair is shown without comment. Much of this is invented around a true episode. Viewers able to weigh a religious superior as the main wrongdoer will find a serious, restrained film.

summary: Anne Fontaine's restrained drama of a French Red Cross doctor who secretly delivers the babies of Benedictine nuns raped by Soviet soldiers in Poland in 1945.
synopsis: Poland, December 1945. Mathilde Beaulieu, a young French Red Cross doctor caring for French soldiers before their repatriation, is begged by a nun to come to her convent. She finds that soldiers have raped the Benedictine sisters and that several are pregnant. The abbess, afraid that scandal will destroy the community, insists on secrecy, and some sisters resist examination, fearing it breaks their vows. Mathilde returns in secret, helped by Samuel, a Jewish doctor in her unit with whom she has an affair, and wins the trust of Sister Maria, the novice mistress. As the births come, the abbess says she is placing the babies with families; in fact she leaves one at a wayside cross, and its mother, Sister Zofia, kills herself. Maria confronts the abbess. Mathilde proposes that the sisters take in the town's orphans, and the convent becomes an orphanage; some nuns leave with their children.
inclusion: Fontaine handles a grim subject with restraint. Caroline Champetier's wintry photography, the sung Office and the faces of the sisters do much of the work, and Agata Buzek as Sister Maria and Agata Kulesza as the abbess give strong performances; Brad Miner of The Catholic Thing called Buzek the film's soul. It takes seriously what most films about nuns do not: what vows, enclosure and prayer mean to women who have suffered this. Critics praised it widely, and it had four César nominations. Dissent centres on the ending. Kevin Jagernauth in The Playlist thought the first two-thirds a nuanced study of devotion meeting a modern outlook, but found the rosy finale dishonest and one character clumsily pushed into a villain's role. A. G. Harmon, writing in Image, admired its account of faith enduring in a ruined place. It is for adults.
themes: The film's question is how faith survives violation. Without a priest the community has no Mass and lives by the Office alone. The sisters fear damnation for a chastity they did not choose to lose, and Maria defines faith as twenty-four hours of doubt and one minute of hope. Some lose their faith, some leave, some endure. Miner reads the film as about hope, its answers given in actions rather than words. The gravest wrong is the abbess's: her fear for the convent leads her to abandon a newborn and to call it Providence, and the film places the moral failure in her rigid authority. The resolution, an orphanage run by the sisters, depends on Mathilde, a non-believer, showing them their duty, and those who leave religious life are treated with sympathy.
history: Madeleine Pauliac (1912-1946) was a French doctor who headed the French Red Cross mission in Warsaw after the war and treated French soldiers awaiting repatriation. Her diary, kept by her nephew Philippe Maynial, records that Soviet soldiers had raped nuns in a convent near Warsaw, and that she delivered babies there in secret. She died in a car accident in 1946, aged 33. The numbers of nuns attacked in Poland in 1945 are not firmly established, and historians treat the story of the abbess abandoning a baby as invention.
liberties: Mathilde is a junior doctor rather than the head of the Warsaw hospital, and Samuel and the affair are not in the published accounts of Pauliac. Her notes say that pregnant nuns raised the question of abortion with her in veiled terms, which the film leaves out. The abbess's abandonment of a baby, Zofia's suicide and the orphanage ending are not attested in the available sources and appear to be invention.
advisories:
The rapes take place before the story and are not shown, but they are described. Soviet soldiers at a checkpoint come close to assaulting the heroine.

A brief non-marital bedroom scene between Mathilde and a colleague.

Childbirth scenes, including a Caesarean section; venereal disease; a nun's suicide; an abbess abandons a newborn.

For adults.

A religious superior is the film's chief wrongdoer, and leaving religious life is shown sympathetically.

title: A Birth
decision: PUBLISH: Tentative. The English subtitle file, a poor machine translation, answers the question the record left open. The faith is at the centre: baptisms, including a fellow prisoner's before his death; Kim's ordination as the first Korean priest; an Easter Mass whose consecration is heard in Latin in the traditional form; and a martyrdom presented as a confession of love made without fear, with last words that he gains eternal life by dying for the Catholic faith, followed by his farewell letter. The pioneer material serves the opening of a route for missionaries. Identity: Korean Film Council; treatment: The Fact, Maeil Shinmun and the dialogue check. If the editor wants a reliable translation first, it stays GREY/unverified.
summary: Park Heung-sik's lavish Korean biography of Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean priest, from his seminary years in Macau to his beheading in 1846.
synopsis: The film opens in 1836 with the French missionary Pierre Maubant crossing secretly into Korea, where Catholicism is outlawed. Kim Taegon, a teenager from a Catholic family, is sent with Choe Yang-eop and Choe Bang-je to study for the priesthood in Macau, where he learns Latin, French and Chinese as well as theology. War in China blocks the way home, and he spends time in the Philippines and China before making perilous journeys across frozen country and open sea to open a route for missionaries into Korea, helped by Yu Jin-gil, the Church's interpreter in its dealings with China. In 1845 he is ordained priest in Shanghai, the first Korean to be so, and returns to Joseon in a small wooden boat. Arrested in a new persecution, he is beheaded at Saenamteo in 1846, aged twenty-five.
inclusion: This is the first feature film about Korea's first priest, made for the bicentenary of his birth, and it is the only screen treatment of the Korean martyrs on this scale. Its money is on the screen in snowfields, storms at sea and the streets of Macau. Yoon Si-yoon plays Kim and speaks four languages; the reviews single him out, and Ahn Sung-ki adds weight as the interpreter Yu Jin-gil. Park Ji-yoon of The Fact found it crammed, packing ten years of events into a breathless sequence and assuming knowledge many viewers lack. At about 150 minutes it is long. Kim Jung-ki in Maeil Shinmun calls it sincere and praises the lead. Its dialogue keeps the sacraments and the martyrdom at the centre.
themes: Kim's priesthood and martyrdom frame the film, and the faith is at its centre. Converts are baptised, one of them a fellow prisoner shortly before his death; Kim is ordained in Shanghai as the first Korean priest; and at Easter he celebrates Mass, with the consecration heard in Latin in the traditional form. The pioneer material, his maps, the sea route and the Opium War, serves the aim of opening a way for missionaries. He is shown with fears and doubts as well as conviction, and his martyrdom is presented as a confession of love made without fear: his last words are that he gains eternal life by dying for the Catholic faith.
history: Andrew Kim Taegon (1821–1846), from a Catholic family that had already given martyrs, was sent to Macau in 1836 to train for the priesthood. He was ordained in Shanghai in 1845, the first Korean priest, and returned to bring missionaries into the country. Arrested in 1846, he was beheaded at Saenamteo by the Han River in September 1846. With 78 other martyrs of the 1839 and 1846 persecutions, among them Augustine Yu Jin-gil and Pierre Maubant, he was beatified by Pius XI in 1925; the group was canonised in 1984.
advisories:
Persecution, imprisonment and a beheading.

Dangerous sea and winter journeys.

Rated 12 in Korea; about 150 minutes.

Its makers frame Kim chiefly as a pioneer, but the film itself centres on his priesthood and martyrdom. The English subtitles available are a poor translation.

title: Fátima, Terra de Fé!
decision: GREY: Identity, outline and production context are established by the Cinemateca Portuguesa and Público's Cinecartaz. The Cinemateca's programme note and the Diário de Notícias comment on its craft and its place in the Estado Novo's official cinema, but no source assesses how it treats the apparitions or the faith. Settle with a 1943 Portuguese Catholic review (e.g. Novidades, Voz da Fátima) or a recorded viewing of the Cinemateca print, checking especially the staged apparition episode and the fictional cure.

grey.question: The film is well identified: Jorge Brum do Canto's 1943 feature, preserved and screened by the Cinemateca Portuguesa. What has not been assessed is how it treats Fátima. Its story of a sceptical doctor converted by his son's cure is fiction, set beside a staged account of the 1917 apparitions, and the only critical comments, from the Cinemateca and the Portuguese press, concern its craft and its official character under the Salazar regime. A contemporary Catholic review or a recorded viewing would settle it.

summary: Jorge Brum do Canto's wartime Portuguese drama of a sceptical doctor converted by his son's cure, set beside a staged account of the Fátima apparitions.
synopsis: A doctor without faith has become estranged from his family over religion and devotes himself to his patients. When his son is badly injured in an accident, his medicine proves insufficient, and the boy's recovery, attributed to the intervention of Our Lady of Fátima, brings the father to belief. The film sets this invented story against the shrine and includes an episode that reconstructs the 1917 apparitions to the shepherd children. The father's struggle between science and faith is the dramatic spine. The sources found do not describe how the cure is staged, how the family is reconciled or how closely the apparition episode follows the historical accounts.
inclusion: The Cinemateca Portuguesa calls this the classic Portuguese sound film on Fátima. It was an ambitious studio picture, shot at Tóbis Portuguesa as the first production of Filmes Portugueses, the new company of the cinematographer César de Sá. Brum do Canto was one of the leading directors of the period, and the Diário de Notícias presents the film as an example of the Estado Novo's official production. He himself dismissed it as commissioned work with little of himself in it, except the apparition episode and the doctor's religious dilemma. The Cinemateca nonetheless singles out passages of documentary interest and some well-directed sequences. It is a document of how Portugal presented Fátima to itself in wartime, a quarter-century after the apparitions.
themes: The film turns on a healing and the conversion it brings: a man of science confronted with a cure his medicine could not achieve. That pattern reflects Fátima's place as a shrine of pilgrimage and prayer for the sick, and the film adds a staged account of the apparitions themselves. The healing is fiction and should not be mistaken for one of the documented events of Fátima. How the film presents the Lady's message, prayer, penance and the Rosary, has not been described by any source.
history: Three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, reported six apparitions of Our Lady at the Cova da Iria, near Fátima, between May and October 1917, ending with the solar phenomenon seen by a large crowd on 13 October. The Bishop of Leiria declared the apparitions worthy of belief in 1930. By 1942 Fátima was a national shrine, and Pius XII consecrated the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary that October.
liberties: The doctor, his family and the cure are invented for the film. The 1917 apparitions appear as a reconstructed episode within the fiction; how closely it follows Lúcia's accounts is not known.
advisories:

doctrine: The apparitions at the Cova da Iria were reported between 13 May and 13 October 1917. On 13 October 1930 Bishop José Alves Correia da Silva of Leiria declared them 'worthy of belief', which allowed public devotion; this is a judgment that belief is permitted, not a doctrine that Catholics must accept. The Lady's reported message asked for the daily Rosary for peace, prayer and sacrifice for sinners, devotion to the Immaculate Heart and the consecration of Russia. On 31 October 1942 Pius XII consecrated the human race to the Immaculate Heart of Mary in a radio message to Portugal, naming the peoples of Russia, and repeated the act at St Peter's on 8 December 1942. Healings attributed to Our Lady are for the bishop to examine; the film's cure is invented.
production: Jorge Brum do Canto's fourth feature was the first production of Filmes Portugueses, a company set up by the cinematographer José César de Sá, who photographed it and directed production. It was shot at Tóbis Portuguesa in Lisbon and released in 1943 at 102 minutes. Brum do Canto later called it commissioned work, in which he felt closer to the apparition episode and the doctor's religious doubts. The Cinemateca's note praises its documentary episodes and well-directed sequences, and the Diário de Notícias counts it among the official productions of the Estado Novo. It is remembered as the classic sound-era Portuguese film on Fátima. No Catholic review of the time has been found.

title: The Bells of Nagasaki
decision: GREY: identity is secure (Shochiku, NFAJ: 94 min, 22–23 September 1950, script by Shindō, Mitsuhata and Hashida from Nagai's books) and the outline and censorship history are documented (Seid/PFA, Shibata). Treatment of the faith is described only in a paragraph each by Shibata and Seid, who disagree on whether the conversion is shown; Nipponica judges it a good Ofuna-style work but says nothing of faith. Not HOLD because identity and content are established. Settles with a scene-level account (viewing or the 1950 Kinema Junpō review; Tadao Satō) of the conversion, Midori's faith and death, the treatment of the bomb as providence, and the ending.

grey.question: The film's identity is secure, but no critic has described in any detail how it presents Takashi Nagai's Catholic faith. The two scholarly accounts give a paragraph each and disagree on whether his conversion happens on screen. Nagai's own reading of the bomb as a burnt offering to God is disputed, and it is not known whether the film adopts it. A scene-level account of the conversion, his wife Midori's faith and death, and the ending, from a viewing or from the 1950 Japanese reviews, would settle it.

summary: Shochiku's occupation-era melodrama of Takashi Nagai, the Catholic radiologist of Nagasaki, and the first Japanese feature to approach the atomic bombing, made under heavy American censorship.
synopsis: Takashi Nagai, a medical student in Nagasaki, turns to radiology at a time when older doctors scorn the field. He is supported by his wife Midori. His early X-ray work exposes him to radiation, and he learns that he is dying before the war ends. Through the years of war he balances his research against duty to his wife and children, and he is drawn towards the Catholic faith of the city's Urakami Christians. In the last third of the film the atomic bomb falls on Nagasaki; the explosion is seen only as a cloud over the mountains. Afterwards the dying Nagai and the survivors set about rebuilding the city, and the bell of the ruined cathedral rings again.
inclusion: This is the first Japanese feature to approach the atomic bombing, made under Occupation censorship that rejected the first two script outlines and required a hopeful ending of survivors rebuilding their city. It adapts the books of Takashi Nagai, the Catholic radiologist of Urakami, from a script co-written by Kaneto Shindō, with music by Yūji Koseki, whose theme song became hugely popular. The Nipponica encyclopedia counts it among the good films that showed the best side of Hideo Ōba's Ofuna studio style; Steve Seid of the Pacific Film Archive calls it a somewhat sentimental melodrama. Its interest for a Catholic viewer is that a major Japanese studio built a 1950 film round a Catholic convert's faith and death. How fully it shows that faith is the open question.
themes: According to the archive notes and Yuko Shibata's study, the film shows Nagai drawn to the Catholic faith of his wife Midori and of the Urakami Christians, and accepting his own death from radiation with resignation; Shibata says he treats the bombing as a test given by God. The closing bell is the Angelus bell of Urakami Cathedral. Nagai himself taught that the bomb was a burnt offering accepted by God, a reading later criticised by some survivors. Whether the film adopts that theology, and whether it shows his baptism or only his attraction to the faith, has not been established.
history: Takashi Nagai was a radiologist at Nagasaki Medical College who was baptised a Catholic at 26, influenced by his wife Midori's faith. His X-ray work had already given him a fatal dose of radiation when the bomb of 9 August 1945 devastated Urakami, the Catholic district, and killed Midori. His book The Bells of Nagasaki was cleared by the Occupation censors only on condition that it appeared with an account of Japanese atrocities in Manila; it was published in 1949, and the film followed the next year.
liberties: Shibata calls the film a "somehow fictionalized" version of Nagai's story. The Occupation censors forced the omission of many scenes from Shindō's script and required the rebuilding finale. The bombing is shown only as a distant cloud over the mountains. Sources disagree on whether Nagai's conversion is shown within the film.
advisories:
Terminal illness from radiation, and a wife's death in the bombing; the explosion itself is seen only at a distance.

Wartime hardship.

No English-subtitled home-video edition has been found; the Pacific Film Archive holds a restricted subtitled print.

names: Nagasaki no kane (The Bells of Nagasaki, 1949), Kono ko o nokoshite and Rosario no kusari, books by Takashi Nagai

suitability.note: The story centres on a man dying of radiation sickness and on his wife's death in the atomic bombing, though the explosion is seen only as a distant cloud. It is a slow, sentimental drama in Japanese, and no subtitled home edition is known, so it suits older children watching with a parent.

doctrine: Urakami was the home of Japan's hidden Christians. On 17 March 1865 a group of them made themselves known to Père Petitjean at the new church in Nagasaki; persecution resumed in 1867, the Urakami faithful were sent into exile, and many died before the survivors came home in 1873. Nagai entered that community by baptism in June 1934, taking the name Paul. The bell of the title is the Angelus bell of Urakami Cathedral; the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) records the Angelus said morning, noon and evening at the bell, indulgenced by John XXII in 1318 and by Benedict XIII in 1724. Nagai's teaching that the dead of Urakami were a burnt offering accepted by God is his own reading, not a doctrine of the Church. It rests on the traditional teaching that suffering joined to Christ's Passion can be offered in reparation, but the Church has never declared any particular calamity to be such an offering.
production: Shochiku's Ōfuna studio made the film the year after Nagai's book appeared, with the support of Nagasaki City and Prefecture, the Society of St Paul and Toshiba. The script was by Kaneto Shindō, with Sekirō Mitsuhata and Sugako Hashida. The Occupation authorities rejected the first two outlines, many scenes were cut from Shindō's script, and the censors required a finale of survivors rebuilding the city; the bombing was a forbidden subject, so the studio cast the story as melodrama. Hideo Ōba directed, Masao Wakahara played Nagai and Yumeji Tsukioka his wife Midori. Liturgical music was sung by the St Gregory Choir. Yūji Koseki's theme song, with words by Hachirō Satō and sung by Mariko Ike, became hugely popular. The film opened on 23 September 1950, while Nagai was still alive; he died on 1 May 1951. No contemporary Catholic notice of the film has been found.

title: All That Remains
decision: PUBLISH: Respinti's review and the distributor and festival records document a Catholic conversion and family story, the bombing of Nagasaki, Nagai's illness and writing, and an imagined closing reunion; Higgins's account of five years' work and survivor interviews supports the seriousness of the research. Nagai is a Servant of God, not a canonised saint.
summary: A British low-budget hybrid of drama, CGI and archive footage about Takashi Nagai, the Nagasaki radiologist and convert who lost his wife to the atomic bomb.
synopsis: Takashi Nagai is a brilliant, sceptical young doctor in Nagasaki who lodges with a family of Catholics descended from Japan's hidden Christians. Their faith and their daughter Midori draw him, slowly, into the Church, and they marry. He throws himself into pioneering radiology, neglecting his family and his health, and is diagnosed with leukaemia. On 9 August 1945 the atomic bomb falls on Urakami, the Catholic heart of the city. Midori is killed. Nagai, injured and dying, works among the survivors, cares for his two children and, increasingly bedridden, writes the books that made him famous. The film ends with an imagined reunion with Midori at the cathedral, as on their wedding day.
inclusion: Nagai's story is important and little known outside Japan, and the Higgins brothers treat it with care: Dominic Higgins spent about five years on the project and interviewed survivors. The mix of live action, CGI and archive footage is a resourceful answer to a small budget, and Respinti found the archive images of the bombing chilling. Marco Respinti called it a film about the saint who beat the bomb. Its real strength is that faith is not decoration here. Conversion, Christian marriage and a doctor's charity are the story, and the film shows Nagai reading the catastrophe in the light of Providence and the Cross, as he did in his writings.
themes: The film is a conversion story first: an atheist scientist is drawn to Christ through the witness of a Catholic family and community with centuries of hidden fidelity behind them. Marriage is shown as a vocation, and its loss as a real grief. Nagai's response to the bomb, serving the wounded, raising his children and praying, is presented as Christian hope rather than stoicism. The closing reunion is a poetic image of hope in the resurrection. It is not a vision, and nothing in the sources suggests the film claims it is.
history: Takashi Nagai (1908–1951) was baptised in 1934 and married Midori Moriyama, whose family had kept the faith in secret through the persecutions. Already diagnosed with radiation-induced leukaemia, he survived the bombing of 9 August 1945, which killed Midori. He spent his last years in a tiny hut, writing; his books include The Bells of Nagasaki. His cause for beatification was opened in 2021.
liberties: Dialogue is invented and the narrative selects heavily from Nagai's life. The final reunion is imagined. CGI reconstructions stand in for prewar and bombed Nagasaki. The film is a family story and does not attempt a full account of the war or of the decision to use the bomb.
advisories:
Archive images of the atomic bombing and its victims, described by one reviewer as chilling; mass death and severe injury.

Bereavement, terminal illness and children who have lost their mother.

Best for teenagers and adults.
