suitability.note: Archive images of the atomic bombing and its victims, mass death and injury, and the death of a mother with young children. It suits older teenagers and adults.

doctrine: Nagai came to the Church as an adult convert and was baptised in 1934. The Church teaches that Baptism is necessary for salvation and that adults must be instructed and freely seek it (Council of Trent, Session 6; Roman Catechism). His wife's family belonged to the hidden Christians of Urakami. Their ancestors kept the faith after the persecutions of the Tokugawa period without priests, and in 1865 the Christians of Nagasaki made themselves known to Fr Petitjean at Oura. The Church teaches that suffering borne in union with Christ can be offered for the sanctification of the soul. Nagai's own reading of the bomb as a providential sacrifice for peace was his own view and is not Church teaching. He died on 1 May 1951. He is not a canonised saint.
production: Ian and Dominic Higgins made the film for their company Pixel Revolution Films, the makers of the Fátima film The 13th Day. It mixes live action, computer graphics and archive footage. To save money they did the visual effects themselves, and production took almost four years. The film was crowdfunded in its early stages. Members of the local Japanese community appeared as extras. Ignatius Press lists the DVD, with a documentary on Nagai told by Fr Paul Glynn, SM, under a publication date of 6 May 2016. The running time is given as 114 to 120 minutes. It was shown at the Uranium Film Festival in Berlin in 2017.

title: Don Bosco
decision: GREY: identity and production history are secure (ANICA visa, Torino Film Festival restoration, Enciclopedia del Cinema in Piemonte). The only independent critical text read is Cinema Illustrazione (1935), which judges craft, not faith. Pre-conciliar Catholic approval (Segnalazioni cinematografiche; L'Osservatore Romano and Rivista del Cinematografo) is known only at second hand, via Salesian ANS and an unpublished essay quoted by Prono. Salesians wrote the treatment, negotiated the script and later owned the negative. Settles with the 1935 Segnalazioni/Rivista del Cinematografo texts or a documented viewing of the 2021 restoration (dreams, Generala episode, Church–State material).

grey.question: The film's identity and production history are well documented, but no independent critic has described how it treats the faith. Approval from the Catholic film press of 1935 survives only at second hand, in Salesian accounts and an unpublished essay. The Salesians supplied the story, negotiated the script and later owned the film. A reading of the 1935 Catholic reviews, or a documented viewing of the restored version that covers Bosco's dreams, the reshot Generala episode and the Church–State material, would settle it.

summary: Lux's first production, made the year after John Bosco's canonisation: a Turin-shot life of the saint with one professional actor, Gian Paolo Rosmino, and real Salesians around him.
synopsis: A Monferrato farm boy who has lost his father clashes with his older half-brother Antonio and finds a mentor in the old priest Don Calosso, who teaches him Latin. After Calosso's death Giovanni leaves home to study at Chieri, where the death of his friend Luigi Comollo marks him. Ordained, he goes to Turin, where townspeople distrust his rowdy Sunday gatherings of poor boys. Help comes, surprisingly, from anticlerical authorities, who suggest a society whose members keep their civil rights. The Oratory becomes schools and workshops, the Salesians and the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians follow, and missionaries leave for Patagonia. The film ends with his death in 1888 and a coda of his canonisation in St Peter's.
inclusion: It is the first sound feature about Don Bosco and the first production of Riccardo Gualino's Lux, later one of the major Italian studios. It was shot in a snowbound Turin, at Chieri and in the Monferrato, with Gian Paolo Rosmino as Bosco and non-professionals around him, real Salesians among them. Giorgio Federico Ghedini wrote the score. Alessandrini, by his own account not a practising Catholic, said he kept to Bosco's memoirs and the historians and invented only linking scenes. Contemporary opinion was mixed. Cinema Illustrazione's critic praised Rosmino and the death scene but found the film disjointed, often superficial and close to an informational documentary. It failed in first-run cinemas and found its audience in parish halls. The 2021 restoration makes it viewable again.
themes: Salesian accounts and archive synopses agree on the shape: a vocation that grows into institutions, from a priest's Sunday gatherings of poor boys to schools, workshops, two religious congregations and missions in Patagonia. The Salesian historian Fr Rufillo Uguccioni wrote the first treatment, and the order's delegate negotiated the script throughout. The ending turns to the canonisation in St Peter's. How the film presents Bosco's prophetic dreams, his confessional ministry and the anticlerical state, which in this telling helps him found his society, has not been described by an independent critic.
history: John Bosco was born on 16 August 1815 at Becchi near Castelnuovo, Piedmont, and lost his father when he was two. He was ordained in Turin on 5 June 1841. In the 1840s he gathered poor and abandoned boys in the Oratory, which settled at Valdocco in 1846, and added workshops and schools. He founded the Salesians in 1859 and, with Maria Mazzarello, the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians in 1872. His missionaries reached Patagonia in 1875. He died in Turin on 31 January 1888, was beatified in 1929 and was canonised by Pius XI on 1 April 1934.
liberties: The first version, released in April 1935, included an episode at the Generala reformatory that the Salesians considered invented. After their protests the scene was reshot, with a caption stressing Bosco's role, and a second version reached cinemas in September 1935. A third version became the standard print. The 2021 restoration reconstructs the second version. Bosco's real outing with Generala inmates in 1855 suggests the scene dramatised an actual episode, but this is unresolved.
advisories:
Poverty, the death of a friend and a deathbed scene.

An early sound film with period acting and recording; patience required.

No age classification found.

suitability.note: Poverty, the death of a friend and a deathbed scene, all gentle. It is an early sound film in Italian with period acting, so children need patience.

doctrine: Bosco's work was a work of Christian education: to keep poor boys from sin and bring them to the sacraments of penance and Holy Communion. His method, which he called the preventive system, rests on reason, religion and loving-kindness. He founded the Salesian Society in 1859 under the patronage of St Francis de Sales, and Pius IX gave it final approval in 1874. With Maria Mazzarello he founded the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians in 1872. He had a strong devotion to Our Lady Help of Christians, a title whose feast, on 24 May, Pius VII established after his return to Rome. Pius XI, who had known Bosco, beatified him in 1929 and canonised him on Easter Sunday, 1 April 1934. His feast is 31 January.
production: Goffredo Alessandrini directed the film for Lux Film, then run by the industrialist Riccardo Gualino, who had been sent into internal exile on Lipari by the Fascist regime. It was made a year after the canonisation, in the climate that followed the Lateran Pacts of 1929. The script was by Alessandrini, Sergio Amidei and Aldo Vergano, from a story by Onorato Castellino and Rufillo Uguccioni. Gian Paolo Rosmino played Bosco. The film runs about 90 minutes in black and white. Gualino later ceded the negative to the Salesians, who held it in their archive. A restored version made from that negative, deposited at Ivrea in 2016, was shown at the Torino Film Festival in 2021.

title: La mies es mucha
decision: PUBLISH: Ernesto Fayé's detailed 1949 review in Cristiandad, read in full, documents a restrained, humorous and devout missionary drama with named religious advisers and judges the one doubtful Christmas Mass gag innocent; RTVE fixes the plot and audience guidance. The director's role as the Franco regime's official filmmaker and the film's place in national-Catholic cinema are disclosed; neither source shows the film carrying political propaganda.
summary: Sáenz de Heredia's missionary drama sends a young Spanish priest to a plague-stricken Indian village, and balances sacrifice with gentle comedy.
synopsis: Father Santiago, a young Spanish missionary, arrives at Kattinga in India to replace the ailing Father Daniel, who dies soon after. He finds the villagers in the grip of Sandem, a trader and moneylender whose loans end in forced labour in a mine. To free them, Santiago signs for the debts of the whole village. When the note falls due, Sandem demands payment. At the same moment people sick with plague begin arriving, and Santiago gives himself to their care. The comedy of a newcomer learning the mission's ways, including a Midnight Mass where the wrong gramophone record plays, gives way to the cost of staying with his flock.
inclusion: Unlike much Spanish religious cinema of the 1940s, it trusts the facts more than the rhetoric. The 1949 Cristiandad critic praised its 'gran contención': no showy technique, no melodramatic tricks, and humour that makes it a pleasure rather than a seminary lecture. Fernando Fernán Gómez is in the cast. A Vincentian missionary who had served at Cuttack advised on the village, which was reconstructed in Spain, and the Augustinian Félix García advised on religious matters. The story of a priest who pledges himself for his people's debts and then serves them through an epidemic is a clean, strong one. The Indian characters are seen through a 1940s Spanish lens, with all its limits.
themes: The title is Christ's own: the harvest is plentiful and the labourers few. The film's Catholic case is missionary charity in its literal form. The priest takes on his people's debt, then risks and ultimately gives his life in the plague. The Midnight Mass gag, in which an unexpected record replaces the carols, worried some contemporaries. Cristiandad's critic, who was alert to irreverence elsewhere, judged it innocent and typically Spanish, with no offence to the Mass itself. Evangelisation is presented as service to the poor against exploitation, not conquest.
liberties: An original story, not a biography. The Indian setting is reconstructed with Spanish locations and actors in some roles, and the picture of Indian society is simplified. Recorded runtimes vary widely between versions.
advisories:
Plague, illness and the death of priests and villagers.

Forced labour and debt bondage.

RTVE rated its broadcast not recommended for under-12s.

A comic mix-up during Midnight Mass may bother some viewers; contemporary Catholic critics judged it harmless.

suitability.note: Plague, the deaths of two priests and villagers, and debt bondage in a mine; RTVE did not recommend its broadcast for under-12s. The comic first half is easy going, and the priest's self-giving gives older children something to think about.

doctrine: The title is Matthew 9:37: 'The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few.' The years before the film saw the popes press hard for missions: Benedict XV's Maximum illud (1919) and Pius XI's Rerum Ecclesiae (1926) urged the training of native clergy and the support of missionaries, and in 1927 Pius XI named St Francis Xavier, apostle of India, and St Thérèse of Lisieux patrons of the missions. Father Santiago's signing for his people's debts is a corporal work of mercy, the ransoming of captives, and his staying with the plague-stricken follows the traditional teaching that a pastor must give the sacraments to the dying even at risk to his own life. Midnight Mass belongs to the old Christmas privilege by which every priest may say three Masses on the feast.
production: Vicente Escrivá and José Rodulfo Boeta wrote the screenplay, and the film was made under the patronage of Bishop Ángel Herrera Oria of Málaga. José Luis Sáenz de Heredia, a first cousin of José Antonio Primo de Rivera and the regime's leading director, made it in 1948 with Fernando Fernán Gómez as the young missionary. India was recreated in Málaga, in the tropical gardens of La Concepción. Ricardo Torres photographed it and Manuel Parada wrote the score. It was a large box-office success. The Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos gave it its medals for best film and best director, and for supporting performances by Rafael Romero Marchent and Julia Caba Alba. It belongs to the national-Catholic cinema of the 1940s, and Catholic critics such as Cristiandad's praised it partly as a credit to Spanish missions.

title: Le Sorcier du ciel
decision: GREY: identity is secure (CNC visa 8067, Unifrance, Cinematografo). A brief pre-conciliar Catholic critical judgment now exists: Séquences no. 16 (January 1959) cites the film as an example of the artifice Pius XII warned against, the director having gone astray by chasing the sensational side of the saint, notably the devil. Kind 'reservations' rather than 'unverified' because the concern is now stated by an independent source. Not REJECT: Vianney was canonised in 1925. Settles with the Centrale Catholique cote, a 1949 Radio-Cinéma or La Croix review, or a documented viewing of the devil scenes.

grey.question: The question is one of emphasis. Le Sorcier du ciel gives the Devil a speaking part and stages the Curé d'Ars's night-time struggles with him as set-pieces. Writing in 1959, the Quebec film review Séquences cited it as an example of the artifice Pius XII warned against: the director went astray chasing the sensational side of the saint's life, and spiritual combat sits badly in a presbytery bedroom. No fuller review has been found. A contemporary French Catholic review or rating, or a documented viewing, would show whether the saint or the spectacle dominates.

summary: A French life of the Curé d'Ars, with Georges Rollin as Vianney facing a hostile village and a Devil who argues with him at night.
synopsis: In 1818 the young priest Jean-Marie Vianney is sent to Ars, a village of unbelievers and anticlericals, and is met with jeers from the blacksmith Sanson and the innkeeper Mairey, whose wedding is being celebrated. Poor and worn by work and fasting, he preaches boldly, while the Devil works against him and the two of them argue at night. Falsely accused of plotting against the government, he is about to be arrested when he cures Mairey's crippled son, and the father returns to the faith. His fame grows, and he confesses day and night and reads souls. He tries to flee the celebrity but is brought back. At the end only Sanson resists, until the old curé's death.
inclusion: The subject is the patron of parish priests, and the film builds its story round what made him famous: preaching, penance, the long hours in the confessional and a village won back to the faith. Georges Rollin plays Vianney, Marie Daëms plays his helper Catherine Lassagne, and René Jolivet wrote the script. Unifrance records a selection at Venice in 1949. It is one of the few films to take the saint's reported struggles with the devil literally and put them on screen, which is exactly what its critics questioned. Made two years before Bresson's Diary of a Country Priest, it is a useful point of comparison for anyone interested in how French cinema of the period filmed the priesthood.
themes: The film presents the conversion of a parish through a priest's suffering and prayer: preaching against the tavern and the dance, the confessional as the place where souls are won, and the devil's attacks as a sign that the work is succeeding. The cure of the innkeeper's son and the last holdout's conversion at Vianney's death make grace visible. The Devil is a speaking character who argues with the priest at night. In 1959 Séquences judged that Blistène had gone astray in pursuing the surprising side of the saint's life, and that spiritual combat is poorly contained in the closed, material space of a presbytery room.
history: Jean-Baptiste-Marie Vianney became parish priest of Ars in 1818, when his bishop warned him there was little love of God in the parish. He made the church his home and disciplined himself with vigils and fasts. In his last years he spent sixteen hours or more a day in the confessional and was credited with reading souls and healing the sick, especially children. He longed to flee into solitude but never abandoned his post. He died at Ars on 4 August 1859, was beatified in 1905 and canonised in 1925.
liberties: Unifrance's synopsis says the film presents his life "en forme un peu romancée". The named village antagonists and the false political accusation have not been checked against the historical record. The departure and return compress his recorded longing to leave Ars into a single episode. The Devil appears as a speaking character, a dramatic device Séquences considered misjudged.
advisories:
Night scenes in which the Devil harasses and argues with the priest; these may frighten children.

Village hostility and mockery of a priest; a crippled child; a deathbed.

General-audience classification in France (CNC).

doctrine: The film turns on the sacrament of penance. The Council of Trent (Session 14, 1551) taught that priests have the power to forgive sins, and that sacramental confession of all mortal sins is necessary to salvation. Vianney spent sixteen to eighteen hours a day in the confessional in his last years. The Church also holds that devils are fallen angels who were created good (Fourth Lateran Council, 1215) and who tempt men but cannot compel them. Accounts of Vianney's harassment by the devil are traditional, but the film dramatises them freely. Vianney was beatified in 1905 and canonised by Pius XI on 31 May 1925. Pius XI named him patron of parish priests in 1929. His feast is 4 August.
production: Marcel Blistène directed from a screenplay by René Jolivet, for Ydex Films, in black and white. Georges Rollin played the Curé. Raymond Loyer was Satan as a voice or shadow. The film was released in France on 14 October 1949 and runs about 100 minutes. It was shown in Italy as Il paese senza Dio. The film loosely fictionalises Vianney's life, giving him invented adversaries in the village. Little is recorded about its shooting or reception.

title: Caterina da Siena
decision: PUBLISH: The contemporary judgment of the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico (preserved in the Italian bishops' film-commission archive) approves the film for all audiences as made with elevated intentions, finds Catherine's mysticism well conveyed and asks parish halls to cut one bedroom scene; ANICA and Film Atlas establish identity and the 1947 censorship certificate. Intermezzo's hostile review and Gianluca della Maggiore's account cover craft and reception. The weak craft and the parish-hall cut are disclosed; neither is a doctrinal problem. Distinct from Palella's later Io, Caterina (1956).
summary: Oreste Palella's modest postwar life of St Catherine of Siena, from her childhood vision to her death in Rome, approved by Italy's Catholic film office.
synopsis: In Siena, the young Caterina Benincasa has a vision of Christ and gives herself to prayer and penance. Her forceful mother, Lapa, wants her married; Caterina answers that she is already the bride of Jesus, and her father and her confessor take her side. She joins the Mantellate, the Dominican women of penance, while still living at home, and the order approves her teaching. After a stay in Florence she returns to nurse the victims of plague in Siena. In 1376 she persuades Pope Gregory XI to bring the papacy back from Avignon to Rome, and miracles are attributed to her. She dies in Rome on 29 April 1380, her last words recorded as 'Blood, blood, blood.'
inclusion: This is an early screen life of Catherine of Siena, made in the poverty of postwar Italy by Oreste Palella, a minor director who returned to the saint in Io, Caterina (1956). Regana De Liguoro plays Catherine, with Rina De Liguoro as her mother. The script by Fernando Leonardi and Palella draws on Catherine's life and letters. The contemporary verdicts are mixed. Italy's Catholic Film Centre found passages of good workmanship and judged Catherine's mysticism well conveyed, but thought the whole rather fragmentary and her political work poorly drawn; it praised the score. The magazine Intermezzo was harsher, saying such a subject needed more preparation and less limited means. The historian Gianluca della Maggiore records that it won over neither critics nor audiences. It is a period piece rather than a lost classic, and copies are hard to find.
themes: Catherine's mystical life is the centre of the film: the childhood vision, her refusal of marriage because she is already given to Christ, penance, and her life as a Dominican tertiary living in the world. Her nursing of the plague-stricken shows prayer turning into charity. Her mission to Gregory XI presents loyalty to the Pope as part of the same holiness, though the Catholic Film Centre thought this public side the weakest part of the film. Its moral verdict was that the film had been conceived and made with elevated intentions and could be shown to everyone in public cinemas.
history: Caterina Benincasa (1347–1380), the daughter of a Sienese dyer, joined the Dominican Mantellate as a laywoman and became known for her prayer, her penances, her care for the sick and her letters to popes and princes. She urged Gregory XI to return the papacy from Avignon to Rome, which he did in 1377. Her Dialogue and nearly four hundred letters survive. She was canonised by Pius II in 1461 and named a patron of Italy by Pius XII in 1939.
advisories:
Plague scenes and a deathbed.

The Catholic Film Centre passed it for all audiences in public cinemas, but asked parish halls to cut a first-half sequence showing the character Monna Gioiosa in her bedroom or dressing room.

Cheaply made and, by contemporary accounts, fragmentary; copies are scarce.

doctrine: Catherine was canonised by Pius II in 1461 and Pius XII named her a patron of Italy in 1939 together with St Francis. Her feast is 30 April (the 1962 calendar). The film touches the Mantellate, the lay branch of the Dominican Third Order, whose members live at home under the Dominican rule. It also touches the Church's teaching on the Roman Pontiff as Christ's vicar: Catherine's letters call him 'the sweet Christ on earth' and urge Gregory XI to return from Avignon, which he did in January 1377. The Italian Catholic Film Centre passed it for all audiences in public cinemas but asked parish halls to cut a sequence in which Monna Gioiosa is shown in her room. title: John of the Cross
decision: GREY: Identity settled: 1997, Saint Luke Productions, directed by K. C. Lynch (Spirituality & Practice and Katoflix; the IMDb credit to Leonardo Defilippis likely reflects his role as producer-performer), with Leonardo and Patti Defilippis in the main roles; 56–60 minutes by edition. Content is clear from the producer's description and a brief Spirituality & Practice notice, but no independent review assesses its treatment, and how it frames the Calced–Discalced conflict is unchecked. A transcript or independent review would move it to PUBLISH or to reservations.
summary: Saint Luke Productions' hour-long drama of John of the Cross, from a poor childhood to the prison cell where he wrote his poems, played by a husband-and-wife company.
synopsis: John grows up in poverty and is drawn early to contemplative prayer. As a young Carmelite friar and priest he finds his order lax, and his austerity offends many of his brethren, including his superiors. In 1567 he meets Teresa of Ávila, who is seeking a partner for her reform; she makes him prior of the first house of Discalced friars, and he later serves as confessor at her convent. Friars opposed to the reform seize him and shut him in a cell for nine months. There he composes much of his poetry and reaches the mystical union he has longed for, before an escape the producers call miraculous. The story is told through the eyes of one of his patrons, and passages from the Spiritual Canticle run through it.
inclusion: Saint Luke Productions, a small American Catholic theatre company led by the actor Leonardo Defilippis, made this as a modest video drama: Defilippis and his wife Patti play the principal roles, with about sixty extras and a score by Randall DeBruyn. It is one of very few English-language films about John of the Cross, and it puts his poetry at the centre rather than treating him as a footnote to Teresa. Frederic and Mary Ann Brussat of Spirituality & Practice, a multifaith review site, describe a drama of the saint's longing for union with God, built round his meeting with Teresa and his imprisonment. Mother Angelica of EWTN endorsed it, according to the producer. At under an hour it is necessarily a sketch, and the tiny cast limits its scale; it is pitched at parish and classroom use.
themes: The film treats John's life as a path to union with God through suffering: the Carmelite rule taken seriously, Teresa's reform, and the dark cell where he writes. Its religious content is traditional: the contemplative vocation, obedience and the cross. The framing invites one caution. The producer's copy says his brethren imprisoned him out of resentment at his holiness, and the Brussats speak of an order that found his devotion excessive and of corruption in it. The real conflict was a jurisdictional dispute between Calced and Discalced Carmelites under the Church's law, and a holy-reformer-against-the-institution reading would distort it. How the film itself presents the dispute is unverified.
history: Juan de Yepes (1542–1591) entered the Carmelites at Medina del Campo in 1563 and was ordained in 1567, the year he met Teresa of Ávila. In 1568 he helped found the first Discalced friary at Duruelo. In December 1577 friars of the Observance seized him at Ávila and held him in their Toledo priory, where he composed much of the Spiritual Canticle; he escaped in August 1578. He was beatified in 1675, canonised in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926.

No sexual content or strong language is reported.

grey.question: John of the Cross is a short, devout drama from Saint Luke Productions, a present-day Catholic company. Its content is clear from the producer and a brief notice on Spirituality & Practice, but no independent review assesses how it treats the faith or the history. In particular, it is unverified whether it presents the conflict with the Calced Carmelites as a dispute inside the Church's order and law, or as a holy reformer against a corrupt institution. An independent review or a transcript would settle it.

doctrine: John of the Cross (1542–1591) was beatified by Clement X in 1675, canonised by Benedict XIII in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church by Pius XI in 1926. With Teresa of Ávila he founded the Discalced Carmelites. The conflict that ends in his imprisonment was a dispute of jurisdiction. In 1575 the Carmelite general chapter at Piacenza ordered the reformed houses to close; in December 1577 friars of the old Observance seized him at Ávila and held him in Toledo, where he composed much of the Spiritual Canticle and escaped in August 1578. The papal nuncio's action against the Discalced was contested, and the separation into a distinct province was granted by Gregory XIII in 1580 and made complete by Clement VIII's bull of 20 December 1593. His writings (the Ascent of Mount Carmel, the Dark Night, the Spiritual Canticle, the Living Flame) describe the purgation of the soul on the way to union with God.
production: Saint Luke Productions, a Catholic company run by Leonardo and Patti Defilippis, made John of the Cross as a one-hour film with more than sixty extras and a score by Randall DeBruyn. K. C. Lynch is credited as director in our record. Its content is known only from the producer's own description, which says that a young priest confronts corruption in his Carmelite Order and that his brethren imprison him for nine months, during which he writes his poetry and escapes miraculously. The Spiritual Canticle runs through it. It is sold on DVD by the producer and streamed on FORMED. No independent review has been found, and no Catholic rating.

title: Saint John Houghton
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established only by the producer: the Mary's Dowry product page (archived 2021) and production blog (filming July 2015, editing November 2015, DVD release announced 26 March 2016). Houghton was beatified by Leo XIII in 1886, so rule (a) does not apply; he is styled Bl. No independent treatment exists, so unverified rather than PUBLISH.
summary: A half-hour devotional film from Mary's Dowry Productions on Bl. John Houghton, the Carthusian prior who was the first martyr of Henry VIII's royal supremacy.
synopsis: Mary's Dowry films tell a saint's life through silent reconstructed scenes, a devotional narration and original contemplative music, and this one follows that pattern. Houghton flees a marriage his parents have arranged, studies for the priesthood and later enters the London Charterhouse, where he is elected prior. When Henry VIII demands the oath acknowledging his supremacy over the Church in England, Houghton refuses. He and his companions are imprisoned in the Tower, pressed by Thomas Cromwell, tried at Westminster and condemned for high treason. On 4 May 1535 they are dragged on hurdles to Tyburn, and Thomas More watches them go from his cell. Houghton urges his brethren to confession, goes first to the gallows in his habit and forgives his executioner. The reconstructions show him teaching novices, at prayer, in prison and at Tyburn.
inclusion: Houghton is the protomartyr of the English Reformation, yet he has almost no presence on film, and this short is the only dedicated treatment found. Mary's Dowry Productions, a small family company in West Sussex, has been making low-budget lives of the English martyrs for parishes and schools since 2007, and describes its approach as prayer as much as information: silent tableaux, narration and contemplative music rather than drama. That makes it suitable for a classroom or a quiet evening, and unsuitable for anyone expecting a dramatised biography. The scenes were filmed over a day in July 2015 in a barn beside a parish church in Goring, which gives a fair idea of the scale. No critic has reviewed it.
themes: The Catholic content is unambiguous: the Pope's primacy against the royal supremacy, the Carthusian life of prayer and silence, and a martyrdom met with confession, forgiveness and joy. The producers' text includes More's remark that the monks went to death like bridegrooms to their marriage. As described, it has none of the post-conciliar framing common in recent productions. Its weakness is the reverse: the producers' own account is plain hagiography, with a terrified jury and a horrified crowd, and it leaves out complications such as Houghton's qualified acceptance of the oath of succession in 1534.
history: Houghton, born in Essex about 1487, entered the London Charterhouse in 1516 and was elected prior in 1531. In 1534 he was imprisoned for refusing the oath of succession, then took it with the qualification "as far as the law of Christ allows". In 1535 he and the priors of Beauvale and Axholme refused the oath of supremacy, and on 4 May they were hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn with Richard Reynolds of Syon. Leo XIII beatified him in 1886.
advisories:
The execution at Tyburn is shown in reconstruction; the producers present the film as devotional, not graphic.

Suitable for older children and adults.

The producers call him Saint; he was beatified in 1886 and is styled Bl. John Houghton here.

grey.question: Saint John Houghton is a 30-minute devotional film on the Carthusian prior executed at Tyburn in 1535, made by a small English Catholic company. Its content is known only from the producers' own description and production blog, which show a straightforward account of his refusal of the royal supremacy and his martyrdom, with no modern framing. No review or independent description has been found. A viewing, or any published assessment, would show whether its history is as sound as its intent.

doctrine: Houghton and his companions died for the primacy of the Pope. The Act of Supremacy of 1534 made Henry VIII supreme head of the Church in England, and the oath was required of the clergy. The Church teaches that Christ gave Peter and his successors the primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church, a doctrine defined by the Vatican Council in 1870 but held from the first centuries. Houghton first took the oath of succession in 1534 only with the clause 'as far as the law of Christ allows', and refused the oath of supremacy in 1535. The Carthusians keep silence, enclosure and perpetual abstinence from meat under their Statutes; the order was founded by St Bruno in 1084. Leo XIII beatified Houghton in 1886, with the other English martyrs of that group. The Church allows no one to deny the Faith to save his life.

title: Golgotha
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from Unifrance and AlloCiné; substantive treatment from James Travers's detailed review and K. V. Turley's National Catholic Register essay, which together establish Scripture-based dialogue for Christ, a reverent Passion and a depicted Resurrection. The portrayal of the Temple authorities is disputed in secondary comment and is flagged rather than treated as resolved by silence.
summary: The first sound film of the Passion: Duvivier's dark, crowded Holy Week, with Jean Gabin's Pilate and Harry Baur's Herod, and a crucifixion staged as a cosmic storm.
synopsis: Christ enters Jerusalem to the crowd's acclaim. The high priests, fearing his popularity, plot with Judas and press the Roman authorities. At the Last Supper Christ foretells his betrayal. He is arrested, taken before Caiaphas, Herod and Pilate, mocked and scourged. Pilate, warned by his wife Claudia, tries to release him, but the crowd chooses Barabbas. Christ carries the cross to Golgotha and is crucified as a storm breaks over the city. The film continues past his death and burial to the Risen Christ.
inclusion: Duvivier keeps Christ at a distance for the first half, seen from behind or across a crowd, and lets us read him through the people around him: Our Lady, Peter, Judas, Caiaphas, Herod, Pilate. K. V. Turley, writing for the National Catholic Register, finds the method illuminating and the film well judged at about ninety minutes. Robert Le Vigan speaks only words from the Gospels and plays them quietly. The supporting cast is the strength: Harry Baur's massive Herod, Gabin's tired, almost decent Pilate, Edwige Feuillère as his wife. Jules Kruger's photography and Ferdinand Earle's Jerusalem give it real scale for a French production, and James Travers rightly singles out the crucifixion sequence. The script is thin and the characters stay at arm's length; some viewers will find it stiff.
themes: The Passion is played straight from the Gospels, without invented speeches for Christ. Travers stresses the film's emphasis on Christ's humanity and suffering; that is a matter of emphasis, not denial, since the film shows the Risen Christ with the wounds of the nails, and Turley calls it a cinematic icon for praying through Holy Week. Our Lady's presence is reverent. The Last Supper is staged after Leonardo. The film locates guilt in a small group of conspirators and in Pilate's weakness, though some later viewers find the Temple authorities visually stereotyped.
liberties: Pilate is made more sympathetic than the Gospels require, and Claudia Procula's role is enlarged. Herod's scene is built up for Harry Baur. Some reports say the film ends with the Ascension, others with the Resurrection; the ending was not verified.
advisories:
Scourging, mockery and crucifixion, shown without modern graphic detail but with real force.

Some viewers consider the costuming and casting of the Jewish authorities stereotyped in the manner of 1930s European films.

Suitable for older children and up; the crucifixion storm is frightening.

suitability.note: The scourging, mocking and crucifixion are not graphic by modern standards but are shown with force, and the storm at the crucifixion can frighten younger children. It is a French black-and-white film of about 95 minutes, best for older children who already know the Gospel story.

doctrine: The film's reverent Last Supper and its Resurrection follow the Creed: Christ 'suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried', and rose again. On the question the film is sometimes asked about, who killed Christ, the Roman Catechism of the Council of Trent is plain. Under the Fourth Article it teaches that our sins consigned Christ to the cross, that sinners were the 'authors and ministers' of his Passion, and that 'this guilt seems more enormous in us than in the Jews', since they would not have crucified the Lord had they known him, while Christians who know him deny him by their deeds. Claudia Procula, Pilate's wife, is named in tradition, and the Greek Church keeps her feast on 27 October.
history: The film follows the last week of Christ's life as the four Gospels tell it, from the entry into Jerusalem to the Resurrection. Pontius Pilate governed Judaea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36, an unusually long term, and was recalled after complaints from the Samaritans. The Gospels name Caiaphas as high priest and Annas as his father-in-law, and St Luke alone records that Pilate sent Christ to Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee. St Matthew alone records the message from Pilate's wife about her dream. Golgotha, the place of the skull, lay outside the walls of Jerusalem.
production: The project began with Canon Joseph Reymond, who wrote the scenario. Duvivier took it on after Maria Chapdelaine, and the film was shot in 1934 for the company Ichthys Film, with exteriors at Fort-de-l'Eau near Algiers and interiors at Boulogne. Jean Perrier built solid sets, and Ferdinand Earle painted the view of Jerusalem. It was a costly production by French standards. Jacques Ibert's score makes extensive use of the ondes Martenot, an electronic instrument then still a novelty, and Ibert later drew a concert suite from it. Golgotha opened in France in April 1935, played across Europe, and reached the United States in 1937 as Behold the Man, when the National Board of Review named it the sixth best foreign film of the year. The British censors refused it. No Legion of Decency rating has been found.

title: Miracle of Saint Thérèse
decision: PUBLISH: Unifrance confirms identity (FAF / Films Fernand Rivers, released 29 August 1952); Steven Greydanus's Decent Films review (A+, +4, nothing objectionable) gives detailed evidence of a reverent biography that presents the Little Way, Carmelite life and her death faithfully. Main checks against Thérèse's own Story of a Soul show no material distortion; minor chronological points are noted.
summary: A plain, reverent French biography of St Thérèse of Lisieux, from her childhood at Les Buissonnets to her death in Carmel, framed by her cause for canonisation.
synopsis: Framed by documentary-style scenes of her canonisation cause, the film tells Thérèse Martin's life. A pious child in a devout family, she hears her father read about Joan of Arc and wants to be a saint. Gravely ill as a girl, she is cured when a statue of Our Lady seems to smile at her. She follows two sisters into the Carmel of Lisieux, overcoming the objections of the convent's ecclesiastical superior. Inside, a prioress rebukes her ambition to be a saint as presumptuous; she answers with Christ's call to be perfect. As novice mistress she teaches her 'little way' of spiritual childhood. She dies young of tuberculosis after a painful illness.
inclusion: Greydanus gives it his highest grade and calls it an excellent, reverent biopic, and the reasons are clear from his account: it takes Thérèse's spirituality seriously instead of turning her into a sugary icon. Her 'little way' is shown in friction with the more severe piety around her, and the film is willing to show a young nun quietly correcting her elders. France Descaut is a sincere Thérèse, Jean Debucourt plays her father, Suzanne Flon is among the nuns, and the black-and-white photography and convent sets are convincing. The canonisation-process frame is stiff, and the titles in both languages promise something it is not. The only English home release is dubbed.
themes: The film is about sanctity in small things. Thérèse wants to be a saint, is told that this is presumption, and replies that Christ commanded it. Her 'little way' is love expressed in ordinary duties and acceptance of suffering; as novice mistress she spares a novice a harsh penance that harms body and work. Greydanus draws out her childhood devotion to Joan of Arc and her love for the missions. The Marian cure and a snowfall are shown as signs of grace without exaggeration, and her death of tuberculosis is treated as a consuming of love rather than a defeat.
history: Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in 1873. In May 1883, aged ten, she was cured of a grave illness when the statue of Our Lady seemed to smile at her. On 20 November 1887 she asked Leo XIII to let her enter Carmel at fifteen; he replied that she would if it was God's will. She entered on 9 April 1888 and died in 1897. She was canonised in 1925.
liberties: Greydanus's account places her cure at about eight; she was ten. The film's snowfall at her entry to Carmel may shift a later event. Convent dialogue is invented. Some English-language summaries wrongly say her father opposed her vocation; in the film, as in history, the opposition came from the convent's superior.
advisories:
A long final illness and death from tuberculosis.

Greydanus finds nothing objectionable and rates it for children and up. The English DVD is dubbed, without the French track.

doctrine: Benedict XV declared Thérèse's virtues heroic on 14 August 1921 and presented her way of spiritual childhood, reliance on God and surrender to His guidance, as a way for all the faithful. Pius XI beatified her on 29 April 1923 and canonised her on 17 May 1925. On 14 December 1927 he named her principal patroness of the missions, equal with St Francis Xavier, although she never left her cloister: a recognition that prayer and sacrifice in an enclosed convent serve the apostolate. Pius XII named her secondary patroness of France, with St Joan of Arc, on 3 May 1944. Her feast is 3 October. The film includes the murderer Henri Pranzini, for whose conversion she prayed in 1887; reports that he kissed the crucifix before his execution illustrate the Church's teaching on prayer for sinners.
production: Procès au Vatican was made by Les Films Fernand Rivers with Les Films Artistiques Français. André Haguet directed and wrote the screenplay and dialogue with André Legrand; photography is by Lucien Joulin and music by Maurice-Paul Guillot. The film runs 115 minutes and opened in France on 29 August 1952; it was also known as La Vie de Sainte Thérèse de Lisieux. In America Ellis Films released it as Miracle of St. Therese (formerly Trial at the Vatican), and the National Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: Teresa de Jesús
decision: PUBLISH (judgment call): Fernando Sanz Ferreruela's archival study (Artigrama, 2023) establishes identity (Agrupa Films; shot September to December 1961; Madrid premiere 14 May 1962; Interés Nacional, 8 June 1962) and shows that the Carmelite objections often attached to this title were made against an earlier, banned script; the filmed script was passed by a Carmelite adviser appointed by the Order and by the Bishop of Madrid in July 1961. Tracie Amend's scene-by-scene study guide supplies substantive treatment. The invented courtship and forced entry are a real distortion and are disclosed.
summary: Aurora Bautista plays St Teresa of Ávila from courted girl to dying foundress in Juan de Orduña's long-delayed, Carmelite-approved Spanish biography.
synopsis: In Ávila the young Teresa is courted by her cousin Pedro and by Álvaro. When the two men duel in the garden, her father sends her to the convent of the Encarnación the next morning. Years later, as a nun, she fasts and scourges herself until she collapses, and her prioress calls it pride. Learned men fear her prayer is the devil's work and her confessor burns her books, until St Francis Borgia tells her to obey God and found a reformed house. With Doña Guiomar's help she opens a poor convent despite a hostile town. She travels Castile founding more houses, drives the Princess of Eboli out of Pastrana and answers the Inquisition in Seville. She dies asking her daughters' pardon.
inclusion: Aurora Bautista, Orduña's star from Locura de amor, carries the film, and the verdicts on her divide: Fernando Méndez-Leite counted it among her best performances, while Eduardo Gil de Muro thought casting her a mistake. Sanz Ferreruela, who reconstructed the production from the censorship file, calls the finished script a hagiography full of commonplaces, and he regrets the bolder script the censors banned. The conventional choices are mostly sound ones, though. The film follows Teresa's own account of long trial by suspicious confessors, Borgia's discernment, the poverty of St Joseph's, the road with her coachman, Pastrana and Seville. Its picture of a mystic who is tested by the Church, not set against it, is the right one.
themes: The film is about testing a vocation. Teresa's early penances are sincere but excessive. The prioress who calls them pride is not a villain, and Teresa confesses pride more than once. Her prayer is treated as genuine, yet the learned men's fear that it may be diabolical is given full weight, and she herself panics that the devil has taken Christ's form. The reform is about poverty and enclosure, set against an Encarnación whose parlour has become a salon for well-dressed visitors. At the trial she answers that she was led by God and denies calling herself a saint. Her death is quiet and penitent.
history: Teresa de Ahumada (1515–1582) was sent by her father to the Augustinian nuns of Ávila to be educated. In November 1535 she entered the Carmelite Incarnation, leaving home without his consent; he then yielded. After years of illness, St Francis Borgia and St Peter of Alcántara guided her through her mystical experiences. She founded St Joseph's at Ávila on 24 August 1562, and later houses included Pastrana and Seville. Jerónimo Gracián's appointment as apostolic visitor was followed by four years of persecution of the reform. She died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582 and was canonised in 1622.
liberties: The opening is invented, and it reverses the history. There were no rival suitors and no duel, and her father did not order her into the convent the next morning: he sent her to the Augustinians for schooling, and she entered Carmel against his wishes. Álvaro's later visits and roses are also fiction. The Encarnación's laxity is sharpened for drama; a Carmelite historian asked in 1957 that the script not show the Order as persecuting innocence. One detailed summary has her travelling to Ávila to die, but she died at Alba de Tormes.
advisories:
Self-flagellation and fasting to the point of collapse, shown as excess and rebuked.

An opening arrest of a fraudulent stigmatic, with a bloody knife; a sword duel; a torch-bearing mob; Inquisition interrogations; a deathbed scene.

Suitable for teens and older; younger viewers may find the penances disturbing.

doctrine: Teresa was beatified by Paul V in 1614 and canonised by Gregory XV on 12 March 1622 with Ignatius Loyola, Francis Xavier, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer. Her feast is 15 October, because the Gregorian reform of 1582 skipped the days after the night of her death. Her reform of Carmel returned the order to the primitive rule, with strict enclosure, poverty and silence, in the spirit of Trent's decrees on religious life (Session XXV). The film shows her obedience to confessors and the testing of her visions. The Church's teaching is that private revelations are not part of the deposit of faith, are to be tried by learned directors, and may be believed only with human faith. The Transverberation, the piercing of her heart by an angel's flaming dart, was given its own feast in the Carmelite calendar.
production: Juan de Orduña directed this Spanish religious drama, which was filmed in 1961 and released in 1962. The screenplay is by José María Pemán, Antonio Vich and Manuel Mur Oti. Eduardo Manzanos produced it for Estela Films and Agrupa Films Cooperativa Cinematográfica. Aurora Bautista, the star of Orduña's Locura de amor (1948), played Teresa. The film runs 131 minutes and was distributed by CEA. In 1962 it won the special prize of the Sindicato Nacional del Espectáculo. In 1984 Spanish television made a series, Teresa de Jesús, starring Concha Velasco, and a film cut of it, which Spanish Wikipedia describes as based on Orduña's film.

title: The Gospel According to St. Matthew
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and awards confirmed by the Italian Cultural Institute (Venice Special Jury Prize; OCIC prize); Greydanus's detailed Decent Films review (A+, +4) shows near-verbatim fidelity to Matthew, matter-of-fact miracles and a contemplative rather than political Christ. Pasolini's Marxism and unbelief are a documented context, but the critical evidence shows the text of the Gospel is not reinterpreted; the film shows the Resurrection.
summary: An atheist Marxist poet filmed St Matthew's Gospel almost word for word, with peasants for actors and southern Italy for Palestine, and made the most austere of Jesus films.
synopsis: The film follows Matthew's Gospel in order. Joseph learns that Mary is with child and is reassured by an angel; Christ is born, the Magi come, the Holy Family flees and Herod kills the infants. John baptises in the Jordan. Jesus, young and severe, calls fishermen, preaches, heals, walks on water, and confronts the scribes and Pharisees. The Sermon on the Mount comes as a barrage of close-ups. He enters Jerusalem, drives the traders from the Temple, eats the Passover with the Twelve, is betrayed, denied by Peter, tried and crucified, watched by his aged mother. On the third day the tomb is empty and he sends his disciples to all nations.
inclusion: Pasolini took no liberties with the words: the dialogue is Matthew's, cut and sometimes reordered, but not rewritten. He cast non-professionals, including a Spanish student as Christ and his own mother as the older Mary, and shot in central and southern Italy, including the cave dwellings of Matera. The result looks like no other Bible film: weathered faces, bare landscapes, abrupt cuts, and long stretches where the images carry the narrative that Matthew's own voice would supply. Greydanus gives it his highest artistic grade and calls it one of the most contemplative Jesus films made. It is demanding: long silent passages assume you know the text, and the Passion is notably restrained. But few films let the Gospel speak so directly.
themes: The film's faith is the Gospel's own. Miracles happen without fuss: an angel simply stands there, Christ walks on the water, the loaves multiply. Enrique Irazoqui's Christ is urgent, stern and human without being diminished. Pasolini called himself an unbeliever with a nostalgia for belief, and critics have long read the film as a Marxist allegory of the poor; Greydanus answers that the text is not bent to politics. Our Lady is played in youth by a silent teenager and at the Cross by Pasolini's own mother. The Resurrection and the command to baptise all nations close the film.
history: Pasolini had been convicted in 1963 of insulting the state religion for his short film La ricotta. The Gospel premiered at Venice on 4 September 1964 and won the Special Jury Prize and the prize of the Office Catholique International du Cinéma. Pasolini dedicated it to the memory of John XXIII, who had died the year before.
liberties: Matthew's genealogy and the Transfiguration are omitted; some episodes are reordered or compressed. The Pharisees' tall hats are borrowed from Renaissance painting. Settings are southern Italian, not Palestinian, and the music is anachronistic by design.
advisories:
Massacre of the Innocents and the Crucifixion are shown, but with little blood.

No sexual content. Greydanus rates it suitable for children and up; its pace and silence suit older children and adults better.

title: The King of Kings
decision: PUBLISH: AFI Catalog identity; Steven Greydanus's detailed Decent Films review, Charles Musser's Criterion essay and K. V. Turley's National Catholic Register piece establish a reverent Gospel film with a Eucharistic Last Supper, a reverent Our Lady and a careful handling of guilt for the Crucifixion. The invented Magdalene prologue, Protestant-default intertitles and one unscriptural intertitle are disclosed rather than disqualifying.
summary: DeMille's silent life of Christ opens as a lurid Hollywood spectacle, then settles into a surprisingly reverent Gospel film, with H. B. Warner's quiet Christ and a Resurrection in colour.
synopsis: Mary Magdalene, a rich courtesan, is told that her lover Judas has gone off after a carpenter from Nazareth. She drives out in a chariot drawn by zebras to win him back, meets Jesus, and is freed of seven devils. The film then follows Christ through healings, the call of the disciples, conflict with the Temple authorities and the Roman occupiers, and into Holy Week: the Last Supper, Gethsemane, Judas's betrayal, the trial before Pilate, the way of the cross and the Crucifixion, cut against Judas's suicide, with an earthquake that splits the Temple. The Resurrection follows, in colour.
inclusion: Greydanus calls it flawed but powerful, and that is fair. The first reel is pure DeMille: a half-dressed Magdalene, an orgy, zebras. Then the tone changes. H. B. Warner, past fifty and rather old for the part, gives Christ dignity and gentleness; his scenes with children, including one where he mends a child's doll, are the warmest in the film. DeMille's craft is formidable: the crowds, the lighting, the cutting between the Crucifixion and Judas's death, the storm that follows. Musser, in his Criterion essay, finds Warner's divinity rendered by lighting rather than acting and some of the halo effects kitsch, and he has a point. But for a silent epic it holds attention, and its seriousness about the Passion is unmistakable.
themes: The Last Supper is handled with reverence: Peter holds the chalice to his heart, while Judas crumbles the host and lets it fall, a clear sign that the film treats the Eucharist as sacred. Our Lady appears with dignity throughout. The intertitles are mostly from the King James Bible and the sensibility, as Greydanus says, is Protestant by default, but nothing in it attacks Catholic belief. Turley objects to one intertitle in which Mary urges her Son to go back to Nazareth, which is unscriptural. On the Crucifixion, the film places guilt on Caiaphas as a Roman appointee and has him plead that he alone is guilty, a deliberate attempt to avoid blaming the Jewish people.
liberties: The opening, with Mary Magdalene as a courtesan and Judas's lover, is invented. Events are rearranged thematically: episodes about taxes are merged and crowd scenes moved. Caiaphas's final prayer is DeMille's invention. The 1927 roadshow version (about 155 minutes) and the 1928 general release (about 112) differ; the longer cut adds an exorcism and other material but also puts the opening in colour, which weakens the colour Resurrection.
advisories:
The opening shows a decadent party and a scantily dressed Magdalene; it is brief.

The scourging and Crucifixion are restrained by modern standards; Judas's suicide is cut against the Crucifixion; earthquake and storm.

Silent with intertitles. Greydanus rates it suitable for children and up, with these caveats.

suitability.note: The brief opening party with a scantily dressed Magdalene, the scourging and the Crucifixion are restrained, and the Legion of Decency rated it A-I. Silent with intertitles, so younger children may need the cards read to them; the Last Supper and the colour Resurrection make it worth the effort.

doctrine: The Last Supper scene rests on the Church's teaching on the Real Presence: the Council of Trent (Session XIII, 1551) defined that after the consecration Christ is truly, really and substantially present under the appearances of bread and wine, which is why Judas's dropping of the host reads as sacrilege. The film follows the old Latin tradition, accepted by St Gregory the Great and set out in the Catholic Encyclopedia, that Mary Magdalene is the sinful woman of Luke 7 and the sister of Lazarus; her feast was kept on 22 July. Her deliverance from seven devils is from Luke 8:2. On guilt for the Crucifixion, the Roman Catechism (Part I, article 4) teaches that sinners of every age are its cause, a point the film approaches by making Caiaphas, not the Jewish people, bear the blame.
history: Jesus of Nazareth taught and worked in Galilee and Judaea under the emperor Tiberius. Pontius Pilate governed Judaea as procurator from AD 26 to 36, a term that covers the whole of Christ's public ministry, and Caiaphas was high priest in Jerusalem at the time of the Passion. The Gospels record that Christ was betrayed by Judas, condemned by the Sanhedrin, handed over to Pilate, crucified outside the city at Passover, and rose on the third day.
production: After The Volga Boatman (1926) DeMille dropped a planned film about the Flood when he learned Warner Bros. was making Noah's Ark; Denison Clift suggested the life of Christ instead, and Jeremiah Milbank put up the money. Jeanie MacPherson wrote the screenplay. H. B. Warner was cast as Christ in June 1926. It was shot in 1926 on Santa Catalina Island and at the DeMille Studios in Culver City, with the opening and Resurrection in two-colour Technicolor. It premiered in New York on 19 April 1927 and opened Grauman's Chinese Theatre on 18 May. It cost about $1.27 million and earned about $2.64 million. The Memphis censors ordered 900 feet cut, mainly the scourging and crucifixion, and the London County Council banned it. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: The Nun's Story
decision: PUBLISH (adults and older teens): The AFI Catalog and Greydanus's Decent Films review show a serious, largely respectful account of pre-conciliar religious formation whose heroine leaves by lawful dispensation after judging herself unable to keep obedience, not a film that attacks the vows. Zinnemann deliberately withholds a verdict on her departure (AFI: no end-title music for that reason); Greydanus calls it neither anti-religious nor anti-Catholic. The film's ambiguity about whether the Rule or the nun is at fault is recorded plainly in the text and advisories.
summary: Audrey Hepburn plays a Belgian surgeon's daughter who becomes a nursing sister, serves in the Congo, and after years of struggle with obedience asks to be released from her vows.
synopsis: In the 1920s Gabrielle Van der Mal enters a nursing order in Bruges, hoping to serve in the Congo. As Sister Luke she learns the Rule: silence, custody of the eyes, obedience to the bell. Her superiors test her pride; one even urges her to fail an exam as an act of humility. She is sent to an asylum, then at last to the Congo, where she works beside a brilliant, irreligious surgeon and falls ill with tuberculosis. Recalled to Belgium, she faces the German occupation. Ordered to show charity to the enemy, she secretly helps the Resistance, and when her father is killed she finds herself full of hatred. Concluding that she can no longer be a true nun, she asks for release, signs the papers, changes into a dress and walks out of the convent.
inclusion: No Hollywood film before or since has shown the formation of a religious so carefully. The first hour, which the New York Times likened to a documentary, explains the vows through the words of superiors, and the rituals of the novitiate are filmed with patience. Hepburn is superb, entirely inward; Edith Evans is formidable as a superior, and Peter Finch plays the atheist surgeon who tells her she is a 'worldly nun' and that her real illness is the struggle to conform. Franz Planer's photography of Bruges and the Congo is beautiful. The film is long and its second half loses some of the first half's concentration. It is not a happy story. But it treats the religious life as a real and serious calling, and its sisters include warm and holy women as well as harsh ones.
themes: The film is about obedience. Sister Luke's struggle is not with faith in God but with the surrender of her will: leaving a dying patient at the sound of the bell, accepting humiliation, forgiving the men who killed her father. The Rule is presented in its own terms, and the superiors explain why the sacrifice of liberty matters. Greydanus notes that the bad advice to fail an exam is later corrected by another superior. The Congo scenes include a priest serving lepers in penance for his sins, and a sister murdered by a man in thrall to a witch doctor, whose fellow nuns' forgiveness draws villagers to the Christmas Eve service. Where the film is open to question is its refusal to judge the outcome: it never settles whether the fault lies with the Rule, the community or Sister Luke herself, and some viewers will read her departure as liberation. Read faithfully, it is the story of a vocation honestly found wanting, not of a vocation exposed as false.
history: Kathryn Hulme's 1956 novel was based on Marie-Louise Habets, a Belgian nursing sister of the Sisters of Charity of Jesus and Mary, who left religious life during the Second World War. Hulme met her among refugees in 1945. The novel changes names and events.
liberties: Names and some events are fictionalised from Habets's life by way of Hulme's novel. The Resistance episodes and the doctor's role are shaped for drama. The order is not named in the film.
advisories:
A violent attack in a mental asylum and a murder in the Congo; wartime bombing; scenes in a leper colony.

No sexual content, but unspoken attraction between the nun and the surgeon.

The heroine leaves religious life at the end, and the film does not say whether she was right. Greydanus rates it for adults; it suits mature teens with discussion.

names: The Nun's Story, novel by Kathryn Hulme (1956)

suitability.note: Rated A-II by the Legion of Decency. A violent attack in an asylum, a murder, leprosy wards and wartime death, but the real difficulty is the ending, where the heroine leaves religious life and the film does not judge her. It needs a parent ready to discuss vows.

doctrine: Religious profession binds by the three vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. A vow, once made to God, obliges in conscience until the Holy See or the competent authority dispenses it. The religious state is, in the traditional teaching, the way of the evangelical counsels, and the vow of obedience is the surrender of one's own will to a lawful superior, as the film shows. Obedience does not require sin. Under the 1917 Code the Holy See grants dispensations or secularisation to religious of simple vows, which is why Sister Luke has to wait for her release. The Church holds that a woman may leave her Institute only by lawful permission. The film does not state that her departure is right.
production: Warner Bros. consulted the Production Code Office in March 1956. The Catholic Church in Belgium disliked the novel and at first refused to cooperate. The Sisters of Charity of Jesus and Mary at Ghent then submitted their own version of the script, many of whose suggestions were used, and allowed observation and guidance but refused to appear on camera. Henry Blanke produced, Fred Zinnemann directed and Robert Anderson wrote the script. Filming was in the Belgian Congo, near Stanleyville, with Belgian interiors made in Rome (Cinecittà) and exteriors in Bruges. Hepburn prepared by meeting Kathryn Hulme and Marie Louise Habets. The final scene has no music. It premiered at Radio City Music Hall on 18 June 1959, cost $3.5 million and took $12.8 million in the US. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II, 'morally unobjectionable for adults and adolescents'. It earned eight Oscar nominations but won none.

title: Barabbas
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (Christ, St Peter, the Roman martyrs), Legion of Decency A-II (Motion Picture Exhibitor Legion tables, 1962), independent reviews (Hannan, Cinefile). Reservation: the hero's faith stays ambiguous to the end, and his doubt of the Resurrection and his part in the burning of Rome are the core of the story; Peter's rebuke and the martyrs' witness keep it from contradicting doctrine. Would move to PUBLISH if the Founder accepts an ambiguous convert as protagonist. The English subtitle file confirms the rebuke (the fire is Nero's, not God's, 02:11:56–02:12:40) and Peter's consolation that Christ has never left Barabbas's side (02:13:44–02:13:59); the last words are addressed into the dark without naming God (02:16:23–02:16:35).
summary: Anthony Quinn's Barabbas, freed in Christ's place, spends twenty years haunted by the man who died for him, in Richard Fleischer's grim and intelligent epic.
synopsis: Pilate offers the crowd Jesus or Barabbas, and they choose Barabbas. Freed, he finds that his lover Rachel has become a follower of the condemned man. He watches the Crucifixion under a darkened sky, finds the tomb empty and refuses to believe; Rachel preaches and is stoned. Back at his old trade, he is caught and sent for life to the sulphur mines of Sicily, chained to Sahak, a Christian. An earthquake frees them, and they are taken to Rome to be trained as gladiators. Sahak is executed for his faith; Barabbas wins his freedom in the arena. When Rome burns he thinks the end of the world has come, sets fires himself and declares himself a Christian. In prison St Peter tells him Christians do not do such things. He is crucified with the Christians.
inclusion: Barabbas is the most searching of the epics of its era. Dino De Laurentiis made it in Italy with real ambition: Christopher Fry wrote the script from Pär Lagerkvist's novel, and Brian Hannan reports that the darkness over Calvary was filmed during an actual eclipse. Anthony Quinn plays a slow, bewildered man who keeps failing the people around him, and Hannan rightly calls the performance excellent and the film overlooked. Fleischer keeps piety at arm's length; the mine, the arena and the burning of Rome are brutal and convincing. The dialogue can be stiff, and David Clare at Cinefile finds it a Christian-era Spartacus without that film's vision. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.
themes: The film is about grace resisted and, at the last, half understood. Barabbas lives because Christ died, and he cannot escape that fact. Rachel, Sahak and Peter are clear witnesses; Barabbas is not. He doubts the Resurrection, mistakes the fire of Rome for the end of the world, and joins in the arson for which the Christians are blamed. Peter's rebuke is plain: the fire is Nero's work, not God's. In prison Peter tells him that Christ died for him because he was farthest away, and has never left his side. Barabbas dies on a cross among the martyrs, giving himself up 'into your keeping' in the dark, without saying to whom. Catholic Culture's Criteria podcast calls him an archetype of human resistance to grace.
history: The Gospels say only that Barabbas, held for insurrection and murder, was released at the Passover instead of Jesus. His later life is unrecorded. The Great Fire of Rome broke out in July AD 64; Nero blamed the Christians, and the persecution that followed is described by Tacitus. Tradition places the martyrdom of Peter and Paul at Rome in Nero's reign.
liberties: Barabbas's later life is wholly invented. Against the novel, the film sends him to Sicilian sulphur mines rather than copper mines in Cyprus, frees him by an earthquake rather than a sympathetic overseer, and adds the gladiatorial scenes.
advisories:
Brutal violence: a stoning, a mine disaster, gladiatorial combat, the burning of Rome and mass crucifixions.

Barabbas's relationship with Rachel is implied.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The hero's faith is left ambiguous, and he takes part in the burning of Rome believing he serves the Christians.

grey.question: Barabbas is a film about a man who cannot believe. He doubts the Resurrection, helps set fire to Rome in the belief that he is serving the Christians, and dies on a cross with words that may be faith or only surrender. The martyrs around him, Rachel, Sahak and St Peter, are drawn with conviction, and Peter corrects his error plainly. The film's power lies in that ambiguity. Viewers who want a clear conversion story will not find one; those willing to watch a portrait of resistance to grace will.

sources.title: The Passion of Christ (Gospel Accounts)
sources.claims: Pilate's offer of Barabbas in the Gospel accounts

suitability.note: Rated A-II by the Legion of Decency. A stoning, a mine disaster, gladiatorial killing, the burning of Rome and mass crucifixions, with a brutal tone throughout. It is also long, at 137 minutes, and its hero never plainly believes.

doctrine: The Gospels record that at the Passover Pilate offered the crowd Jesus or Barabbas, a prisoner held for insurrection and murder, and the crowd chose Barabbas (Matthew 27, Mark 15, Luke 23, John 18). Christian writers have long seen in the exchange a picture of the Atonement: the guilty man goes free because the Innocent One dies. Trent teaches that Christ merited justification for us by His Passion, and that men can resist grace. Peter, the first Pope, was crucified in Rome under Nero according to ancient tradition. The fire of Rome in July AD 64 was blamed on the Christians by Nero, as Tacitus records. The film's Barabbas takes part in the burning of Rome believing he serves the Christians; the Church holds that no good end justifies a wicked act.
production: Pär Lagerkvist, a Swedish Nobel laureate, published his novel in 1950. Dino De Laurentiis produced the film, with Christopher Fry as the main writer, helped uncredited by Nigel Balchin, Diego Fabbri, Ivo Perilli and Salvatore Quasimodo. Richard Fleischer directed. It was shot in Verona and Rome. The darkness at the Crucifixion was filmed during the total solar eclipse of 15 February 1961. Yul Brynner was considered for the title role. Mario Nascimbene's score has a theme based on the Kyrie of Mass XI. The film changes the novel: the mines are in Sicily rather than Cyprus, and the gladiator scenes are added. It opened in Italy on 23 December 1961 and in the US on 10 October 1962, running 137 minutes, and took $2.9 million in the US and Canada. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

title: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ
originalTitle: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (AFI Catalog, BFI) and the treatment is established by Greydanus (moral/spiritual +3, Kids & Up*), who calls it arguably the best version of the story. Christ is shown reverently, never with his face, in Technicolor sequences framing the drama: the Nativity, the cup of water, the raising of a child, the healing of the lepers on the way of the cross, the Crucifixion. Two reservations stop it at PUBLISH: Christ is the background to a revenge melodrama from a Protestant novelist rather than its centre, and the restored version contains brief nudity (bare-breasted women in a procession, a nude galley slave) that censors cut in 1931.
summary: MGM's silent Ben-Hur sets Lew Wallace's revenge tale inside the life of Christ, from a Technicolor Nativity to the Crucifixion, with a still-astonishing sea battle and chariot race.
synopsis: The film opens in Bethlehem with Joseph and Mary, the birth in the cave, the shepherds and the Magi. Years later in Jerusalem, Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince, is betrayed by his Roman boyhood friend Messala; Judah is sent to the galleys and his mother and sister are imprisoned. On the road a young carpenter of Nazareth gives him water. Judah survives a sea battle, wins his freedom and returns to defeat Messala in the chariot race. He gathers men to fight for the foretold king, but the Nazarene, carrying his cross, heals Judah's mother and sister of leprosy, and before the Crucifixion Judah lays down his sword when Christ speaks of a kingdom not of this world.
inclusion: This was the most expensive silent film ever made, shot partly in Italy and finished in California, and it still looks it. Greydanus judges the sea battle the best of any version and the chariot race at least equal to the 1959 remake; Kevin Brownlow compared the race to the Odessa Steps in Potemkin. Ramon Novarro plays Judah, and at around two and a half hours it is an hour shorter than Wyler's version and better paced; Greydanus notes that it delays the rescue of Judah's mother and sister, which helps the drama. The Christ scenes were shot in two-strip Technicolor, considered lost until the 1980s and restored in 1987, so the Gospel episodes literally glow against the tinted story. Photoplay singled out Betty Bronson's Madonna.
themes: Christ is never seen full-face; he is a hand, a figure, a presence, and the title cards quote the Gospels. That restraint is the film's best religious decision. The Nativity is staged with Mary and Joseph at the centre and treated with reverence. Judah's journey moves from vengeance towards Christ: he plans an army for a political Messiah and learns at the foot of the cross that the kingdom is not of this world. Greydanus approves of keeping the Gospel in the background, but notes that Hollywood's melodramatic spectacle sits uneasily with sacred subjects. The novel's author, Lew Wallace, was a Protestant, and the faith in the film is a broad, undogmatic Christianity.

grey.question: Christ appears in Ben-Hur with real reverence, in the Nativity, the healing of the lepers and the Crucifixion, but the film belongs to Judah's revenge and the chariot race, and its faith is the general Christianity of Lew Wallace's novel rather than anything specifically Catholic. The full restoration also includes brief nudity cut by censors in 1931. Viewers will want to decide whether a spectacle in which Christ is the frame, not the subject, belongs alongside films about Him.

history: The film's frame is the Gospel history: the birth of Christ at Bethlehem under Herod, the ministry in Judaea under Roman rule, and the Crucifixion at Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate, prefect from AD 26 to 36. Judah Ben-Hur, Messala and the Ben-Hur family are inventions of the novelist Lew Wallace, a Union general who published the book in 1880. The Roman galleys and chariot racing are period colour, not recorded events.
liberties: Judah, Messala and the Ben-Hur family are Wallace's inventions. The film follows the novel's main line but ends at the Crucifixion, whereas the novel continues into the reign of Nero. Christ's words and the healing of the lepers are placed on the way of the cross for dramatic effect.
advisories:
Battle violence at sea, galley brutality and the chariot race crash.

Brief partial nudity (women in a procession, a galley slave) and a sequence of mild sensuality.

The Crucifixion is shown without graphic detail.

Greydanus rates it Kids & Up with these cautions; better for older children.

names: Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ, novel by Lew Wallace (1880)

suitability.note: A galley sea battle, brutal treatment of slaves and a fatal chariot crash, with the Crucifixion shown without gruesome detail. The restored print has brief partial nudity (a galley slave, women in a procession), so parents may prefer to preview it; the Nativity and Gospel scenes are reverent and worth showing to older children.

doctrine: The film frames Wallace's tale with the Incarnation: the Nativity at Bethlehem, the shepherds and the Magi. Judah's error is the one the Gospels record in the disciples, the hope of a political Messiah. Christ's answer to Pilate, 'My kingdom is not of this world' (John 18:36), is the turning point. Pius XI taught the same truth in Quas Primas (11 December 1925), less than three weeks before the film opened, when he instituted the feast of Christ the King. The film never shows Christ's face, which accords with the long Christian custom of reverence in depicting Him. The cure of lepers and the cup of water are Wallace's inventions, not Gospel episodes; the Crucifixion is Gospel history, and the Church holds that Christ died for all men.
production: The 1880 novel was a stage hit for twenty-five years before Goldwyn bought the film rights in 1922. Shooting began in Rome in October 1923 under Charles Brabin; Fred Niblo is the credited director. George Walsh was fired as Ben-Hur and replaced by Ramon Novarro. After two years of trouble the production moved to MGM at Culver City, resuming in spring 1925. Costs reached about $3.9 million, then the most for any silent film. About 200,000 feet of film were shot for the chariot race, cut to 750 feet. William Wyler was an assistant director. The Christ scenes were in two-colour Technicolor. It premiered in New York on 30 December 1925 and was reissued in 1931 with a musical score and sound effects added. It took $10.7 million but showed a loss after costs. Reports say about a hundred horses died during the race scenes.
