title: The Prisoner
decision: PUBLISH: Catholic-centred (a cardinal's faith under communist interrogation). Pre-1965 Catholic judgments are favourable: Grand Prize of the International Catholic Office for the Cinema 1956 (AFI, citing the NYT of 12 July 1956), commendation by Cardinal Griffin (Wikipedia), Legion of Decency A-II. Independent treatment from the Monthly Film Bulletin and NYT (via Wikipedia) and Roger Moore (2023). The open question about the cardinal's motives is disclosed.
summary: Alec Guinness plays a cardinal in a communist state whose interrogator breaks him not by torture but by turning his own humility against him.
synopsis: In an unnamed country of eastern Europe after the war, the government arrests its popular cardinal for treason. He resisted the Nazis and survived their torture, so his interrogator, a former comrade from the Resistance now loyal to the party, avoids physical violence. Forged evidence fails. Instead the interrogator uses sleeplessness, solitary confinement and the disruption of every routine, and searches the cardinal's past for a weakness. He finds it in his poor childhood, and in his fear that he became a priest out of vanity and a wish to escape it. Broken, the cardinal confesses at a show trial to everything he is charged with. His sentence is commuted so that he cannot become a martyr, and he walks out into a silent crowd. A subplot follows a young guard and a married woman.
inclusion: Guinness and Jack Hawkins have the film almost to themselves, and their duel is the reason to see it. The Monthly Film Bulletin praised Peter Glenville's first film and Guinness's soberly convincing cardinal, while finding the manner sometimes portentous; the New York Times called it grim and gripping. Its origin as a stage play shows. Roger Moore, reviewing it in 2023, found it stagebound and the guard's romance corny. In 1955 it was attacked from both sides: banned in Ireland as communist propaganda, dropped from Cannes and refused at Venice as anti-communist. The International Catholic Office for the Cinema gave it its Grand Prize for 1956, and Cardinal Griffin of Westminster commended it. Everyone saw the model: Mindszenty, and Stepinac.
themes: The film is about a priest's interior life under assault. The cardinal's strength is his faith, and the interrogator wins only by persuading him that his vocation was mixed with pride. The confession that follows is false, but it is also an act of self-abasement, and in the dock he seeks forgiveness from God, not from the court. He then accepts his survival, discredited, as a penance. The film leaves open how far his self-accusation is true; it never doubts the faith itself, and it is the interrogator who is left unsettled. Glenville insisted the film was not a tract for either side but the encounter of a man of God and a man of the State.
history: József Mindszenty, Archbishop of Esztergom and Primate of Hungary, was arrested on 26 December 1948 and in February 1949 sentenced to life imprisonment after a show trial in which he confessed to treason and currency offences. He had said beforehand that any confession of his would be the product of duress. The Hungarian rising freed him in October 1956 and he took refuge in the American legation in Budapest, where he stayed until 1971. In Yugoslavia, Alojzije Stepinac, Archbishop of Zagreb, was sentenced in October 1946 to sixteen years in prison and later confined to his village; Pius XII made him a cardinal in 1953. The film's cardinal is fictional.
liberties: The cardinal and his country are fictional, a composite of the Mindszenty and Stepinac cases. The psychological method of the interrogation is the play's invention, not a reconstruction of either trial.
advisories:
Psychological cruelty: sleep deprivation, solitary confinement and humiliation; no torture is shown.

A subplot about a guard's love for a married woman; nothing explicit.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The cardinal's false confession, and his doubts about his own motives, are central and partly left open.

names: The Prisoner, play by Bridget Boland (1954)

suitability.note: No torture is shown, but the psychological cruelty is sustained and the cardinal's collapse is hard to watch. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II; it is talky, slow and best suited to teenagers who can follow an argument.

doctrine: The Church teaches that a confession or act extorted by fear is not freely made. The film's cardinal is broken by sleep deprivation and solitary confinement rather than by torture. His real struggle is inward: the interrogator exploits his fear that he entered the priesthood from pride. Trent taught that the efficacy of the Church's ministry does not depend on the priest's worthiness (Session 7, can. 12). The Holy Office decree of 1 July 1949 excommunicated Catholics who knowingly profess and spread communist doctrine. The Church honours those who endure imprisonment for the Faith as confessors, a title below that of martyr.
production: Bridget Boland's play opened in London in 1954. Peter Glenville, who had directed it on stage, made his film debut with it, with Alec Guinness as the Cardinal. The cardinal was inspired by Mindszenty and Stepinac. It was shot in England and in Ostend and Bruges. It was controversial: Ireland saw it as pro-Communist, France as anti-Communist, it was banned from the Venice Film Festival, and some Italian critics called it anti-Catholic. It won a Catholic film award. Because of the resemblance to Stepinac it was not shown in Yugoslavia until after communist rule ended. It received five BAFTA nominations, including Best Film and Best British Actor for both Guinness and Hawkins.

title: The Robe
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified the finished film A-I (morally unobjectionable for general patronage) and it received a Christopher Award, both pre-conciliar Catholic judgments recorded in the AFI Catalog; the Legion had warned against Lloyd C. Douglas's novel in 1948 (B), so the A-I marks a deliberate judgment on the film itself. Greydanus (B-, moral/spiritual +2, Kids & Up) establishes reverent content with Christ seen only from outside and St Peter as leader of the community, and is candid about its dramatic weakness. Christ, the Passion, Peter and martyrdom are central; nothing contrary to Catholic teaching is reported. Protestant authorship is disclosed.
summary: The first CinemaScope film follows the Roman tribune who crucified Christ and won His robe, through guilt and conversion under St Peter, to martyrdom under Caligula.
synopsis: Marcellus Gallio, a dissolute Roman tribune, is posted to Jerusalem after offending Caligula, taking with him the Greek slave Demetrius. He commands the detail that crucifies Jesus and wins the robe in a dice game at the foot of the cross. Demetrius, who has seen Christ on Palm Sunday, follows Him. Marcellus is tormented by guilt and fits of madness. The Emperor Tiberius sends him back to Palestine to find and destroy the robe and to spy on the Christians. In Cana he meets the followers of Jesus, among them Peter, comes to faith and joins them. Back in Rome he helps rescue Demetrius, who has been tortured, and Peter's prayer restores him. Caligula, now emperor, tries Marcellus for treason. He confesses Christ and walks to his death with Diana, who chooses to die with him.
inclusion: The Robe is best known as the film that launched CinemaScope, and it won Oscars for its sets and costumes. Leon Shamroy shot it in Technicolor and Alfred Newman wrote the score; it was nominated for Best Picture. As drama it is uneven. Greydanus singles out the Roman prologue and Demetrius's frantic search through Jerusalem on Holy Thursday night, and Peter's account of his denial and forgiveness, but finds Richard Burton stiff, the action scenes weak beside Ben-Hur, and the conversion more a matter of special effects than of a changed life. Bosley Crowther and Richard L. Coe were also unimpressed at the time. Its virtues are reverence and clarity, and Greydanus rates it suitable for children.
themes: Christ is never shown full-face: Demetrius is overwhelmed by a glance on Palm Sunday, and Calvary is seen through the soldiers who carry out the sentence. The robe is treated almost as a relic, an idea Greydanus finds intriguingly sacramental, though the film does not develop it. Peter, played as a gentle shepherd, recounts his triple denial and Christ's forgiveness, and leads the community that receives Marcellus. The ending is a confession of faith before the emperor and a martyrdom accepted freely. The film's Christianity is broad, from a Lutheran-trained novelist, but its subjects, the Passion, repentance and martyrdom, are wholly within Catholic tradition.
history: Pontius Pilate was prefect of Judaea from about AD 26 to 36 and ordered the crucifixion of Jesus under Tiberius. St John records that the soldiers divided Christ's garments and cast lots for the seamless tunic. Caligula became emperor in AD 37 and was murdered in AD 41. Marcellus Gallio, Demetrius and Diana are creations of Lloyd C. Douglas's novel. The Gallio family name comes from the proconsul of Achaia before whom St Paul appeared at Corinth (Acts 18:12), but the tribune is not a historical figure. The accounts of Roman persecution of the first Christians belong to a later period than the film places them.
liberties: Marcellus, Diana, Demetrius and their story are fictional. Greydanus notes the film exaggerates the prominence of the early Church in Rome and invents a direct clash with Caligula, for which there is no historical basis. Peter is gentler than the Peter of the Gospels and Acts.
advisories:
Stylised action violence, a sword duel and the torture of a prisoner.

The Crucifixion is seen at a distance; mild Passion imagery.

Some veiled innuendo at Caligula's court.

Legion of Decency A-I; suitable for children.

names: The Robe, novel by Lloyd C. Douglas (1942)

suitability.note: A duel, the torture of a prisoner and a distant Crucifixion, none of them graphic, and a decadent Roman court handled by innuendo. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I, and older children can follow it, though the story is long and talky.

doctrine: The seamless tunic for which the soldiers cast lots is in St John's Gospel (19:23-24). The Fathers read it as a sign of the unity of the Church. Marcellus Gallio is invented, but tradition names the centurion who confessed Christ at the cross as Longinus, whom the Roman Martyrology keeps as a saint. The film's Peter is the leader of the disciples. The Church holds that Christ made Peter the rock on which the Church is built (Matthew 16:18), a primacy that the Vatican Council defined in 1870. Marcellus is converted by grace and by the witness of the faithful, and he ends in martyrdom, which the Church honours as the highest proof of faith. Two relics claim to be the seamless robe (Trier and Argenteuil). The Church has never defined that either is authentic.
production: Producer Frank Ross bought the film rights to Lloyd C. Douglas's novel in 1942, before the book was finished, for $100,000. A first attempt at RKO stalled and the property passed to Twentieth Century-Fox. Jean Peters was first cast as Diana, but became pregnant and was replaced by Jean Simmons. Victor Mature signed as Demetrius in December 1952. The film was the first released in CinemaScope, with each scene shot in both wide and standard versions. Filming ended on 30 April 1953, two weeks early. It opened at the Roxy, New York, on 16 September 1953 and was the top US film for nine weeks. It won Oscars for art direction and costume design and the Golden Globe for best drama. The Legion of Decency classified it A-I.

title: The Trouble with Angels
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog settles identity and source. Independent secular criticism (Films and Filming, quoted by TCM; Christian Sauvé) and Simcha Fisher's Catholic review (used for content) agree that the film treats the sisters and Mary's vocation with sympathy, with religious life in its pre-conciliar form shown as normal. No doctrinal problem is reported; the only advisory is a few leering gags. A 1966 Catholic film-office classification was not found and would strengthen the record.
summary: Ida Lupino's convent-school comedy follows Hayley Mills as a prank-playing pupil whose long war with Rosalind Russell's Mother Superior ends in a vocation.
synopsis: Mary Clancy arrives at St Francis Academy, a girls' school run by nuns, and at once teams up with Rachel Devery. Over three years the pair stage a string of pranks that test the patience of the Mother Superior, who comes close to sending Mary away; Mary's uncle, her guardian, lets her stay on. When Mother Superior learns what lies behind Mary's behaviour, she shows mercy and sees promise in her. Left at school over Christmas, Mary watches the sisters at Midnight Mass from the wings of the chapel. When old Sister Liguori dies in her sleep, Mary slips into the chapel and sees Mother Superior's private grief. At graduation Mary announces that she will stay and enter the order. Rachel feels betrayed, but comes to accept her friend's choice.
inclusion: This is a mild studio comedy, but an unusually honest one about a vocation. It comes from Jane Trahey's memoir of a Catholic girls' school in the 1930s, and the sisters are individuals rather than saints or tyrants: Simcha Fisher notes that several carry painful pasts and share real friendships. Rosalind Russell, a devout Catholic, gives Mother Superior dry wit and authority, and her grief at a sister's death is the best scene in the film. Hayley Mills is better than her material. The weaknesses are real. Variety found the plotting repetitive, most contemporary critics thought it formulaic, the slapstick has dated, and Fisher would cut twenty minutes. The turn from farce to vocation is abrupt; Christian Sauvé finds the late revelation forced. It was Lupino's last feature, and it remains a good family film that treats the convent as a real way of life.
themes: Religious life is shown as it was before the Council: full habits, community prayer, Midnight Mass and obedience to a superior. The film takes the vocation seriously without preaching. Mary is not converted by argument. She is drawn by seeing the sisters at prayer at Christmas and by the quiet way the community meets a death, and her choice is presented as a free answer, not an escape. Mother Superior's authority rests on charity: she disciplines, then forgives. There are no doctrinal statements to weigh. The Catholic content is the witness of a community living its rule, seen through the eyes of a girl who begins by mocking it.
history: Jane Trahey published Life with Mother Superior in 1962, drawing on her own schooldays at a Catholic girls' school near Chicago in the 1930s; she was a day pupil, while the book's school is a boarding school. Filming began in August 1965 under the title Mother Superior, with exteriors at a Pennsylvania mansion and interiors at Columbia's Hollywood studio. A sequel, Where Angels Go, Trouble Follows, followed in 1968 without Mills.
advisories:
Slapstick pranks and mild mischief.

The death of an elderly nun, handled gently.

Simcha Fisher notes a few gags in which the camera lingers on schoolgirls' legs and bottoms for laughs.

Suitable for families; older children will enjoy it most.

names: Life with Mother Superior, memoir by Jane Trahey (1962)

suitability.note: Slapstick pranks, a few cheeky jokes and the gentle death of an elderly nun. Children will enjoy the schoolgirl mischief, though a few gags dwell on the girls' legs.

doctrine: The film shows convent life as it stood before the changes of the later 1960s: the habit, the grand silence, rule and obedience to the Mother Superior, and the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience that bind a religious. Mary Clancy asks what a vocation is and finds it is a call from God, tested over time, not a taste for the cloister. The 1917 Code (canons 487 and following) defines the religious state as a stable manner of life in common in which the faithful take on the evangelical counsels. The Church holds that the religious life is a higher state than marriage, as the Council of Trent defined in session XXIV, canon 10.
production: Ken Donnellon and Jacqueline Babbin bought the rights to Jane Trahey's 1962 book, but Columbia acquired them in 1964. Ida Lupino directed. Shooting began in August 1965 under the title Mother Superior. Interiors were made at Columbia in Hollywood and most exteriors at Greystone Mansion, while the school's exteriors were filmed at what is now Lindenwold Castle in Ambler, Pennsylvania. The budget was $2 million. It opened on 30 March 1966, ran 112 minutes and earned $4.1 million in rentals. Reviews were mostly good, though Variety found it repetitive. A sequel, Where Angels Go, Trouble Follows, came in 1968.

title: Vision
originalTitle: Vision – Aus dem Leben der Hildegard von Bingen
alternateTitles: Vision: From the Life of Hildegard von Bingen
decision: GREY: Rule (a) does not apply. Hildegard was never formally canonised in the Middle Ages, but she was venerated as a saint and her name stands in the Roman Martyrology, as the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) records; Benedict XVI's 2012 extension of her cult adds nothing needed here. Identity (filmportal.de) and content (Christianity Today, Time Out, One Guy's Opinion, Wikipedia) are established. Reservations: von Trotta's feminist framing, ambiguity over whether Hildegard feigns illness, little sense of the mystical, and an intense, possessive attachment to Richardis.
summary: Margarethe von Trotta's handsome, measured life of St Hildegard of Bingen, with Barbara Sukowa as the visionary abbess who founds her own convent against male resistance.
synopsis: Hildegard is given as a child to the Benedictine house at Disibodenberg, where she grows up among the nuns enclosed beside the monks' abbey. As a nun she has visions, which she keeps hidden until the monk Volmar encourages her to write them down. Elected to lead the sisters, she clashes with Abbot Kuno over penitential severity, the study of medicine and the sisters' welfare, and her visions are examined and in the end accepted by Church authority. Deeply attached to the young nun Richardis, she resolves to found her own convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen, against the monks' opposition. A nun's pregnancy and suicide shake the community. When Richardis's family secures her an abbacy elsewhere, Hildegard fights bitterly to keep her and is devastated by her departure. At the end Hildegard announces that she will go out and preach.
inclusion: Hildegard was a composer, a writer on medicine and nature, a correspondent of popes and emperors and a reformer of her own community, and von Trotta's film gives a solid outline of that life. It was shot in surviving medieval monasteries, including Maulbronn and Eberbach, and Kenneth Morefield in Christianity Today credits it with careful research and much detail of convent life. Barbara Sukowa's Hildegard is formidable, even haughty, and her chant runs through the film. It is slow and severe. Joshua Rothkopf in Time Out finds the performance over-restrained and the abbess's famous independence in short supply, and a reviewer at One Guy's Opinion warns that the pacing is very deliberate. It is most alive in the Richardis story, which von Trotta called its emotional climax. Its value is as an introduction to a great medieval figure rather than as a portrait of a mystic.
themes: The visions are treated as real events, and they are tested and approved by the Church, but Morefield, citing the medievalist Elizabeth Rambo, finds little sense of the transcendent; the Hildegard on screen can look more like a shrewd politician than a mystic. Von Trotta frames the story around a woman resisting male superiors, and the film leaves open whether some of Hildegard's illnesses are feigned to get her way. The Benedictine life itself, with its Office, enclosure and obedience, is shown with respect, and questions of penance and learning are raised, though not resolved. Hildegard's possessive love for Richardis is presented as an intense friendship; Rothkopf hints at an unspoken subtext, while One Guy's Opinion finds nothing improper.
history: Hildegard (1098–1179) entered religious life as a child at Disibodenberg and in about 1147–48 settled with eighteen sisters at Rupertsberg near Bingen, where she died. The Catholic Encyclopedia records that no formal canonisation ever took place, though Gregory IX and Innocent IV ordered inquiries; she was venerated as a saint, her name is in the Roman Martyrology and her feast is 17 September. Benedict XVI extended her cult to the whole Church in 2012.
liberties: The film compresses decades into a few conflicts, concentrated on Abbot Kuno and on Richardis. Morefield notes that it raises disputes over penance and secular learning and then drops them. The nun's pregnancy and suicide and Hildegard's possible feigned illness are dramatic conjecture rather than documented fact.
advisories:
Two scenes of self-flagellation, and nuns removing a belt of thorns from a dead sister's scarred body.

A nun becomes pregnant and later takes her own life; no sexual activity is shown.

Rated 12 in Germany; suitable for teenagers and adults.

The film reads Hildegard partly through a modern feminist lens.

grey.question: Vision gives a careful, well-researched outline of St Hildegard's life and treats Benedictine life with respect. The question is the angle. Von Trotta frames the abbess as a proto-feminist resisting male superiors, lets the film wonder whether some of her illnesses were feigned to get her way, and conveys little of the mystical depth of her visions. Her attachment to Richardis is shown as intense and possessive, and some critics read more into it. Viewers can judge whether this is a fair portrait or a modern projection.

title: A Man for All Seasons
alternateTitles: Robert Bolt's A Man for All Seasons
decision: PUBLISH: The TNT film follows Bolt's play more literally than the 1966 film (Wikipedia, Cinema e Medioevo), and the play text (1960 edition, archive.org) was checked: More calls the divorce a matter for the Holy See, refuses a heretic son-in-law, and argues at his trial that Parliament cannot confer a spiritual supremacy. A contemporary Catholic review of the play (Theophilus Lewis, America, 1961) is the independent judgment. The Bolt 'self' caveat is the same as in the 1966 record. No independent review of the 1988 production itself could be opened (TCM and KQEK pages failed); if the editor wants one, GREY/unverified is the fallback.
summary: Charlton Heston directs himself as Thomas More in a close, stagy version of Bolt's play that keeps the Common Man the 1966 film dropped.
synopsis: Henry VIII wants his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled and needs his Lord Chancellor, Sir Thomas More, to approve. More will not. He resigns the chancellorship and keeps silent, trusting the law to protect a man who says nothing. Thomas Cromwell sets out to break him, with the help of the ambitious Richard Rich. More refuses to let his daughter Margaret marry William Roper while Roper holds heretical views, and he will not take the oath required by the new Act. Imprisoned in the Tower, he resists the pleas of his wife Alice and his friend the Duke of Norfolk. Rich's perjury convicts him, and only then does More speak his mind on the Act before going to the block. The Common Man steps in and out of the action as chorus and plays several small parts.
inclusion: Heston had played More on stage and adapted his own production for TNT, the network's first made-for-television film. He told critics that Paul Scofield's screen performance was definitive and that he was not trying to copy it. The production is plainly theatrical: it runs about half an hour longer than Zinnemann's film and follows Bolt's text more literally. The cast is strong. John Gielgud plays Wolsey, Vanessa Redgrave plays Alice, Richard Johnson plays Norfolk, and Roy Kinnear plays the Common Man. Redgrave's casting earned a Golden Globe nomination. The reason to see it beside the 1966 film is the text: this is Bolt's play much as he wrote it, with the Common Man's ironic commentary restored and More's argument for the Church given in full. Those who know the Zinnemann film will find it stagier and less polished, but closer to the play.
themes: More dies for the papacy and for the indissolubility of marriage. In Bolt's text he calls the King's case a matter for the Holy See, refuses Roper while Roper is a heretic, and at his trial argues that Parliament cannot give the King the Supremacy of the Church because it is a spiritual supremacy, adding that the Church's immunity is promised in Magna Carta and the coronation oath. Bolt's preface describes More as a man who would not retreat from the place where he located his self, and that modern language of selfhood colours the play. On stage, though, his reasons are God and the Church. Theophilus Lewis, reviewing the Broadway production for America in 1961, called it magnificent and read More as a man of conscience rather than a seeker after martyrdom.
liberties: Bolt compresses More's last years and leaves out his record as Lord Chancellor against heretics. The Common Man is Bolt's invention, a chorus figure who comments on the action and plays servants, officials and the executioner's kind. Rich's perjury follows the traditional accounts of the trial.
advisories:
More's execution ends the film.

No sexual content or strong language. Long dialogue and legal argument suit teenagers and adults more than young children.

The play omits More's part in the prosecution of heretics, so it is not a complete biography.

title: Acts of the Apostles
decision: GREY: Identity (MUBI; Brunette) and content established by independent scholarship (Peter Brunette, UC Press 1996; Tag Gallagher, Senses of Cinema 2004; Adriano Aprà via Bible Films Blog). Not PUBLISH because the adaptation removes the Ascension and almost all the miracles and frames the faith in humanist terms; not REJECT because Luke's text and the apostles' preaching are largely kept and no explicit heterodox thesis is voiced in the film. The editor may prefer REJECT; a subtitle check of Pentecost and Peter's sermons would decide.
summary: Rossellini's five-part RAI series stages the Acts of the Apostles in Tunisian locations, from the first community in Jerusalem to Paul in Rome, with the miracles almost all removed.
synopsis: The series begins in Jerusalem after Christ has gone, with the apostles gathered and waiting; Rossellini leaves out the Ascension. It follows the first conversions and baptisms, the life of the community and its sharing of goods, disputes over the meaning of Christ's words and over the Law, the stoning of Stephen and the persecution led by Saul, Philip's baptism of the Ethiopian eunuch, and Saul's conversion. The later episodes follow Paul on his journeys, preaching to Jews, Greeks and Romans, through riots, arrests and trials, to his arrival in Rome. Most of the healings and wonders by which Peter and Paul show their authority in Luke's account are omitted, and the great events are given no more weight than the business of daily life.
inclusion: Tag Gallagher calls it perhaps the aesthetic culmination of Rossellini's late historical work, and Adriano Aprà ranks it the warmest of his television films. Shot in south-east Tunisia, with the mosque of Kairouan standing in for the Temple, it looks like no other Bible film: long takes, slow zooms, white light, largely non-professional actors, and constant attention to how people ate, worked, kept accounts and prayed. Jacques Siclier in Le Monde called it anti-dramatic, the objective description of a phenomenon. It is also long, talky and deliberately flat, and its padded costumes and painted backdrops have been mocked. It drew an average of 8.6 million homes per episode on RAI. For patient viewers it is the most serious attempt on film to show the Church of the Acts as a real community in a real world.
themes: Much of Luke's text is there: the community of goods, baptism, Stephen's martyrdom, Paul's conversion and his argument that salvation comes through faith in Christ, not the letter of the Law. The difficulty is what Rossellini leaves out and why. He omits the Ascension and nearly all the miracles, and, as Peter Brunette notes, refuses any outside confirmation that the apostles are guided from heaven. Rossellini said he made the series because Christianity changed man's relation to nature and so made Western civilisation, and Brunette concludes that it shows Christianity as a carrier of Hebrew ideas rather than as the true religion. The Church's beginnings are respected as history; its supernatural foundation is muted.
liberties: Rossellini invents speeches for Saul before and after his conversion and adds detailed scenes of daily life; Aprà notes that he synthesises, expands, cuts and invents freely within Luke. The Ascension and most of the apostles' miracles are left out.
advisories:
The stoning of Stephen, riots and a food riot, staged without gore.

Very long: about 340 minutes in five episodes; a shorter theatrical version exists.

Suitable for older children and adults with patience.

The supernatural is largely removed; viewers should know Luke's account.

title: A.D.
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred in its apostolic core, which follows Acts and Eusebius (McNulty; Unger in the Christian Science Monitor, 1985). But a large share of the running time goes to invented romance and Roman court drama, with some sexual content (McNulty rates sex and nudity 3/10). That is a reservation a reader can weigh. A detailed episode guide or a subtitle check of the Roman episodes would settle how much sexual material there is.
summary: A six-part account of the Apostles from Pentecost to Nero's persecution, half the Acts of the Apostles and half Roman court drama and invented romance.
synopsis: After the Crucifixion, the Apostles in Jerusalem receive the Spirit at Pentecost and begin to preach. Peter and John stand before the Sanhedrin, Stephen is stoned, Philip baptises the Ethiopian, and Saul the persecutor is converted. After his vision, Peter visits a Roman officer. Alongside the Church's story runs the history of the Caesars, from Tiberius through Caligula and Claudius to Nero, and two invented love stories between Jews and Romans: the Zealot Caleb becomes a gladiator in Rome while searching for his sister Sarah, who is enslaved and then marries the soldier Valerius. After the fire of Rome, Nero blames the Christians. Peter is crucified head downwards and Paul is beheaded. At the end Linus, Peter's successor, entrusts an orphaned boy to Caleb and Corinna.
inclusion: This was the last of Vincenzo Labella's biblical productions with Anthony Burgess, after Moses the Lawgiver and Jesus of Nazareth, and it has the same kind of large international cast. Denis Quilley's Peter and Philip Sayer's Paul are its core, and Ed McNulty singles them out. Arthur Unger, in the Christian Science Monitor, found it a serious, perhaps too serious, attempt to recreate the years after the Crucifixion rather than camp spectacle, and praised James Mason's Tiberius and Anthony Andrews's Nero. He also found the Jerusalem episodes slow and the Roman ones livelier, which points to the problem: the Acts material is good, but it has to be extracted from a great deal of imperial intrigue and fiction. The DVD runs about six hours, cut from a broadcast that took nine with commercials.
themes: The apostolic material is substantial. Pentecost, the Apostles before the Sanhedrin, Stephen's martyrdom, Philip and the Ethiopian, Peter's vision and visit to the Roman officer, Saul's conversion, and the house church of Aquila and Priscilla in Rome are all dramatised, drawing on Acts and on Eusebius. Peter's crucifixion upside down follows the tradition Eusebius records, and the closing scene with Linus shows the succession continuing in Rome. McNulty notes, as a quibble, that baptisms are by pouring. The weakness is proportion: much of the running time goes to the Caesars and to invented romance, which at times pushes the Apostles to the margins.
history: Acts records Pentecost, Stephen's death, Philip and the Ethiopian, Peter and Cornelius, Paul's conversion and his journeys, and ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome. Peter's crucifixion and Paul's beheading under Nero come from early tradition recorded by Eusebius. Tacitus records that Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of 64. Linus is listed as Peter's first successor as bishop of Rome.
liberties: Caleb, Sarah, Valerius and Corinna are invented, and their stories, including Corinna's turn as a gladiator and two love affairs between Jews and Romans, take up much of the series. The imperial scenes draw on Suetonius rather than Acts. The final scene with Linus is invented. Burgess novelised the material as The Kingdom of the Wicked.

Persecution and martyrdom: stoning, crucifixion, beheading and arena violence. McNulty rates the violence 5 out of 10.

title: Anthony of Padua
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency classed the American release A-I (1951-52), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment, and The Exhibitor's 1952 review gives an independent account: made with care and sincerity, with Aldo Fabrizi's Ezzelino sequence the best thing in it. The content (vocation, preaching, bilocation, raising a dead man to clear his father, confronting Ezzelino) follows the traditional legends. Anthony was canonised in 1232.
summary: Pietro Francisci's modest biography of St Anthony, framed by a modern mother's prayer, moves from Lisbon to the Franciscans and ends with the saint facing down the tyrant Ezzelino.
synopsis: After the First World War a young mother refuses to believe her husband has been killed. She almost agrees to marry a rich suitor, but her prayers to St Anthony are answered and her husband comes home. Her small son becomes fascinated by the saint's story, which the film then tells. Fernando, son of a noble family in Lisbon, enters the Augustinian canons and later becomes a Franciscan, taking the name Antonio. He preaches in Africa, France and Italy. Preaching in Paris, he learns that his father is on trial in Lisbon for murder; by bilocation he appears in the court and raises the dead man, who names his real killer. Settled in the Veneto, he confronts the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano, whose massacres have become unbearable, and persuades him to open his prisons. He dies near Padua.
inclusion: This was the first sound feature on St Anthony, made by Pietro Francisci a few years before his Hercules films, with Mario Bava as cinematographer and Silvana Pampanini, soon a star, as the mother in the frame story. It is a small film. The Exhibitor found it made with care and sincerity but limited in appeal, and singled out the one sequence with Aldo Fabrizi as Ezzelino as easily the best in it. What it offers is the popular St Anthony: the preacher, the wonder-worker of the bilocation and the Lisbon trial, the patron who answers prayers, and the friar who stands up to a tyrant. The modern frame shows why he was the most invoked saint in Italian homes. It suits families who want a plain, devout saint's life rather than a work of art.
themes: The frame story is about intercession: a widow's prayers to St Anthony are answered, and her son's devotion leads into the saint's life. That life is told through his vocation, first as an Augustinian canon and then as a Franciscan, his preaching against heresy and sin, and his miracles, which the film presents as real: bilocation and the raising of a murdered man to save an innocent. The confrontation with Ezzelino shows the saint's preaching as a public force, persuading a tyrant to release prisoners. It is devotional in the traditional sense, close to the Fioretti-style legends rather than to critical biography.
history: Fernando Martins de Bulhões was born in Lisbon about 1195, joined the Augustinian canons and in 1220 became a Franciscan after seeing the relics of the friars martyred in Morocco. Shipwrecked in Sicily on the way back from Africa, he became a celebrated preacher in Italy and France. He died near Padua in June 1231 and was canonised by Gregory IX in 1232; Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1946.
liberties: The bilocation to Lisbon and the raising of the murdered man are traditional legends, presented as fact. His preaching in Africa is a stretch: he went to Morocco to seek martyrdom but fell ill and never preached there. The modern frame story is invented. The meeting with Ezzelino follows a later legend.
advisories:
Violence: a murder trial, massacres ordered by a tyrant.

A widow nearly remarries while her husband is missing in war.

Suitable for older children and up.

doctrine: Anthony died near Padua on 13 June 1231 and was canonised by Gregory IX on 30 May 1232, less than a year later, at Spoleto. His feast is 13 June. Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1946 with the title Doctor Evangelicus, honouring his sermons, which were built on Scripture and aimed at heresy and at the sins of usury and tyranny. The Council of Trent (Session 25, 1563) taught that the saints reign with Christ, offer their prayers to God for men, and that it is good and useful to invoke them. The film's frame, a mother asking the saint's help for a missing husband, rests on that teaching. Anthony's tongue was found incorrupt when his relics were moved in 1263, in the presence of St Bonaventure. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the story of Ezzelino's humbling is legend, though Anthony's plea for prisoners at Verona is documented.
production: Pietro Francisci directed and co-wrote the film for Oro Film, with Mario Francisci as producer. Mario Bava, later known for horror films, was the cinematographer. The cast was led by the unknown Aldo Fiorelli as Anthony, with the comic star Aldo Fabrizi in a serious part as the tyrant Ezzelino da Romano and Silvana Pampanini as the saint's mother. The film runs 81 minutes and was released in Italy in June 1949. It was later shown in the United States in the Trans-Global dubbed version, reviewed in the trade press as an Italian-made picture. Francisci went on to make the 1950s Hercules films.

title: Augustine of Hippo
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from the Pacific Film Archive catalogue record (Italy 1972, made for Italian television, 120 min, screenplay Rossellini, Mariani, Scaffa) and the Gulbenkian programme. Peter Brunette's chapter (UC Press, 1996) is an independent, scene-aware treatment showing a film centred on the bishop's defence of Catholic unity against the Donatists, with Augustine given the answer to the pagans' objections. No hard rule applies; the 1972 date is noted and no post-conciliar framing is reported. The absence of Pelagius and the didactic flatness are stated.
summary: Rossellini's spare RAI film follows St Augustine as Bishop of Hippo, defending the unity of the Church against the Donatists while the Western Empire falls apart.
synopsis: The film skips the Confessions and begins with the bishop. Valerius, the aged Bishop of Hippo, chooses the reluctant Augustine (Dary Berkani) as his successor, and Augustine leaves his home for his new diocese. After the sack of Rome, Romans blame the Christians, and Augustine argues that the empire fell through its own corruption and that hope lies with the Church. Much of the film follows his long struggle with the Donatists, who reject Catholic unity and attack other Christians, and his eventual recourse to Roman law against them. He sits as judge in a civil case and insists that justice matters more than legality; he persuades a Christian magistrate that public duty and the law of charity cannot be separated; he answers pagans who accuse the Christians of hating beauty and pleasure. The Vandal advance on Roman Africa darkens his last years.
inclusion: Rossellini wanted to film a turning point in civilisation, and he chose not the convert of the Confessions but what Peter Brunette calls the life of a small-town bishop. That choice is the film's strength. Shot among the ruins of Pompeii, Paestum and Herculaneum and composed like a late Roman mosaic, it shows how a fifth-century bishop preached, judged disputes and held his flock together while the world he knew collapsed. Brunette reports that the Catholic critic Trasatti thought its religious inspiration the highest in Rossellini's work. It is austere and talky, the acting is deliberately flat, and anyone hoping for Augustine the theologian of grace will find little of him. As a portrait of the Church holding a falling civilisation together, it is unusual and serious.
themes: The theme is the unity of the Church. Augustine fights the Donatists because, in a line Brunette quotes, they want to destroy the unity of the Church of Christ, and the film shares his view that truth and unity go together. Original sin is stated through a pagan who mocks the Christians for calling human nature wounded, and Augustine answers the pagans that Christians do not reject art or history but see through them the Word made flesh. The scenes with the magistrate teach that morality is one, in public office as in private life. Brunette notes the irony that Augustine finally calls on Roman law to suppress the schismatics; the film does not condemn him for it.
history: Augustine (354–430) was ordained priest at Hippo in 391 and, from about 396, was coadjutor and then successor to the aged Bishop Valerius, holding the see for thirty-four years. The Donatist schism dominated his early episcopate; at the Conference of Carthage in 411 the Catholic case prevailed and imperial authority enforced it. He also wrote against the Pelagians. He died on 28 August 430 while the Vandals besieged Hippo.
liberties: The film omits Augustine's youth, his conversion and his mother, St Monica, and gives almost no room to his writings or to the Pelagian controversy. Its debates with pagans, magistrates and litigants compress arguments into short set-piece scenes.
advisories:
Donatist mobs attack other Christians; little else in the way of violence.

No sexual content; Augustine's early life is left out.

Slow and dialogue-heavy; best for adults and older students.

title: Barabbas
decision: GREY: Same story and grounds as barabbas-1961 (GREY): Christ's Passion, St Peter and the Roman martyrs surround a protagonist who never clearly believes. This version is closer to the source, since Lagerkvist co-wrote it, and the novel ends with Barabbas surrendering his soul to the darkness. Identity from the Cannes festival record and Wikipedia; content from the novel and a Church of Sweden screening note. No review of the film's own treatment was found. A review, or the film's final dialogue, would settle whether the ending is despair or a hidden act of faith.
summary: Alf Sjöberg's austere Swedish film of Pär Lagerkvist's novel about the robber freed in Christ's place, who spends his life unable either to believe or to forget.
synopsis: The film follows Lagerkvist's novel. Barabbas, a brigand condemned to death, is released by Pilate at the Passover in place of Jesus, and watches the crucifixion from the crowd. The event takes hold of him. He seeks out the followers of the crucified man and questions them, but what they say does not match what he has seen, and he cannot share their faith. Years later he is a slave in the mines, chained to a Christian, Sahak, who believes and who dies for it. Taken to Rome, Barabbas still tries to understand. When fire breaks out in the city he joins in, thinking he is serving the Christians, and is imprisoned with them. St Peter is among the prisoners. Barabbas is crucified with them, and dies alone.
inclusion: This is the first film of Lagerkvist's novel, which helped win its author the Nobel Prize in 1951, and Lagerkvist shares the screenplay credit. Sjöberg was Sweden's leading stage and film director before Bergman, and the film was in competition at Cannes in 1953. Ulf Palme plays Barabbas, Erik Strandmark St Peter. It is much harder to see, and much less spectacular, than the 1961 Hollywood version with Anthony Quinn, and it is likely to be closer to the book's bleak, questioning spirit. That is both its interest and its difficulty. It suits viewers who know the novel and want its most faithful screen form.
themes: The story is told from outside faith. Barabbas wants to believe but must first understand, and never does. Around him are believers who understand less and believe more: Sahak, the martyrs in Rome and Peter. The novel's great antithesis is that Christ dies among friends and speaking to God, Barabbas alone and speaking to the darkness. Read as a Catholic, it is a portrait of a soul resisting grace and of what faith asks: trust before understanding. The danger is that the film, like its author, may leave the darkness the last word.
liberties: Barabbas's life after his release is wholly invented by Lagerkvist; the Gospels say nothing of it. The novel's account of the Christians setting fire to Rome reflects Nero's accusation, not their guilt, and Barabbas's part in it is his own mistake.
advisories:
The Crucifixion and later crucifixions; harsh slavery in the mines; a martyr's death.

No sexual content of note is reported.

A bleak story of unbelief; for adults and older teenagers.

grey.question: This is a film about a man who cannot believe. Barabbas is freed in Christ's place, haunted by the crucifixion, surrounded by believers who die for their faith, St Peter among them, and yet he never reaches faith himself. In Lagerkvist's novel, which he co-adapted, Barabbas dies on a cross speaking to the darkness. Viewers should know that the film is a study of unbelief that respects the believers but may give doubt the last word; whether its ending leaves any opening to grace has not been verified.

title: Cardinal Messias
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and morally clean - the Legion of Decency classed the US release A-I (1951-52), and Italian reviews of 1939 and The Exhibitor (1952) agree on a dignified missionary drama. The reservation is political and historical: made in Italian East Africa three years after the conquest of Ethiopia, funded partly by a religious order, awarded the Coppa Mussolini, and described by the Museo Nazionale del Cinema as a manifesto of italianità and of the regime. Massaia is a Servant of God (declared Venerable only in 2016); rule (a) does not apply and he is not given a title.
summary: A Fascist-era epic of the Capuchin bishop Guglielmo Massaia's mission in Ethiopia, his friendship with Menelik and his expulsion, shot on location and awarded the Coppa Mussolini.
synopsis: Massaia, a Capuchin bishop who has spent years in Ethiopia, travels on foot with his companion Fr Leone, caring for the poor and freeing a slave. Menelik, King of Shewa, receives him warmly and lets him found a mission; the two become friends. Massaia fights an epidemic with a rough smallpox vaccine and settles his mission among the people he has nursed. His success provokes the Coptic Abuna Atanasio, who excommunicates anyone who deals with him and persuades the Emperor Yohannes to demand his expulsion. Menelik refuses and war follows; a princess slighted by Menelik joins his enemies. Massaia, knowing he is the pretext, offers to give himself up. Yohannes wins with the help of the Galla, spares Menelik but orders Massaia out to satisfy the Copts. Fr Leone dies on the journey, and crowds escort the bishop to the border.
inclusion: Camillo Pilotto's Massaia was widely praised: Mario Gromo in La Stampa called the film a major achievement and admired Pilotto and Enrico Glori's ambiguous Menelik, and Umberto Barbaro found it dignified and serious though spectacular and crudely edited. The battle and crowd scenes, shot in Eritrea with thousands of extras, were what impressed contemporary audiences. The Exhibitor, reviewing the American release in 1952, admired the authentic background but felt the film never got below the surface of its political and religious struggle. The Museo del Cinema's programme note, presenting a restored copy in 2009, judged that Massaia himself is spared the propaganda rhetoric given to other characters. It is worth knowing as a serious missionary portrait made in the wrong cause.
themes: Massaia is presented as an apostle in the full sense: he preaches, baptises, heals and frees slaves, and he is ready to give himself up to prevent bloodshed. The Coptic hierarchy, in the person of Abuna Atanasio, is shown as envious and political, using excommunication to drive out the Catholic mission. The Church's work is given a clear supernatural purpose, the salvation of souls and works of mercy, but the film also makes the missionary a forerunner of Italian influence in Ethiopia and celebrates Italy as a civilising power.
history: Guglielmo Massaia (1809-1889), a Piedmontese Capuchin, was named Vicar Apostolic of the Galla in 1846 and worked in Ethiopia for some thirty-five years, much of it in Shewa under Menelik, whose favour he won partly through medicine, including vaccination against smallpox. He was expelled by the Emperor Yohannes IV in 1879, returned to Italy, wrote his memoirs and was made a cardinal by Leo XIII in 1884. His cause for beatification is open.
liberties: The plot compresses decades of missionary work into a single conflict, and the princess and some episodes are dramatised. The film presents Italian interest in Ethiopia through a friendly Menelik, passing over the later war of 1896 and the invasion of 1935-36, which the film was made to justify.
advisories:
Battle scenes with many deaths; an epidemic.

Slavery, including a slave being freed.

Suitable for older children and up.

The film was made as colonial propaganda and presents Fascist Italy's claims in Ethiopia favourably.

grey.question: The missionary portrait is sound and the Legion of Decency passed the film for all audiences. The question is its purpose. It was shot in occupied Ethiopia in 1939, won the Coppa Mussolini, and is described by the Museo Nazionale del Cinema as a manifesto of Italian identity and of the regime: Massaia's mission is presented as the forerunner of Italy's civilising role in Africa. Viewers should weigh how far the film enlists a missionary bishop for the Fascist colonial cause.

title: Near the City
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a young priest's first parish and his catechism of the children). Identity and outline are established (Spanish Wikipedia), and decine21 gives a short descriptive note. No independent or contemporary Catholic assessment of how the film treats the priest and the faith was found. A Spanish Catholic rating (the 1950s Oficina Nacional Permanente de Vigilancia de Espectáculos or Ecclesia listings) or a 1952 review would settle it.
summary: Luis Lucia's modest Spanish social drama of a newly ordained priest who takes charge of a destitute parish on the edge of Madrid and wins it over through its children.
synopsis: Padre José, newly ordained and the son of a variety ventriloquist, is sent as curate to a poor parish on the outskirts of Madrid. He arrives to find that the parish priest has died, and he must run the church himself until the bishop decides what to do. The district is poor in every sense: bad housing, poor health and moral neglect. Ramón, the old sacristan, explains its troubles to him. Doña Casilda, owner of the best house in the neighbourhood, practises her religion in her own fashion. With the help of the sacristan, a doctor who gives his services, and Pepito, his father's ventriloquist's dummy, the young priest begins to draw the neighbourhood's children to catechism, the first step in reclaiming a parish that has drifted from the Church.
inclusion: It belongs to a strand of early-1950s Spanish films that put a priest among the urban poor. Adolfo Marsillach, later a leading theatre director, plays the young curate, with the great character actor Pepe Isbert as the sacristan. The film won a 300,000-peseta prize from the Sindicato Nacional del Espectáculo. Decine21 calls it an interesting example of the social cinema of the period, though it rates it only 4 out of 10. The ventriloquist's dummy as an instrument of catechesis is an engaging, unusual idea. Beyond that, no critical account of the film's quality survives in the sources found.
themes: The subject is the pastoral care of a dechristianised suburb. The young priest's tools are humble: catechism for the children, the help of a sacristan and a charitable doctor, and a dummy that makes the children laugh. The film appears to set the priest's patient work against both material poverty and a self-satisfied piety, in Doña Casilda, who keeps religion on her own terms. How much the film shows the sacraments, and whether it treats the priest's mission as spiritual or chiefly social, is not recorded in the available sources.
advisories:
Poverty and illness in a shanty district.

Nothing objectionable is reported.

Suitable for families on the available evidence.

title: Demetrius and the Gladiators
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred enough under the Bible-epic rule (a Christian's fall and repentance, St Peter as shepherd, the relic of Christ's robe), and the Legion of Decency rated it A-II. The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the shape and sharpens the reservation: the apostasy is explicit (he swears there is no king but Caesar and sacrifices to Isis), the return is private prayer without any sacramental reconciliation, and the middle third relishes the arena killings, an attempted gang rape and the affair with Messalina. The robe is handled correctly as a memorial, not a charm. AFI, Bryant Frazer and Wikipedia remain the critical sources.
summary: Fox's sequel to The Robe sends the Christian freedman Demetrius into the arena, out of his faith and into Messalina's arms, before St Peter brings him back.
synopsis: After Marcellus and Diana are martyred, Peter leaves Christ's robe in the keeping of Demetrius, the Greek freedman who knew Christ. Caligula, who believes the robe can make him immortal, has it hunted; Demetrius strikes a soldier and is sentenced to the gladiator school owned by Claudius. In the arena he refuses to kill. Messalina, Claudius's wife, takes an interest in him. When gladiators assault Lucia, the Christian girl who loves him, and she seems to die, Demetrius cries out against God, kills his opponents, declares before Caligula that there is no king but Caesar, sacrifices to Isis and becomes Messalina's lover. Peter visits and is mocked. Sent to seize the robe, Demetrius finds Lucia alive but sunk in a stupor; he prays for forgiveness and she wakes. Caligula's test of the robe fails, the Praetorians kill him, and Claudius promises loyal Christians safety.
inclusion: It was a bigger hit than many better films, and contemporary critics liked it more than The Robe: Bosley Crowther enjoyed its mix of spectacle, action, sex and reverence, and Richard L. Coe found it less stuffy. Delmer Daves directs with energy and makes good use of CinemaScope, Susan Hayward is a vivid Messalina, and Jay Robinson's Caligula is grand camp. Victor Mature is wooden. Bryant Frazer gives the honest modern view: a Bible picture that condemns its hero's killing and adultery while letting the audience enjoy both, then turns preachy. Its religious core, a believer's fall and return through prayer and the patience of Peter, is real, and stronger than its reputation as a gladiator movie suggests. Michael Rennie's Peter, who answers mockery with pity, is the best thing in it.
themes: The subject is apostasy and repentance. Demetrius loses his faith when God seems to let Lucia die, and the denial is explicit: he swears there is no king but Caesar and offers sacrifice to Isis. Peter does not argue him back. He comes to the villa, is mocked, and answers with pity; later he tells Demetrius that if he wants the robe he must pray for it, as he once knew how. The return is a prayer to the Father for forgiveness, set against Christ's words from the cross, and Lucia's waking answers it. The robe is treated as a relic and memorial: Demetrius says its only spell is memory, and when Caligula fails to raise a murdered man with it, he is told no one ever claimed it had powers. The repentance stays private; nothing sacramental is shown.
history: Caligula reigned from 37 to 41 and was murdered by officers of the Praetorian Guard led by Cassius Chaerea, who appears in the film. Claudius succeeded him; Messalina was his wife. There is no evidence that Claudius protected Christians, and he expelled Jews from Rome in about 49, an episode that may have involved early Christians.
liberties: Demetrius, Lucia and the robe's history are fiction from Lloyd C. Douglas's characters. The film makes Messalina a predator at Caligula's court who publicly renounces her adultery at the end, and has Claudius promise the Christians they have nothing to fear while they stay loyal, which is invention. Peter's presence in Rome under Caligula is unhistorical.
advisories:
Arena combat, with killings; tigers; an attempted gang rape of a young woman.

An adulterous affair with Messalina, implied rather than shown.

The hero denies Christ and sacrifices to Isis before his repentance.

Legion of Decency A-II (adults and adolescents).

title: The Galilean
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from filmdienst.de (45 min, tinted, restored 1996 by the Bundesarchiv-Filmarchiv) and the 4enoch catalogue. Grzegorz Nadgrodkiewicz's scholarly article (Kwartalnik Filmowy 87–88, 2014), an independent source drawing on Reinhold Zwick's study, establishes a Gospel Passion adapted from the Fassnacht family's Freiburg play, itself based on the Oberammergau text, with the Christ–Judas conflict at its centre. Reservation stated in advisories: the Sanhedrin priests are drawn with anti-Jewish stereotyping.
summary: Dimitri Buchowetzki's film of the Fassnacht family's Freiburg Passion play, a self-styled Oberammergau, with Adolf Fassnacht as Christ and his brother Georg as Judas.
synopsis: The film follows the last days of Christ as the Passion plays did. Christ enters Jerusalem on foot at the head of a great crowd and heals a blind man, while Judas watches from the edge, apart and hostile. Other teachings and miracles are reported by the characters in the titles rather than shown. Parallel scenes show the Last Supper, staged after Leonardo, and Judas before the Sanhedrin taking the thirty pieces of silver; he returns to the upper room and faces Christ in silence. The arrest, the trial and the way of the cross follow, ending with the Crucifixion. Throughout, the drama turns on Christ and his betrayer rather than on Pilate or the crowd.
inclusion: The Galilean is the founding film of German religious cinema and a record of a popular Passion play that has otherwise vanished. The Fassnacht family had toured Germany with a Passion 'after Oberammergau' before settling in Freiburg in 1921, where they built a huge open-air stage. Buchowetzki, fresh from his hit Danton, filmed it that September with more than 3,000 extras. Nadgrodkiewicz shows that he did more than record the play: the entry into Jerusalem is cut quickly from several angles, and the Last Supper is intercut with Judas's bargain and closes on alternating close-ups of Christ and Judas. Other passages remain static and stagey. Reviews in 1921 were mixed but praised the crowd scenes. In America, as The Passion Play, it helped launch the Fassnachts' 1929 tour.
themes: The film is a straightforward Gospel Passion drawn from a Catholic popular tradition: the Fassnachts' text was an adaptation of the Oberammergau play as revised by its parish priest, Joseph Alois Daisenberger. Christ is shown praying before the miracle at the gate, instituting the Eucharist at the Last Supper and going to his death. Judas is the dramatic counterweight, a brooding loner bought with silver, not a political rebel. The Sanhedrin is another matter: Nadgrodkiewicz notes that the priests are drawn as stereotypes, with sneers and horned caps, a feature for which the Fassnachts' stage play drew protests in America.
history: The Fassnachts claimed descent from a Freiburg Passion going back to 1264, a claim Nadgrodkiewicz treats as publicity. In 1921 the Oberammergau players sued over the use of their name, and the film was released as Der Galiläer, a mystery in five acts. Its German premiere was delayed to 1923; in the United States it was released in the mid-1920s as The Passion Play. The Fassnacht company performed the play at the New York Hippodrome in 1929.
advisories:
The scourging and Crucifixion, in the restrained manner of a stage Passion.

The Jewish priests of the Sanhedrin are drawn as hostile caricatures.

Silent; tinted restoration of about 45 minutes.

Suitable for older children and up.

title: Don Camillo and the Youth of Today
originalTitle: Don Camillo e i giovani d'oggi
decision: GREY: Identity from ComingSoon and Avvenire (Fulvio Fulvi, 2025); content from ComingSoon's plot and Gordiano Lupi's review (Futuro Europa, 2015). The film satirises post-conciliar novelties from the side of tradition (so not rule b), but it is set inside the reformed Church, and how it shows the new liturgy and Don Camillo's relation to his bishop is unverified; it is also weak by all accounts.
summary: The last Don Camillo film, with Gastone Moschin and Lionel Stander, sets the old rivals against 1968's youth and a young curate determined to reform everything, liturgy included.
synopsis: Peppone (Lionel Stander) has a rebellious son, Michele, whose long-haired gang splits his party, and a Maoist cell gives him further trouble. Don Camillo (Gastone Moschin) is saddled with his niece Caterina, a young protester, and with a curate, don Francesco, who wants to reform everything, the liturgy included. Caterina wins a contest at the Communist Festa dell'Unità and causes a scandal, and the bishop, who also wants to take away the old wooden crucifix Don Camillo talks to, transfers him to a small mountain parish. To repair matters Caterina pretends to have fallen in love with don Francesco, who falls into a spiritual crisis and asks to go to the mountain parish himself. Don Camillo quietly helps Peppone win re-election, and Michele and Caterina, now in love, are married in church with the traditional rite.
inclusion: Guareschi's last, unfinished book, Don Camillo e don Chichì, turned his parish priest against a new adversary: not Communism but the fashions that followed 1968 and the Council. A first version with Fernandel and Gino Cervi was abandoned in 1970 when Fernandel fell ill; he died the next year, and Mario Camerini remade it with a new cast. The film keeps Guareschi's central idea: the old priest, the crucifix that answers him, and the folly of a reforming curate and a bishop who would clear it all away. The execution is weak. Gordiano Lupi finds Moschin and especially Stander shouting where Fernandel and Cervi were restrained, and the humour mild and rose-tinted. It is mainly of interest to admirers of the series and of Guareschi's resistance to the post-conciliar changes.
themes: The faith here is under pressure from within. Don Camillo's crucifix, the voice of Christ throughout the series, is threatened by a bishop who wants it removed, and his parish by a curate who would remake the liturgy; the film takes Don Camillo's side, and it ends with a church wedding in the traditional rite. Guareschi's point, kept here, is that the novelties of 1968, in Church and party alike, are fashions that pass, while the old priest's plain faith and charity remain. What the sources do not establish is how the reformed liturgy and the bishop's authority are shown on screen, or whether Don Camillo's resistance ever becomes disobedience.
history: Guareschi died in 1968 without finishing Don Camillo e don Chichì, the last part of his Mondo piccolo, and his children prepared the text for publication. Christian-Jaque began filming it with Fernandel and Cervi at Brescello in July 1970; Fernandel collapsed on set on 31 July and died in February 1971. Camerini's film, with Moschin and Stander, used a revised script approved by Guareschi's children and had little success.
advisories:
Fights between rival youth gangs.

Caterina feigns a romance with the curate as a trick, and some accounts say a pregnancy; nothing is shown.

Miniskirts and mild sensuality around Carole André's character.

Suitable for teenagers and adults.

title: Judas' Kiss
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred Gospel drama of the betrayal, told from Judas's side, with Christ's face kept off screen. Identity is secure (Wikipedia; Venice 1954 competition list). Content comes from decine21 (present-day, content only), Entreletras and viewers' reviews; none examines the film's account of Judas's motive and end, and an OCIC mention at Venice claimed by decine21 could not be confirmed (the 1954 OCIC prize went to On the Waterfront). A contemporary review or Catholic rating would settle it.
summary: Rafael Gil's large-scale Spanish Passion drama tells the story of the betrayal through Judas Iscariot, played by Rafael Rivelles, with Christ seen only from behind or in part.
synopsis: The film follows the public life and Passion of Jesus as Judas Iscariot lives it. Judas joins the disciples driven by ambition, and over time his ambition and greed harden into betrayal. He sells Jesus to the priests for thirty pieces of silver and identifies Him with a kiss. A young Roman soldier, Quinto Licinio, comes to plead for clemency for the man he recognises as the Son of God, and Pilate, under pressure, gives Jesus up to be crucified. Judas lives on to see the suffering he has caused.
inclusion: This was the most ambitious production of the religious cycle Rafael Gil made with Vicente Escrivá for their company Aspa: 82 sets by Enrique Alarcón, exteriors shot in the Holy Land in 1953, and dramatic black-and-white photography by Alfredo Fraile, which viewers still single out. The press of the day was dazzled by its scale. It was shown in competition at Venice in 1954 and declared of National Interest. Rafael Rivelles gives Judas an intense, brooding presence, and Francisco Rabal, as the Roman soldier, tends to overact. Viewers note that the film is at its best when it stays close to Judas in a dark, almost noir mood, and weaker when it retells the Gospel at a distance. Entreletras calls it monumental and dogmatic, and finds it has aged into a curiosity.
themes: The Passion is seen from the traitor's side. Judas betrays out of ambition and greed, as the Gospels suggest, and the film shows him watching the consequences of what he has done. Christ is never shown full-face: His figure is seen from behind or in part, a reverent convention of the period. Licinio's plea for 'the Son of God' affirms Christ's divinity within the drama. Entreletras reports that the film presents the betrayal as a step in the work of Redemption; how it handles Judas's freedom, guilt and despair, and whether his suicide is shown, is not recorded in the sources found.
advisories:
The scourging and Crucifixion; Judas's end may be shown.

Nothing sexual of note is reported.

Suitable for older children and adults.

title: The Cock Crow
decision: PUBLISH: The film's dialogue (Spanish auto-captions, read in machine translation, 2026-10-12) settles what was unverified. The priest's denial, his refusal of confession to a dying man and his betrayal of a fellow priest are named as grave sins; the enforced cohabitation is explicitly chaste; the climax is sacramental confession to a bishop, with absolution and a penance, followed by restitution to the dead man's companion and the commissar's reconciliation before death. Identity from Wikipedia (Bentley) and the SSIFF 1996 record; craft from Decine21. No contemporary Catholic rating found; the captions are imperfect, so wording is approximate but the substance is unambiguous.
summary: Rafael Gil's Cold War parable on Peter's denial: a priest under a Communist regime disowns his priesthood to save his life, sinks further, then confesses, does penance and returns.
synopsis: Communist troops raid a church refuge in Hungary and beat Father Gruber to death. Father Muller (Francisco Rabal) flees, is arrested and denies he is a priest; in the cells he refuses to hear a dying prisoner's confession. The commissar Gans (Gérard Tichy), his old schoolfellow, spares him once he signs a statement that he has deceived the people, and lodges him with Elsa, a hard-drinking woman separated from her husband. Neighbours discover him; he is made to marry a young couple, and to save himself he points out a fellow priest, then tries in vain to retract. Drunk, he proclaims his priesthood. After the war he confesses to his bishop, who absolves him and sends him back to his old parish as penance, and he tells the dead prisoner's companion what he did. When Gans, now hunted, returns, Muller offers him God's forgiveness, and the commissar dies reconciled.
inclusion: Rafael Gil and the writer-producer Vicente Escrivá made a run of Catholic films in 1950s Spain, and this is one of their Cold War pair with Rabal, after Murió hace quince años. Its idea is a good one: Peter's denial at cockcrow transposed to a priest in a Communist state, so the drama is weakness and return rather than heroic resistance. Rabal, a few years before Buñuel's Nazarín, plays the fallen priest without vanity, and Tichy's commissar, a man whose hatred of God is grief, won a Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos medal. The Spanish site Decine21 finds it well made and tense despite its political message, with a memorable chase through the sewers and touches of film noir. The confession scene with the bishop is the heart of it. The regime declared it of national interest. It is hard to see outside Spain.
themes: The film follows Peter's denial closely and treats the priest's fall with Catholic precision. Muller's sins are named in his own confession: refusing a dying man the sacrament, denying his priesthood in writing, betraying a brother priest and living under one roof with a woman, an arrangement the film makes clear stays chaste. The bishop answers with Peter, the power to bind and loose, and the joy over one sinner who repents; he calls Muller's despair and his wish for martyrdom forms of pride, absolves him and imposes a penance. The priesthood is indelible: even drunk and apostate, Muller insists his hands can still absolve and consecrate. The ending carries the same logic to his persecutor. A passing scene has a mother rebuked for calling a cure miraculous before the Church has judged.
advisories:
The killing of a priest in a raid (heard, not shown); a shoot-out and a pursuit through the sewers; nothing graphic.

The priest is made to live in the same room as a hard-drinking woman; the film states plainly that nothing happens between them. Soldiers' drunken advances to her.

For teenagers and adults.

A priest's apostasy and betrayals are central before his confession and penance.

title: The Judas
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a village Passion play as the means of a sinner's conversion; a monk of Montserrat as counsellor). Identity and outline are established by independent Spanish reviews (Alberto Mateos at Camino de Emaús; DQVlapeli; Entreletras). None describes the ending in detail, and no contemporary Catholic assessment was found; Entreletras reports that Catholic critics of the time argued over it. The ending and the period Catholic verdict would settle it.
summary: Ignacio Iquino's drama, shot at the Esparreguera Passion play with its villagers, about a grasping man who schemes his way into the role of Christ and is changed by it.
synopsis: In Esparreguera, a Catalan town famous for its Holy Week Passion play, Mariano Torné is cast as Judas, and in life he resembles him: proud, envious, a usurer who has ruined neighbours and cheated his own brother Fermín of his inheritance. He wants the part of Christ for his vanity, not from any belief. He frames Jaime Soler, the man cast as Jesus, for thefts at the textile mill where Jaime works, and takes over the role. Rehearsing the Passion begins to work on him. A conversation with a monk of Montserrat shakes him, and the people he has wronged, the children he drove off, a shopkeeper he meant to evict, relatives he cheated, return to confront him. The performance of the Way of the Cross becomes his own Calvary.
inclusion: Iquino, a prolific Barcelona genre director, made this in 1952, the year of the International Eucharistic Congress in Barcelona, and filmed it in Esparreguera with the town's own Passion company as cast and extras; only Antonio Vilar and Manuel Gas were professionals. Reviewers single out Vilar's embittered Mariano and Iquino's skill in weaving rehearsals into the story without trying to stage the whole Passion. Alberto Mateos compares the use of non-actors to Italian neorealism. Entreletras finds it the more lasting of the two Spanish Judas films of the period, against Rafael Gil's monumental Judas' Kiss, and notes the expressionist chiaroscuro of Pablo Ripoll's photography. It is an unusual, sincere piece of popular religious cinema.
themes: The film rests on an old Catholic idea: that representing the Passion can convert the one who represents it. Mariano begins as a Judas in fact, playing Christ out of vanity, and the role, the monk's counsel and the reappearance of those he has injured press him toward repentance. Entreletras describes salvation in the film as an uncertain, interior process, and reports that Catholic critics at the time argued whether a man who played Judas could aspire to holiness. Whether the film ends in sacramental confession, restitution or only inner change is not recorded in the sources found.
advisories:
The Passion is re-enacted, with the Way of the Cross.

Fraud, usury and family betrayal; threats of revenge.

Nothing sexual of note is reported.

Suitable for older children and adults on the available evidence.

title: The Martyr of Calvary
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred life of Christ from the call of the Apostles to the Resurrection, with Our Lady present. Identity from Wikipedia (citing the Cannes festival record); content from Infobae (2021, secular press) and blog and user reviews that call it faithful to the Gospels. No substantive independent critique or contemporary Catholic rating was found (it is not in the US Legion list). A 1952 Mexican review or a Legión Mexicana de la Decencia rating would settle it.
summary: Mexico's best-loved Holy Week film: a studio-bound, theatrical life of Christ with Enrique Rambal, still shown on Mexican television every Lent.
synopsis: The film follows Jesus from the gathering of His first disciples to His Resurrection on the third day. It takes in the Sermon on the Mount, the multiplication of the loaves and fishes, the healing of a blind child and of a paralytic, His disputes with the scribes and Pharisees, the repentance of Mary Magdalene and the raising of Lazarus. Peter, Andrew and the other Apostles follow Him, and His Mother is present through the story. Judas, played by Manolo Fábregas, betrays Him to the priests. He is condemned, handed over by Pilate, scourged and crucified on Calvary. The film closes with the Resurrection.
inclusion: For Mexican Catholics this is the Passion film, broadcast every Lent and still a fixture of Holy Week. Its reputation rests on Enrique Rambal, a Valencian actor of 28, whose voice and bearing became the model for later portrayals of Christ in Mexico, including the great Passion of Iztapalapa. Miguel Morayta, a Spanish Republican exile, shot it entirely on interior sets at the Tepeyac studios on a small budget, and it looks like a stage play. Admirers find that its plainness gives it force, and Fábregas's Judas was hated by audiences of the day. It was shown in competition at Cannes in 1954. Viewers used to later, grander Gospel films will find it stiff; those who value an unembellished telling may find its simplicity moving.
themes: The film keeps close to the Gospel narrative, according to its admirers, and presents the miracles and the Resurrection without softening them. Christ is shown as a Man who teaches, heals and suffers, and the Passion is the climax. Our Lady, played by Consuelo Frank, has a place throughout. The film was made as Holy Week devotion for a Catholic audience and has served that purpose for seventy years. No source records any departure from Catholic teaching, but no detailed independent account of its treatment of the Last Supper or of Mary's role has been found.
advisories:
The scourging and Crucifixion are shown with some force.

Nothing sexual of note; Magdalene's past is treated discreetly in the accounts available.

Suitable for older children and families in Holy Week.
