title: Fabiola
alternateTitles: Fabiola ou a igreja das catacumbas
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Silent Era's Progressive Silent Film List and home-video page; Wikipedia citing Sorlin). The cast list (St Sebastian, St Agnes, St Cecilia, Fulvius, Eurotas, Quadratus, Afra, Lucina) shows it follows Cardinal Wiseman's novel of the Diocletian persecution, but no source describes the film's own treatment or its ending. The 1949 remake is GREY for a different reason (CCC reservation). An independent description of the surviving print would settle it.
summary: Guazzoni's silent Fabiola brings Cardinal Wiseman's novel of the Diocletian persecution to the screen, with St Sebastian and St Agnes among the martyrs.
synopsis: No published account describes the film's plot scene by scene, so this summary follows the cast list and the novel it adapts. In Rome under Diocletian, Fabiola is a rich and proud pagan woman. Around her are the hidden Christians of the city: the soldier Sebastian, the young Agnes and Cecilia, and Fabiola's own slave Afra among her household. The informer Fulvius and his servant Eurotas hunt the Christians for profit, and the persecution claims Agnes and Sebastian among others. In Wiseman's novel, the witness of the martyrs and of those close to her leads Fabiola to the faith and to baptism. The film runs about 85 minutes in its surviving form.
inclusion: Enrico Guazzoni had made the Quo Vadis of 1913 that defined the Italian Roman epic, and Fabiola, produced by Palatino Film in 1918, belongs to the same tradition of crowds, arenas and catacombs. Its source is one of the most widely read Catholic novels of the nineteenth century, written by Cardinal Wiseman to show the life of the early Church. The cast includes Elena Sangro, later a star of the 1924 Quo Vadis, and Amleto Novelli as Fulvius. A print survives; an 87-minute version with English intertitles is available on disc, probably from a 16mm reduction print. Beyond these facts, no critic has written about how the film handles its story.
themes: The source gives the film its Catholic shape: martyrdom as witness, the hidden life of the Roman Church in the catacombs and the conversion of a proud pagan through the example of the Christians around her. The saints in the cast, Sebastian, Agnes and Cecilia, are among the best-known martyrs of the Roman calendar. Whether the film keeps the novel's emphasis on conversion and the sacraments, or reduces it to spectacle and romance as the 1949 remake did, is not documented.
history: Nicholas Wiseman, first Archbishop of Westminster and a cardinal, published Fabiola, or the Church of the Catacombs in 1854. It is set in Rome around 302–305, during the persecution under Diocletian, and weaves the martyrdoms of St Sebastian, St Agnes and others into the fictional story of Fabiola's conversion.
advisories:
Persecution and martyrdom, including arena scenes typical of the genre (not described in detail by any source).

Silent; the surviving copy has English intertitles.

Age guidance cannot be given until the content is described.

grey.question: Fabiola adapts Cardinal Wiseman's novel of the Roman persecution, and its cast list names St Sebastian, St Agnes and St Cecilia. But no critic or archive has described what the film itself shows: how it treats the martyrs, whether Fabiola's conversion and baptism are kept, and how much is romance and spectacle. A detailed description of the surviving print, or its English intertitles, would settle whether it is faithful to the novel.

title: Father Brown, Detective
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and full synopsis from the AFI Catalog (PCA no. 374; passed by the National Board of Review). Independent reviews (Home Theater Forum, 2025; Editor Eric's Chesterton essay) establish a priest whose aim is the thief's soul: he lures Flambeau, lets him go without the diamonds, prays for him, and Flambeau gives himself up. Softer and more romantic than Chesterton, as the reviewers note, but no doctrinal problem. Pre-Legion list; no rating found.
summary: The first Father Brown film: Walter Connolly's priest guards a diamond cross from Paul Lukas's Flambeau, less to catch the thief than to save him.
synopsis: The jewel thief Flambeau falls for Evelyn Fischer and announces that he will steal the ten diamonds of the 'Flying Stars': six belong to her uncle, Sir Leopold, and four are set in a gold cross that Father Brown keeps for his church. Father Brown wants to reform Flambeau before the police catch him. When Flambeau turns up at the presbytery posing as a stranded motorist, the priest recognises him and hides the stones in a glass of milk. Flambeau steals the Fischer diamonds, but Evelyn rejects him because of what he is. At a Eucharistic Congress in London, Flambeau, disguised as a priest, tries for the cross again; Father Brown leads him on a trail of odd incidents that brings the police, then lets him escape without the jewels. Father Brown prays for him, and Flambeau gives himself up.
inclusion: This is a modest Paramount programme picture of 68 minutes, built from 'The Blue Cross' and 'The Flying Stars', and it is the screen's first Father Brown. Walter Connolly's priest is warm and avuncular rather than Chesterton's sharp little paradox-monger, and Editor Eric's essay regrets the loss of the books' cleverness and the romance that does much of the converting. Paul Lukas has a rogue's charm, though one reviewer notes that his accent gives away every disguise. Home Theater Forum's 2025 review calls it a quick B-picture that punches above its weight and one of the underrated Father Brown adaptations. The chase across London, taken from 'The Blue Cross', is the highlight. Kino Lorber issued it on Blu-ray in 2025 with a commentary by Jason A. Ney.
themes: The film keeps Chesterton's central idea: the priest's business is the criminal's soul, not his punishment. Father Brown sets the cross where Flambeau can reach it, beats him at his own game and then lets him go free, trusting grace to finish the work. The climax is prayer: Father Brown prays for Flambeau, and Flambeau surrenders of his own will. The setting of the Eucharistic Congress places the Church in public view. The weakness, as reviewers note, is that Evelyn's love does as much as the priest to reform the thief.
history: G. K. Chesterton, who became a Catholic in 1922, published the first Father Brown story, 'The Blue Cross', in 1910, and the collection The Innocence of Father Brown in 1911. In the stories Flambeau, the great French thief, is gradually converted by the priest and becomes a private detective and his friend.
liberties: The film combines 'The Blue Cross' and 'The Flying Stars', invents the romance with Evelyn Fischer as a motive for Flambeau's reform, and compresses his conversion, which in the stories takes several adventures, into one.
advisories:
No violence beyond a car accident and a chase.

Flambeau enters Evelyn's bedroom after the theft; nothing improper occurs.

Suitable for all ages.

title: Miraculous Fátima
decision: GREY: Identity is established by the contemporary trade advertisement and news item in Cine – Revista Mensal (October 1928) and the Cinemateca Portuguesa's 2017 Fátima cycle as reported by Diário de Notícias. Content is known only in outline (Time Out Lisboa): an impoverished noblewoman serving incognito in Lisbon goes on pilgrimage to Fátima to obtain the cure of a paralysed girl, with footage of the 1927 pilgrimage. Time Out calls it melodrama, devotion and propaganda. No independent assessment of its treatment; survival in full not confirmed.
summary: The first fiction feature about Fátima: Rino Lupo's melodrama of a ruined noblewoman's pilgrimage for a paralysed girl's cure, built round real footage of the 1927 pilgrimage.
synopsis: Maria Helena, a noblewoman from an impoverished provincial family, takes work as a servant in the house of a Lisbon aristocrat without revealing who she is. The butler's young daughter is paralysed. Maria Helena first asks Our Lady of Lourdes for help, but the girl does not recover. She then goes on pilgrimage to Fátima, joining the crowds that travel to the Cova da Iria, and the girl is cured. The pilgrimage sequences use documentary images of the great pilgrimage of 1927.
inclusion: Fátima Milagrosa is the oldest fiction feature about Fátima, made only eleven years after the apparitions and two years before the bishop of Leiria declared them worthy of belief. Rino Lupo, an Italian who had founded an acting school in Porto, brought the realist method of his Mulheres da Beira and Os Lobos to a popular melodrama, and he worked in footage of the 1927 pilgrimage, the oldest known film of the subject. Manoel de Oliveira made his screen debut in a small part, which he did not later care to remember. It was a provincial hit: in October 1928 the magazine Cine reported bookings across the country until the end of the year. Time Out Lisboa sums it up as melodrama, devotion and propaganda.
themes: The film's religious content is the devotion of pilgrimage and the hope of a cure through Our Lady's intercession, shown through a woman who gives up her rank to serve. The 1927 pilgrimage footage records the crowds at the Cova da Iria in the years before the Church's approval. One element needs care: according to Time Out, the story makes Fátima succeed where a prayer to Our Lady of Lourdes has failed, which sets one Marian shrine above another, a promotional rather than a theological idea. How the cure and the apparitions are presented has not been described.
history: Three shepherd children reported apparitions of Our Lady at the Cova da Iria, near Fátima, between May and October 1917, ending with the 'miracle of the sun' on 13 October. Pilgrimages grew through the 1920s. The bishop of Leiria declared the apparitions worthy of belief in October 1930.
advisories:
No violence or sensual content reported.

Silent, with Portuguese intertitles.

Suitable for all ages.

The story is said to set Fátima above Lourdes.

grey.question: Fátima Milagrosa is the earliest fiction film about Fátima, a melodrama about a cure obtained by pilgrimage, with real footage of the 1927 crowds. What is known of it comes from short notices; no critic has described how it presents the cure, Our Lady or the shrine, and one summary says the story sets Fátima above Lourdes. A screening report or archival description of the Cinemateca Portuguesa's copy would settle it.

title: Philip of Jesus
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred: a life of St Philip of Jesus, the Mexican Franciscan crucified at Nagasaki in 1597 and canonised in 1862, ending with his martyrdom and the legendary flowering of the dead fig tree. Identity and plot are established by the English encyclopaedia entry and a reproduction of Jesús Ibarra's account. The reservation is the invented love story that fills most of the film: the novice leaves his convent for a married woman, takes the blame for her stabbing her husband, and meets her double, a leprous prostitute, in Manila. A Mexican critic later noted its sensuality and ironic commentary. No contemporary Catholic rating was found.
summary: Julio Bracho's life of the Mexican martyr of Nagasaki, which surrounds his conversion and crucifixion with an invented double romance.
synopsis: In sixteenth-century Mexico City, the young Felipe de las Casas, a novice, falls in love with Rosalía, who is engaged to another man, and leaves the friary. When she stabs her husband Cristóbal in her bedroom, Felipe takes the blame, and he escapes punishment by enlisting and sailing for the Philippines. In Manila he meets María, a prostitute who is Rosalía's double and has leprosy. He returns to religious life as a Franciscan, and when he sets sail for home María stows away on his ship, where the crew nearly burn her as a witch. Storms drive the ship to Japan. There Felipe joins the friars preaching the faith, until the authorities arrest the missionaries and their converts; they are crucified, and Felipe is pierced with lances. In Mexico City, a dead fig tree bursts into bloom.
inclusion: Felipe de Jesús is the first canonised saint born in Mexico, and his crucifixion at Nagasaki in 1597 is the high point of this film; the miracle of the fig tree, a beloved piece of Mexico City legend, closes it. Julio Bracho, one of the leading directors of the Mexican golden age, made it for Clasa Films Mundiales with Ernesto Alonso as Felipe, Rita Macedo in the double role of Rosalía and María, and Julio Villarreal as Fray Pedro Bautista, the leader of the martyrs. Jesús Ibarra describes a film that was controversial in its day but has come to be valued as a work of art. Its value is in the closing martyrdom; the hour of invented melodrama before it is another matter.
themes: The film is built as a conversion story: a worldly young man who abandons his vocation for a woman is led back, through sin, guilt and the sight of misery in Manila, to the Franciscan habit and finally to a martyr's death. The double role of Rosalía and María makes the point that the woman he once desired becomes the sick and outcast soul he must serve. The Japanese episode presents the martyrs as missionaries dying for preaching Christ, and the flowering fig tree as Heaven's answer. The romance, the bedroom killing and the prostitute plot, however, take up much of the film.
history: Felipe de las Casas was born in Mexico City around 1572, entered the Franciscans, left, travelled to Manila, and there returned to the order. Sailing home in 1596, his ship was wrecked on Japan, and he was crucified at Nagasaki on 5 February 1597 with twenty-five companions. He was beatified in 1627 and canonised in 1862, and is the patron saint of Mexico City.
liberties: Rosalía, the stabbing of Cristóbal, Felipe's taking of the blame and his enlistment, and María the leprous prostitute who stows away on his ship are all invented. Felipe's real youthful waywardness is known only in outline from the hagiographical tradition. The fig tree is a popular legend, not part of the canonisation record.
advisories:
A love affair with an engaged and then married woman; a stabbing in a bedroom; a prostitute and a near-burning as a witch.

The crucifixion and lancing of the martyrs.

For adults and older teenagers.

The invented romance occupies much of the running time.

grey.question: The film ends well, with St Philip's martyrdom at Nagasaki and the miracle of the fig tree. But it fills his life with an invented double romance: a married lover who stabs her husband, a prostitute double, and a sensual treatment that a later Mexican critic remarked on. The saint's real waywardness was nothing like this. Viewers should weigh whether the invented sins illuminate his conversion or simply exploit it. A check of the dialogue would settle how the romance is presented.

title: St. Francis
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and sincere by the account of the one independent critic found (James Steffen, TCM), with Pope Innocent III's approval of the Rule and the Canticle of the Creatures at its close. The reservations: a large amount of invented material, including a childhood friendship between Francis and Clare from the opening scenes, and a framing that, in Steffen's words, sets Francis's spirituality of nature and the poor against faith coerced through fear, which risks the familiar opposition of the free saint and the institutional Church. Contemporary Italian praise (l'Unità) reads it in modern terms of fraternity, peace and simplicity. Subtitles would settle how Clare's vocation, the Pope and the Church are framed against the clare-and-francis threshold.
summary: Michele Soavi's two-part Canale 5 life of St Francis, with Raoul Bova, from a childhood alongside Clare to the Canticle of the Creatures.
synopsis: The film opens in Francis's childhood in Assisi, where the boy plays with the young Clare, who is already carrying bread to lepers and the poor. Grown up, Francesco (Raoul Bova), son of the cloth merchant Pietro di Bernardone (Mariano Rigillo), carouses with friends, rides to war and comes back a prisoner. Shaken, he gives away his goods, breaks with his father before the bishop, dresses in rags and nurses lepers. Companions join him: Bernardo (Gianmarco Tognazzi), Pietro, Silvestro and others, and Clare (Amélie Daure) follows him into poverty. Francis goes to Rome and wins Innocent III's (Toni Bertorelli) blessing for his brotherhood. As the brotherhood grows, Francis, worn out, dies singing the Canticle of the Creatures.
inclusion: Soavi, known for horror films such as The Church and Cemetery Man, made a serious and ambitious life of Francis, over three hours long, with a strong sense of medieval texture and faces. James Steffen (TCM) found Raoul Bova lively and charismatic and his portrait credible, and preferred the film to Zeffirelli's Brother Sun, Sister Moon. He also found the style overwrought, with too much slow motion and a clichéd score, and called it no masterpiece but worth a look. It was a ratings success on Canale 5, and l'Unità praised lines such as Francis's answer that the Gospel speaks a language he understands. Rossellini's Flowers of St Francis and Curtiz's Francis of Assisi remain the better films.
themes: The film covers Francis's conversion, his embrace of poverty and the lepers, the Gospel as rule of life and the approval of his order by Innocent III. Francis says the Gospel speaks a language he understands. Clare is present throughout, from an invented childhood to her own consecration. The weaker side is framing. Steffen describes a contrast between Francis's reverence for nature and the poor and a faith imposed by fear, and Italian praise in 2002 read it as a message of fraternity, peace and simplicity. How far it presents Francis against the Church of his time, rather than within it, is the open question.
history: Francis of Assisi (c. 1181–1226), son of a cloth merchant, was a prisoner of war after the battle of Collestrada, renounced his inheritance before the Bishop of Assisi, and in 1209 or 1210 received oral approval of his rule from Innocent III. Clare joined him in 1212. He received the stigmata in 1224 and died in 1226; he was canonised in 1228.
liberties: Reviewers note much speculative material: the first hour, before Francis's break with his father, is largely invented, and Francis and Clare are shown as childhood companions, which the sources do not support.
advisories:
Battle violence and the suffering of lepers; Francis's illness and death.

No sexual content reported.

Suitable for older children and up.

Much invented material, including an early bond between Francis and Clare; the film's picture of the Church of his time should be weighed.

title: The Passion of St. Francis
alternateTitles: A Vida Humilde de S. Francisco de Assis
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Silent Era's Progressive Silent Film List: I.C.S.A., 3,700 m, April 1927, from a story by Johannes Jørgensen; US release 1932 as The Passion of St. Francis). Content is known from Christensen's and Van Yperen's scholarship as summarised in the Anglican Third Order survey: a complete life from youth to death at the Portiuncula, with the Sultan and the stigmata, plus an invented melodramatic subplot with a villain, Clare's uncle Monaldo. No independent assessment of its treatment, and its survival is uncertain (Silent Era: unknown; TSSF: lost, with fragments online). Settled by locating a print and a description of it.
summary: Giulio Antamoro's big-budget life of St Francis for the saint's seventh centenary, from a story by the Danish Catholic writer Johannes Jørgensen, with Alberto Pasquali as Francis.
synopsis: Francis, son of a cloth merchant, works in his father's business, fights in the war with Perugia, is wounded and sets out as a knight for Apulia, then turns away from war. Before the crucifix of San Damiano he hears the command to rebuild the church, and he strips himself before the bishop of Assisi to renounce his inheritance. He receives Clare when she runs away to a life of poverty, and goes to Rome with his first followers to seek Innocent III's approval. A melodramatic subplot gives the story a villain in Clare's uncle Monaldo. Later Francis goes before the Sultan and receives the stigmata. Sick and failing, he returns to Assisi on a donkey, hailed by the crowd, and dies at the Portiuncula.
inclusion: Frate Francesco was the third Italian film about the saint and much the most ambitious, made by the director of the 1916 Christus for the 700th anniversary of Francis's death. The story came from Johannes Jørgensen, whose 1907 biography of Francis was widely read. The Sole 24 Ore describes it as a blockbuster with wide international distribution: it reached Portugal and Spain, and in 1932 America, where it was cut heavily and reissued in 1934. Scholars note how it stages Francis as a second Christ: wounded at Perugia, he is held like the dead Christ in a Pietà; he stands before the San Damiano crucifix with arms outstretched; and he returns to die riding a donkey, as on Palm Sunday. Whether a complete copy survives is not clear.
themes: On the scholarly accounts, the film keeps the traditional life complete: conversion, renunciation, Clare's vocation, papal approval, the Sultan, the stigmata and a holy death. Its distinctive idea is the conformity of Francis to Christ, carried through the staging from the Pietà image to the entry into Assisi. The invented Monaldo plot is melodrama rather than theology. Jørgensen was a Catholic convert and his life of Francis is devout. No critic's account suggests the Church is shown as an opponent.
history: Francis Bernardone (c. 1181–1226) fought for Assisi against Perugia and was imprisoned, renounced his inheritance before the bishop, restored San Damiano and won verbal approval of his rule from Innocent III. Clare joined him in Lent 1212. He went before the Sultan in Egypt in 1219, received the stigmata in September 1224 and died at the Portiuncula on 3 October 1226; Gregory IX canonised him in 1228.
liberties: The villain Monaldo, Clare's uncle, and his subplot are invented melodrama. The repeated staging of Francis as a figure of Christ is the film's own emphasis rather than the early biographers'. The American release of 1932 cut the film heavily.
advisories:
War scenes at Perugia; Francis is wounded.

Silent; survival of a complete copy is uncertain, and the American version was heavily shortened.

Suitable for older children and up.

grey.question: Frate Francesco is a full life of St Francis, from the Perugian war to the stigmata and his death, made for the 1926 centenary from a story by Johannes Jørgensen. Scholars describe its staging of Francis as a second Christ and an invented melodramatic villain. Two things are unsettled: no independent critic has assessed how it treats the faith, and it is not clear that a complete copy survives. Locating a print and an archival description of it would settle both.

title: Brother Sun
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Wikipedia, citing the Cineteca Milano listing; IIC Beirut; the TSSF survey). Content is described by the IIC Beirut screening note and by two Third Order (Anglican Franciscan) viewers quoted in the TSSF survey, who note an invented strand in which Clare guides Francis and sees his stigmata in a vision. No independent critical assessment of the religious treatment exists. A detailed review of the restored print would settle it.
summary: Mario Corsi's four-part 'Franciscan recreation' follows St Francis and St Clare from the kiss of the leper to the stigmata, restored by the Cineteca Italiana in 1998.
synopsis: The film is in four episodes. In the first, Francis, the pleasure-loving son of a merchant, is drawn to God through the prayers and example of Clare, who has turned down rich suitors to give herself to God; she shames him into kindness to a beggar, and he overcomes his disgust to embrace a leper. In the second, he gives to the poor and hears a voice telling him to rebuild the church, and followers gather round him. The third episode, called Time in some sources and The Temple in others, follows the growth of the brotherhood and Clare's religious life. In the last, Francis receives the stigmata on La Verna, and Clare, in her distant cell, sees it in a vision.
inclusion: Mario Corsi, a writer and critic from Pistoia, made Frate Sole soon after coming back wounded from the front, with the playwright Ugo Falena. He billed it as a 'Franciscan recreation in four cantos', with a sacred poem for orchestra and chorus by Luigi Mancinelli, and the episodic structure anticipates Rossellini's Flowers of St Francis. The Sole 24 Ore calls it one of the historical masterpieces of early Italian cinema, though that is a passing judgment rather than a review. The 70-minute restoration by the Fondazione Cineteca Italiana has been shown with live music in Foligno, Assisi, Manila and Beirut. Viewers who have written about it find the vignettes somewhat disjointed. Its unusual feature is the weight it gives to Clare.
themes: The film's Franciscan content is traditional: conversion through the leper, poverty, the call to rebuild the church, the brotherhood and the stigmata. What is unusual is Clare's role. One Third Order viewer noticed that she takes the moral lead: she prays for Francis's conversion, rebukes him over a beggar and explains to him what his embrace of the leper meant. Historically Clare followed Francis, not the reverse. The vision in which she sees his stigmata from afar is invented, though it is in the spirit of the legends. None of this touches doctrine, but it changes the shape of the story.
history: Francis's embrace of a leper, recorded by his early biographers, marked his conversion. He restored San Damiano after hearing a voice there. Clare, a noblewoman of Assisi, joined him in Lent 1212 and founded the Poor Clares at San Damiano. Francis received the stigmata on La Verna in September 1224 and died in 1226.
liberties: Clare's guiding role in Francis's conversion is invented: in the early sources she joined him years after it. Her vision of the stigmata is also invented. The four-episode form leaves out most of the familiar events, such as the renunciation before the bishop and the papal approval, as far as the available descriptions show.
advisories:
A leper is shown; no violence or sensual content reported.

Silent, with Italian intertitles.

Suitable for children.

title: Joan of Arc at the Stake
decision: PUBLISH: A filmed staging of Claudel and Honegger's Catholic oratorio on St Joan of Arc (canonised 1920). Identity from the Cinema e Medioevo filmography and the oratorio's record; independent substantive treatment from Phil Hall (Film Threat, 2005) and Hal Erickson (AllMovie, quoted by Cinema e Medioevo): Joan's unwavering faith, the saints' voices, her ascent to heaven. The satire of her judges as beasts is Claudel's, aimed at a tribunal the Church itself later annulled; it is disclosed.
summary: Rossellini's filmed staging of Claudel and Honegger's oratorio, with Ingrid Bergman as St Joan reliving her life from the stake before her soul rises to heaven.
synopsis: The film opens with a cosmic flourish: statue-like angels descend in a spiral while Joan's soul rises. Joan, at the moment of her death at Rouen, is met by Brother Dominic, who leads her back through her life so that she can understand it. She sees her trial again, in which her judges appear in the masks of beasts, the presiding bishop as a pig, and then, in gentler scenes, her childhood at Domrémy and the voices of St Catherine and St Margaret that called her. Returned to the stake, she breaks her chains and goes to the fire with joy, as the voices of heaven receive her and she ascends among the angels.
inclusion: It is a strange, neglected film by a major director: Rossellini filmed his own stage production of the oratorio, first given at the San Carlo in Naples in December 1953, in Gevacolor and largely on painted sets. Ingrid Bergman, too old for Joan, compensates with conviction; Phil Hall calls her performance extraordinary, and Hal Erickson finds her more impressive than the presentation. Honegger's score, with its choruses and unusual orchestra, carries much of the film. It was a box-office failure, partly because the Bergman–Rossellini scandal was stale news, and the French version was never released. Hall argues it is far better than its reputation, and the opening flight of angels is pure cinema. It is static and theatrical, and suits those who know the music or the play.
themes: Claudel wrote the oratorio as a Catholic meditation on Joan's death, and the film keeps it. Her faith never wavers, Hall notes, and the voices of the saints confirm her place in heaven. The mocking of her judges as animals is Claudel's judgment on the court at Rouen, which condemned her for political ends and whose sentence the Church overturned in 1456; it does not mock the Church. The childhood scenes set her holiness in the simple piety of a French village, and the end is the triumph of a martyr, not a victim. The Virgin is among the heavenly voices of the score.
history: Joan of Arc (c.1412–1431) led French forces from 1429, was captured, tried for heresy at Rouen by a court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burnt on 30 May 1431. A papal commission annulled the sentence in 1456. She was beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920.
liberties: This is not a historical reconstruction but an oratorio: the trial is allegory, with Cauchon as a pig and the assessors as animals, and the events of her life return as memories in no strict order. Brother Dominic is Claudel's invention as her guide.
advisories:
Death by burning, stylised rather than realistic.

The judges are shown as grotesque animals in a satirical trial.

Nothing sexual of note.

Slow and theatrical; best for adults and older teenagers who know the music or the play.

title: Guilty of Treason
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified it A-I (1936–59 list on archive.org), a contemporary Catholic judgment. The AFI Catalog establishes the content: the arrest, interrogation and show trial of Cardinal Mindszenty, with a priest as technical adviser and the Cardinal's public papers as a source. Dennis Schwartz's independent review confirms the treatment while judging it cheap propaganda. Mindszenty is not a canonised saint, so rule (a) does not arise.
summary: A low-budget, urgent dramatisation of the communist persecution and 1949 show trial of Hungary's primate, Cardinal József Mindszenty, with Charles Bickford in the role.
synopsis: At a meeting of the Overseas Press Club, the American correspondent Tom Kelly tells what he saw in Soviet-dominated Hungary in 1948. He meets Stephanie Varna, a music teacher in love with a Russian officer, Colonel Melnikov, and the two visit Cardinal Mindszenty at his mother's farm. The Cardinal expects to be arrested and says so. Stephanie refuses to sign a petition demanding his arrest and is taken by the secret police. The regime spreads lies about the Cardinal, arrests him and interrogates him for more than thirty days; a police doctor recommends a drug to break his will. Stephanie, charged with espionage, refuses to confess and dies under torture. Melnikov, faced with what he has served, is shot by his own side. The Cardinal is tried, convicted of treason and sentenced to life imprisonment.
inclusion: This was Hollywood's rapid response to a trial that shocked the Catholic world in February 1949, made within months of the verdict by an independent company after Warner Bros. dropped the subject. Charles Bickford gives the Cardinal a stolid, unshowy dignity, and the film draws on Mindszenty's own public statements. It is not good cinema. Dennis Schwartz calls it cheaply made and over-moralising, and the framing device of a journalist addressing a press club is stiff. The love story was pushed in the advertising because the anti-communist message did not sell. Its value is as a document: an American film that treated the persecution of a Catholic bishop as front-page news, and that shows the methods of the show trial plainly.
themes: The Cardinal is shown as a pastor who expects arrest and meets it calmly, with Bickford playing him as steady rather than heroic. The film's interest is in how a regime destroys a churchman: slander, a manufactured petition, prolonged interrogation and the use of drugs to obtain a confession. Stephanie's refusal to sign against him is the lay counterpart of his witness, and she dies for it. Religion appears less as worship than as the conscience the state cannot own. The Catholic content is the persecution of the Church through its primate.
history: József Mindszenty (1892–1975), Archbishop of Esztergom and Primate of Hungary, was arrested on 26 December 1948 and, after weeks of interrogation, tried in February 1949 and sentenced to life imprisonment. Freed briefly in the 1956 uprising, he took refuge in the United States legation in Budapest until 1971 and died in exile in Vienna in 1975.
liberties: Stephanie Varna, Melnikov, Tom Kelly and the commissar Belov are fictional. The trial is compressed, and the film's account of drugging reflects contemporary Western reports rather than established fact. The final sentence and the dedication follow the real record.
advisories:
Torture is depicted, and a young woman dies under interrogation; a beating; a man is shot.

No sexual content of note.

Legion of Decency A-I. The political propaganda is heavy; it suits older children and adults.

title: The Poor Man of Assisi
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Il Cinema Ritrovato's 2008 programme record of the Cineteca Nazionale print). Content is known in outline from Kevin Harty's plot summary (quoted in the Anglican Third Order's 2025 survey) and the Italian Cultural Institute's screening note. The only critical comments (Elena Mosconi via Il Cinema Ritrovato) concern direction and acting, not the treatment of the saint. Nothing suggests a problem; an independent assessment of the content would settle it.
summary: The first film about St Francis: a 24-minute Cines short, shot in Assisi, with Emilio Ghione as the saint and the main episodes of his life in tableaux.
synopsis: Francis, son of a rich Assisi merchant, has a dream in which poverty appears to him in person. He breaks with his father, Pietro Bernardone, and gives himself to poverty and the service of the poor, and other men join him. Clare becomes his spiritual companion. Francis travels to the East and preaches before the Sultan at Damietta, who treats him with respect but will not be converted. The Pope approves his order, and in one scene Francis dictates the Canticle of the Sun. At the end, dying, he blesses Assisi, surrounded by his friars, Clare and her sisters.
inclusion: This is where St Francis on film begins. Enrico Guazzoni, who two years later made the Quo Vadis that set the pattern for the Italian epic, shot it in Assisi itself for the Turin International Exhibition of 1911. It made Emilio Ghione's name: the notes for the 2008 Il Cinema Ritrovato screening say his first leading role was his first big success, and quote critics on a performance that held together the worldly young man and the ascetic. Elena Mosconi praised the direction and Ghione's restraint. It is a short film, and by the account of its plot it moves through the familiar episodes rather than dramatising any of them. The Cineteca Nazionale in Rome holds a copy.
themes: On the evidence of its plot, the film follows the traditional life: the call to poverty, the break with his father, the founding of the friars, Clare's companionship, papal approval of the order, the Canticle, a holy death. The visit to the Sultan is shown as an act of preaching, with the Sultan respectful but unconverted, which matches the early sources. No account suggests that the Church is cast as an obstacle, as in later Francis films. How much of this is staged, and how, has not been described by an independent critic.
history: Francis Bernardone (c. 1181–1226) renounced his inheritance before the bishop of Assisi and restored the chapel of San Damiano. Clare joined him in Lent 1212. In 1219 he sailed for the East and was taken before the Sultan in Egypt. He received the stigmata at La Verna in September 1224, died at the Portiuncula on 3 October 1226 and was canonised by Gregory IX in 1228.
advisories:
No violence or sensual content reported.

Silent, with Italian intertitles; short.

Suitable for children.

grey.question: This 1911 short is the earliest film about St Francis, and its outline is known: the vision of poverty, the break with his father, Clare, the Sultan, papal approval, the Canticle of the Sun and a holy death. Festival notes praise Ghione's performance and Guazzoni's direction. What no independent critic has yet described is how the film handles its religious material scene by scene. A detailed review or archival study of the surviving Cineteca Nazionale print would settle it.

doctrine: Francis died at the Portiuncula on the evening of 3 October 1226 and was canonised by Gregory IX at Assisi on 16 July 1228. His feast is 4 October. In September 1224, at La Verna, he received the stigmata, the first recorded case of a stigmatist; Benedict XI later allowed the Friars Minor a feast of the Impression of the Stigmata, and Paul V extended it to the universal Church in 1615. Francis was never a priest. He was ordained deacon and obtained from Innocent III in 1209 verbal approval of his Rule, which Honorius III confirmed in 1223. The Order he founded holds the Church's teaching on poverty as a counsel of perfection, not a duty on all, and Francis insisted on obedience to the Pope and reverence for priests. Clare took the veil from him in 1212 and founded the Poor Clares.
production: Il poverello di Assisi was made in 1911 by Cines of Rome, the leading Italian studio, and directed by Enrico Guazzoni, who made Quo Vadis? for the same company in 1913. The story is credited to a Contessa Salimei. Emilio Ghione, later famous as the Parisian-gangster hero of Italian serials, played Francis, and Fernanda Negri-Pouget played Clare. The film is 443 metres long, about 24 minutes, in black and white with Italian intertitles. The surviving print comes from the Cineteca Nazionale in Rome and was shown at the Il Cinema Ritrovato festival in Bologna in 2008. The Third Order of St Francis lists it as the first film about the saint.

title: I.N.R.I.
decision: GREY: Identity and content are established (Wikipedia citing Jung and Schatzberg's Beyond Caligari; Paul van Yperen's notes; the Humanities Institute study guide giving a scene-by-scene account of the Gospel section). The Gospel story is told conventionally, and Christ affirms that he is the Son of God. Reservations: the source is Peter Rosegger's novel, in which a condemned anarchist writes his own Gospel; the frame story (often cut) concerns a political assassin; Judas is reconceived as a disillusioned political revolutionary; and the surviving version ends at the death on the cross, with no Resurrection. Not REJECT because the core Gospel content is orthodox in the account available.
summary: Robert Wiene's star-studded Passion, after Rosegger's novel, sets the Gospel inside the story of a condemned Russian anarchist and makes Judas a disappointed revolutionary.
synopsis: In the full version, a revolutionary in modern Russia assassinates a minister and is sentenced to death. Waiting for execution, he begins to doubt the meaning of what he has done, and the story of Christ unfolds. It runs from the Nativity and the boy Jesus in the Temple through the healings, the blessing of children and Mary Magdalene washing his feet, to the entry into Jerusalem, where the crowd hopes he will break the Roman yoke. He drives out the money-changers. Judas, who wanted a leader of revolt, betrays him for silver. Christ is tried before Annas, where he declares himself the Son of God, and before Pilate, who finds him innocent but releases Barabbas. He is crucified, forgives his executioners and dies; a centurion declares him a righteous man.
inclusion: I.N.R.I. was the biggest film Robert Wiene made after Caligari: ninety days at the Staaken studios in 1923, expensive sets, hundreds of extras and a remarkable cast, with Gregori Chmara as Christ, Henny Porten as Mary, Asta Nielsen as Mary Magdalene, Werner Krauss as Pilate and Alexander Granach as Judas. The film's staging was praised, but German reviews were mixed and it soon left cinemas. Censors objected to the modern Russian scenes, and most prints omit them. In 1933 it was reissued in America with music and narration as Crown of Thorns. As a document of Weimar cinema at full stretch, and of how European film treated the Gospel in the 1920s, it has real interest.
themes: The Gospel section is conventional and largely scriptural. Christ heals and raises the dead, declares himself the Son of God before the high priest and a king whose kingdom is not of this world before Pilate, institutes the Eucharist and forgives his executioners. The questions lie around it. Peter Rosegger's novel was a free retelling of the Gospel by an imprisoned anarchist, and Rosegger reinterpreted many dogmas symbolically. Wiene's Judas betrays Christ out of political disappointment, a reading meant to tie the Gospel to the assassin of the frame. The version described ends at the death on the cross, with no Resurrection.
history: Peter Rosegger (1843–1918), the Styrian novelist, published I.N.R.I.: Frohe Botschaft eines armen Sünders in 1905, in which a man awaiting execution writes his own account of the life of Christ. Wiene's adaptation premiered in Berlin on Christmas Day 1923. Some sources give 1925 for the premiere of the cut version.
liberties: Judas's motive is changed from greed to political disillusionment, though he still takes the silver. The frame story of a Russian assassin is added from Rosegger's premise and transplanted to Russia. Mary is given a prophecy that his followers will desert him. The film stops at the Crucifixion.
advisories:
The scourging, mocking and Crucifixion, not graphic by later standards.

An assassination in the frame story (absent from many prints).

grey.question: I.N.R.I. tells the Passion conventionally, and its Christ declares himself the Son of God. But it comes from Peter Rosegger's novel, a Gospel rewritten by a condemned anarchist, and it frames the story with a modern political assassin. Judas becomes a revolutionary who betrays Christ out of political disappointment, and the surviving version ends at the death on the cross without the Resurrection. Viewers should weigh whether the frame and these choices bend the Gospel towards a merely humanitarian Christ.

title: My Name Is Bernadette
decision: GREY: Identity from Offi and French Wikipedia; content from distributor material and one short independent review (Unidivers) that judges craft rather than treatment. The subject is pre-conciliar (apparitions approved 1862). Subtitles or a substantive review of the apparition, Peyramale and Nevers scenes would settle it.
summary: Jean Sagols's modest French retelling of Lourdes, from Bernadette's visions at Massabielle through her trials with clergy and officials to the convent at Nevers.
synopsis: In February 1858 Bernadette Soubirous, the fourteen-year-old daughter of a destitute family in Lourdes, sees a Lady in the grotto of Massabielle. Over eighteen apparitions, ending in July, the crowds grow until a town of four thousand is overrun by pilgrims. The parish priest, Abbé Peyramale, is gruff and suspicious; Commissioner Jacomet questions her, and the imperial prosecutor, Vital Dutour, is charged with restoring order. Her parents, Louise and François, suffer poverty and gossip, and Bernadette is examined by the town doctor. She holds to her account, will not embellish it, and has to fight to be heard by Church and State alike. The film then follows her into religious life at Nevers.
inclusion: This was the first cinema feature for Jean Sagols, a veteran of French television serials, and it was made on modest means, much of it in old villages in Portugal standing in for the Pyrenees. Its strength, by every account, is Katia Miran as Bernadette, a determined, unsentimental girl who will not be talked out of what she saw; she won a best-actress prize at the Mirabile Dictu festival in 2013. A solid supporting cast fills out the officials: Michel Aumont as Peyramale, Francis Huster as the prosecutor, Francis Perrin as the police commissioner. The distributor says the script draws on Abbé René Laurentin's documentary volumes on Lourdes. Critics were lukewarm: David Norgeot of Unidivers found the direction and story thin and preferred Jean Delannoy's two Bernadette films of 1988.
themes: The subject is the apparitions and Bernadette's fidelity to them: a poor, unlettered girl who reports what she has seen, asks nothing for herself and submits to questioning by the Church and the State. Unidivers found the spiritual message conveyed with some warmth but felt the film reduced the drama to a contest between those two authorities. French Wikipedia describes a strong-willed Bernadette who suffers for her testimony. No independent source describes in detail how the film handles the apparitions, the Lady's words, the clergy or Bernadette's religious life at Nevers.
history: Between 11 February and 16 July 1858 Bernadette Soubirous reported eighteen apparitions at the grotto of Massabielle outside Lourdes. In 1862 the bishop of Tarbes declared the faithful justified in believing them. Bernadette later entered the Sisters of Charity of Nevers, where she died in 1879. She was beatified in 1925 and canonised in 1933.
advisories:
No reported sexual content, violence or bad language.

Interrogations, official harshness and scenes of family poverty.

No content guide was found; it appears suitable for older children and up.

grey.question: My Name Is Bernadette tells a canonised saint's story from the traditional sources, and nothing reported about it raises a doctrinal problem. But the only independent review found, a short notice in Unidivers, judges its craft rather than its handling of the faith, and the distributor's claim that it follows Abbé Laurentin's documentation has not been checked. A detailed review, or the dialogue of the apparition and Nevers scenes, would settle it.

title: Joan of Arc
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and content are well documented (Wikipedia drawing on the Méliès catalogue scholarship; Cinemedioevo's catalogue entry; Antti Alanen's and an archive.org note collected on The Early Silent Era blog). The film presents Joan's voices as real, her condemnation as unjust and closes on her reception in heaven. No doctrinal question. A ten-minute tableau short, so 'Silent feature' is the nearest format.
summary: Méliès's hand-coloured pageant tells St Joan's story in a dozen painted tableaux, from her voices at Domrémy to the stake at Rouen and her welcome in heaven.
synopsis: At Domrémy, Joan is visited by St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, and leaves home against her parents' pleas. At Vaucouleurs she wins over the captain, Robert de Baudricourt, who gives her men to lead. Orléans greets her with a long triumphal procession, and Charles VII is crowned in the cathedral at Reims. At Compiègne she is captured during an assault on the castle. In prison she has a second vision. Brought before her judges, she refuses to sign a retraction and is condemned as a heretic. She is burned in the market-place at Rouen. In a final apotheosis she rises into heaven, where God and the saints receive her. The surviving print lacks the opening scene.
inclusion: This was Méliès's second long tableau film after Cinderella, and his most ambitious to that date: twelve scenes, each with its own painted set, running about ten minutes when most films lasted one or two. It was a hit in France and abroad, reaching Montreal and Havana, and Edison sold pirated copies in America. Thought lost, it was found in 1982 in a hand-coloured print, and the colour is the main pleasure: bright costumes against the painted backdrops and a sudden red at the burning. The staging is frankly theatrical. The procession at Orléans is padding, with the same extras running behind the backdrop to cross the frame again. Antti Alanen places the film at the head of the lavish Joan tradition, the opposite of Dreyer's and Bresson's austerity.
themes: The film takes Joan on her own terms. Her voices are not explained away: the saints appear to her at Domrémy and again in prison, and her mission is from God. Its fulfilment is the coronation at Reims. Her trial is an injustice, and she is condemned for refusing to deny what she has seen. The closing apotheosis shows her received into heaven by God and the saints, two decades before Rome canonised her in 1920. It is popular French devotion of its day, told as a sequence of holy pictures rather than examined.
history: Joan was born at Domrémy, probably in 1412. Guided by the voices of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, she persuaded Robert de Baudricourt at Vaucouleurs to send her to the Dauphin, entered besieged Orléans on 30 April 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims on 17 July. She was captured at Compiègne in May 1430, tried at Rouen by a court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon, and burned as a relapsed heretic on 30 May 1431. A later process reversed the sentence; she was beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920.
liberties: The film compresses Joan's career into single images. Orléans appears as a victory procession rather than a siege, Chinon and the recognition of the Dauphin are left out, and the trial is reduced to one interrogation and her refusal to sign.
advisories:
The burning at the stake is shown briefly and in stylised form, with the flames coloured red.

Silent; the surviving print lacks its first scene.

Suitable for children.

title: Joan the Maid
alternateTitles: Jeanne la Pucelle I: Les Batailles
Jeanne la Pucelle II: Les Prisons
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred, serious and close to the record: Joan names St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, is examined and approved at Poitiers, recants her abjuration with 'God sent me', receives Communion before the stake and dies calling on Jesus. The reservation is Rivette's stance. Rosenbaum calls it a 'materialist version' with no miracles, and Dennis Schwartz finds it sceptical of her voices and of the miracles attributed to her; the Church at Rouen is shown as a political instrument. A reader can weigh that; it is reticence, not Besson's psychological debunking.
summary: Jacques Rivette's two-part, five-and-a-half-hour chronicle of St Joan, with Sandrine Bonnaire as a down-to-earth Maid, witnesses speaking to camera and no miracles on screen.
synopsis: In the first part, Les Batailles, Joan (Sandrine Bonnaire), a farm girl from Domrémy who has heard St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret since she was thirteen, persuades the captain at Vaucouleurs to send her to the Dauphin. At Chinon she convinces Charles (André Marcon); at Poitiers churchmen examine her for weeks and approve her. She relieves Orléans, is wounded, and brings Charles to his crowning at Reims. In the second part, Les Prisons, the court loses interest. She is captured at Compiègne, held by the Burgundians and sold to the English. At Rouen the bishop's court tries her for heresy; she abjures to save her life, is put back in an English prison, resists an attempted rape, and takes back her abjuration. She receives Communion and is burned on 30 May 1431. Participants address the camera throughout.
inclusion: Rivette made the most patient and historically grounded of the Joan films. It runs over five hours in its full version and is built on long takes, real landscapes and the plain business of medieval war: horses, mud, waiting, councils. Sandrine Bonnaire's Joan is a believable country girl, devout and stubborn, who giggles, weeps and is frightened. Jonathan Rosenbaum calls it a plausible portrait of the teenage Joan, and Glenn Kenny calls it 'essential cinema'. The second part, on her captivity, is the stronger. It lacks the intensity of Dreyer and the spiritual concentration of Bresson, and Dennis Schwartz finds it more pleasing than scintillating. For a viewer who wants Joan's whole public career shown soberly, it has no rival.
themes: Joan's faith is shown as real and simple: her saints, her prayers, her loyalty to the anointed king, and her refusal at Rouen to deny that God sent her. She receives Communion before her death and dies calling on Jesus. The film's own stance is cooler. Rivette shows no miracles and keeps the camera outside her visions, so her mission is presented as something she believes rather than something the film affirms. The Rouen trial is a political deal between Church and English power, which matches the history of a partisan court but leaves out the Church that later annulled the verdict and canonised her.
history: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) was examined by theologians at Poitiers in 1429 before relieving Orléans. Captured at Compiègne in 1430, she was tried at Rouen under Pierre Cauchon, signed an abjuration in May 1431, resumed male dress days later and was burned as a relapsed heretic on 30 May. A papal retrial annulled the sentence in 1456; she was canonised in 1920.
liberties: Few factual inventions are reported. The main choices are omissions and stance: no visions or miracles are shown, and witnesses address the camera as if testifying. The US home-video version cuts the 336-minute original to about 226 minutes.
advisories:
Battle scenes, wounding and an attempted rape in prison; the burning at the stake.

Long and slow by design; the full version runs over five and a half hours in two parts.

Suitable for teenagers and adults.

The film shows no miracles and keeps its distance from Joan's voices; the Church at Rouen appears as a political tool.

title: Jeannette: The Childhood of Joan of Arc
decision: GREY: Content from Greydanus (Decent Films, B+, and Arts & Faith), Tushnet (The American Interest), Wikipedia and Eyefilm. The text is Péguy's and its theology is corrected within the film; the deliberately incongruous staging and the unresolved revolt are reservations a reader can weigh, not sacrilege presented approvingly.
summary: Bruno Dumont stages Charles Péguy's verse drama of Joan's childhood vocation as a musical for untrained children, from a cappella song to thrash metal, on the dunes of northern France.
synopsis: Domrémy, 1425, during the Hundred Years' War. Eight-year-old Jeannette minds her sheep, shares her bread with refugee children and cannot accept that God permits the war, the suffering and the damnation of souls; she turns the Our Father into a lament. Her friend Hauviette counsels trust. A Franciscan nun, Madame Gervaise, answers her at length: evil is real and all share in it, but Christ's redemption is present now, and Jeannette's wish to suffer hell in place of the damned is blasphemous. Jeannette is not fully satisfied. She has a vision of three saints, who call her to lead France against the English. Years later she persuades her uncle to help her reach the army, hesitates at the last moment, and finally slips away on the pretext of nursing a relative.
inclusion: Nothing else looks like it. Dumont shot on the dunes of the Côte d'Opale, cast local children who sing off-key and dance awkwardly to Philippe Decouflé's choreography, and gave the score to the metal musician Igorrr. Every word is Péguy's, from his 1910 Mystère de la charité de Jeanne d'Arc and his 1897 Jeanne d'Arc. The result divides people. Variety's Peter Debruge called it a blasphemous assault; Eve Tushnet found it strange and often thrilling, a portrait of how unpredictably God breaks in; Steven Greydanus gave it B+ and called the eighteen-minute exchange with Madame Gervaise sublime, if close to ridiculous. Most agree the second half drags. Cahiers du cinéma placed it second in its 2017 list.
themes: The first half is a real theological drama: the problem of evil and the damnation of souls, posed by a child and answered by a nun. Gervaise's reply is orthodox: the Redemption is present, suffering can be offered, and no one may wish to take on the pains of hell for others. The film leaves Jeannette restless rather than convinced, which is Péguy's point but also a risk. The vocation scene treats the saints' call as real. Against this, the style is deliberately incongruous: nuns pull off their wimples and headbang, and the dances are comic. Greydanus and Tushnet argue it is playful, not mocking; Dumont himself is an unbeliever. The second half, from Péguy's earlier socialist play, is more patriotic than religious.
history: Joan was born at Domrémy, probably in 1412, and first heard the voices of St. Michael, St. Margaret and St. Catherine in the summer of 1425, aged about thirteen. In 1428 and again in 1429 she went to Vaucouleurs, accompanied by a kinsman, to seek Robert de Baudricourt. She was burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431, her sentence was annulled on appeal a quarter of a century later, and she was beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920.
liberties: Dumont uses Péguy's words but cuts them heavily and stages them anachronistically, with modern dance, rap and metal. Joan's first call is moved from about thirteen to eight. Madame Gervaise is Péguy's invention, and the long theological debate is his, not the historical record's.
advisories:
No violence beyond talk of war; no sexual content or bad language.

Long sung theological disputation; children are more likely to be baffled than harmed.

Nuns headbang and the dancing is comic; some viewers will find this irreverent.

Jeannette's revolt against the damnation of souls is answered by the nun but not settled in her.

grey.question: Dumont, an unbeliever, stages Péguy's Catholic verse as a punk and metal musical: children dance, a nun pulls off her wimple and headbangs, and the saints sing. Catholic critics who know the film well, Greydanus and Tushnet, find it playful rather than mocking and orthodox in substance; Variety called it blasphemous. Jeannette's revolt against the damnation of souls is answered but leaves her unconvinced. Viewers must decide whether the style serves the text or cheapens it.

title: Everyman
decision: PUBLISH: Hofmannsthal's text (Projekt Gutenberg) is a Catholic morality: contrition, a monk's cleansing and the sacrament, faith joined to good works, and the Devil answered with Christ's atonement. Paimann's Filmlisten (contemporary Austrian trade review, via de.wikipedia) found the film faithful to the play apart from Salzburg-inspired settings, choreography and costumes, and the film-dienst review (organ of the German Catholic film commission, carried in the Lexikon des internationalen Films) called it a remarkable screen record of the Salzburg staging. Identity: filmdienst.de, Wikipedia.
summary: Gottfried Reinhardt films the Salzburg Festival's Everyman, Hofmannsthal's morality play of a rich man summoned by Death, deserted by friends and money, and saved by Faith and Good Works.
synopsis: God, grieved that men forget him, sends Death to summon Everyman (Walther Reyer), a rich man in his prime. Before Death comes, Everyman turns away a poor neighbour, has a debtor taken off to prison, brushes aside his mother's pleas to think of his soul, and feasts with his mistress (Ellen Schwiers). Death interrupts the banquet. Everyman begs for company on his journey and is refused by his friends, his cousins and his servants; Mammon (Paul Dahlke) mocks him. His Good Works (Sonja Sutter) are too weak to stand. Her sister Faith (Paula Wessely) teaches him the mercy of God and the power of contrition. He goes to be cleansed and returns in a white robe; the Devil (Heinrich Schweiger) comes to claim him and is turned away. Everyman goes into his grave with Good Works beside him.
inclusion: Hofmannsthal's Everyman has opened the Salzburg Festival almost every summer since Max Reinhardt first staged it on the cathedral square in 1920. This film preserves the 1961 production, directed by Max's son Gottfried, with Walther Reyer, the festival's Everyman through the 1960s, and Paula Wessely as Faith; Ernst Krenek wrote the music. It was Austria's submission for the foreign-language Oscar. Paimann's Filmlisten found it faithful to the play, and the film-dienst review called it a remarkable screen record of the Salzburg staging. It is filmed theatre and best taken as such: rhymed verse, pageantry and a strong ensemble rather than cinema. For anyone who cannot get to Salzburg it is the nearest thing, and the play itself is one of the great Catholic dramas of the century.
themes: The play is a Catholic morality: death and the particular judgement, the uselessness of wealth and friends at the end, and salvation through faith joined to works. Faith hears Everyman recite the articles of the Creed learned in childhood, teaches him Christ's atonement and the transforming power of contrition, and sends him to a monk to be cleansed; he later says he has received the sacrament. Good Works, crippled by his neglect, rise and go with him into the grave, and Faith answers the Devil that Christ has paid the debt. His mother, on her way to early Mass, hears the angels.
history: Hofmannsthal drew on the late-medieval morality plays, the English Everyman, the Dutch Elckerlijc and Hans Sachs's Hekastus among them. Max Reinhardt first staged it in Berlin in December 1911, and in 1920 it opened the first Salzburg Festival in front of the cathedral. Gottfried Reinhardt directed the festival production in 1961 and 1962, and the film was made during the 1961 festival. It premiered in Vienna and Salzburg on 24 November 1961.
advisories:
No violence; Death and the Devil may frighten young children.

A banquet with the rich man's mistress; nothing explicit.

Filmed theatre in German verse; English subtitles may be hard to find.

title: Jesus of Nazareth
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred by subject: the first Mexican sound film on the life and Passion of Christ, with José Cibrián as Jesus and Aurora Walker as Our Lady. Identity is established by the New York State Motion Picture Division's licence record and a 2024 Mexican press article. But no source I could open describes how the Gospel is treated, which episodes are included or invented, or how Our Lady and the Apostles are presented, and no contemporary Catholic rating was found. Unverified, not PUBLISH, until the content is checked.
summary: José Díaz Morales's life of Christ, the first made in Mexico in the sound era, with José Cibrián as Jesus.
synopsis: The film follows the life of Christ as told in the Gospels, from His public ministry to the Passion and Crucifixion, with Aurora Walker as the Blessed Virgin, Adriana Lamar as Mary Magdalene, José Pidal as Judas and José Baviera as Pontius Pilate. Its cast list points to the familiar Gospel episodes: John the Baptist, the Samaritan woman at the well, the woman taken in adultery, the rich young man, the supper at Simon the Pharisee's house, Nicodemus, the trials before Annas, Caiaphas, Herod and Pilate, Barabbas, Veronica, and the two thieves crucified with Christ. The sources I could open do not say whether the film shows the Nativity or the Resurrection, or how far it adds invented incidents. A fuller synopsis must wait for the dialogue script or a viewing.
inclusion: Made by Pereda Films in 1942 and released in the United States through Cinespano in 1943, Jesús de Nazareth was the first Mexican feature on the life of Christ, and it made a star of José Cibrián in the title role. The director, José Díaz Morales, was one of the Spanish exiles newly arrived in the Mexican studios, as were many of his crew. The film belongs to the cycle of Mexican religious pictures of the 1940s that also produced La Virgen Morena and Felipe de Jesús. Its place in the catalogue depends on how faithfully it renders the Gospel, which has not yet been established.
themes: As a Passion film, its themes are given by the Gospels: Christ's teaching and miracles, His rejection by the authorities, the betrayal by Judas, the trial before Pilate and the Crucifixion. The cast list suggests the familiar emphases of the period: the sorrowing Mother, the penitent Magdalene and a Judas given motives of his own. Whether the film presents Christ's divinity and the Sacrifice of the Cross as the Church teaches, or reduces Him to a moral teacher, is the question still open, as is whether Our Lady is shown with due reverence.
history: Mexico's film industry boomed during the Second World War, and religious subjects were popular with audiences. Spanish exiles who had fled after the Civil War found work in the Mexican studios, including Díaz Morales. The film was licensed for exhibition in New York State in 1943 at 8,463 feet.
advisories:
The scourging and Crucifixion of Christ.

Suitable for families, subject to confirmation of the content.

The film's fidelity to the Gospel has not been checked.

title: Jesus, Our Lord
decision: GREY: Identity from Wikipedia and Hispanopedia (both thinly referenced; García Riera's Historia documental del cine mexicano is the print source cited for production history). No treatment source of any kind was found; nothing contrary to the faith is reported. Close to HOLD on evidence; kept GREY/unverified because identity and outline agree across sources and the subject is plainly Catholic-centred.
summary: The last of Miguel Zacarías's Mexican Gospel trilogy, with Claudio Brook as Christ, covers the public ministry, Passion and Ascension and was released on Holy Thursday 1971.
synopsis: Drawn from the four Gospels, the film covers Christ's public life (Claudio Brook) from his baptism by John to his death and the Ascension. Among its documented scenes are the baptism, at which the young apostle John is shown seeking the Messiah through the Baptist; the Sermon on the Mount, filmed with Popocatépetl behind the crowd and with the Our Father placed in it; and the entry into Jerusalem, shot in the streets of Guanajuato. Rita Macedo appears as Our Lady. After the Crucifixion the film passes directly to Christ's appearance to the apostles and the Ascension, without showing the burial or the empty tomb. It was shot mainly in 1969, finished in 1970 and released in Mexico on Holy Thursday, 8 April 1971.
inclusion: Mexican cinema produced a steady line of Gospel films, and Miguel Zacarías, a veteran of the industry, closed his trilogy, after Jesús, el niño Dios and Jesús, María y José, with this account of the ministry and Passion. It is a popular colour production made for Holy Week and shot on Mexican locations, with the volcano and colonial streets standing in for Galilee and Jerusalem, and Claudio Brook cast as Christ on his return to Mexico from Europe. Beyond that, little is documented. No review of its quality or its treatment of the Gospel has been found, so it should be approached as a devotional film of its period whose merits are untested.
themes: The film is based on the four Gospels and keeps the familiar shape of a Life of Christ: the baptism, the preaching, the Sermon on the Mount with the Lord's Prayer, the entry into Jerusalem, the Passion and Crucifixion, and the Ascension, with Our Lady present. The one documented departure of substance comes at the end, where the burial and the Resurrection itself are passed over and the film moves straight from the Cross to the risen Christ among the apostles. How it handles the miracles, the Last Supper and Christ's claims to divinity has not been checked.
liberties: Documented departures from the Gospels: the apostle John appears at the Baptist's preaching seeking the Messiah; the Our Father is placed within the Sermon on the Mount; and the burial and Resurrection are skipped between the Crucifixion and the appearance to the apostles before the Ascension.
advisories:
The Passion and Crucifixion are shown; their intensity is not documented.

No other content concerns are reported.

No review has been found; this description rests on reference entries.

title: Joan of Arc
alternateTitles: Joan of Arc: The Virgin Warrior
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and broadly sympathetic, and St Joan was canonised in 1920. Not PUBLISH because the independent reviewer (Jim McLennan) notes the film declines to say whether her voices came from God, and the history is bent in ways that change the meaning of her trial: Cauchon is made Charles VII's own spiritual adviser and Charles is made more responsible for her death than the evidence allows, with hints of a romance with Jean de Metz. The only Catholic endorsement is from its present-day distributor, Ignatius Press. Subtitles of the voices and trial scenes would settle whether the treatment of her mission is sceptical or simply reticent.
summary: Christian Duguay's lavish two-part CBS/CBC Joan of Arc, carried by Leelee Sobieski's steady Joan and Peter O'Toole's Emmy-winning Cauchon, with large liberties in the politics.
synopsis: The film opens with Joan's burning and then returns to Domrémy, where a girl her parents (Powers Boothe and Jacqueline Bisset) had not wanted begins at eleven to hear voices. When soldiers burn the village and kill her blind friend, the voices tell her to put the Dauphin on the throne. At Vaucouleurs she wins an escort; at Chinon she sees through a courtier posing as Charles (Neil Patrick Harris) and convinces him. She raises the siege of Orléans and sees Charles crowned at Reims, but the court tires of her. Captured at Compiègne, she is sold to the English and tried at Rouen by Bishop Cauchon (Peter O'Toole), a churchman the film has placed at Charles's side. Abandoned by the king she crowned, she is condemned and burned.
inclusion: This is the most widely seen Joan of the television era: thirteen Emmy nominations, with an award for O'Toole's Cauchon, and a cast that includes Shirley MacLaine, Maximilian Schell, Olympia Dukakis and Robert Loggia. Leelee Sobieski, herself a teenager, plays Joan with a calm, unforced certainty that reviewers single out; Jim McLennan finds it the thing that holds the film together. The early scenes, with Joan feeding the poor and putting heart into her village, give her charity as well as courage. Its weaknesses are a slow middle, nearly bloodless battles, a Middle Ages filmed in Czech snow, and a script that reshapes the politics freely. It is a respectable family Joan, below Dreyer, Fleming and Bresson.
themes: Joan's voices, her loyalty to the anointed king and her trial before churchmen are all central. The film shows her praying, receiving guidance and holding to it under interrogation. But reviewers note it does not commit itself on whether the voices were from God, and its star said publicly she was undecided. The trial is presented as a political manipulation, which matches the history, but by making Cauchon the king's own adviser the film shifts blame from the English party towards Charles and the Church at large. Her canonisation in 1920 is the Church's answer.
history: Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) left Domrémy in 1429, relieved Orléans and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims. Captured at Compiègne in 1430, she was sold to the English and tried for heresy at Rouen by a court under Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, a partisan of the Anglo-Burgundian side. She was burned on 30 May 1431. A papal retrial annulled the verdict in 1456; she was beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920.
liberties: Cauchon is made Charles VII's spiritual adviser, though he was always of the English and Burgundian party. Charles is shown as more responsible for her death than the evidence supports. Joan is an unwanted daughter whose blind friend is killed; her brother dies in battle, though in fact he lived to see her rehabilitated; a romance with Jean de Metz is hinted at. Several supporting characters are composites.
advisories:
Battle scenes, mostly bloodless; a village burned and a child killed; Joan's burning at the stake, shown at the start and end.

No sexual content beyond hinted romantic feeling.

Suitable for older children and up.

The film is non-committal about the source of Joan's voices, and it misplaces Cauchon at Charles's court.

title: The Annunciation of Marie
decision: PUBLISH: A faithful adaptation of Claudel's play, Catholic-centred throughout. Séquences (1992) gives a substantive independent account of its treatment: Violaine's threefold sacrifice, the communion of saints and the Christmas-night miracle. 24 Images (1992) dissents on style only. The 1992 Berlin ecumenical jury prize is a post-conciliar body and is cited for fact only.
summary: Alain Cuny's only film as director is a severe, stylised staging of Claudel's medieval mystery: a girl kisses a leper, loses everything, and revives her sister's dead child.
synopsis: On the farm of Combernon in medieval Champagne, Violaine Vercors is betrothed to Jacques Hury. Pierre de Craon, a master builder working on a church at Reims, has leprosy, and Violaine gives him a kiss of pity in farewell. Her sister Mara, who wants Jacques for herself, sees it and uses it against her. Violaine catches the disease and is cast out to live apart as a leper, and Jacques marries Mara. Years later, on Christmas night, Mara brings her dead baby to Violaine and demands that she give the child back to her alive. The child lives, and opens eyes the colour of Violaine's. At the end Violaine is brought home to die at the great farm table, as her father, Anne Vercors, returns.
inclusion: Cuny acted in Claudel's plays for decades, and before the poet died in 1955 he asked Cuny to film this one. Cuny made it in his eighties with a largely non-professional cast, shooting in Quebec and in rural France. The result is formal to the point of rigidity: tight framing, slow, measured movement, and verse spoken with deliberate solemnity. Opinion split along that line. Séquences, in 1992, called it a work of sublime elevation that asks the viewer to leave everyday concerns behind. 24 Images found Cuny's emphatic acting and over-worked photography at odds with the Bressonian austerity he was reaching for, while granting it some real moments of grace. It is not an easy film, but it is a faithful one, made by the actor who knew the play best, and a 4K restoration was released in French cinemas in 2022.
themes: Claudel's subject is sacrifice and the communion of saints. As Séquences notes, following Claudel, Violaine gives herself three times: in pity for the leper, in love for the sister who takes her betrothed, and in faith, when she obtains the child's life. The miracle comes on Christmas night, and its sign, the child's new eyes, binds the two sisters together. Suffering is shown as something that can be offered for others, a fully traditional idea. Cuny keeps the religious world of the play in view: a crucifix on the farmhouse wall, and the dalmatic lent by the nuns of Monsanvierge that Violaine wears at her betrothal. Nothing in the sources suggests any departure from Claudel's orthodoxy.
liberties: The film follows Claudel's text and keeps its verse, so the changes are of staging rather than story. Exteriors were shot partly in Quebec, standing in for medieval Champagne, and the cast is largely non-professional.
advisories:
Leprosy is shown, and a dead infant is central to the climax.

No sexual content or strong language; a kiss of pity sets the plot in motion.

Slow, formal and spoken in verse; best for adults and older teenagers.

title: The Apparition
decision: GREY: Content from Greydanus (NCRegister), Brad Miner (The Catholic Thing), Aleteia, Johnny Alucard and CNC; identity from CNC and Wikipedia. Respectful and orthodox where it touches doctrine, but agnostic, set in the present-day Church, with a twist not yet verified. Subtitles are needed to state the ending exactly; if it mocks the faith rather than exposing a deception the Church was right to doubt, REJECT.
summary: Xavier Giannoli's long, serious mystery puts an agnostic war reporter on a Vatican commission examining a young novice's claim that the Virgin Mary appeared to her in south-eastern France.
synopsis: Jacques Mayano, a veteran reporter for Ouest-France, is back from the Middle East, where his photographer friend was killed. An official of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith asks him to join a canonical inquiry. In a small town in south-eastern France, Anna, an eighteen-year-old novice raised in foster homes, says she has seen the Virgin; thousands of pilgrims are coming. Her mentor, Father Borrodine, defies his bishop on her behalf, and a German Catholic promoter, Anton Meyer, is marketing her. The commission includes a sceptical theologian and a psychiatrist who wants to believe. Anna guards a bloodstained cloth she says Mary gave her. Jacques's search into her past leads to a missing friend, Meriem, and finally to the Middle East, where the truth about the apparition comes out.
inclusion: This is one of the few recent European films to take Catholic piety and Church procedure seriously. Giannoli built it from an article on canonical inquiries, and the detail of the process, the archive work, interviews and medical examinations, and the commerce round a new shrine, is unusually exact. Vincent Lindon is excellent as the grieving investigator, and Galatéa Bellugi keeps Anna opaque. Greydanus calls it an earnest, curious exploration of doubt and faith; Brad Miner calls it a very Catholic film; Aleteia's critic found it honest and respectful of the Church's judgment. Its faults are length (144 minutes), sprawling subplots and a resolution that Greydanus finds clever but thinly worked out.
themes: The film treats the Church's caution as a virtue: the commission exists to separate fact from fraud, and Jacques's honesty is put at its service. Anna's message, to help the poor and build a house of prayer, is simple and orthodox, and her prayer is shown as sincere. Greydanus corrects the film's sceptical theologian, who argues that Mary cannot be linked with violence, by pointing to the Sorrowful Mother. The relic is the weak point, since apparitions do not traditionally leave objects behind. The ending is agnostic about the supernatural; its interest is in the cost of truth. The setting is the present-day Church, presented without irony.
advisories:
Brief medical nudity: a woman's breasts are exposed during defibrillation.

Several obscenities.

Disturbing images and themes, including war trauma and a death; better for older teenagers and adults.

An agnostic film about faith: it leaves the supernatural open, and its ending turns on a lie and a sacrifice.

grey.question: The Apparition treats the Church's investigation of a claimed apparition with respect and its visionary with sympathy, but it is agnostic about the supernatural, and its twist settles the case in a way that critics found contrived. A Franciscan defies his bishop, a promoter sells the visionary, and the Church shown is the present-day one. Viewers should know it is an inquiry into belief rather than a film of faith.
