title: The Birth, the Life and the Death of Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from Silent Era's Progressive Silent Film List and Wikipedia (citing Abel, McMahan, Hebron and Foster); Dennis Schwartz's independent review and the scholarship summarised by Wikipedia establish a traditional 25-tableau Gospel life from Bethlehem to the Resurrection, modelled on Tissot's Bible, with Jesuit consultants per Guy's memoirs (via McMahan). The NCRegister piece is present-day Catholic and used for content only. No doctrinal objection.
summary: Alice Guy's Gaumont Life of Christ stages the Gospel in 25 tableaux modelled on Tissot's paintings, from the arrival at Bethlehem to the Resurrection.
synopsis: Mary and Joseph arrive in Bethlehem, Christ is born and the Magi come to the manger. Short scenes of the public life follow: the Samaritan woman, the raising of Jairus's daughter and the woman who washes Christ's feet. After the entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday and the Last Supper, the film follows the Passion closely: the agony in the garden, the night watch, Judas's betrayal, Christ before Caiaphas, Peter's denial, the trial before Pilate, the scourging and the Ecce Homo. On the way of the cross Christ falls, Veronica wipes his face and the procession climbs to Golgotha. After the Crucifixion, the agony and the descent from the cross, Christ is laid in the tomb. The last tableau is the Resurrection.
inclusion: Gaumont's answer to Pathé's Passion was the most ambitious film Alice Guy made in France: about 33 minutes, some 300 extras and 25 sets by Henri Menessier, sold whole or scene by scene. Guy based the sets and costumes on James Tissot's watercolours of the life of Christ, and the compositions often look like them. She also shot exteriors in the forest of Fontainebleau, which gives the film more air than its rivals. Historians single out a cut-in to a medium shot as Veronica holds out the veil, and a pan following the climb to Golgotha, both unusual in 1906. Richard Abel notes the attention given to the women around Christ. The acting is broad and the camera mostly static, and for a long time the film was credited to her assistant, Victorin Jasset.
themes: This is a traditional Gospel harmony in Catholic dress. Most of the running time goes to the Passion, which follows the order of the Gospels and adds the third-century tradition of Veronica's veil, a scene of the Stations of the Cross. Christ's miracles and his forgiveness of the penitent woman are shown plainly, and the film ends with the Resurrection rather than at the tomb. Guy recalled in her memoirs that she hired two Jesuits who had recently been in the Holy Land as advisers. Gwendolyn Audrey Foster criticises its casting of Black figures, apart from one of the Magi, in hostile roles.
history: Alice Guy (1873–1968) was Gaumont's head of production and among the first directors to make fiction films. She bought the Tissot Bible, a bestseller published in French in 1896, and used its 365 gouaches of the life of Christ as documentation for the film. The film was released in France and the United States in January 1906; the American release, from the Biograph company, followed in January 1907. Older histories credited it to Victorin Jasset, who handled the exteriors and extras.
advisories:
Stylised scourging and Crucifixion.

Silent, with title cards naming each scene; viewers need to know the Gospel story.

Suitable for children.

title: The Virgin of Guadalupe
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency classed it A-I as The Virgin of Guadalupe (La Virgen Morena), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Independent contemporary reviews in Motion Picture Herald (John Stuart Jr.), The Exhibitor and Variety (May-June 1943) describe a reverent, well-made telling of the Tepeyac apparitions within a story of the Church defending the Indians against Spanish soldiers. The scenario was by the Jesuit Carlos M. de Heredia and carried the Archbishop of Mexico's endorsement. Juan Diego (beatified 1990) is a character, not the subject; rule (a) does not apply, and he is not given a title.
summary: Gabriel Soria's account of the 1531 apparitions at Tepeyac, written by a Jesuit historian of the shrine, sets Juan Diego's vision against the last struggle between Spaniards and Aztecs.
synopsis: December 1531. Spanish soldiers under a ruthless captain burn and pillage villages of Indians who have become Christians. The Bishop of Mexico begs the Viceroy to stop the cruelty, which is turning the Indians against the faith and keeping the Aztec prince Temoc from agreeing a truce. In reprisal Temoc seizes the Viceroy's daughter, Doña Blanca, as a hostage; the captain recovers her and nearly wipes out the prince's people. Temoc, who has fallen in love with her, brings her back himself and surrenders. Meanwhile the Virgin appears to a poor Indian, Juan Diego, on the hill of Tepeyac and asks for a church there. The bishop's household demands a sign. She sends him to gather roses, and when he opens his cloak before the bishop and the people, her image is on it. Temoc kneels, and the Viceroy has the captain arrested.
inclusion: This is the more straightforward of the two Guadalupe films Mexico made in 1942, and the better documented. Its story came from Fr Carlos M. de Heredia, SJ, a historian of the shrine, and the film opened in May 1943 with the endorsement of the Archbishop of Mexico. The trade press in New York liked it: Motion Picture Herald called the screenplay well contrived and the production values excellent, The Exhibitor found it attention-holding and authentic, and Variety said it was done in excellent taste. José Luis Jiménez, as Juan Diego, was named Mexico's outstanding screen discovery of 1942. The score by Julián Carrillo used his microtonal 'Sonido 13' for the apparition scenes, a rare experiment in Mexican cinema. The invented romance between the Aztec prince and the Viceroy's daughter is the kind of sub-plot the period demanded.
themes: The apparition is presented as a real miracle and as the turning point in the conversion of Mexico. The film sets the bishop and the friars against the soldiers: the Church defends the converted Indians, and their faith is threatened by Spanish cruelty, not by the Gospel. Our Lady appears to the poorest of them, the bishop asks for a sign as prudence requires, and the image on the cloak convinces both the Spanish and the Aztec prince, who kneels in submission to the faith. Motion Picture Herald summed up its theme as the simple, sincere faith that is credited with evoking miracles.
history: According to the tradition recorded in the Nican Mopohua, Our Lady appeared four times in December 1531 to Juan Diego, a baptised Indian, on the hill of Tepeyac north of Mexico City, asked that a church be built there, and left her image on his tilma as a sign for Bishop Juan de Zumárraga. The image is venerated in the basilica at Tepeyac; it was crowned in 1895 and Our Lady of Guadalupe was declared patroness of Latin America in 1910.
liberties: Temoc, Doña Blanca, the captain and the hostage story are inventions to dramatise the conquest. The reviews describe the bishop's household doubting Juan Diego and the image appearing before a large gathering; tradition has the tilma opened before the bishop in his house. The 'last battle between Spaniards and Aztecs' in 1531 is a dramatic licence: Tenochtitlan fell in 1521.
advisories:
Burning of villages, battle scenes and killings.

An abduction; a chaste romance between the prince and the hostage.

Suitable for older children and up.

title: The Miracle Roses
decision: GREY: Identity (Wikipedia citing García Riera, Historia documental del cine mexicano) and outline (ADN40, Posta) are established: a conquest-era drama ending in the 1531 Guadalupe apparitions and the miracle of the roses. No review or Catholic rating found. Juan Diego (beatified 1990) is a character, not the subject; rule (a) does not apply, following la-virgen-que-forjo-una-patria-1942. Unverified.
summary: Julián Soler's historical drama of the conquest of Mexico and the 1531 apparitions of Our Lady of Guadalupe to Juan Diego, ending with the roses and the image.
synopsis: The film is set in the years of the Spanish conquest. Its cast includes Moctezuma (Crox Alvarado), an Aztec high priest (Andrés Soler) and invented Aztec characters, among them Tlaltecalzin (Armando Silvestre), Nanoaltzin (Jaime Fernández) and Citlali (Magda Urvizu), with Hernán Cortés (Manuel Calvo) and Bishop Juan de Zumárraga (Francisco Jambrina) for the Spaniards. The story leads to 1531, when the Virgin (Lilia del Carmen Camacho) appears to the Indian Juan Diego (Jorge Martínez de Hoyos) at Tepeyac and asks for a church to be built there. The title refers to the sign she gives: Castilian roses gathered out of season, and her image on Juan Diego's cloak before the bishop. How the invented characters' stories lead to the apparitions is not documented in the sources found.
inclusion: Mexican cinema returned several times to Guadalupe, and this 1960 version, written by Alfonso Patiño Gómez and directed by the experienced Julián Soler, sets the apparitions against the conquest itself, with Moctezuma, Cortés and an Aztec priest among the characters. Jorge Martínez de Hoyos, a respected character actor, plays Juan Diego. Present-day Mexican press pieces call it a forgotten landmark and describe a mix of historical drama and spirituality in which the Virgin's image is offered as a sign of hope for the Indian people. No critical review, old or new, has been found, so its quality is unknown. Emilio García Riera covers it in his documentary history of Mexican cinema.
themes: The subject is the apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe in 1531, long venerated and approved by the Church, and the foundation of Mexican Catholic devotion. By the press accounts, the film presents the Virgin's image as a sign of hope for the Indians and dramatises the meeting of Aztec religion and the Catholic faith. The miracle of the roses and the image on the cloak give the film its title and climax. How it shows Aztec religion and the conquest, and whether it presents the conversion of the Indians as the Virgin's work, is not established.
advisories:
Conquest-era conflict and Aztec religion are part of the story; how violence or sacrifice is shown is not documented.

As far as is known, suitable for families.

Juan Diego was beatified only in 1990; he is a character here, not the subject, and is given no title.

title: The Satin Slipper
decision: PUBLISH: A Catholic-centred adaptation of Claudel's play. Gonçalves (Études littéraires) establishes that it keeps the essentials of Claudel's text, and two independent critics, R. Emmet Sweeney and Joe Bendel, document the religious frame: the Jesuit's prayer for his brother, the slipper left with the Virgin, the Guardian Angel and the lovers' renunciation. The adulterous love is renounced, not approved, and that is stated in the advisories. No contemporary Catholic rating was found.
summary: Manoel de Oliveira films most of Claudel's vast Catholic drama as open theatre: a married woman and a conquistador love each other, renounce each other, and are parted for decades.
synopsis: Spain's Golden Age, with the whole world for a stage. A Jesuit lashed to the mast of a sinking ship prays for his younger brother, Rodrigue, that he may come to God even by way of his passions. Doña Prouhèze, married to an older nobleman, loves Rodrigue and is loved in return. Before going to meet him she leaves her satin slipper with a statue of the Virgin, so that if she runs towards evil it will be with a limping foot. Her Guardian Angel keeps watch over her. The King sends Rodrigue to govern in the Americas and Prouhèze to hold the African fortress of Mogador. Her letter reaches him ten years late. When he finally comes to Mogador they are kept apart, and she dies in the fortress. Years later the maimed and disgraced Rodrigue meets her daughter, Sept-Épées.
inclusion: Claudel's play, published in 1929, runs about eleven hours uncut and is rarely staged. Oliveira's version keeps the essentials of the text, as Luís Carlos Pimenta Gonçalves notes, and refuses to make it realistic. It opens on an audience filing into a theatre; the camera is mostly static, the takes are long, the sea is painted papier-mâché and the whales are cardboard. Joe Bendel argues that this stylisation lets the angel scenes work where 1980s effects would have failed, and he singles out Patricia Barzyk's Prouhèze as a great tragic heroine. R. Emmet Sweeney credits the film with making the religious fire of Claudel's world recognisable again. The cost is real: it is talky, heavy with exposition, and some of the comic interludes drag. For viewers willing to give it seven hours, it is the only complete screen version of one of the major Catholic dramas of the century.
themes: The play's subject is desire offered up rather than indulged. Prouhèze's gesture with the slipper is its emblem: she does not trust herself, so she binds herself through Our Lady. The Jesuit's prayer in the opening scene and the Guardian Angel who argues with her make it plain that grace, not fate, is at work in the lovers' separation. The question the play asks is how God can use even a forbidden love, and its answer is renunciation, not consummation. The setting is the Spanish Catholic empire at full stretch, and Rodrigue's worldly ambitions are judged as well as admired. Claudel's frankness about passion can startle, but the moral order of the play is never in doubt.
history: Paul Claudel (1868–1955) published Le Soulier de satin in 1929. It was first staged in 1943 in an abridged version prepared by Claudel and Jean-Louis Barrault; complete stagings came only later, notably at the Avignon Festival in 1987. Oliveira's film was shown at the Venice Film Festival in 1985, where it received the Sergio Trasatti Award, and in a drastically shortened version at the New York Film Festival the same year.
liberties: Oliveira keeps the play's structure and most of its text, so the changes are of form rather than substance. He frames the action as a performance, opens on an audience entering a theatre, and keeps painted backdrops and visible stage artifice throughout. Some secondary material is shortened.
advisories:
No sexual scenes: the love is spoken of, not shown, and the lovers never consummate it.

Very long (about seven hours, with an intermission) and wordy; for patient adults and older teenagers.

The central love is adulterous in desire. The play judges it, and its resolution is renunciation.

title: Miracles of Thursday
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (apparitions, popular devotion, St Dismas); the Spanish Church's rating was 3R, adults with reservations (La Cabecita), and the censorship history is from es.wikipedia (citing Marcos Molano and Álvarez Sanz, 2019). The English-subtitled version read 2026-10-12 is the pious one: the stranger calls himself a good thief saved by a miracle, cures seem real, the parish priest keeps his distance from the fraud, and the closing reveal identifies Martino as St Dismas. Reservation stands: the 'saint' works through mirrors, staged illnesses and a gold bribe, the mockery of credulous devotion remains, and the plotters' confession is a farce.
summary: Berlanga's satire of a spa town that fakes a saint's apparition to bring back visitors, turned by the censors into a fable in which the real St Dismas intervenes.
synopsis: Fontecilla's spa is dying. Envying Lourdes and Fátima, five notables, the mayor, the doctor, the schoolmaster, a landowner and the spa owner, stage an apparition of St Dismas, the Good Thief, with one of them dressed as the saint. Fireworks fool Mauro, the village simpleton; the next Thursday a devout woman sees it too, and crowds gather. The parish priest, Don Fidel, takes their money for the poor but will not endorse a miracle. On the third Thursday the stunt collapses. A mysterious stranger, Martino (Richard Basehart), then arrives, knows all about the hoax and seems to help it along with tricks of his own, while a lost dog comes home and a sick child recovers. When the plotters try to confess publicly, the crowd will not listen. In his long-empty room they find a picture of the real St Dismas: the stranger himself.
inclusion: Berlanga, the great Spanish satirist of the 1950s, took the idea from reported apparitions at Cuevas de Vinromá and wanted a sharp comedy about the commercial use of religion. The censors banned the first script for showing a false miracle; the production passed to a company close to Opus Dei; a Dominican, Father Garau, was imposed as adviser; and extra scenes were shot by Jorge Grau. The result is two films in one: a funny, well-cast village comedy with José Isbert and Manuel Alexandre, and a pious fable grafted on. It flopped on its Spanish release in 1959 and drew objections from both traditionalists and progressives. Spanish critics now count it among Berlanga's classics, and the Filmoteca Española has restored it from two versions.
themes: Its real subject is the abuse of devotion: notables who manufacture a miracle for money, and the gullibility of the faithful. The imposed ending turns this round. The stranger calls himself a thief made good by a miracle, says St Dismas will return with a single word, faith, and is finally revealed as the saint, so grace works through and despite human fraud. But his methods are tricks, staged illnesses and a bribe of gold, which leaves the miraculous ambiguous. The parish priest is the sanest figure: he refuses to call it a miracle, warns that priests are not miracle workers, and clears the church of a mob seeking cures. The mockery of credulous piety remains.
history: In the 1950s reports of the Virgin appearing to children every Thursday at Cuevas de Vinromá, in Castellón, drew pilgrims; Berlanga visited the site with his family. Censors rejected his first script in 1956; filming began that June, and further scenes were shot in 1957 at the authorities' order. The film opened in Italy as Arrivederci Dimas in August 1957 and in Madrid only in February 1959, where it ran ten days.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content of note.

Comic mockery of credulous devotion and a staged apparition; the 'saint' uses tricks and a bribe.

For teenagers and adults. The Spanish Catholic rating was 3R (adults, with reservations).

Two versions exist; the English-subtitled copy reviewed has the pious ending.

title: Magnificat
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (Holy Week, a pilgrimage to a Marian monastery, the monastic office, a girl's entry into the cloister) and taken seriously by independent critics, who call it Avati's best film and a study of the human need for faith. The reservations are content and stance: graphic executions (a drowning and a drawing and quartering), a young couple subjected to the jus primae noctis, a concubine's desperate efforts to bear a son, and a narrator who stresses the period's superstition; La Stampa's critic asked whether it is a religious work at all. Its Italian age rating is 16+. No CCC/CNVF judgment has been traced.
summary: Pupi Avati's austere Cannes competition film follows pilgrims, an executioner and a girl entering the cloister through one Holy Week in tenth-century Italy.
synopsis: In Holy Week of the year 926, in a small kingdom of the Pentapolis, several journeys converge on the Monastery of the Visitation at Malfole. The executioner Folco, still grieving for his son, takes on a young assistant, Baino, and travels to carry out a drowning and a quartering. The king's concubine Roza, pregnant, goes to the monastery, whose relic of Our Lady's garment is said to protect women in childbirth. Margherita, a fourteen-year-old girl, is brought there by her father to enter the cloister. A monk tours the religious houses recording those who died over the winter. The dying lord of Malfole divides his goods among his bastard sons, and a young peasant couple marry under their lord's right to the wedding night. A narrator comments on the customs and fears of the age.
inclusion: Avati, better known abroad for comedies and gialli, made this as a near-documentary of belief in the early Middle Ages, and Italian critics often name it his best work. It has no single plot. Matt Blake (The Wild Eye) compares it to Pasolini's medieval films with the bawdiness removed and calls it an almost anthropological study of trials, executions, weddings, childbirth and monastic rule; he finds it slow and unstructured but compulsive. Cesare Bastelli's photography of Abruzzese abbeys and churches, Riz Ortolani's spare score and the costumes, which won a Ciak d'oro, are its strengths. The Christian Science Monitor's Cannes reviewer called it brilliant and noted how one faith yields both brutal violence and the comfort of the Church's rites.
themes: The film's subject is faith in a hard world: Holy Week, pilgrimage, relics, monastic life and death, set under the title of Our Lady's canticle. Avati said he went back a thousand years to a time when faith was needed to face God's silence. Margherita's entry into the cloister is its clearest image of consecration. But the film is as interested in superstition and cruelty as in grace. Christian justice is shown through executions, and a lord's claim on a peasant bride stands unchallenged. Whether the film presents the faith of the age as true or only as consolation is the question critics raised.
advisories:
Graphic executions: a woman drowned and a man drawn and quartered.

A lord exercises the 'right of the first night' over a peasant bride; a concubine's pregnancy; implied sexual content.

Rated 16+ in Italy. For adults.

The narrator stresses medieval superstition; the film's own view of the faith it shows is open to question.

grey.question: Magnificat is built around Holy Week, a pilgrimage to a Marian monastery and a girl's entry into the cloister, and critics read it as a film about the need for faith. But it lingers on cruelty: a drowning and a drawing and quartering are shown, a lord claims a peasant bride's wedding night, and a narrator stresses the superstition of the age. One leading Italian critic asked whether it is a religious film at all. It is for adults, and viewers must judge whether it treats medieval faith as true or only as a refuge.

title: Marcellino
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (friary, foundling, crucifix in the attic) with identity established (offi.fr, Movieplayer, Box Office Mojo), and the original author, Sánchez Silva, shares the screenplay credit. No review of how it treats the faith was found. Subtitles of the crucifix scenes and the ending would settle it.
summary: Luigi Comencini's remake of Marcelino, pan y vino: a foundling raised by friars, who longs for his mother and finds a friend in the crucifix in their attic.
synopsis: A baby boy is left at a small, poor friary. The friars cannot trace his parents and raise him themselves. Marcellino grows up happy and mischievous, but he longs for the mother he has never known, whom he imagines as the Virgin Mary. A local count takes him in and has him educated, but the boy runs back to the friars. In the attic he finds a large crucifix, and a friendship begins between the child and the Christ on the cross that changes his life. In the original story the boy brings food to the figure, Christ speaks to him, and the friendship ends with the boy's death as he asks to see his mother; how far the remake follows that ending is not established by the sources.
inclusion: José María Sánchez Silva's story was filmed by Ladislao Vajda in 1955 as Marcelino, pan y vino, and that version is the classic. Comencini, best known for his films about children, among them Incompreso and the television Pinocchio, remade it near the end of his career. Sánchez Silva shares the screenplay credit with Comencini and Ennio De Concini. The cast includes Fernando Fernán Gómez as the prior, Alberto Cracco as Brother Eusebio, and Nicolò Paolucci as the boy. There is no substantial critical record of the film in any language found, so its quality is unknown. The credits are serious, and the author's involvement suggests the story's religious core was kept, but that has not been confirmed by any review.
themes: The original story turns on a child's simple charity towards Christ crucified, answered by Christ himself, and on the boy's longing for his mother, fulfilled in death. Comencini's version keeps the friary, the foundling, the boy's longing for a mother he pictures as Our Lady, and the crucifix in the attic. The episode with the count who adopts and educates the boy is the remake's main addition. Whether the ending, the boy's death and reunion with his mother, is kept, and how the Christ figure speaks, are not established by any source found.
liberties: The remake adds a nobleman who takes the boy in and has him educated before he returns to the friars. Sources disagree on the period: one Italian listing places it in fifteenth-century Italy, a French one in seventeenth-century Tuscany.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content is reported.

The original story ends with the death of the child; whether the remake keeps that ending is unverified.

Made as a family film.

title: Margaret of Cortona
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred life of St Margaret of Cortona (canonised 1728); identity and plot are established (Italian and English Wikipedia). The Legion of Decency rated it A-I, but only for prints shown in the continental United States, which implies the Italian original differed. The film recasts her nine years as a nobleman's mistress as a doomed romance with invented villains. No critical review of its treatment was found. A review or a full Italian synopsis would settle it.
summary: Mario Bonnard's Italian life of the thirteenth-century penitent St Margaret of Cortona, from a shepherd girl's love affair with a nobleman to her service of the sick.
synopsis: Margherita, a beautiful shepherd girl of Laviano near Cortona, lives with her father and a young stepmother, Lucia. She falls in love with Arsenio, a young nobleman she meets while minding the sheep. When a rival, Marco, betrays the affair, her father has her sent to a convent, but Arsenio takes her to his house. Marco and Rinaldo degli Uberti murder him, and Francesca, the woman promised to Arsenio, poisons herself. Margherita is despised and persecuted by the villagers and begins to receive visions. When plague strikes the district, she nurses the sick, and she stays at the side of her stepmother, Lucia, until Lucia dies of the disease. Through the epidemic the outcast becomes the town's servant.
inclusion: St Margaret of Cortona is one of the great penitents of the Franciscan tradition, and this is the only feature film of her life. It was the screen debut of Maria Frau in the title role, and it was made with solid craftsmen: Leonida Barboni photographed it and Virgilio Marchi, a leading Italian designer, built the sets. Bonnard was a veteran of Italian costume pictures. It reached New York in 1957. What has not survived is any critical account of it, and the plot as recorded owes as much to melodrama as to the saint's legend: murderous rivals, a jilted fiancée's poisoning and a vigil at a stepmother's deathbed. It is a curiosity for those devoted to the saint.
themes: The film's arc is conversion: a girl's sin, the death that ends it, rejection and humiliation, and then penance expressed as service of the sick. Margaret's visions after Arsenio's death mark the turn, as they do in her legend. Charity in time of plague, and her care for the stepmother who had never loved her, are the visible signs of her change. How directly the film acknowledges that she lived for years as a mistress, and how it shows her penances, is not recorded in the available sources.
history: Margaret (1247–1297) left her father's house at about seventeen to live with a young nobleman near Montepulciano. She lived with him for nine years and bore a son. After he was murdered, his hound led her to the body. Refused a home by her stepmother, she went to Cortona, became a Franciscan tertiary, lived in severe penance, and founded a hospital for the sick poor. She was canonised in 1728.
liberties: Per the plot recorded, the film invents the rival Marco, the murderers, and Arsenio's fiancée and her suicide, and appears to make the affair a brief romance rather than nine years' cohabitation. Her son, her years in Cortona under Franciscan direction, and the founding of her hospital are not mentioned in the synopses. The plague-nursing and reconciliation with the stepmother are dramatised.
advisories:
An unmarried love affair, implied.

A murder and a suicide by poison.

Plague deaths.

Legion of Decency A-I, but only for the US prints; the Italian version may differ.

title: Mary of Nazareth
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred, from a director whose two Bernadette films are in the same vein, and nothing in the available accounts suggests unsound content: all the infancy episodes, Cana, the Passion with Mary at the Cross, John taking her in, and the Resurrection announced to her by John. But no independent critical assessment has been found, only database entries, audience comments and a 2024 ACI Prensa recommendation, and it was co-produced by the Catholic broadcasting committee C.F.R.T. A contemporary French review (La Croix, Télérama, Le Monde, March 1995) or the subtitles would settle it.
summary: Jean Delannoy's last film, made at 87, tells the Gospel from the Annunciation to the Resurrection through the eyes of Our Lady, played by Myriam Muller.
synopsis: In Nazareth under Herod and Augustus, the young Mary (Myriam Muller) receives the angel's message and is betrothed to Joseph (Francis Lalanne). The film follows all the infancy episodes, from the Visitation and the birth at Bethlehem to the threat from Herod (Marc de Jonge). In the public ministry, the wedding at Cana is the only miracle shown. Mary follows her Son (Didier Bienaimé) to Jerusalem and watches his condemnation by Pilate (Jean-Marc Bory) and his scourging and crucifixion. From the Cross Jesus entrusts her to John. The film does not show the risen Christ appearing to the disciples; John brings Mary the news of the Resurrection. Georges Wilson narrates.
inclusion: Jean Delannoy had made Bernadette (1987) and La Passion de Bernadette (1988) late in a long career, and he called this third religious film his testament. It is one of very few features centred on Our Lady, keeping to the Gospel episodes in which she appears and adding her presence at others. It was shot in Morocco, with sets by the Spanish designer Gil Parrondo and Georges Wilson as narrator. No press reviews have been traced. French audience comments call it stagey and literal but faithful, and praise Muller's simple performance; one English-language comment finds the North African settings handsome but the rest flat, and another notes that much of the film is about Jesus rather than Mary. ACI Prensa recommended it in 2024 as an intimate, human portrait.
themes: Mary's divine motherhood is the frame: the Annunciation and the virgin birth, her watch at the foot of the Cross, and her entrustment to St John, the scene tradition reads as her motherhood of the Church. The film follows the Gospels closely and is described by viewers as strongly Catholic in tone. Its restraint with miracles, showing only Cana, keeps the focus on Mary's part. The Resurrection is told to her rather than shown. How the film handles the brethren of the Lord, Joseph's doubt, and Mary's sinlessness has not been checked.
liberties: Mary is placed in scenes where the Gospels do not mention her. Most public-ministry miracles are omitted; Cana is the only one shown. The deposition is not shown, and the Resurrection is reported by John rather than seen.
advisories:
The scourging and crucifixion are shown, at a level suitable for a 'tous publics' French certificate.

No sexual content or strong language reported.

Suitable for families.

No independent review of its treatment has been found; see the question above.

title: Marie's Story
decision: GREY: Identity from NZIFF and Wikipedia; content from independent reviews (Independent Ethos, NZIFF notes) and Catholic sources (The Record; a note by the French bishops' Jeunes & Vocations service, interested). Pre-conciliar religious life shown positively, but no independent source describes how the film handles doctrine or Marie's religious instruction. Subtitles would settle it and could move it to PUBLISH.
summary: Jean-Pierre Améris's restrained true story of a nun at Larnay in the 1890s who teaches a deaf-blind girl to communicate, with Isabelle Carré as the ailing Sister Marguerite.
synopsis: In 1895 a poor artisan brings his daughter Marie, born deaf and blind, to the convent of Larnay near Poitiers, where the Daughters of Wisdom run a school for deaf girls. A doctor has advised an asylum. Marie is wild and violent, and the Mother Superior refuses her, since the sisters have never taught a deaf-blind child. Sister Marguerite, young and already ill, persuades her to relent and takes Marie on. For months she tries to reach her by touch, through tantrums and physical struggles. The breakthrough comes when Marie grasps that a sign made in her hand stands for an object, starting with her treasured knife. Language opens the world to her. Then Marguerite's illness confines her to bed, and she must teach Marie what death means.
inclusion: Améris spent time at Larnay and among deaf-blind people while preparing the film, and he cast Ariana Rivoire, a deaf teenager, as Marie; her physical performance carries the first half. Isabelle Carré, who learned tactile signing for six months, gives Sister Marguerite both delicacy and stubbornness. The camera keeps its distance and the emotion stays low-key; Hans Morgenstern of Independent Ethos praised it for refusing to manipulate, and the NZIFF notes call the climax moving. Comparison with The Miracle Worker is unavoidable, and the film holds up. Its other value is a plain, respectful picture of a teaching congregation before the Council: sisters in habit, a superior with real authority, and a nun who believes it is God's will that she reach this child.
themes: Sister Marguerite sees Marie as a soul imprisoned and believes God wills that she free her; the NZIFF notes describe the story as driven by a divine mission. She presses this against her superior's caution, and the conflict is settled within obedience rather than against it. The convent is a working community, and its charity is concrete. Death is handled seriously: Marguerite prepares Marie for her own, and the Mother Superior tells the grieving girl that faith does not make loss less painful. No independent source says whether the film shows Marie being taught about God, prayer and the sacraments.
history: Marie Heurtin (1885–1921), born deaf and blind at Vertou, was brought to Notre-Dame de Larnay in March 1895. Sister Sainte-Marguerite of the Daughters of Wisdom taught her tactile signs, the alphabet and Braille, and Marie learned to read, write and knit; she later helped teach her deaf-blind sister Marthe. Louis Arnould made the case famous in Âmes en prison (1910). Sister Marguerite died in 1910 and Marie at Larnay in 1921.
advisories:
Marie's early tantrums and the struggles to restrain and wash her are long and sometimes rough; a frightened, violent child may upset younger viewers.

A death from illness, and grief.

No sexual content or bad language reported. Suitable for older children and up.

grey.question: Marie's Story shows a pre-conciliar teaching congregation with evident respect, and its Catholic setting is integral to the story. What has not been established is how much of the faith itself is on screen: whether Marie is taught about God, prayer and the sacraments, as the real Marie was, or whether religion stays a matter of habit and good works. Independent reviews praise the film but say little on this; its dialogue would settle it.

title: Mater Dei
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred life of Our Lady, made by the Society of St Paul from a treatment by its founder, Fr Giacomo Alberione. Content is established by Virgilio Fantuzzi's review of the 2005 restoration in La Civiltà Cattolica (present-day Catholic outlet: content only) and production facts by Fabrizio Natalini's study in Schermi (2017). No independent or pre-1965 assessment of its treatment was found. A Centro Cattolico Cinematografico rating or a 1950–51 review would settle it.
summary: The Pauline Fathers' naive, devotional life of the Virgin Mary, from the Fall to the Assumption, shot in a Roman crypt and billed as Italy's first colour feature.
synopsis: The film opens in Eden after the Fall and then follows Mary's life in a sequence of episodes linked by narration: her childhood, the Annunciation, the Visitation, the Nativity, the visit of the Magi, the flight into Egypt, Christ's public life, Calvary, the Resurrection and the Assumption. The second half moves from the Gospel to the Church. Mary, now in heaven, watches over the faithful, guides and protects them, and receives the devotion of people of every condition, which the film presents as an offering to her. The episodes are arranged much like the mysteries of the Rosary.
inclusion: This is an early example of what Virgilio Fantuzzi calls catechetical cinema, made by a religious congregation for its own network of parishes and halls. Fr Giacomo Alberione, founder of the Society of St Paul, wrote the treatment and asked a young Pauline priest, Emilio Cordero, to direct. The whole community took part: the sisters made the costumes, Alberione appears performing a baptism, and the superior of the Daughters of St Paul plays the prophetess Anna. It was shot in Ansco colour in the crypt of the Regina Apostolorum church in Rome, with prints made in New York. Fantuzzi likens its scenes to a gallery of ex-votos, simple and naive. Cordero himself put its faults down to his inexperience. Its interest is as a document of popular Marian piety in the year of the Assumption dogma.
themes: The structure is Marian doctrine in pictures: a story that begins with the Fall, then Mary the Mother of God at the Annunciation and the Nativity, the Mother of Sorrows at Calvary, and the Queen assumed into heaven. The film was planned for the definition of the Assumption by Pius XII on 1 November 1950. Its second half shows her intercession and the devotion of the faithful. Fantuzzi compares the whole to a Biblia pauperum, a picture-book of the faith. The treatment follows Scripture and tradition; nothing in the available accounts departs from Catholic teaching, but no independent critic has assessed it.
advisories:
The Crucifixion is depicted.

Nothing else of concern is reported.

Simple, slow and amateur in places; suited to families and parish audiences.

title: Ash Wednesday
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a priest serving in hiding under the Calles persecution) but lurid: the premise is a priest's rape of the heroine, much is set in her brothel, and she tries to seduce the hidden priest. Content from the San Sebastián 2019 retrospective record and a fan page reproducing García Riera's documentary history. No Catholic rating found. Editor may prefer REJECT if the priest-rapist premise is judged too grave to weigh.
summary: María Félix plays a brothel-keeper who hates the Church after being raped by a priest, until she falls for a doctor who is secretly a priest during the Cristero persecution.
synopsis: In the 1920s, during the Cristero conflict, young Victoria Rivas falls from a boat on Lake Pátzcuaro and is assaulted by the man who rescues her. At the Ash Wednesday service she recognises him as the priest. Hardened, she leaves the Church, becomes a rich brothel-keeper in Mexico City and informs for the government against the Cristeros. On a train she meets Dr Federico Lamadrid (Arturo de Córdova), who treats the wounded of both sides; later she finds a notebook of his that could ruin him and keeps it rather than betray him. He reveals that he is a priest in hiding and insists on bringing confession to a dying girl in her house. Victoria, in love with him, tries to seduce him and fails. He compares her to Mary Magdalene and leaves her.
inclusion: Gavaldón was one of the great directors of Mexico's golden age, and this was a prestige production, entered at the 1958 Berlin festival, with two of the country's biggest stars. Its interest is the portrait of the priesthood under the Calles persecution: a priest who serves in secret as a doctor, tends the wounded of both sides and risks exposure to bring the sacraments to the dying. Arturo de Córdova had played priests before, and Félix's hard, glamorous Victoria is a role built for her. The story, from Luis G. Basurto, is lurid melodrama, and its premise is a priest's crime. The San Sebastián festival revived it in its 2019 Gavaldón retrospective.
themes: Two priests stand at either end of the film. The first commits a grave crime against Victoria and drives her from the faith; the second, Federico, lives his priesthood in hiding, keeps his vows when she tries to seduce him and seeks to bring a dying woman to confession. The film sets the faithful priest against the unworthy one, and shows Victoria's hatred of the Church resting on one man's sin. The Cristero war is background: Victoria informs against the rebels, while Federico treats both sides. Whether her final tears become repentance is not clear from the sources.
advisories:
The rape of a young woman by a priest is the premise (reported as taking place off screen).

A brothel setting; a woman's attempt to seduce a priest.

Civil-war violence, including a train hold-up and wounded men.

For adults.

A priest's sexual crime is central; the film sets a faithful priest against it.

title: White Mission
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and established in detail by Diana Arbaiza's 2020 study and the Claretians' own account: a young missionary in Spanish Guinea, his abandoned father turned brutal planter, the father's repentance and death in his son's arms. The reservation is the colonial-nationalist frame. The film opens by praising missionaries for sowing 'religion and the fatherland', presents the natives as childlike, and its key flashback has a missionary cut Our Lady's mantle to make a Spanish flag, then offer the flag back to her. Arbaiza is independent; no contemporary Catholic rating was found.
summary: Juan de Orduña's Spanish missionary melodrama, shot in Guinea: a young priest finds that the brutal planter terrorising the Africans of his mission is his own father.
synopsis: Fr Javier arrives at a Spanish mission in continental Guinea to work under the veteran Fr Urcola, who runs the church and school of a peaceful Christian village. The neighbouring lands belong partly to Brisco, a fugitive Spanish banker who fled the country after a great fraud and now runs a lumber mill with the whip, beating his workers Minoa and Souka. Javier tells him plainly that the Africans hate him because he mistreats them. Brisco is in fact Javier's father, who abandoned him long ago. Brisco burns Urcola's chapel; the old priest rescues a Spanish flag from the fire and explains, in a flashback, how as a young missionary on Annobón he made that flag from altar curtains and the red mantle of the Virgin to turn away a foreign warship. In the end the repentant Brisco dies in his son's arms.
inclusion: Misión blanca was a big popular success in 1946 and was declared of National Interest, with a special medal from the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos for Manuel Luna's Brisco. It was shot partly on location in Spanish Guinea, with Julio Peña as Javier, Jorge Mistral and a young Fernando Rey, and a priest, Fr Olangua, advising on the script. Arbaiza argues that its melodrama, with emotional music, close-ups and sentimental acting, makes the missionaries' sacrifice more convincing than the regime's documentaries managed, and that it quietly criticises colonial exploitation by concentrating it in one villain. The father-son story of sin, rejection and deathbed repentance is the film's real engine. Its picture of Africans, in broken Spanish and as easily led children, has dated badly.
themes: The missionaries are shown living among the people, teaching, baptising and defending them against exploitation; a priest's line that the mission must sometimes save 'the black souls of white men' sums up its moral. Brisco's story is one of conversion: a fugitive and a cruel master, confronted by the son he abandoned, who repents and dies reconciled. Against this sits the film's equation of the Church's mission with Spain's empire, most strikingly in the flashback where Our Lady's mantle is cut up to make a national flag, which the old priest presents as an offering to her.
history: The Claretian missionaries ran most of the Catholic missions in Spanish Guinea from 1883. The Annobón episode is based on Fr Joaquín Juanola, a Claretian who died in Guinea in 1912; according to the Claretian historian Tomás Luis Pujadas, as cited by Arbaiza, he simply pointed out the Spanish flag already flying to a German commander, rather than improvising one under fire.
liberties: Fr Urcola's flag made under fire from a warship dramatises a much smaller incident involving Fr Juanola. Brisco, Javier and the rest are fictional. The film places colonial brutality in the past and in one villain, while forced labour on Guinea's plantations was still common when it was made.
advisories:
Beatings and whipping of African workers; a chapel burned; a deathbed.

Racial caricature typical of its time: African characters speak broken Spanish and are portrayed as childlike.

Suitable for older children and up, with explanation.

The film equates the Catholic mission with Spanish imperial patriotism.

grey.question: The missionary drama is sound: priests serve and defend the Africans, and a cruel colonist repents in his son's arms. But the film fuses the faith with Franco-era imperial nationalism. It opens by praising missionaries for sowing religion and the fatherland together, it portrays Africans as childlike, and its emotional climax has a missionary tear Our Lady's mantle to make a Spanish flag, presented as an act of devotion. Viewers should weigh that use of a sacred object and the patriotic frame.

title: Monsignor Quixote
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred, with identity established (Wikipedia; BAFTA shortlist) and content established through Greene's novel. But the film's handling of Quixote's doubts, of the satirical bishop and of the delirious Mass with communion given to an unbeliever has not been verified against the film itself. If the dialogue has Quixote voicing heterodoxy that goes uncorrected (for example, rejecting hell), move it to REJECT under the editor precedent. If it is faithful to the novel's sympathetic but ambiguous ending, keep it as reservations.
summary: Alec Guinness plays Graham Greene's unworldly Spanish priest, made a monsignor by chance, on a road trip across post-Franco Spain with the Communist ex-mayor he calls Sancho.
synopsis: Father Quixote, parish priest of El Toboso in La Mancha, believes he is a descendant of Cervantes's knight. After he helps a stranded Italian bishop, Rome makes him a monsignor, to the displeasure of his own bishop, who sends him on holiday. He sets out in his old Seat 600, Rocinante, with the town's Communist former mayor, Sancho (Leo McKern). Their arguments about the Church and Marx bring them closer and unsettle each of them. Recalled and suspended by his bishop, Quixote escapes and takes to the road again. He is hurt trying to rescue a statue of Our Lady from a procession where people pin money to her. Sheltered at a Trappist monastery, he rises in delirium and says Mass in the night with no bread or wine, gives communion to Sancho, and dies in his arms.
inclusion: Guinness and Leo McKern are a well-matched pair, and their scenes together are what viewers remember. The film was shot on the real locations of Greene's novel, including the Valley of the Fallen, and Greene himself co-produced it for Thames Television. It was shortlisted for the BAFTA for best single drama, and Guinness for best actor. Greene's story is a comedy of ideas: a believer and a Marxist on holiday, each finding the other more human than his creed allows. Its sympathy is with the old priest, who keeps the old Mass and is an embarrassment to his suspicious bishop. That makes it warmer towards the Church than much of Greene, but its Catholicism is the doubting kind, and its ending raises real questions.
themes: Quixote's faith is simple and sincere. Greene also gives him doubts, and lets the Communist argue his case, so the faith is tested rather than simply affirmed. In the novel the climax is a Mass in the old rite said in delirium, with nothing on the altar, followed by communion given to an unbeliever. It is a moving scene, but it raises plain questions: a Mass without matter is no Mass, and communion is not given to a man outside the faith, yet the scene is presented as an act of love. The bishop who suspends Quixote is drawn satirically. The Spain of the film is post-Franco and post-conciliar, but the story's sympathy lies with the priest who keeps the old ways.
advisories:
Long theological arguments between a priest and a Communist, some left unresolved.

The novel's comic episodes touch on sexual subjects; how the film handles them has not been checked.

The ending shows a Mass said in delirium without bread or wine, and communion given to an unbeliever.

Suitable for adults and older teenagers.

title: Murder in the Cathedral
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-I (1936–59 list on archive.org), a contemporary Catholic judgment. Identity from the BFI. Independent substantive treatment from Wheeler Winston Dixon (Senses of Cinema, 2016) and Tom Birchenough (The Arts Desk, 2015): a faithful, austere film of Eliot's play on the martyrdom of St Thomas Becket (canonised 1173). Eliot was an Anglican, but the subject is a Catholic archbishop who dies defending the liberty of the Church, and nothing in the play contradicts Catholic teaching.
summary: George Hoellering's severe, verse-spoken film of T. S. Eliot's play about the last days and martyrdom of St Thomas Becket, with Eliot himself as the unseen fourth tempter.
synopsis: December 1170. Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, returns from long exile in France to a cathedral city that fears what his return will bring. A new opening scene, written by Eliot for the film, shows the quarrel with King Henry II that drove him abroad. At Canterbury four tempters come to him in turn: one offers him safety and the pleasures of his youth, one power as the King's chancellor again, one an alliance with the barons against the King. The fourth, the most dangerous, urges him to seek martyrdom for the glory it will bring. Becket refuses them all. On Christmas Day he preaches on the meaning of martyrdom. Four knights arrive from the King and demand that he submit. He will not, and they cut him down in his own cathedral.
inclusion: It is one of the very few serious British films about a saint, and one of the strangest. Hoellering, an Austrian émigré who ran London's Academy Cinema, worked closely with Eliot, who recorded the whole play to guide the actors and wrote new scenes. Becket is played by Fr John Groser, a London East End clergyman with no acting experience; Tom Birchenough finds his calm dignity remarkable, and Bosley Crowther, no admirer of the film, praised it in 1952. The chorus of Canterbury women, the stark interiors and the bleak exteriors give the film the severity that Dixon compares to Dreyer and Bergman. It won the production design prize at Venice in 1951. It is static and wordy, and some will find the verse hard going. The 114-minute cut is the director's preferred version.
themes: The film is about what makes a martyr. The fourth temptation, to die for one's own glory, is the heart of it: Becket must die for God and the Church, not for his reputation, and Dixon reads his death as the King's act rather than one Becket contrived. The quarrel is the liberty of the Church against the Crown, and Becket's refusal to yield the rights of his see is presented as fidelity, not pride. The Christmas sermon sets his coming death against the feast of Christ's birth and the martyrs who follow it. Eliot, an Anglo-Catholic, keeps the drama within the Church's own understanding of martyrdom.
history: Thomas Becket (c.1119–1170), Henry II's chancellor, became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162 and resisted the King's claims over the Church. After six years in exile he returned in December 1170 and was murdered in his cathedral by four knights on 29 December. He was canonised by Alexander III in 1173, and Henry did public penance at his tomb.
liberties: The film adds an opening that dramatises the conflict with Henry, who is seen on screen, unlike in the play. At Hoellering's request Eliot cut most of the knights' direct address to the audience after the murder and replaced it with a shorter speech. A church in St John's Wood stood in for Canterbury.
advisories:
The murder at the altar is brief, with one bloody image (BFI rates it PG).

No sexual content or bad language.

Verse dialogue and a slow pace; best for older teenagers and adults.

Legion of Decency A-I.

title: Word and Utopia
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a Jesuit's vocation, missions and preaching, much of it in Vieira's own sermons) and seriously reviewed by independent critics (Rosenbaum, BAMPFA, the São Paulo Mostra). The reservation is framing: the Inquisition trial is the spine, and the film presents Vieira as a 'freethinking' champion of Indians, slaves and New Christians persecuted by the Holy Office, whereas the trial actually turned on his prophetic writings (the Fifth Empire) and Rome later exempted him from the Portuguese tribunal. Vieira is not a canonised subject, so rule (a) does not apply. Subtitles of the trial scenes would show whether the film's case against the Inquisition goes beyond the history.
summary: Manoel de Oliveira's film of the Jesuit preacher António Vieira, three actors playing him across seventy years, built from his own sermons and his trial by the Inquisition.
synopsis: In 1663 the Jesuit António Vieira, once the intimate of King João IV, is summoned before the Portuguese Inquisition at Coimbra. Court intrigue and a misunderstanding have cost him his protection. Before his judges he goes over his life: a boyhood in Brazil and his novitiate at Bahia (Ricardo Trêpa), his first triumphs in the pulpit and his campaign for the Indians of Maranhão (Luís Miguel Cintra). Forbidden by the Inquisition to preach, he goes to Rome, where his sermons make him famous and Queen Christina of Sweden (Leonor Silveira) wants him as her confessor. Homesick, he returns to Portugal, but the new king, Pedro, receives him coldly, and the old man (Lima Duarte) goes back to Brazil, where he dies.
inclusion: Oliveira, who had already made a short tribute to Vieira, here gives the greatest preacher in Portuguese a feature built largely from his own words. Jonathan Rosenbaum notes that the sermons and letters are treated almost as libretti, with settings and period art arranged around them, and that Oliveira, in his nineties, directs his actors with unusual vigour; Renato Berta's photography is rich. The three Vieiras, Trêpa, Cintra and the Brazilian star Lima Duarte, chart youthful zeal, rhetorical mastery and the anger of age. It is demanding: more than two hours of speech, static compositions and little conventional drama. For viewers who want to hear Baroque Catholic preaching at full stretch, nothing else on film comes close.
themes: Vieira's vocation, his sermons and his missions to the Indians are the core, and the preaching is Catholic through and through: Scripture, the Fathers, the duties of kings and masters before God. The film's sympathies lie with his defence of the Indians and of Portugal's converted Jews, and the Inquisition appears as the obstacle. The historical case was narrower: his prophetic speculations on a Portuguese Fifth Empire drew censure, and Rome later freed him from the Portuguese tribunal. The BAMPFA note calls his views on God and prophecy unorthodox; how far the film endorses those prophecies, and how it frames the Holy Office, is the question.
history: António Vieira (1608–1697), born in Lisbon and raised in Bahia, entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1625. Preacher and diplomat to João IV, he led the missions in Maranhão and opposed the enslavement of Indians. Cited by the Inquisition for propositions 'smacking of heresy', chiefly his defence of Bandarra's prophecies of a Fifth Empire, he was held at Coimbra from 1665 to 1667 and forbidden to preach. In Rome he preached before the cardinals and returned with a papal bull exempting him from the Portuguese inquisitor. He died in Bahia.
liberties: Oliveira compresses seventy years into a trial frame and lets the sermons carry the story. The film emphasises Vieira's social causes over the prophetic writings that were the actual matter of his trial. Little else is reported as invented.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content reported.

Long, static and dialogue-heavy; best for adults and older students.

The Inquisition is shown as the persecutor of a reforming priest; the doctrinal content of his trial is underplayed.

title: Pastor Angelicus
decision: PUBLISH: Produced by the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico itself in 1942, and its American version, The Story of the Pope (1946), was classed A-I by the Legion of Decency. Independent treatment: Motion Picture Herald's 1946 review (good, though technically limited) and Cristina Formenti's 2017 study in Schermi. Focus, the British Catholic film review, praised it in 1951. The only question is political: Fascist circles withdrew it in January 1943 for its 'pacifist tendency'. That is history, not a reservation.
summary: The Italian bishops' film office's portrait of Pius XII for his episcopal jubilee, the first feature where a reigning pope appears himself; withdrawn by the Fascist authorities within weeks.
synopsis: The film traces Eugenio Pacelli's life from his Roman boyhood, ordination and legal training through his years as nuncio in Germany and Secretary of State to Pius XI, to the conclave of 1939 and his coronation. It then shows the Pope at work: receiving pilgrims and soldiers in audience, celebrating the great ceremonies of St Peter's, and directing the Church's relief in wartime, including the Vatican's information bureau for prisoners and missing persons. Scenes of the basilica, the Vatican palaces and Raphael's paintings are set to music and the singing of the Sistine Choir. The American version, The Story of the Pope, recut the material with a commentary by Mgr Fulton Sheen, an introduction by Cardinal Spellman and newsreel of the 1946 consistory.
inclusion: Pastor Angelicus matters as the first film made by the Church's own film office about a living pope, and as the first in which a pope appears on screen as himself. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico deliberately released it without names in the credits, so that it would read as the Church's film rather than a director's; the paperwork credits Romolo Marcellini, a documentarist from the Istituto Luce. Formenti shows that it was modelled on The March of Time's Vatican films and aimed at an international audience. Motion Picture Herald admired the Sistine Choir and the material but noted slow movement, poor editing and uneven sound. Focus, reviewing the British release, called it an excellent film essay and urged Catholic groups to ask cinemas to book it. It is a period piece, but a rare one.
themes: The film presents the Pope as father of all the faithful and as a peacemaker above the warring nations. The office of Peter is shown in its liturgy, its audiences and its charity: the Pope receiving soldiers of every nation, the relief and information work of the Holy See, the ceremonies of St Peter's. Focus singled out the scene of wounded soldiers of different countries waiting to be received by the Pope. The title comes from the prophecy of popes attributed to St Malachy, which the film uses as a devotional epithet. Its Catholic content is straightforward and devotional; its political subtext, that the Pope rather than Mussolini spoke for peace, is what got it withdrawn.
history: In December 1941 Luigi Gedda pressed the CCC, the Italian Catholic Action film office, to produce its own feature on Pius XII for his episcopal silver jubilee. The film received its Italian censorship certificate on 17 December 1942 and opened that month, but the Fascist authorities withdrew it on 8 January 1943, reportedly for a 'pacifist tendency'. It circulated in Europe after the war; Chapel Films released the American version in December 1946, and it was shown in France as Pastor Angelicus.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable; suitable for all ages.

Newsreel footage of wartime suffering and wounded soldiers.

The English-language version differs substantially from the Italian original; check which one you are watching.

title: Quo Vadis
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Il Cinema Ritrovato 2024 record of the EYE Filmmuseum print; Wikipedia citing Ricci and Scodel–Bettenworth). Maria Wyke's programme notes, an independent scholarly treatment, describe a film that pushes Sienkiewicz's story to decadent extremes: half-dressed women thrown to Nero's eels with erotic underwater shots, orgies, attempted rapes and lurid martyrdoms, with the Christians emerging only late from the catacombs. The Catholic substance is real but subordinate to Nero's spectacle; the sensual material is a reservation a reader can weigh. The batch lead's 2012 Vatican Library print could not be verified and is omitted.
summary: UCI's lavish silent remake of Sienkiewicz's martyr novel is dominated by Emil Jannings's grotesque Nero and its decadent spectacle; the Christians come into their own only late.
synopsis: In Nero's Rome, the young officer Marcus Vinicius falls in love with Lygia, a Christian hostage in a Roman household, protected by her giant servant Ursus. Vinicius tries to take her by force; she escapes, and his pursuit of her draws him towards the Christians who shelter her. At court, Nero amuses himself with cruelties and banquets, egged on by Poppaea and Tigellinus, while the elegant Petronius watches with irony. Nero has Rome burned and blames the Christians, who are seized from the catacombs and sent to the arena or turned into living torches in his gardens. Lygia is exposed in the arena and saved by Ursus. Petronius and his slave Eunice take their own lives, and Nero's reign collapses.
inclusion: This was one of the most expensive Italian films of its day, an attempt by the Unione Cinematografica Italiana to recover the world market Guazzoni's Quo Vadis had conquered in 1913. Its biggest asset is Emil Jannings, whom Maria Wyke calls a satanic grotesque of a Nero; the New Yorker found him the one thing besides boredom in the film. It was over budget and troubled, with German money forcing in Georg Jacoby as co-director and a lead actor replaced mid-shoot. The New York Times thought it excellent as spectacle but tedious. It failed, and ended its producer's career. A restoration led by the Nederlands Filmmuseum, from two incomplete original negatives and a Dutch tinted print, allows it to be seen today.
themes: Sienkiewicz's novel is a story of conversion and martyrdom: a pagan learns from the Christians he despises, and the Church of Rome under St Peter wins by suffering. On Wyke's account, this film is more interested in the emperor's gaze than in the faith. The Christians appear only when they leave the catacombs, and their martyrdoms are staged as lurid spectacle rather than witness. The arena, the human torches and the Way of the Cross glimpsed in a vision of Christ are there, but the film's energy goes into Nero's palace.
history: Henryk Sienkiewicz published Quo Vadis in 1895–96; it helped win him the Nobel Prize in 1905. The novel draws on Tacitus's account of the fire of Rome in 64 and Nero's persecution of the Christians, and on the tradition of St Peter's martyrdom.
advisories:
Sensual material: half-dressed women thrown into a fountain of eels, with erotic underwater shots; an orgy; attempted rapes.

Lurid martyrdoms in the arena and Christians burned as torches.

The pagan Petronius and Eunice commit suicide.

Adults only.

grey.question: This Quo Vadis keeps the shape of Sienkiewicz's story of conversion and martyrdom, but its emphasis is on Nero's court. Maria Wyke describes erotic scenes with half-dressed women, an orgy, attempted rapes and lurid martyrdoms, with the Christians emerging only late in the film. Viewers should weigh whether the witness of the martyrs survives a production that dwells so long on decadence. Only adults should consider it.

title: The Holy Queen
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred: a life of St Elizabeth of Portugal, the Aragonese princess who became Queen of Portugal, canonised in 1625, made by Rafael Gil in a Spanish-Portuguese co-production. Identity is established by the Spanish and English encyclopaedia entries; the Spanish entry records good reviews and commercial success. But the sources give only an outline, centred on the queen's troubled marriage to King Dinis and a court intrigue, and no contemporary review describing its religious content, nor any Catholic rating, was found. Unverified until the content is checked.
summary: Rafael Gil's Spanish-Portuguese costume picture about St Elizabeth of Portugal, patient wife of an unfaithful king and peacemaker of her kingdom, with Maruchi Fresno.
synopsis: Elizabeth, daughter of the King of Aragon, is married as a girl to King Dinis of Portugal. At the Portuguese court she meets coldness and intrigue, led by the ambitious Nuño de Lara, and she bears with patience the infidelities of her husband, while devoting herself to prayer and to the poor. The film follows her through the troubles of her marriage and of the kingdom, in which she works to make peace within the royal family. Beyond this outline, the sources I could open do not say which episodes of her life and legend the film includes, such as the miracle of the roses, her intervention between her husband and their rebellious son Afonso, or her last years as a Poor Clare tertiary at Coimbra. A fuller synopsis must wait for a viewing or a contemporary review.
inclusion: Reina santa was one of the prestige productions of Spanish cinema in 1947, made by Rafael Gil, who released La fe the same year, for Cesáreo González's Suevia Films, in co-production with Portugal and in separate Spanish and Portuguese versions. Madeleine Carroll was first announced for the title role and withdrew; Maruchi Fresno played the queen, with the Portuguese star António Vilar as King Dinis, Luis Peña as Nuño de Lara and the young Fernando Rey, and a score by Ruy Coelho. The Spanish encyclopaedia entry, citing Diego Galán, records good reviews and strong takings. Its subject, a married saint who was also a queen and a peacemaker, is rare in the cinema.
themes: The life of St Elizabeth offers a model of sanctity in marriage and in public life: fidelity and patience towards an unfaithful husband, charity to the poor, and the work of a peacemaker between king and heir and between kingdoms. The outline the sources give stresses the marriage and the court intrigue; whether the film gives equal weight to her prayer, her charity and her miracles, or treats her mainly as the heroine of a royal melodrama, is not established.
history: Elizabeth of Aragon (1271-1336), great-niece of St Elizabeth of Hungary, married King Dinis of Portugal in 1282. Known for her charity and her repeated reconciliations between Dinis and their son Afonso, she became a Franciscan tertiary after her husband's death and lived beside the Poor Clares at Coimbra. She was beatified in 1516 and canonised by Urban VIII in 1625.
advisories:
The king's infidelities and court intrigue.

Suitable for families, subject to confirmation of the content.

The film's treatment of the saint's religious life has not been checked.

It is listed here pending a check of how it presents her faith, her charity and her miracles, and whether the saint or the royal melodrama is at its centre.

title: Rita of Cascia
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred: a life of St Rita of Cascia, canonised in 1900, made with a priest as ecclesiastical adviser and shot on location at Cascia. Identity is established by the Italian and English encyclopaedia entries and FilmTV.it. But the only descriptions of the content are a one-line plot and two short modern judgments, both of which find the film weak; no contemporary review or Catholic rating was found, and nothing shows how the saint's forgiveness of her husband's killers, her prayer for her sons and her entry into the Augustinian convent are handled. Unverified until the content is checked.
summary: Antonio Leonviola's debut, a modest wartime life of St Rita, the wife and widow of Cascia who forgave her husband's murderers, with Elena Zareschi.
synopsis: In fourteenth-century Umbria, the young Rita longs to become a nun, but at her parents' wish she marries Paolo di Ferdinando, a violent and dishonest man, hoping by patience and prayer to reform him. Her husband is murdered in the feuds of the time, and her two sons grow up determined to avenge their father. Beyond this outline, the sources I could open do not describe how the film handles Paolo's change of heart, Rita's forgiveness of his killers, the deaths of her sons before they could take revenge, her repeated attempts to enter the Augustinian convent at Cascia, or the wound of the thorn and the other miracles of her last years. A fuller synopsis must wait for a viewing or a contemporary review.
inclusion: Rita da Cascia was the first film directed by Antonio Leonviola, who later remade the story as Il suo più grande amore. It was produced by Titanus in 1943, with Elena Zareschi as Rita and Ugo Sasso as Paolo, a screenplay by Celestino Spada and Leonviola, and Fr Vittorino Callisto Vanzin as ecclesiastical adviser; the exteriors were shot at Cascia itself, with local people as extras. Modern judgments are lukewarm: FilmTV.it's editors find it poorly made but lifted by Zareschi's performance, and a viewer's review calls it harmless and anonymous. Its interest lies in its subject, one of the most popular saints in Italy, and in its being one of the few films about her.
themes: St Rita's story is about marriage borne as a cross: a wife's patience and prayer for a violent husband, his conversion, and his murder. Its crux is forgiveness, since Rita pardons her husband's killers and prays that her sons should die rather than commit murder in revenge. It ends with the widow's long-delayed entry into religious life. The outline the sources give covers the vocation, the marriage and the sons' wish for vengeance; whether the film keeps the saint's prayer for her sons, which modern versions often soften, is not established.
history: Margherita Lotti was born at Roccaporena near Cascia around 1381, married young, and was widowed when her husband was killed in a feud. After her two sons died, she entered the Augustinian convent of St Mary Magdalene at Cascia, where she lived for some forty years and received a wound on her forehead from a thorn of the Crucifix. She died in 1457, was beatified in 1627 and canonised in 1900.

A murder and a family feud.

title: Rosa de Lima
decision: GREY: Identity is established (UC3M Cine de movilidad catalogue; Decine21 credits), and the subject, canonised in 1671, raises no hard rule. The only treatment source is Decine21, a present-day Catholic-oriented Spanish site, which cannot make it PUBLISH. A 1962–63 Spanish review or Catholic classification (Hemeroteca Digital BNE, ABC hemeroteca) would settle it.
summary: José María Elorrieta's modest Spanish biography of St Rose of Lima, with María Mahor as the girl who refuses marriage to give her life to God and the poor.
synopsis: The film opens with the arrival in Peru of a Spanish arquebusier in the service of Philip III, and follows the life of his daughter Isabel, called Rosa, born in Lima in the late sixteenth century to him and María de Oliva. Her parents intend her for marriage, but Rosa has privately vowed her virginity to God. She refuses the match and gives herself instead to prayer and to the care of the poor and sick of the city, against the wishes of her family. The film follows her to her early death in Lima in 1617, at about thirty-one, after which the city took her as its patron.
inclusion: Films about St Rose are rare, and this is the main screen biography of the first canonised saint of the Americas. It was a Spanish production made for the Spanish-speaking world, with a script credited to Juan Antonio Verdugo, Elorrieta, Manuel Sebares and César González Ruano, and it made María Mahor's name. What is known of its quality is limited. Decine21, a Spanish site that reviews films from a Catholic standpoint, gives it 4 out of 10 and calls the production humble but dignified; no contemporary review has been found. It suits viewers who want a straightforward, devotional life of a saint whose story is little known outside Latin America, and who can accept the conventions of a low-budget Spanish religious film of its time.
themes: The film is built around a vow of virginity: Rosa refuses the marriage her family intends because she has already given herself to God, and spends herself on prayer and on the poor. That is also the core of her historical cult. According to the Catholic Encyclopedia she received the Dominican habit at about twenty, lived almost as a recluse in a grotto in the family garden and practised extreme penances. How the film handles those penances and her mystical life has not been established from any review. The sources describe a respectful biography; none reports anything contrary to Catholic teaching.
history: Isabel Flores de Oliva was born in Lima in 1586. She took the habit of St Dominic in her twentieth year, lived in seclusion in a small grotto built with her brother's help in the family garden, leaving mainly to visit the Blessed Sacrament, and practised severe fasting and mortification. She died in 1617. Clement IX beatified her in 1667 and Clement X canonised her in 1671, the first saint of the Americas.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content is reported; Decine21 rates it suitable for all ages.

The saint's penances may be shown; how is not documented.

The description rests on short listings; no full review has been found.

title: Mystic Rose
decision: GREY: Identity from Rotten Tomatoes and the Biblioteca Nacional del Perú; content from Sebastián Zavala's Cinencuentro review (independent, substantive) and director interviews (El Comercio, Cinencuentro). Subject canonised 1671. Serious about penance but ambiguous on sanctity, with invented symbolic scenes: a reservation a reader can weigh.
summary: Augusto Tamayo's long, austere Peruvian portrait of St. Rose of Lima's penances and mystical life, which leaves open whether she was a saint or a troubled girl.
synopsis: Lima, early in the seventeenth century. Rosa, daughter of Gaspar and María, refuses the marriage her ambitious mother wants for her and deliberately spoils her looks to avoid it. She also declines to enter a convent, choosing instead to live at home in prayer and penance. She fasts, scourges herself and prays through the night, and her health gives way. She cares for the sick, confronts an old man she believes is the devil, and falls into ecstasy before a crucifix. Several priests counsel and question her, and a woman friend encourages her. Her mother calls her mad. The film is arranged in thematic chapters rather than as a continuous life, and its opening announces it as an interpretation.
inclusion: Tamayo, one of Peru's senior directors, worked on the project for some forty years, and the care shows in its colonial interiors: Sebastián Zavala of Cinencuentro praised its churches and cathedrals, and above all Fiorella Pennano, who carries the film. It is slow, close to two and a half hours, shot with a restless hand-held camera, and its chapters do not always make Rosa's choices clear. Its interest is that it takes the penitential and mystical life seriously as a subject at all. Tamayo, who says he is not a believer, rejects the clinical diagnoses that have been made of her and insists she was not mad. He says most episodes come from documented testimony.
themes: The film puts St. Rose's penances, fasting, scourging and sleepless prayer, at the centre and does not soften them. Tamayo argues that bodily suffering has meant sacrifice, offering and forgiveness in every religious culture, and that modern incomprehension is the problem, voiced in the film by her mother. But he treats Rosa as a human figure, not an object of devotion, and Zavala found the film cool and leaning towards a psychological reading: Rosa appears capricious and manipulative with her parents, and her holiness is played down. Some symbolic scenes are Tamayo's own. Grace is left as one possible explanation among others.
history: Rose of Lima was born in Lima in 1586 and took the name Rose at her confirmation. In her twentieth year she received the Dominican habit and lived in severe penance, with fasting, a spiked crown hidden under roses and an iron chain, while caring for the sick and poor. She died in 1617. Clement IX beatified her in 1667 and Clement X canonised her in 1671, the first saint of the Americas.
liberties: Tamayo calls the film an interpretation rather than a biography and says so on screen. Episodes are grouped by theme, and some are invented symbols, notably a chapter in which Rosa drinks putrefied blood and a slave bears a wound in the place of Christ's. Her baptismal name, Isabel, is never used.
advisories:
Self-scourging and other bodily penances shown at length; the film opens with a warning.

Rosa drinks a sick woman's blood; scenes of illness among hospital patients.

No sexual content reported. For adults and older teenagers.

The film leaves open whether Rosa's mystical life was grace or illness.

grey.question: Mystic Rose takes St. Rose's penances and mystical life seriously and refuses to call her mad, but its director, an unbeliever, presents her as a human figure rather than a saint. The Peruvian critic Sebastián Zavala found it cool, sparing with her holiness, and likely to leave viewers leaning towards illness as the explanation. Some symbolic scenes are invented. Viewers should weigh whether its open question respects her sanctity or undercuts it.
