title: Paul the Apostle
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (St Paul's conversion and the apostolic Church, with Peter, John and Our Lady present) and with no reported doctrinal error, but Peter Chattaway's independent review finds it the weakest of Lux Vide's Bible films: much invented material, above all an invented Sadducee, Reuben, whose wedding night includes nudity (the US distributor recalled the first video release for a censored version), while Paul's own missions are compressed into montages and his martyrdom is not shown. Under the clare-and-francis threshold the inventions do not change the saint's own choices, so not REJECT; the nudity and dilution make it a reservation.
summary: Lux Vide's two-part Acts of the Apostles for Rai, with Johannes Brandrup as Saul turned Paul, padded with invented intrigue and short on Paul's missions.
synopsis: In Jerusalem the young Pharisee Saul (Johannes Brandrup), a pupil of the tolerant Gamaliel (Franco Nero), joins the persecution of the followers of Jesus and approves the stoning of Stephen. His friend Reuben, a Sadducee, later turns against him, and Reuben's young wife Dinah is drawn to the new faith. On the road to Damascus Saul is struck blind; Ananias restores his sight, and he escapes the city by night. The second part follows the Church in Jerusalem under Peter (Ennio Fantastichini), Herod's persecution, and Paul's work with Barnabas (G. W. Bailey) at Antioch and Lystra, his dispute with Peter over eating with Gentiles, and his break with Barnabas. His later journeys pass in montage, and the film ends with his arrival as a prisoner in Rome.
inclusion: Films about the Acts of the Apostles are rare, and this one gives a full three hours to the early Church in Jerusalem, Saul's persecution and conversion, and the first Gentile mission. Its best scenes are the early ones: Gamaliel's counsel, Stephen's death and the Damascus road. It was popular in Italy, drawing over 8.7 million viewers, and Corriere della Sera's Aldo Grasso called the direction honest and expository. Peter Chattaway, who has written more on Bible films than any other critic, is blunter: it is one of the weakest of the Bible Collection, spends far too long on invented characters, and tells rather than shows key events such as Cornelius's baptism. The 1981 Peter and Paul, with Anthony Hopkins, is the better film about the Apostle.
themes: Paul's conversion is presented as a real encounter with the risen Christ, followed by baptism and a life given to preaching him to the Gentiles. Peter appears as head of the Jerusalem Church, and Our Lady is among the disciples. The dispute at Antioch over eating with Gentiles is described rather than shown, and the reconciliation of Jew and Gentile in one Church is the film's concern. Its weakness is proportion rather than doctrine: Paul's letters and theology barely feature, and his martyrdom, the crown of his life in Catholic tradition, is left out.
history: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel, persecuted the Church and consented to the death of St Stephen before his conversion near Damascus (Acts 9). With Barnabas he evangelised Cyprus and southern Galatia, then made further journeys through Asia Minor and Greece. Arrested in Jerusalem, he appealed to Caesar and reached Rome about AD 60. Tradition holds he was beheaded at Rome under Nero.
liberties: Reuben, a Sadducee friend turned enemy, and his wife Dinah, who becomes a Christian, are invented and given much screen time. Pharisees wrestle semi-naked; Herod's execution of Peter's guards is extended; Roman officials encourage a stoning; Barnabas laughs at the Lystrans' acclaim. Paul's journeys after Acts 15 are compressed into montages, and the film ends at Rome without his death.
advisories:
Stonings and Herod's executions of soldiers; persecution violence.

Brief nudity on an invented character's wedding night (removed from the later censored US video); semi-nude wrestling.

Suitable for teenagers and up, or for younger viewers with the censored version.

Much of the drama is invented; Paul's missions and martyrdom are barely covered.

title: Satan Never Sleeps
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and supported by a contemporary pre-1965 Catholic judgment: Legion of Decency A-III in Motion Picture Exhibitor's 1962 alphabetical tables, with the Exhibitor's own review and the AFI Catalog. Reservation: the rape plot and the marriage of the victim to her repentant attacker, which critics (Poague, via Wikipedia) read as leaving her no choice; a weak film by all contemporary accounts.
summary: Leo McCarey's last film casts William Holden and Clifton Webb as missionary priests in 1949 China, harried by a Communist commander who was once a mission boy.
synopsis: In 1949, as the Communists overrun China, young Father O'Banion (William Holden) arrives at a remote mission to relieve the elderly Father Bovard (Clifton Webb). Siu Lan (France Nuyen), a girl whose life O'Banion once saved, follows him there and declares her love, which he rebuffs. Colonel Ho San (Weaver Lee), raised at the mission before he renounced Christianity, wrecks the dispensary, desecrates the chapel and jails the priests for refusing to confess to crimes against the state. With O'Banion tied to a chair, he rapes Siu Lan, who later bears his son. When his superiors order the killing of Christians, his own parents among them, Ho San turns and tries to smuggle the group out. Father Bovard puts on Ho San's coat and cap and draws the pursuers' fire, dying so the others can escape. In Hong Kong O'Banion marries the couple and baptises their child.
inclusion: McCarey made Going My Way and The Bells of St. Mary's, and his last film tries to carry the same pairing of a young and an old priest into the persecution of the Church in Communist China. Its interest is the subject. Few Hollywood films dealt with the harassment and expulsion of missionaries there, and this one shows a desecrated chapel, priests jailed for refusing false confessions, and an old priest who gives his life for others. Webb's dry delivery is the best thing in it. Contemporary judgments were poor. Motion Picture Exhibitor found it over-long, with awkward and embarrassing scenes; the New York Times called it a lacklustre imitation of Going My Way; and the studio's ending, which according to McCarey's biographer replaced his own, is pat. The Legion of Decency classed it A-III, unobjectionable for adults.
themes: The faith is shown under persecution. The priests lose their mission and staff, are imprisoned and threatened with torture for refusing to confess to crimes against the state, and Father Bovard lays down his life so that a mother, her child and his fellow priest may escape. O'Banion keeps his vow of celibacy against Siu Lan's open infatuation, which is played largely for comedy. The ending is a return to the sacraments: Ho San, a lapsed mission boy, comes back to the faith, marries the woman he wronged and has their son baptised. Whether a woman should marry her attacker is the film's real moral problem. It presents the marriage as reparation; the film scholar Leland Poague has argued that it leaves her no real choice.
history: The film is set during the Communist victory in China in 1949. It was based on a story by Pearl S. Buck, The China Story, published as the novel Satan Never Sleeps in 1962, with a screenplay by Claude Binyon and McCarey. Fox shot it in England and Wales, and it opened in London, as The Devil Never Sleeps, and in New York in February 1962.
advisories:
A rape is part of the plot, committed while a priest is tied up nearby; the victim later bears a child.

A chapel is desecrated; priests are threatened with torture; a priest is shot dead.

The Legion of Decency rated it A-III (adults).

The ending has the victim marry her attacker, presented as reparation.

title: Say One for Me
decision: GREY: Priest-centred, with real ministry (a baptism, an alcoholic helped to sobriety, a marriage); Legion of Decency A-II (1958-59), no objection recorded. Content from AFI and Motion Picture Exhibitor (17 June 1959). Reservation: much of the film is set in a cheap nightclub with showgirl numbers, and the faith content is thinner than in Going My Way. Editor may prefer PUBLISH by analogy with Going My Way.
summary: Bing Crosby's third New York priest runs a show-business parish, rescues a drunken songwriter and steers a chorus girl away from a playboy, in a slack CinemaScope musical.
synopsis: Father Conroy (Bing Crosby) has a parish in New York's theatre district, where he says a 2 a.m. Mass for performers. When the old vaudevillian Harry LeMaise has a heart attack, Conroy promises to look after his daughter Holly (Debbie Reynolds). She secretly takes a job as a showgirl in a cheap nightclub, where the entertainer Tony Vincent (Robert Wagner) sets out to seduce her. Conroy keeps watch, has a chorus girl's baby baptised with Tony as godfather, and helps the alcoholic songwriter Phil Stanley (Ray Walston) back to sobriety and work. To separate Tony from Holly he offers him a place on a televised charity show. Tony, conscience-stricken, gives the spot to Phil's new song, and Conroy marries Tony and Holly.
inclusion: It is the last of Crosby's priest films after Going My Way and The Bells of St. Mary's, and it shows why the formula ran out. The parish is loosely modelled on St Malachy's, the actors' church off Broadway, and that is the most interesting thing about it: a priest whose flock is chorus girls, comics and drunks. Motion Picture Exhibitor found it a warm crowd-pleaser; Variety thought something went wrong and Crosby was oddly inhibited; Bosley Crowther called it pleasant. It runs nearly two hours, with Cahn and Van Heusen songs and nightclub routines, and Stella Stevens made her debut in it. It was a hit. As a priest film it is thin, but Conroy's ministry is real.
themes: Conroy is a parish priest whose work is pastoral rather than doctrinal: he moves his Mass times to suit his people, brings an unmarried mother's child to baptism, helps an alcoholic to sobriety and protects a young woman's chastity. The film ends with a church wedding that redeems the playboy's intentions. What is missing is any sense of the supernatural beyond good counsel, the criticism also made of Going My Way, and more of the running time goes to nightclub numbers than to the parish. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II and recorded no objection.
advisories:
Nightclub showgirl numbers with costumes revealing for 1959; a playboy's pursuit of a young woman.

Alcoholism; an unmarried mother.

For teenagers and up. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The priest's bargain with the playboy may strike some as manipulative.

title: The Song of Sister Maria
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a singer's vocation, convent hospital work and death on the missions). Identity is established (Wikipedia, Cervantes Virtual Rabal archive) and the plot by an independent Spanish review (DQVlapeli, which judges it one of the weakest of Gil's religious films) and decine21 (present-day, content only). No contemporary Catholic rating or substantive independent assessment of its religious treatment was found; the 'clandestine recordings' episode raises an unanswered question about obedience. A 1952 Spanish Catholic rating or review would settle it.
summary: Rafael Gil's comedy-drama of a famous singer who becomes a nursing sister, cheerfully bends convent ways to save its hospital, and gives her life on the missions in India.
synopsis: Soledad, a celebrated singer, astonishes her family, the press and the public by giving up her career to enter a convent, where she becomes Sor María de la Asunción. She works in the order's hospital, whose finances are failing, and her unconventional, high-spirited methods at first disconcert her superiors. She brings about a conversion and wins half a million pesetas from a television impresario in exchange for recordings of her voice, which save the hospital. Her goal is a leper settlement in India. There, a local couple are expecting a child; bandits threaten their lives, and Sor María gives her own life so that the newborn can be baptised.
inclusion: It belongs to the cycle of religious films Rafael Gil made with the writer Vicente Escrivá for their company Aspa, alongside La señora de Fátima, La guerra de Dios and Judas' Kiss. The French actress Dominique Blanchar plays the singer-nun, with Francisco Rabal, Pepe Isbert and Julia Caba Alba in support. It received the state's National Interest classification and the first prize of the Sindicato Nacional del Espectáculo. The DQVlapeli reviewer admires Gil's handling of the early comic and pathetic scenes, a false Christmas and the cure of a crippled boy in a wheatfield among them, but finds the Indian third act rushed, under-financed and poorly motivated. Decine21 praises its restraint, Alfredo Fraile's photography and Blanchar. It is an uneven popular piece.
themes: The film's subject is a vocation that costs everything: fame, family approval and finally life. Sor María's religious life is active rather than contemplative, nursing the sick and raising money for the order's hospital, and it ends in missionary self-sacrifice for the baptism of a child, a clear statement of the value the Church places on that sacrament. The weakness is the cheerful view of convent discipline: her methods disconcert her superiors before they approve, and the recordings that save the hospital are made in secret. How the film reconciles this with religious obedience is not recorded.
advisories:
A violent bandit attack and the heroine's death.

Nothing sexual of note is reported.

Suitable for families on the available evidence.

title: St. Patrick: The Irish Legend
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (St Patrick's slavery, vocation, ordination and mission as bishop to Ireland, drawn in part from his Confession and the early Lives by Muirchú and Tírechán), with no sex or language problems. The reservation is its picture of the Church: the main antagonist is a corrupt British bishop, Quentin, who tries to have Patrick excommunicated after he refuses to collect church taxes, and Patrick's churches are shown accommodating clan customs, a pattern that plays to the popular myth of a free Celtic Church set against a grasping institution. Critics (Variety, VideoHound) and Alan Bates's biographer judge it historically careless. A weighable reservation, not a heterodox thesis.
summary: A Fox Family television life of St Patrick, with Patrick Bergin as the slave turned bishop and Malcolm McDowell as a scheming British churchman.
synopsis: In fifth-century Roman Britain, Patrick, son of the decurion Calpurnius (Alan Bates) and Concessa (Susannah York), is seized at sixteen by Irish raiders and sold as a slave to a harsh Druid chieftain. Herding animals for six years, he turns to prayer, and a vision tells him a ship is waiting. He escapes home, but dreams of the Irish calling him back. He trains for the priesthood in Gaul and returns to Ireland as its first bishop (Patrick Bergin), facing the Druids, winning converts such as the boy Benignus and founding churches. At home in Britain, Bishop Quentin (Malcolm McDowell) regards the Irish as heathens, suspects Patrick of founding a church of his own, and moves to have him excommunicated when he will not collect the British church's dues.
inclusion: There are very few films about St Patrick, and this one covers the essentials of his own account: the raid, the years of slavery and prayer, the escape after a vision, the call back to the people who had enslaved him. It was shot on Irish locations, with music by Inon Zur and contributions from The Chieftains and Clannad, and Patrick Bergin gives the saint a quiet authority. The Dove Foundation's reviewer found its picture of faith growing under trial worthwhile. Other critics were cool: Variety praised the cast and scenery but called it a well-meaning, absurd costume drama, VideoHound found it bland, and Alan Bates's biographer Donald Spoto said it had no historical accuracy and treated Patrick chiefly as a wonder-worker.
themes: The film's strength is Patrick's conversion in slavery and his choice to return as a missionary to his captors, which is the heart of his own Confession. Prayer, visions and the courage to face the Druids carry the story, and the Dove reviewer notes its emphasis on salvation through Christ's sacrifice and God's mercy. The weakness is its Church. The British clergy are corrupt and unloving, Patrick is set against them over money, and his accommodation of clan customs is presented as a virtue against them. Rome and the Pope do not figure. Patrick's real complaint against his British elders, in the Confession, concerned a sin of his youth, not taxes.
history: Patrick, a Romano-Briton of the fifth century, was captured at sixteen and spent six years as a slave in Ireland before escaping. Ordained, he returned as a bishop and spent the rest of his life evangelising the Irish. His Confession, written late in life, answers charges brought by church elders in Britain. Muirchú and Tírechán wrote the first Lives in the seventh century.
liberties: Bishop Quentin and the tax dispute are invented; the film turns the elders' charges mentioned in Patrick's Confession into a corrupt prelate's vendetta. Patrick's miracles are staged freely from the later legends. The Roman connection of his mission is omitted.
advisories:
A raid with several killed and bloodied bodies; Patrick's capture and enslavement; Druid menace.

No sexual content or bad language.

Approved for 12+ by the Dove Foundation; suitable for older children.

Church authority is shown mostly through a corrupt British bishop; the history is loose.

title: St. Wenceslas
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Wikipedia citing ČSFD and Czech Radio; the Czech Government Office and Czech Radio on the 2010 restoration). Content is known only in outline: St Wenceslas raised a Christian by his grandmother St Ludmila, opposed by his mother Drahomíra and a plotter, murdered by his brother Boleslav. Official sources say it stresses Czech statehood and peace (with the Germans, per the title of Petr Kopal's Cinepur article, not opened). No independent assessment of its religious treatment was found. A Czech critical study (Kopal 2009; Filmový přehled's 'Saint Wenceslas in film', which returned 403) would settle it.
summary: Czechoslovakia's costly millennium epic of the martyr-duke St Wenceslas, raised in the faith by St Ludmila and murdered by his brother Boleslav.
synopsis: Wenceslas is brought up as a Christian by his grandmother Ludmila, while his mother Drahomíra holds to the old gods. After his father's death, a schemer named Skeř stirs up Drahomíra, Wenceslas's younger brother Boleslav and the duke of Zlič against Ludmila and Wenceslas, and Ludmila is murdered. Wenceslas comes to the throne and rules as a Christian prince, seeking peace with his German neighbours, and the film stages great battles with thousands of extras. Boleslav finally kills his brother. Afterwards, according to the plot summaries, Boleslav regrets what he has done.
inclusion: St. Wenceslas was the most expensive Czech film yet made: a state-backed epic for the thousandth anniversary of the duke's death, with 5,000 extras, castle sets built at the Strahov stadium, location shooting in the Šumava forest and at Křivoklát, and a cast that included Vera Baranovskaya, Pudovkin's Mother, as Ludmila. Zdeněk Štěpánek plays Wenceslas. It arrived in April 1930, a silent film just as sound took over, without the orchestral score by Oskar Nedbal and Jaroslav Křička that had been planned, and it flopped; most of its audience were schoolchildren. A 1971 reconstruction was supervised by Kolár himself. In 2009 the lost score was found in Czech Radio's archives, and in 2010 the restored film was shown with it, live, at the Rudolfinum.
themes: The film's subject is a martyr-king: a Christian prince formed by a saintly grandmother, opposed by pagan and political enemies within his own family and killed by his brother. Both Wenceslas and Ludmila were venerated as martyrs long before 1965. The official accounts of the 2010 restoration say the film puts strong emphasis on Czech statehood and peace, and the title of Petr Kopal's article suggests that peace with the Germans was its political theme. How far the faith is the motive of the drama, rather than national history, is not documented.
history: Wenceslas, born probably in 903, was raised a Christian by his grandmother St Ludmila, murdered in 921 at the instigation of his pagan mother Drahomíra. He ruled Bohemia as duke, placed it under German protection and favoured Latin-rite clergy. He was murdered by his brother Boleslav at Stará Boleslav, probably on 28 September 935, and his relics were moved to St Vitus in Prague. He became patron of Bohemia.
advisories:
Battle scenes, the murder of Ludmila and the killing of Wenceslas.

Silent; the 2010 restoration carries the original orchestral score.

Suitable for older children and up.

grey.question: St. Wenceslas tells the life and martyrdom of the Bohemian duke, raised in the faith by St Ludmila and murdered by his brother, in a costly state-funded epic of 1930. Its outline is known, and official accounts say it stresses Czech statehood and peace with the Germans. No independent critic has yet been found who describes how it treats Wenceslas's faith and death. A Czech critical study of the restored version would settle whether the saint or the national myth is its centre.

suitability.note: Battle scenes and the murders of Ludmila and Wenceslas are staged with restraint, and the film is silent and long. Children who like history and knights will cope; younger ones will lose the thread.

doctrine: Wenceslas was killed on 28 September 935 as he went to Mass, and the Church counts him a martyr although he was killed by his brother for political as well as religious reasons. His feast is 28 September. His grandmother St Ludmila, who taught him the faith, was strangled in 921 and is also honoured as a martyr. Wenceslas favoured the Latin rite and German priests and placed Bohemia under the protection of the German king, which the Catholic Encyclopedia records. He is the patron of Bohemia. The film's 1929-30 date marks the thousandth anniversary of his death as then reckoned. Methodius, who appears in the cast, was the Apostle of the Slavs with his brother Cyril; Hadrian II approved their Slavonic liturgy in 867-869, and Wenceslas's period saw tension between the Slavonic and Latin rites.
production: The Czechoslovak government made the film part of the 1929 millennium celebrations and lent the producers 1 million crowns, and another million when filming nearly stalled. Prime Minister František Udržal also supplied army equipment and personnel. Jan S. Kolár directed and co-wrote it, and five cameramen shot it, among them Otto Heller. It had more than a hundred principals and about 5,000 extras, and was called the most expensive Czech film to date. Shooting began in September 1929, moved indoors in December and took 82 days. A 40-piece orchestra played at the premiere in April 1930, since plans to record the music failed. It was not a commercial success. František Balšán reconstructed it in 1971, the lost score was found in Czech Radio's archive, and it was shown with live orchestra at the Rudolfinum on 28 September 2010.

title: The Awakening
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a missionary sister's vocation, obedience and charity). The contemporary Italian Catholic notice (Segnalazioni cinematografiche vol. 40, 1956, via Cinematografo) judged the very delicate subject not handled adequately or convincingly and called for more discretion. Legion of Decency A-II (Awakening (Ital.), 1957-58). Reservation, stated.
summary: Anna Magnani plays a missionary nun sent to close a failing island convent who reopens its school instead, and grows too attached to an abandoned boy.
synopsis: After twenty years in the African missions, Sister Letizia (Anna Magnani) is sent to an island in the Gulf of Naples to wind up a struggling convent, close it and take its last nuns back to the mother house. Offers for the land come quickly. Instead she takes pity on Salvatore, a fatherless boy whose mother Assunta (Eleonora Rossi Drago) means to leave him behind to go away with Peppino (Antonio Cifariello), who will not have the child. Against her superiors' wishes Letizia takes in Salvatore and other children and reopens the convent school. Her love for the boy grows possessive, and the other sisters notice. Recalled, she plans to take him with her, until the Mother Superior's words, and the boy himself, show her she must let him go. She goes to Naples and persuades Peppino to marry Assunta and take Salvatore in.
inclusion: The film is a vehicle for Magnani, and her energy carries it: a forceful nun with years of mission work behind her who cannot leave a problem alone. Mario Camerini directs from a story by Cesare Zavattini and Camerini, and Gianni Di Venanzo photographed it; Magnani won a Nastro d'Argento for the part. Its subject, rarely handled, is maternal feeling in a consecrated woman, and the danger that charity turns into possession. The contemporary notice in Segnalazioni cinematografiche, the Italian Catholic film office's review, was unconvinced: it found the delicate subject handled neither adequately nor convincingly, wanted more discretion, and thought the role did not suit Magnani's temperament, for all her spontaneity and passion. Columbia handled it in Italy, and it reached the US as The Awakening.
themes: Religious life is treated as a real vocation with real demands. Letizia's virtues, zeal, pity and practical energy, lead her into disobedience: she ignores her instructions and keeps the convent open on her own authority. Her love for Salvatore then becomes an attachment that draws her from her duties. The ending restores order: counselled by the Mother Superior, she gives the boy up for his own good and works to reunite him with his mother within a marriage. So the film closes on obedience and self-denial. What the Catholic reviewer doubted was not that conclusion but the handling of a nun discovering herself as a mother.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content reported.

A child is abandoned by his mother; emotional scenes.

For older children and up. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

A nun disobeys her superiors and becomes possessively attached to a child; the film resolves this through obedience.

title: Tepeyac
decision: GREY: Identity is established (Il Cinema Ritrovato 2017 record of the Filmoteca UNAM 2K restoration; UNAM Gaceta; Wikipedia citing Wilt and Schroeder Rodríguez). Content is established by Shari Kizirian's San Francisco Silent Film Festival essay and the UNAM restorers: a 1917 frame story enclosing a reverent re-enactment of the 1531 apparitions, based on Becerra Tanco's account. No independent assessment of its religious treatment exists. Juan Diego (beatified 1990) is a character, not the subject: rule (a) does not apply, and he must not be called saint or blessed.
summary: Mexico's oldest surviving fiction feature: a woman praying to Our Lady of Guadalupe for her missing fiancé reads the story of the 1531 apparitions, which the film re-enacts.
synopsis: Lupita Flores is engaged to Carlos Fernández, a diplomat who has to sail for Europe during the war. News comes that his ship has been sunk by a German submarine. Lupita prays to Our Lady of Guadalupe for his safety and, unable to sleep, reads the story of the apparitions. The film then tells it: in December 1531 the Virgin appears to the Indian Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac and asks for a church to be built there. Bishop Juan de Zumárraga doubts him and asks for a sign. The Virgin sends Juan Diego to gather roses in winter; when he opens his tilma before the bishop, her image is on it. Back in the present, Carlos turns out to have survived, and the couple visit the Basilica of Guadalupe on 12 December.
inclusion: Tepeyac matters first as history. Made by Films Colonial in 1917, when the war had cut off European and American imports, it is the oldest surviving feature-length fiction film from Mexico and the first Mexican film about Guadalupe. The writer José Manuel Ramos and the painter Carlos E. González had little experience and modest equipment, and the frame story is simple melodrama. The apparitions are staged as a pious re-enactment based, according to the Filmoteca UNAM, on Luis Becerra Tanco's seventeenth-century account and Ignacio Manuel Altamirano's La fiesta de Guadalupe. It also preserves documentary images: a procession to Tepeyac carrying the banner Hidalgo raised in 1810. The Filmoteca UNAM's digital restoration, with a score by José María Serralde, cleaned some 49,000 frames by hand.
themes: The film's Catholic content is direct. A woman in danger of losing the man she loves turns to Our Lady of Guadalupe, and her prayer is answered; the framing makes the 1531 story a lesson in trust. The apparition is told as the tradition tells it: the Virgin asks for a church, the bishop asks for a sign, and the roses and the image on the tilma give it. Shari Kizirian notes that the film presents what many believe to be historical fact. The film was made in the year of Mexico's anticlerical constitution, when the cult was politically charged.
history: According to the tradition, the Virgin appeared to Juan Diego at Tepeyac, near Mexico City, in December 1531 and left her image on his cloak as a sign for Bishop Zumárraga. Kizirian's essay outlines later Church history: an inquiry in 1666, approval in the eighteenth century and the title 'Empress of the Americas' in 1945. The hill had been a sanctuary of the Aztec goddess Tonantzin. Juan Diego was beatified in 1990 and canonised in 2002.

A detailed review of the restored Filmoteca UNAM version, or a reading of its intertitles, would settle it.

title: The Big Fisherman
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-I (1958-59), and the dialogue (English, read 2026-10-12) removes the main reservation. Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi is given in full, with Christ's answer naming him the rock on which he will build his Church, promising that the gates of hell will not prevail and giving him the keys of the kingdom. The Sermon on the Mount, the Our Father, John the Baptist's rebuke of Antipas and his death, a healing by Christ and a healing by Peter in the holy name are all dramatised. The invented Arabian plot is long, but Peter's office is not left undeveloped, and nothing contrary to Catholic teaching was found.
summary: Frank Borzage's last film, a three-hour Lloyd C. Douglas epic in which Howard Keel's Simon Peter becomes Christ's chief disciple while an Arabian princess plots to kill Herod Antipas.
synopsis: Fara (Susan Kohner), a princess half Arab and half Jewish, learns that her father is Herod Antipas (Herbert Lom), who abandoned her mother. After her mother's death she vows revenge and rides to Galilee disguised as a boy. Robbed of her horse, she is taken in by Simon (Howard Keel), a big, self-reliant fisherman sceptical of the preacher from Nazareth. John the Baptist, soon imprisoned and beheaded for rebuking Antipas, points her to Jesus, whose teaching against vengeance she resists. Simon becomes Jesus' chief disciple and confesses him as the Christ. When Fara has her chance to kill Antipas, she remembers Christ's words and lowers the knife. Peter takes her back to Arabia, where he heals a jealous prince who later breaks his promise to reform and dies. Fara's suitor Voldi (John Saxon) becomes king; she will not marry him, and sails for Galilee to carry on Christ's work.
inclusion: Borzage was one of Hollywood's great romantic directors, and this was his last film: a 70mm Panavision production released by Disney's Buena Vista, with Oscar nominations for its photography, costumes and art direction. Motion Picture Exhibitor's reviewer was impressed by its scale and by religion presented in palatable form. Most critics were not: Variety called it pious but plodding, and Halliwell leaden. Keel makes a good physical Peter, the fisherman who trusts his own strength until he learns to trust Christ. The trouble is proportion: Lloyd C. Douglas's invented Arabian romance takes most of the running time. But the Gospel scenes, when they come, are given whole and without hedging, Peter's confession and commission above all. The Legion of Decency classed it A-I.
themes: Peter's conversion is the spiritual line: from self-reliance to dependence on Christ, from fisherman to the disciple called to be a fisher of men. The film gives his confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Christ's reply in full: Peter is the rock, the Church will be built on him, hell will not prevail against it, and he receives the keys. Christ's teaching against revenge, from the Sermon on the Mount, is the turning point of Fara's story, and her renunciation of vengeance is the film's main moral act. Peter prays for a healing and later heals a prince in God's name; the prince breaks his vow to reform and dies. The film ends before the Passion, so neither the Cross nor the Resurrection is shown.
liberties: Fara, Voldi and the whole Arabian plot are Douglas's inventions. They grow from a historical fact: Herod Antipas married a daughter of the Nabataean king Aretas IV and divorced her for Herodias. The Gospel events are compressed and seen through Peter and Fara, and Peter's journey to Arabia and his healing of a prince there are invented.
advisories:
Fights and deaths; John the Baptist's execution, not shown graphically.

A chaste romance subplot.

For families, though very long. The Legion of Decency rated it A-I.

Most of the story is invented, and the film ends before the Passion and Resurrection.

title: The End of the Affair
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a vow to God, a priest's direction, a secret Catholic baptism, a conversion) and passed A-II by the Legion of Decency (1954-55). The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the reservation and refines it: the affair is told with sympathy and never named as sin by the priest, Sarah is not shown receiving any sacrament and dies without a priest, her last letter speaks loosely of the lovers being part of God, and no miracle follows her death. In its favour, the vow is kept, the priest's counsel is sound, the childhood baptism is kept, and Bendrix ends conceding God's existence. Treatment established by AFI, Sterritt (TCM) and Schwartz.
summary: Deborah Kerr plays Graham Greene's adulteress who, believing her lover killed in an air raid, vows to give him up if God spares him, and is held by the promise.
synopsis: In London during the flying-bomb raids, the writer Maurice Bendrix (Van Johnson) is having an affair with Sarah Miles (Deborah Kerr), wife of the civil servant Henry (Peter Cushing). A bomb wrecks his flat; Sarah, finding him under a fallen door and thinking him dead, prays and promises God to give him up if he lives. He walks in, and she leaves him without explanation. A year later the jealous Bendrix hires a detective, Parkis (John Mills), who obtains her diary. It records her vow, her visits to a priest, and her talks with Smythe, an atheist orator whose hatred of God convinces her that God exists. She resolves to break the vow, then promises Henry she will not leave him. Bendrix pursues her through the rain to a church. She falls ill and dies; her mother reveals she was secretly baptised a Catholic, and her last letter declares her belief.
inclusion: Greene's novel is one of the central Catholic novels of the century, and this first film of it keeps its spine: a vow made in desperation that turns out to bind, and a woman drawn to God against her own inclinations. Deborah Kerr was widely praised. Van Johnson was miscast, as Greene himself said, and Columbia's recut of Dmytryk's flashback structure leaves the film talky. Bosley Crowther found it muddy and Sarah irrational, while Picturegoer called it distinguished and provocative. David Sterritt, writing for TCM, thinks it tame beside Neil Jordan's 1999 remake but more thoughtful than most religious films of its day. It is the version for anyone who wants Greene's story without the remake's sexual explicitness.
themes: The film takes seriously the idea that a promise made to God in terror binds. Sarah, who says she is not a Catholic, keeps her vow without knowing why. The priest first asks why she should keep a vow made to a God she does not believe in, then reminds her that God gave her free will to use for him or against him; later he tells her that one moment of acknowledging God was the first step of a long journey, and that to seek God is already to have found him. Smythe's hatred convinces her that God exists. The film keeps Greene's revelation that her mother had her baptised a Catholic at two. Her last letter professes belief in loose words, and Bendrix ends conceding that God exists while asking for time.
liberties: Lenore Coffee's script reorders Greene's flashbacks, and Columbia recut the film again after shooting. The sexual side of the affair is softened. The miracles after Sarah's death, including the healing of Smythe's disfigurement, are omitted; his affliction is mentioned but nothing follows. Bendrix's reluctant turn toward belief is reduced to a few closing lines.
advisories:
An adulterous affair is the starting point; it is treated sympathetically but not explicitly, and the priest never addresses it.

Wartime bombing; a woman's illness and death.

For adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The vow is presented as binding and as the work of grace, but Sarah is not shown receiving any sacrament, and her last letter's language about God is loose.

Sarah Miles promises God to give up her lover if he survives a bomb, keeps the vow against her own wishes, seeks out a priest, and comes to belief; the film keeps Greene's revelation that she was secretly baptised a Catholic as a child. title: The Fighting 69th
decision: GREY: The Legion of Decency classed it A-I, and Film Daily's January 1940 review calls it an outstanding war picture whose second strand is a finely etched study of Fr Duffy, played reverently by Pat O'Brien. The chaplain drives the redemption of the coward Plunkett. The open question is scope: the film is first a regimental saga and patriotic melodrama, and the sources do not show whether Duffy's ministry is presented in sacramental Catholic terms or as generic chaplaincy. Precedent (Men of Boys Town) rejects priest-led films whose subject is not religious; this one is closer to the line. A transcript would settle it.
summary: Warner Bros.' First World War saga of New York's Irish regiment, in which Fr Francis Duffy (Pat O'Brien) refuses to give up on a cowardly braggart (James Cagney).
synopsis: When America enters the war, Jerry Plunkett, a cocky New Yorker, joins the 69th Infantry, the old Irish regiment, sneering at its traditions and boasting that he will beat the Germans alone. In his first action he panics. Fr Francis Duffy, the regimental chaplain, believes the man can change and persuades Major 'Wild Bill' Donovan to give him another chance. On a night patrol Plunkett betrays the squad's position and several men are killed, including two brothers of Sergeant Big Mike Wynn. He is court-martialled and sentenced to death. Duffy visits him in his cell and refuses to help him escape. A German shell wrecks the prison; Plunkett frees himself, pulls Duffy from the rubble and watches him tend the wounded. He returns to the line, works a mortar for Wynn's crew, and dies throwing himself on a grenade to save Wynn.
inclusion: This is one of the classic Warner Bros. pictures of the period, with Cagney and O'Brien in their familiar pairing, George Brent as Donovan and Jeffrey Lynn as the poet Joyce Kilmer, and Tony Gaudio's photography of the battle scenes. Film Daily ranked it with the best war pictures made and praised O'Brien as born to play Duffy reverently and humanly. Later critics are cooler: Dennis Schwartz calls it a sentimental recruiting-poster account, sugary and patriotic, with exciting battle scenes and a fine Cagney breakdown. Its interest here is Fr Duffy, a real priest whose statue stands in Times Square, shown as a chaplain who will not give up on a soul. It suits those who enjoy old-fashioned war films with a priest at their moral centre.
themes: Duffy is the film's conscience. He sees good in a man everyone else has written off, argues for his second chance, visits him under sentence of death, refuses to connive at desertion, and keeps ministering to the wounded under shellfire. Plunkett's change of heart follows from seeing that example, and the film presents his self-sacrifice as redemption. The regiment's Irish Catholic identity is part of its colour, and Kilmer, a Catholic convert, is among the characters. What the sources do not show is how explicitly Catholic Duffy's ministry is: whether confession, absolution or the last rites are shown, or whether his role is that of a generic chaplain.
history: Fr Francis P. Duffy (1871-1932), a Canadian-born priest of the Archdiocese of New York, was chaplain to the 69th New York (165th Infantry) in France and was much decorated. William Donovan commanded a battalion; the poet Joyce Kilmer, a sergeant, was killed in July 1918. Training at Camp Mills, the Rouge Bouquet dugout collapse and the Ourcq crossing are drawn from the regiment's history. Duffy's statue stands in Duffy Square, Times Square.
liberties: Plunkett is fictional, and his cowardice-and-redemption story, the court-martial and the shell that frees him are inventions. The film compresses the regiment's campaigns and shapes them around his personal story.
advisories:
Extensive battle violence and deaths; a soldier killed by a grenade.

A death sentence for cowardice.

Suitable for older children and up.

Open question: whether the film's religion is specifically Catholic or a general patriotic piety.

grey.question: Fr Duffy is the moral centre of this war film: he refuses to give up on a coward, visits him under sentence of death and leads him, by example, to a redemptive death. But the film is first a patriotic regimental saga, and the sources do not show how Catholic Duffy's ministry is on screen - whether confession or the last rites appear, or whether he is simply a good chaplain. Viewers should judge whether the faith is the film's substance or its colour.

title: The Garden of Allah
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency classified it A-I (unobjectionable for general patronage, 1936–37 list), the contemporary pre-conciliar Catholic judgment. Identity and plot from Wikipedia (citing Thomson and Greene) and the Legion list; independent treatment from Graham Greene (Spectator, 1936, via Wikipedia), Sister Celluloid and Silver Screenings. A Trappist who fled his monastery marries without telling his wife; when his past is discovered she lets him return to make reparation. Vows upheld. The romance is foregrounded and the film is generally judged weak; stated in the prose.
summary: Selznick's Technicolor desert romance: Marlene Dietrich marries Charles Boyer, not knowing he is a Trappist who has broken his vows, and lets him go back.
synopsis: After her father's death, Domini Enfilden visits the convent where she was raised, and the Mother Superior suggests the solitude of the Sahara. At a Trappist monastery in Tunisia, Brother Antoine, the only monk who knows the secret of the house's famous liqueur, has fled. On a train Domini meets a troubled stranger who calls himself Boris Androvsky. In the desert he shows a strange hostility to religion, but they fall in love, and Father Roubier, uneasy, marries them. On their honeymoon caravan they rescue a lost patrol, and an officer recognises Boris as the runaway monk. Boris confesses his past and his vows. Domini, who loves him, lets him go back to the monastery to make reparation, and they part at its gate.
inclusion: The Garden of Allah is remembered for its colour. It was one of the first features in three-strip Technicolor, and the cinematographers received a special Academy Award; Max Steiner's score was nominated. As drama it is generally thought a failure. Graham Greene admired its surreal look and mocked its 'superhumanly pious' Church. Modern reviewers are blunt: Silver Screenings calls it a mess with miscast leads and stilted dialogue, though Basil Rathbone and C. Aubrey Smith are good; Sister Celluloid enjoys it as gorgeous, ridiculous romance. Its interest here is that a big Hollywood studio made a love story whose ending sends the hero back to the cloister because his vows bind him.
themes: The story turns on the permanence of solemn vows. Boris has fled the Trappists and lives in torment, hostile to the faith he has betrayed. His marriage to Domini, made by a priest who does not know his past, cannot stand, and the film does not pretend otherwise: once the truth is out, Domini, raised by nuns and herself devout, gives him up so that he can return and do penance. The film's sympathy is with the lovers, and the cloister is a sacrifice rather than a home, but the Legion found nothing objectionable in that resolution.
history: Robert Hichens published The Garden of Allah in 1904, and it became a bestseller. It had already been filmed in 1916 and 1927 before Selznick's version, the third feature made in the new three-strip Technicolor process, with a script by W. P. Lipscomb and Lynn Riggs.
advisories:
A love story between a woman and a runaway monk who has hidden his vows; an invalid marriage, treated with restraint.

A tense scene with a dancer and her jealous lover; desert hardship.

Rated A-I by the Legion of Decency; suitable for older children and up.

title: The Left Hand of God
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-II, and AFI records the Production Code condition that Carmody is never shown hearing confessions or saying Mass. The dialogue (Portuguese subtitles, read 2026-10-12) settles the reservation in the film's favour: he refuses absolution to a dying man and leads only common prayers, declines to say Mass, performs none of the pending weddings or baptisms, calls his imposture a sacrilege, and submits to whatever the Church decides. The bishop's envoy rebukes him for letting a 'miracle' story grow, and the ruling to leave in priest's dress is framed as protecting the people's faith while he goes to judgement.
summary: Humphrey Bogart plays an American flier who escapes a Chinese warlord by posing as a dead priest at a remote mission, and finds the role changing him.
synopsis: China, 1947. James Carmody (Humphrey Bogart), an American pilot who has spent years in the service of the warlord Mieh Yang (Lee J. Cobb), escapes by taking the identity of a dead priest, Father O'Shea, and arrives at a Catholic mission as its new priest. Pleading that his chalice and vestments were lost, he avoids the sacraments; the mission doctor and his wife (E. G. Marshall, Agnes Moorehead) depend on him, and the nurse Anne Scott (Gene Tierney) falls in love with a man she believes is a priest. He confesses the truth to a Methodist minister and writes to the bishop. When Yang comes for him and threatens the villages, Carmody stakes his life on a game of dice and wins their safety. The bishop's envoy, Father Cornelius, rebukes him and orders him to leave still dressed as a priest and face judgement elsewhere.
inclusion: It is a star vehicle and an adventure, but its subject is what a priest is. Bogart, near the end of his career, plays a hard man who takes up the cassock as a disguise and grows into what it stands for, without the film pretending that a disguise makes a priest. To win Production Code approval the studio agreed that Carmody would never be shown hearing confessions, saying Mass or doing anything sacrilegious for a layman, and the script keeps to it with some care. Franz Planer's colour photography is handsome. Critics were cool: Crowther found it lacking credibility, the Monthly Film Bulletin disliked its mock religiosity, and the dice game strains belief. The New Yorker thought Bogart did a fine job.
themes: The film is about the difference between the office and the man. Carmody is not a priest and knows it: at a dying man's bed he gives no absolution and leads only the Our Father and Hail Mary, he finds excuses not to say Mass, and the weddings and baptisms waiting for him are never performed. The Methodist minister he confides in tells him he has offended the Church and must write to his bishop. After the dice game he insists there was no miracle, only luck, and that nothing he did had any authority. The bishop's envoy calls the imposture a sacrilege and doubts his sincerity for letting a miracle story grow. The ruling that he keep the cassock until he leaves is made to spare the people's faith, not to excuse him.
advisories:
Warlord violence, killings and threats; a tense game of dice for lives.

A nurse falls in love with a man she believes to be a priest; nothing improper occurs.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

A layman impersonates a priest throughout; he administers no sacrament, and the imposture is called a sacrilege.

title: The Miracle
decision: GREY: The Marian legend frames the film and is told straight; Legion of Decency A-II (Motion Picture Exhibitor Servisection; Legion list 'Miracle (War.) A-II'). The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the frame (a habited 'Teresa' seen in the convent while she is away, the empty pedestal and drought, her prayer for forgiveness, her return and the rain) and corrects the plot: she is a postulant without vows, and her gypsy lover is shot before the wedding, so there is no marriage. Reservation unchanged: two hours of sympathetic romance, her open denunciation of Christianity, and religious life barely seen.
summary: Carroll Baker plays a Spanish postulant who runs off after a British officer while Our Lady takes her place, in Warner Bros.' Technicolor version of the legend.
synopsis: Salamanca, 1812. Teresa (Carroll Baker), a postulant at the convent of Miraflores, nurses a wounded British officer, Michael (Roger Moore), and falls in love. After praying for a sign she follows him; behind her the convent's statue of the Virgin vanishes from its pedestal, a figure in Teresa's habit is seen in her place, and drought follows. Teresa is taken in by gypsies and turns against her faith; Guido (Vittorio Gassman) means to marry her, but is shot before the wedding. In Madrid she becomes a celebrated singer, courted by a bullfighter who dies in the ring and by an old count. Believing she brings death to those she loves, she meets Michael in Brussels before Waterloo, sends him away, prays in a church for the first time since her flight and asks a priest for help. She returns to Miraflores, kneels at the empty pedestal, and the rain comes.
inclusion: Karl Vollmoeller's wordless spectacle The Miracle, staged by Max Reinhardt, was one of the theatrical sensations of the century, and Warner Bros. turned it into a Napoleonic romance in Technirama, produced by Henry Blanke after his success with The Nun's Story. The legend at its heart, the Virgin taking the place of a runaway nun, is a medieval Marian tale. The film keeps its frame: the empty pedestal, the drought, the return and the restored statue. Between them come two hours of gypsies, bullfights and Waterloo. Critics were harsh, and the Monthly Film Bulletin called it a cloying confection. Motion Picture Exhibitor thought it had something for everyone. Elmer Bernstein's score and Ernest Haller's colour photography are handsome.
themes: The legend is about Mary's motherly care for a sinner: she covers the runaway's absence so the community is spared scandal, and waits for her return. The film keeps that shape. The Mother Superior tells Michael that Teresa is now the bride of Christ, and a habited figure is glimpsed in the cloister while Teresa is far away. Her flight is a fall, and her declaration among the gypsies that she is no Christian, and that Christianity betrays its believers, is its lowest point. In Brussels she prays to be forgiven and helped to atone, says a Hail Mary and seeks out a priest. The villagers read the drought as the Virgin's departure from a people who fell away from God, and the rain on her return ends the film with praise of God.
advisories:
A shooting before a wedding, a death in the bullring, the eve of battle; nothing graphic.

A postulant's several romances; nothing explicit.

The heroine renounces Christianity for a time and says so bitterly.

For teenagers and adults. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The miracle is a legend, not an approved apparition.

grey.question: The frame is a medieval Marian legend: Our Lady takes a runaway postulant's place in the convent until she repents and returns. That frame is told straight, with the empty pedestal, the drought, her prayer for forgiveness and the rain on her return, and the Legion of Decency rated the film A-II. But most of its two hours follow Teresa's romances with an officer, a gypsy, a bullfighter and a count, treated with sympathy, and for a time she bitterly renounces Christianity. Religious life is barely seen.

title: The Power and the Glory
decision: GREY: Identity from the BFI record and Wikipedia; the dialogue of the CBS broadcast (English, read 2026-10-12) shows a close adaptation of Greene. In its favour: the priest's theology of the sacraments is stated plainly and more than once (only he can give the people Christ's body and blood; it would not matter if every priest were as bad as he), he returns knowingly to a trap to bring confession to a dying man, and he dies after a prayer of contrition. Against it: the faults the Holy Office objected to in the novel (1953) are all kept, including the child conceived in drunkenness, haggling over baptism fees, the married Padre José refusing him confession, and his admission that he is not sorry for his sin. The pre-conciliar verdict stands as the reservation.
summary: Laurence Olivier plays Graham Greene's hunted whisky priest in this lavish CBS adaptation, with George C. Scott as the police lieutenant who means to stamp out the faith.
synopsis: In a Mexican state where religion has been outlawed, the last priest at large (Laurence Olivier) is a drunkard who misses the boat to safety to visit a dying woman. Padre José (Frank Conroy) has married under the law. A police lieutenant (George C. Scott), an idealist who hates the Church, takes hostages from the villages and shoots them. The priest finds the village where Maria (Julie Harris) is raising their sullen daughter, says Mass and escapes; jailed overnight for carrying brandy, he goes unrecognised and is freed with a coin from the lieutenant. Across the border he baptises for fees and plans for an easier life. A mestizo (Roddy McDowall) lures him back to a dying American gunman, who refuses confession. The lieutenant arrests him. Padre José refuses to hear his confession, and he is shot at dawn.
inclusion: This was one of the most expensive American television dramas of its year. David Susskind produced it for CBS at a reported cost of about $746,000, with a Mexican township built for the set and a cast that runs from Olivier and Scott to Julie Harris, Patty Duke, Keenan Wynn, Mildred Dunnock and Cyril Cusack; Dale Wasserman wrote the script. Greene's novel is one of the great Catholic novels of the century, and Olivier's priest, frightened and weak but faithful at the last, is the reason to see it. Scott's lieutenant is given his argument fairly. The reception was cool: the New York Times called it a milestone and a major disappointment. Surviving copies are of poor picture quality, some with the original commercials.
themes: Greene's subject is the priesthood itself: the sacraments do not depend on the holiness of the minister. The priest says it outright to the lieutenant: drunkard and coward as he is, he can still put God in a man's mouth and give him God's pardon. He stays because only he can bring the people Christ's body and blood, even as hostages die for him. The lieutenant's charge that the Church served the rich is answered with the priest's insistence that damnation is no fairy story. His last night is a prayer of contrition: he has served badly and asks that his death be an atonement. In 1953 the Holy Office judged the novel 'altogether adverse', finding that human wretchedness prevails over the power of God and that the portrait injures the priesthood.
history: Greene wrote the novel in 1938–39. On 17 November 1953 Cardinal Pizzardo of the Holy Office wrote to Cardinal Griffin of Westminster that the verdict on it was adverse, asking him to tell Greene tactfully, to urge more constructive Catholic writing and to secure corrections in future editions. Greene met Griffin in April 1954 and, the rights being with foreign publishers, passed on their names. No listing on the Index is recorded.
liberties: Dale Wasserman's script compresses the novel and gives the broken dentist, Tench, the opening scene. Coral Fellows becomes a girl who brings the priest food and loses her faith at ten, and a native child, not an adult, is the gunman's victim. The novel's closing scene, where a new priest arrives in secret, is replaced by the lieutenant's remark that the priest has more lives than he has bullets.
advisories:
The priest's drunkenness and the child he fathered are central; the conception is described, not shown.

Hostage shootings, the death of a child used as a shield, and the priest's execution by firing squad.

For adults and older teenagers.

The Holy Office judged the source novel injurious to the priesthood (1953); the adaptation keeps the priest's faults.

grey.question: This close adaptation of Greene's novel gives a strong statement of Catholic sacramental faith: a drunken, frightened priest who knows that only he can bring Christ's body and pardon to his people, goes back into a trap to hear a dying man, and dies after a prayer of contrition. But it keeps everything the Holy Office objected to in the novel in 1953: the child he fathered and is not sorry for, the haggling over baptism fees, and a married priest who refuses him confession. Viewers should weigh that pre-conciliar verdict.

title: The Red Danube
decision: PUBLISH: The National Legion of Decency classified the film A-I (its 1936–59 list on archive.org), a contemporary Catholic judgment. Independent secular sources (AFI Catalog, TCM, Jonathan Lewis at MysteryFile) establish a Catholic-centred story from Bruce Marshall's novel. The Spanish-dubbed dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the open points: the Mother Superior tells the dying Maria she has sinned gravely but been given time to repent, and Maria dies repentant, commending her soul to God; no priest is called. The colonel's return to faith is understated, voiced in his refusal of an order as a Christian.
summary: MGM's talky Cold War drama, from Bruce Marshall's novel, sets a fierce Viennese Mother Superior against a faithless British colonel enforcing the forced repatriation of Soviet refugees.
synopsis: Vienna, 1946. Colonel Michael 'Hooky' Nicobar, a one-armed British officer who lost his faith when his son was killed in the war, is billeted with his staff in a convent run by a formidable Mother Superior. His job is to hand Soviet citizens back to the USSR. His aide falls for a ballerina, Maria Buhlen, who turns out to be a Russian the Soviets want. Hooky hands her over, then watches the consequences: a Soviet professor kills himself rather than go back, and on Christmas Eve a train of starving refugees is dumped in the British zone. Maria escapes; Hooky and the nun hide her. The Mother Superior flies to Rome with him and sees the Pope. Hooky refuses an order to return Maria and is relieved of command. Cornered again, Maria throws herself from a window and dies repentant. Forced repatriation ends.
inclusion: It is one of the few Hollywood films of its time to put a nun's argument for God at the centre of a political drama. Ethel Barrymore's Mother Superior is no sweet sister: she is blunt, anti-communist and certain, she apologises when she has been uncharitable, and she spends the film working on Walter Pidgeon's lapsed colonel. Bruce Marshall, a Scottish Catholic novelist, supplied the source. The subject, the Allies' forced return of refugees to Stalin, was real and shameful, and the film says so. Its faults are plain. Critics in 1949 found it too long and too wordy, Variety complained of religious talk, and George Sidney, a musicals director, gives it little visual life. Angela Lansbury drew the best notices. It suits adults and older teenagers interested in the period.
themes: The drama is a conversion story. Hooky's unbelief is grief, and the film adds a pointed detail: his son's last letter said he had come to believe in God and had been received into the Church, which the father dismisses as empty formality. The Mother Superior holds that only men who have abandoned God could treat refugees as the Soviets do, and carries Hooky's complaint about official Christianity to the Pope. The reply she brings back is that God does not abandon man; man abandons God. When Maria throws herself from a window, the nun tells her she has sinned gravely but been given time to repent; Maria asks forgiveness and dies commending her soul to God. No priest is called. Hooky's return is quiet: he refuses an order as a Christian, or one trying to be.
history: In 1945–47 the British and American authorities returned Soviet citizens, including many who did not wish to go, under agreements made at Yalta; many were shot or sent to camps. Bruce Marshall (1899–1987), a Catholic convert, drew on this in Vespers in Vienna (1947). MGM shot background footage in Vienna and Rome.
liberties: The characters are fictional. The film compresses the end of forced repatriation into a single vote and a change of policy, and Hooky's promotion to carry out a humane line is a dramatic convenience. Its picture of Soviet officers is broad Cold War caricature, as reviewers have noted. The order's foundress, a saint said to have flown to Rome on an angel in 1585, is a comic invention.
advisories:
Two suicides: a professor shoots himself off screen, and the young heroine jumps from a window and dies; she repents before death, and her act is called a grave sin.

Refugees in distress; threats of deportation and imprisonment.

title: The Rite
decision: GREY: Identity from AFI and BBFC; treatment from Greydanus (Christianity Today), Moria (agnostic critic), KPBS and Den of Geek. Sound on the reality of the devil and the efficacy of the rite, but its horror content, the invented possession of the exorcist and an uncritical present-day setting are reservations a reader can weigh. Subtitles would settle whether Michael is shown giving sacramental absolution before ordination.
summary: Mikael Håfström's exorcism thriller, loosely drawn from Matt Baglio's book, sends a doubting American seminarian to a Vatican course and to an old Jesuit exorcist in Rome.
synopsis: Michael Kovak, a mortician's son, enters a seminary mainly to get away from the family business. Near the end of his studies he writes to resign, saying he lacks faith. After he ministers to a woman dying in a street accident, his superior, Father Matthew, persuades him to attend an exorcism course in Rome instead. There Father Xavier sends him to Father Lucas Trevant, a Jesuit with long experience, who is treating Rosaria, a pregnant teenager. Michael suspects mental illness and says so; a journalist, Angelina, is chasing the same story. Rosaria dies after a miscarriage, and then Lucas himself shows signs of possession. With Xavier away, Michael, still unsure what he believes, must perform the rite on his own mentor, and in doing so recovers his faith. He goes home, is ordained and is last seen hearing a confession.
inclusion: Steven Greydanus, writing in Christianity Today, called it probably the most sober and realistic treatment of exorcism in Hollywood history, and the most positive picture of the Church and Christian faith he could recall in a recent studio film. The first two thirds earn that. Exorcisms drag on for weeks, holy objects are not magic, and Michael's scepticism is given real weight rather than set up to be knocked down; Fr Lucas tells him to make friends with his doubts. The Roman settings, crucifixes and images of St. Thérèse and the Sacred Heart are used plainly. Anthony Hopkins is the reason to watch. The last half hour is weaker: Den of Geek and Moria both note the lurch into stock horror once Lucas is possessed, and most secular critics were unkind.
themes: The film argues the old point that belief in the devil leads back to belief in God: Michael cannot master the demon until he admits that he believes. The rite is shown as a prayer of the Church, said with crucifix, stole and holy water by priests acting under authority, and its power depends on faith rather than technique. Doubt is treated with respect but not as a resting place. Two weaknesses: the possession of a holy, experienced exorcist is a horror device with no basis in Baglio's book, and the film takes the present-day Church and its training course entirely at face value.
history: Matt Baglio's 2009 book The Rite: The Making of a Modern Exorcist follows Fr Gary Thomas, a California parish priest sent by his bishop to train as an exorcist in Rome, and his apprenticeship to an experienced Italian exorcist, Fr Carmine De Filippis. Thomas consulted on the film and called its exorcisms very accurate, with some expected licences. Baglio wrote the book partly to correct Hollywood clichés about exorcism.
liberties: The middle-aged parish priest of the book becomes a young seminarian without faith. Baglio, a male journalist, becomes Angelina, with a hint of romance. Fr Lucas is a composite based on De Filippis, and his possession, which fills the second half, has no equivalent in the book. The film opens by calling itself a true story; the end credits say only that it was suggested by the book.
advisories:
Sustained scenes of possession and exorcism: contorted bodies, facial markings, a possessed girl beating her pregnant belly, and a bloody miscarriage. Rated 15 by the BBFC and PG-13 in the United States.

A possessed priest strikes a child. Mortuary scenes, including a boy helping prepare his mother's body.

Blasphemous and crude sexual taunts from the possessed; one strong expletive.

No sex scenes. For adults and older teenagers.

Wikipedia's plot summary says Michael absolves a dying woman before his ordination, which only a priest can do.

grey.question: The Rite is a horror film with Catholic convictions. It takes the devil, the rite of exorcism and the authority of the priest seriously, but its climax rests on an invented device, the possession of a holy and experienced exorcist, and it piles up stock shocks, a bloody miscarriage and crude demonic taunts. It also takes the present-day Church at face value. Viewers should weigh whether the horror serves the faith or simply sells tickets.

title: The Silver Chalice
decision: GREY: An apostolic-age melodrama with a reverent conversion thread; Legion of Decency A-II; Motion Picture Daily (1954) records that Basil completes Christ's face only after learning the faith from Peter. The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) confirms the Eucharistic words over the cup, Simon Magus drawn from Acts 8, and Peter called the Christians' acknowledged leader, but also the weight problem: Peter is on screen for a few minutes near the end, Basil is never baptised, and much of the film is his entanglement with Helena after his marriage. Still borderline with REJECT (scope); kept GREY because the Last Supper cup and the apostles drive the plot.
summary: Paul Newman's debut: a Greek silversmith commissioned to encase the cup of the Last Supper finds faith among the apostles while Simon Magus plots to destroy it.
synopsis: In Antioch the young sculptor Basil is cheated of his inheritance and sold into slavery. Luke buys his freedom and takes him to Jerusalem, where the aged Joseph of Arimathea shows him the cup of the Last Supper and commissions a silver casing carved with the faces of the Apostles and of Jesus. Basil can carve the Apostles but not his Lord. He marries Joseph's granddaughter Deborra (Pier Angeli) so that her inheritance can go to the Church, while still drawn to Helena (Virginia Mayo), his childhood companion and now partner of the magician Simon (Jack Palance). Simon sets out to outdo Christ's miracles and destroy the cup before Peter. In Rome Basil meets Peter, who has been watching him in disguise, and at last carves Christ's face. Simon, claiming to be a god, tries to fly before Nero and falls. The cup is lost, and Peter foretells its return.
inclusion: It is worth knowing as a curiosity of the 1950s biblical cycle rather than as a good film. Warner Bros. spent heavily: CinemaScope, an Oscar-nominated score by Franz Waxman, and stylised, nearly abstract sets that Variety thought wrong for the period and Fortnight admired. Jack Palance sneers through Simon Magus, Pier Angeli is the devout Deborra and Lorne Greene plays Peter. Newman, in his first film, later called it the worst picture of the decade, and critics at the time largely agreed; Motion Picture Daily thought the long adaptation of Costain's best-seller drifted into religious soap opera. Its Catholic interest is the premise: the cup of the Eucharist kept as a relic by the first Christians, and a pagan artist who can carve Christ's face only once he has come to love him.
themes: The cup is introduced with the words of institution spoken over it, and Deborra sees a light around it that Basil cannot. His conversion is told through his art and is never formalised; no baptism is shown. He acquires a conscience through his Christian wife, meets Peter, who has watched him disguised as a porter, and hears him pray that Basil will one day see the face of Jesus. He finishes the carving only after asking Jesus to guide his hand. Simon Magus comes from Acts: baptised in Samaria, rebuffed by Peter when he offered money, he now preaches a religion that calls lust and hatred natural and good, and dies boasting that he is a god. Peter is called the Christians' acknowledged leader and heals a cripple. Little else of the Church's life appears.
history: Thomas B. Costain's novel was a best-seller of 1952, and the AFI Catalog records that Costain was pleased with how closely Lesser Samuels's script followed it. Basil, Helena and Deborra are fictional. Simon Magus appears in Acts 8, where he tries to buy the Apostles' power; the story of his attempt to fly in Rome comes from second-century apocryphal writing, not Scripture. The Grail as a relic kept by Joseph of Arimathea is medieval legend.
liberties: The plot is invented around legend. Simon dies through his own boast at Nero's court, refusing the hidden wire his trick depends on, rather than at Peter's prayer as in the apocryphal account, and Helena is forced to repeat the flight. Simon's fake Pentecost is presented as a miracle of Jesus. The Grail and its silver holder are not historical, and Luke, Joseph of Arimathea and Peter are drawn in as supporting characters.
advisories:
Swordplay, killings and Simon's fatal fall from a tower; Christians forced to build the tower; nothing graphic by modern standards.

Helena is a seductive figure in costumes revealing for the period. Basil marries Deborra for her inheritance's sake and, once married, keeps meeting and kissing Helena before he returns to his wife.

For older children and up. The Legion of Decency rated it A-II.

The Grail story is legend; the film presents it as fact.

grey.question: This is a costume melodrama built on legend: an invented silversmith, a love triangle and the medieval Grail, with Peter, Luke and Joseph of Arimathea in support. Its religious thread is reverent: the cup is introduced with Christ's words of institution, Simon Magus comes from Acts, and an artist carves Christ's face only after Peter prays that he will see it. But Peter appears only briefly, Basil is never baptised, and much of the film follows his pull toward Helena after his marriage. Take it as Hollywood legend, not a picture of the apostolic Church.

title: The Singing Nun
decision: GREY: The AFI Catalog and Motion Picture Exhibitor (Legion A-I and a 1966 review) establish a respectful convent drama with religious life in its pre-conciliar form and a nun who chooses obedience and the missions over fame. The 1966 classification comes months after the Council, so it is noted rather than decisive. The reservation is historical: the film presents itself as the story of a real nun whose life contradicted it (TCM).
summary: Debbie Reynolds plays a guitar-playing Belgian Dominican whose song 'Dominique' becomes a worldwide hit, in MGM's sweet, heavily fictionalised version of the Soeur Sourire story.
synopsis: Sister Ann (Debbie Reynolds), a young Dominican who loves to sing and play the guitar, leaves her convent near Antwerp for Samaritan House, a mission in a poor district of Brussels. There she befriends Dominic, a motherless boy whose unemployed, drinking father leaves him to his seventeen-year-old sister, Nicole, and she writes a song for him. Father Clementi (Ricardo Montalbán) brings her to Robert Gerarde (Chad Everett), a record executive who knew her at the Paris Conservatory. With the Church's permission she records an album, and 'Dominique' becomes an international hit; Ed Sullivan sends a crew to film her. Torn between success, Robert's interest in her and her vocation, she seeks Father Clementi's counsel. When Dominic is badly hurt in an accident, she prays for his recovery and promises to give up her music. He recovers, she gives her guitar to Nicole, and she leaves for a mission in Africa.
inclusion: This was MGM's family picture for Easter 1966, built on the surprise success of 'Dominique', the song a Belgian Dominican, Sister Luc-Gabrielle, recorded as Soeur Sourire. Reynolds sings it and the other songs well, Greer Garson is a calm Mother Prioress, and Harry Sukman's score earned an Oscar nomination. Motion Picture Exhibitor called it warm and appealing but found the story too pat to mean much, and TCM's Frank Miller records reviews that mocked its out-of-date wholesomeness. Its value now is as a picture of convent life in full habit at the very end of the pre-conciliar era, and as a story in which a nun chooses her vows and the missions over celebrity. It is sentimental, and it is fiction: the real nun's life went the other way.
themes: The film's question is vocation against celebrity. Sister Ann's music is shown as an overflow of her love of God, but the success it brings, and the attentions of a man from her past, pull her away from the obedience and hiddenness of her life. She turns to her prioress and her confessor, and she settles the matter by prayer and a promise: she offers up her music for the boy's recovery and goes to the missions. Poverty, obedience and charity to the poor are presented as the heart of religious life, and the convent is treated warmly and without irony. Nothing reported in it is contrary to Catholic teaching.
history: Jeanine Deckers entered a Dominican convent as Sister Luc-Gabrielle, and her record 'Dominique', issued under the name Soeur Sourire, became an international hit in the early 1960s. TCM reports that the Church agreed to the film only if her story was fictionalised, and that she left the Church in 1967 to pursue a singing career. Her later life was troubled, and in the 1980s, facing ruin over a tax claim, she died by suicide with her companion.
liberties: Almost everything is invented: the slum mission, the boy Dominic and his family, the record executive who knew her before her vows, the Ed Sullivan crew as shown, and the departure for Africa. The real Sister Luc-Gabrielle did not give up her music for the missions.
advisories:
A child's accident and a father striking his daughter; no other violence.

Nicole has posed for provocative photographs to pay the rent; they are discovered, not dwelt on.

The Legion of Decency rated it A-I (general patronage) in 1966.

The real nun later left the Church; the film is fiction.

grey.question: This is a pious, sentimental fiction: its nun gives up fame for obedience and the missions, and the Legion of Decency passed it for all audiences. The reservation is historical. It is sold as the story of the real Singing Nun, Jeanine Deckers, but its plot is invented, and her life went the other way: she left the Church in 1967 and died by suicide in the 1980s. Take it as a parable of vocation, not as her biography.
