title: The Story of the Vatican
decision: PUBLISH: The Legion of Decency classed it A-I (March of Time-RKO), the pre-conciliar Catholic judgment, and Film Bulletin's August 1941 review gives an independent account: splendid, sepia-toned photography and Sheen's fervent narration, but long and repetitive for general audiences. AFI's synopsis (via TCM) establishes the content: Vatican City's institutions, art and the career of Pius XII. Nothing post-conciliar is involved.
summary: The March of Time's feature-length tour of Vatican City under Pius XII, from St Peter's tomb to the post office, narrated by Mgr Fulton J. Sheen.
synopsis: The film opens with the career of Eugenio Pacelli: Secretary of State to Pius XI, visitor to the United States, and in 1939 the first pope crowned in public on the balcony of St Peter's. It then explains Vatican City as a sovereign state, independent since 1929, with its governor, its diplomatic corps of thirty-eight nations, its own radio station installed by Marconi, its currency, fire brigade, railway and post office. The Polyglot Press and the Osservatore Romano are shown at work, the latter noted as free of Mussolini's censorship. The camera moves through the Vatican Library and its manuscripts, Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling, Raphael's rooms, St Peter's Basilica and the papal crypts. It closes with the Noble Guard, the Swiss Guard, the Roman congregations and the pilgrims who come to Rome every year.
inclusion: This was one of only four full-length features made by The March of Time, and its crew, Jean Pagès and the cameraman Marcel Rebière, were given unusual access inside the Vatican in 1939. Film Bulletin praised the photography as splendid and noted that the whole film was printed in sepia, which gives even the newsreel inserts a warmth. Fulton Sheen, then the best-known Catholic voice on American radio, wrote and spoke the commentary, and the reviewer found it fervent and dramatic. The same reviewer warned that the film would seem long and repetitive to anyone looking for entertainment, and it is essentially an illustrated lecture. Its value now is as a record of the papal court and the Vatican of Pius XII as it looked on the eve of war, decades before the Noble Guard and much of the papal court were abolished.
themes: The film presents the papacy as a visible institution: a sovereign state with its own guard, press and diplomats, serving a spiritual office. The Pope is shown as successor of St Peter, whose tomb lies under the basilica, and as teacher of the world through the Polyglot Press and the Osservatore Romano. The Noble Guard, the Swiss Guard and the Roman congregations, including the one that handles liturgy and canonisations, are shown as parts of a working Church government. It is reverent in tone rather than devotional, closer to a travelogue and art film than to a sermon, and it makes no doctrinal claims beyond the Pope's office.
history: Louis de Rochemont's March of Time persuaded the Vatican in 1939 to allow a crew to film inside the city. Part of the footage became the two-reel issue The Vatican of Pius XII, released in February 1940. The rest was expanded into this feature, which RKO released on 18 July 1941; Spanish, Portuguese and French versions were also made. In 1942 Italy's Centro Cattolico Cinematografico modelled its own film on the Pope, Pastor Angelicus, partly on these two March of Time films.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable; suitable for all ages.

A documentary of about 54 minutes, slow and lecture-like by modern standards.

title: The White Sister
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from the AFI Catalog; independent treatment from Bret Wood (TCM), James Patterson (Silent London) and the contemporary New York Times review (via Wikipedia). The heroine takes final vows believing her fiancé dead, refuses his plea to petition for release when he returns, and forgives the sister who wronged her. The Church advised on every religious scene. Vows upheld; no doctrinal problem. Pre-Legion, so no rating.
summary: Lillian Gish plays an Italian heiress who becomes a nun believing her soldier fiancé dead, and keeps her vows when he comes back, in Henry King's location-shot melodrama.
synopsis: Angela Chiaromonte loves Captain Giovanni Severini, but when her father dies her jealous half-sister, the Marchesa di Mola, burns his will and turns her out penniless. Giovanni leaves for Africa promising to marry her on his return. His camp is attacked and reported massacred. Grief-stricken, Angela is cared for by nursing sisters and decides to become one of them. Giovanni, in fact a prisoner, escapes and reaches Italy on the very day she takes her final vows. He finds her at the hospital and tries to persuade her to ask the Pope for release. She refuses. When Vesuvius erupts, the dying Marchesa confesses in a church and Angela forgives her; Giovanni drowns saving others, and Angela prays to be reunited with him in heaven.
inclusion: Bret Wood opens his TCM essay by saying that seldom has a Hollywood film embraced the Catholic Church with so much passion and reverence. It was shot on location in Rome, Naples and Algeria, with Church officials advising on each religious scene; Gish visited more than thirty enclosed communities before choosing one as a model, and the clothing ceremony took twenty-five hours to film. Ronald Colman, in his first major part, is excellent as Giovanni, and Gish gives a restrained performance that contemporary critics thought among her best. The New York Times found the opening love story among the strongest ever filmed but thought the later disaster plot weakened it, and the film is long at over two hours. It ran six months in New York and was a large commercial success.
themes: The centre of the film is the religious vow. Angela enters religion in grief, but once she has made her profession she treats it as binding, even when the man she loves returns and begs her to seek a dispensation. The film presents her fidelity as right and costly. Wood notes the near-fetishistic detail with which it stages her symbolic marriage to Christ. The church scene at the climax, where Angela forgives the dying sister who ruined her, is a plain picture of forgiveness at the hour of death. The ending looks to reunion in heaven rather than on earth.
history: F. Marion Crawford (1854–1909), an American novelist who lived in Italy, published The White Sister in 1909 and adapted it for the stage with Walter Hackett. It was filmed in 1915, 1923 and 1933, and in Mexico in 1960. Henry King's version was made on location in Italy with Church advice and was a large commercial success.
liberties: James Patterson notes that the novel ends happily while the 1923 film ends with Giovanni's death. The African expedition, the will and the Vesuvius eruption give the story a scale the play lacked.
advisories:
A massacre in Africa (reported), a carriage crash and the eruption of Vesuvius, with deaths.

No sensual content beyond a few embraces between the engaged couple.

Silent, about 2 hours 20 minutes in its full length; shorter release versions exist.

Suitable for older children and up.

title: The White Sister
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and full synopsis from the AFI Catalog; independent treatment from Danny Reid (Pre-Code.com) and the contemporary Variety and New York Times notices (via Wikipedia). Angela takes final vows believing Giovanni dead, refuses to leave the order when he returns and begs her, and he dies holding her cross: the vows are upheld. Pre-Legion (no rating found). Reid's complaint that her vocation is unconvincing is a matter of craft, stated in the prose.
summary: MGM's sound remake moves Crawford's story to the First World War, with Helen Hayes as the nun who keeps her vows and Clark Gable as the airman who returns.
synopsis: Angela Chiaromonte, a prince's daughter, is about to marry an older banker when a collision with the car of a dashing lieutenant, Giovanni Severi, starts a romance. Her father catches them kissing and forbids it. Running to Giovanni, Angela crashes into her father's car and he is killed. Stricken with guilt, she sends Giovanni away, but pledges her love when Italy enters the war. Giovanni is shot down and reported dead. Angela enters a convent, trains as a nursing sister and takes her final vows. Giovanni has survived as a prisoner, escapes in a stolen plane and finds her at a military hospital. He begs her to leave the order; she refuses. He leaves, is shot down by German fire, and dies in her arms holding the cross she gave him.
inclusion: This is a polished MGM production, photographed by William Daniels, with Helen Hayes at the height of her screen reputation and Clark Gable in a part that, as TCM's account has it, was against type. Variety praised Hayes. Mordaunt Hall in the New York Times called it beautifully produced but less real than Henry King's silent version, and Harrison's Reports thought it lacked the earlier film's emotional pull. Danny Reid of Pre-Code.com is harder on it: a respectable, competent melodrama whose romance lacks chemistry and whose heroine's journey never quite convinces. It made a profit. The aerial war scenes borrow footage from Hell's Angels.
themes: As in the 1923 version, the subject is the binding force of religious vows. Angela enters the convent out of grief and guilt, and Reid finds that her spiritual journey is shown more as ritual than as inner change. But once professed she treats her vows as unbreakable, and the film supports her: when Giovanni sees her praying during an air raid, he understands that she no longer belongs to him. The Catholic rites, the veiling and the convent hospital are shown with care. The end, with Giovanni dying in her arms holding the cross she gave him, keeps the renunciation.
history: F. Marion Crawford published The White Sister in 1909 and adapted it for the stage with Walter Hackett. Henry King had filmed it in 1923 with Lillian Gish and Ronald Colman. MGM's remake moved the story from Italy's colonial wars in Africa to the First World War and the air war on the Italian front.
liberties: The novel's African expedition becomes air war on the Italian front. Angela's motive for entering the convent is changed: guilt over her father's death in a car crash replaces the destroyed will of the earlier version.
advisories:
Air combat, a fatal car crash and the hero's death from wounds.

The engaged couple kiss; later he pleads with her, now a nun, and they almost embrace.

Suitable for older children and up.

title: The World of Don Camillo
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred (a priest protagonist and Guareschi's speaking crucifix) and identity established (Wikipedia, Box Office Mojo). The English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) answers the rule (b) question in the film's favour: no Mass is shown or spoken of, Don Camillo wears the cassock, sets a boy to learn the Our Father in Latin, and answers to a bishop who calls himself old-fashioned. The crucifix speaks as Guareschi's Christ does, insisting on baptism, rebuking the priest's temper, bribery and card-sharping, and blessing him into exile; Don Camillo accepts the bishop's transfer as deserved. Reservation: a thin, Americanised remake whose comedy includes a gimmick skydiving wedding, girls roller-skating in church, and the priest's cheating and blackmail, played for laughs before Christ corrects them.
summary: Terence Hill directs himself as Guareschi's hot-tempered priest in a remake that moves his feud with the Communist mayor Peppone into the Italy of the 1980s.
synopsis: In a village on the Po, the parish priest Don Camillo and the re-elected Communist mayor Peppone (Colin Blakely) are old enemies who respect each other, and Don Camillo still talks with the crucified Christ in his church. He refuses to baptise Peppone's son with the name Lenin until Christ rebukes him. He goes poaching on a baron's land, hears Peppone's confession, and does penance by fasting. A football match between his 'angels' and Peppone's 'devils' is lost on a bribed penalty, and the bishop (Cyril Cusack) warns him. He befriends a lonely boy, Magrino, and his divorced mother. When Peppone secretly wins the football pools, Don Camillo extracts a gift for his youth centre. A violent rematch gets him sent to a mountain parish, and the village sees him off.
inclusion: Guareschi's stories were first filmed by Julien Duvivier in 1952 with Fernandel and Gino Cervi, and that film is the one to see. Hill, then best known for comic westerns, produced, directed and starred, working from a script by his wife, Lori Hill, and Guareschi's stories, and shot for five months in the Po valley. The talking crucifix is kept and well used, and the contest between priest and Communist is still the engine of the comedy. Critics were cool. The Filmtv.it reviewer found it a weak directing debut, glossy and Americanised, and argued that the stories lose their point without the post-war struggle between Christian Democrats and Communists. It is mainly of interest to admirers of Hill, or of Guareschi, who already know the originals.
themes: In Guareschi the crucifix is the priest's conscience, and the remake keeps that. Christ tells Don Camillo that he instituted baptism and that a child denied it through spite would be the priest's fault; he forgives those who crucified him and expects the same of his priest; he reminds him that the road to hell is paved with good intentions, that priests serve the king of heaven and not of money, and that winning at cards by trickery is confusing good with evil. Don Camillo does penance for poaching, admits he deserved the bishop's punishment, and goes into exile with Christ's promise to be with him wherever he goes. The parish is shown through baptism, confession, blessings and a procession; no Mass appears.
liberties: The setting moves from the late 1940s to the early 1980s, with football, roller skates, skydiving and cheerleaders in place of the post-war political battles. The football match, the pools win, the baptism and the priest's exile to the mountains come from Guareschi's stories, recombined, and a divorced American mother and her son are added.
advisories:
Comic brawling, a violent football match and a punch-up in the church doorway.

The Filmtv.it reviewer objects to scantily dressed girls on roller skates and cheerleaders at the children's match; the priest lets the girls skate in the church.

The priest bribes, cheats at cards and blackmails for comic effect; Christ rebukes him each time.

Probably suitable for families with older children, with those caveats.

title: Thérèse Martin
decision: PUBLISH: La Cinématographie française's review (June 1939), an independent trade notice, describes a simple, tactful and discreet life of St Thérèse from childhood to her death in the Carmel, with an invented parallel story of a childhood friend whose failing marriage is saved by the saint's death. The trade press reported that Cardinals Verdier and Gerlier saw it in Rome in 1939 and expressed their satisfaction. The Legion of Decency's A-I for 'Saint Therese of Lisieux (French)' (1940-41) very probably refers to this film but is not proved; it is not relied on. Thérèse was canonised in 1925.
summary: Maurice de Canonge's 1939 life of St Thérèse, with Irène Corday in her first role, follows her from a devout childhood to her death in the Lisieux Carmel.
synopsis: Thérèse Martin, the youngest daughter of a devout family in Normandy, loses her mother as a small child and grows up in an atmosphere of fervent faith with her father and sisters. Determined to give herself to God young, she enters the Carmel of Lisieux, where her sisters have gone before her, and lives a short, hidden life of prayer and sacrifice, ending in a long final illness. Alongside her story the film follows a fictional childhood friend, Elisabeth d'Estranges, who grows up, marries, and sees her marriage come close to ruin through misunderstandings. Thérèse's death holds Elisabeth back on the brink and saves her household. The cast includes a scene with Pope Leo XIII, recalling the young Thérèse's petition in Rome to enter the Carmel early.
inclusion: This was the first sound feature about St Thérèse, made fourteen years after her canonisation and shot partly in Lisieux and the Normandy countryside, with a score by Jacques Ibert. La Cinématographie française praised Maurice de Canonge's tact, discretion and feeling with a difficult subject, and the radiance and serenity that the young Irène Corday brought to the role in her screen debut. It was a popular success in France at the start of the war, and later in Canada. The parallel story of Thérèse's friend is a period device to show the 'little way' bearing fruit in an ordinary life, and the reviewer thought it cleverly done. The film is hard to see today, and its interest is partly historical: an early, reverent attempt to film a modern saint whose family and sisters were still alive.
themes: The film's subject is Thérèse's hidden holiness: a pious home, an early call, the Carmel, suffering accepted and offered, and death. Contemporary publicity called her role a love brought into a world of hatred and quoted José Germain on her offering of herself as a holocaust in the Carmel, the language of Story of a Soul. The invented sub-plot puts the doctrine of the communion of saints into narrative form: Thérèse's death and intercession save a friend's marriage, as she promised to spend her heaven doing good on earth. Nothing in the reviews suggests any departure from the Church's understanding of her.
history: Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in 1873, the youngest of nine children of Louis and Zélie Martin. After her mother's death the family moved to Lisieux. She asked Leo XIII in 1887 for leave to enter the Carmel at fifteen, entered in 1888 and died of tuberculosis on 30 September 1897. Story of a Soul made her known worldwide. Pius XI beatified her in 1923 and canonised her in 1925.
liberties: Elisabeth d'Estranges, her family and the doctors in the cast list are inventions, and the friend's marriage plot is wholly fictional. The trade review's summary compresses the Carmel years; details of the papal audience and the illness are not known from the sources.
advisories:
A long final illness and death.

A marriage in difficulty (the fictional sub-plot); nothing explicit is reported.

Suitable for all ages, but slow for young children.

suitability.note: The only distressing matter is Thérèse's long final illness and death, which is shown quietly. The pace is slow for young children, but there is nothing frightening or improper.

doctrine: Thérèse was beatified by Pius XI on 29 April 1923 and canonised by him on 17 May 1925, twenty-eight years after her death. In 1927 he named her, with St Francis Xavier, patron of the missions, although she never left Carmel. She asked Leo XIII for permission to enter Carmel at fifteen during the 1887 pilgrimage, and the Bishop of Bayeux and the Carmel then admitted her in April 1888. Her teaching, the 'little way' of spiritual childhood, is a path of confidence, small offerings and charity for ordinary souls. It rests on the Church's doctrine of grace, merit and the communion of saints, and it does not replace the sacraments, the virtues or the counsels. Her Carmelite name was Sister Thérèse of the Child Jesus and of the Holy Face. Her feast was kept on 3 October in the pre-1960 calendar.
production: The film was made by Atlantic Film and Les Productions Françaises Cinématographiques and distributed by Filmsonor. Maurice de Canonge directed it from a script by Henry Dupuis-Mazuel, Maurice Gleize and Robert Hennion, with music by Jacques Ibert. Irène Corday played Thérèse, and the Russian émigré actor Nicholas Malikov played Leo XIII. The picture ran 90 minutes and was released in France on 7 June 1939.

title: Thunder on the Hill
decision: PUBLISH: Legion of Decency A-II, a contemporary Catholic rating, and the English dialogue (read 2026-10-12) settles the two open questions. The order is plainly Catholic (the convent of Our Lady of Rheims; Mass, Latin prayers, the rosary, a bishop), and the nun's vocation and her reading of events as Providence run through the dialogue rather than decorating it. Her disobedience is named by her as a fault, the one order she refuses is to burn evidence that could save an innocent life, and the ending reconciles her with her superior on the note that being right is worthless without humility. It is a mystery first, and the record says so.
summary: Douglas Sirk's rain-soaked convent mystery: a nursing nun, haunted by guilt, sets out to prove that a condemned woman sheltering from a flood is innocent.
synopsis: Floods cut off the roads in Norfolk, and a convent hospital becomes a refuge. Among those stranded is Valerie Carns, convicted of poisoning her brother, a composer, and on her way to be hanged, with the officers escorting her. Sister Mary Bonaventure, who runs the hospital and entered religion troubled by her own sister's suicide, becomes convinced Valerie is innocent. She crosses the flood by night to fetch Valerie's fiancé and, against her Mother Superior's orders, presses on with the case, refusing to burn a love letter that points elsewhere. A lay sister's hoard of old newspapers yields the clue. The poisoner is the hospital's doctor, who lures Sister Mary into the bell tower and attacks her; the bell is rung, help comes, and he is taken. Sister Mary and her superior are reconciled.
inclusion: Sirk made it a few years before his great Universal melodramas, and it already shows his eye: William H. Daniels's dark, noir-style photography of the storm-bound convent is its chief pleasure. Claudette Colbert is better than her unlikely casting as a nun suggests, Gladys Cooper is a formidable Mother Superior, and Ann Blyth overplays the condemned girl. The source is Charlotte Hastings's 1949 West End thriller Bonaventure. Reviewers agree it is well made but contrived, with the murderer obvious too early. What lifts it is that the nun's inner story is taken seriously: her guilt, her pride in being right, and her superior's patient correction are as much the subject as the poisoning. The Great Detectives reviewer credits it with treating religion more seriously than most Hollywood films of its day.
themes: Sister Mary's vocation is bound up with guilt over her sister's suicide, and the film asks whether that guilt has become charity or only a need to be right. The convent is plainly Catholic: Our Lady of Rheims, Mass, Latin prayers, a rosary said over the potato peeling. She disobeys her Mother Superior, admits there is no excuse for it, and refuses only the order to burn a letter that could save a condemned woman. The superior answers her doubts with Christ's words that he chose his disciples, not they him. The ending reconciles them: the superior apologises, Sister Mary gives the credit to a lay sister, and the last word is that being right is a gift wasted without humility. Facing the murderer, she tells him to think of his soul.
liberties: The story and characters are fictional, taken from Hastings's stage thriller, whose device of a flood stranding a condemned prisoner in a convent the film keeps. Reviewers note that a nun conducting a murder investigation against the police and her superior strains belief.
advisories:
A murder by poisoning is the subject; a violent attack in a bell tower; a newborn in danger.

A sister's suicide is discussed as back-story.

No sexual content of note; an adulterous affair is part of the solution and is not shown.

A nun repeatedly disobeys her superior; the film treats this as a fault and ends in reconciliation.

Legion of Decency A-II (adults and adolescents).

title: True Confessions
decision: GREY: The AFI Catalog and Wikipedia establish identity and content; TCM (David Sterritt), Canby and Ebert (via Wikipedia) are independent. The Bishops' Conference of England and Wales note is post-conciliar and used for content only. Not REJECT: the portrait of clerical worldliness is a moral drama that ends in repentance, not an anticlerical thesis. Reservations: grave sordid material and the institutional portrait; adults only.
summary: Robert De Niro's ambitious monsignor and Robert Duvall's detective brother collide over a 1948 Los Angeles murder in a grim study of clerical worldliness and its cost.
synopsis: In 1948 Los Angeles, Monsignor Des Spellacy (Robert De Niro) is the cardinal's fixer, running the archdiocese's building programme with the help of Jack Amsterdam (Charles Durning), a former hoodlum turned contractor. His brother Tom (Robert Duvall), a homicide detective who once collected payoffs for Amsterdam, deals with the death of a priest in a brothel and then the murder of a young woman found cut in two. The trail leads to a stag film and to Amsterdam. The cardinal's office decides to honour Amsterdam as layman of the year and then drop him; Tom confronts him at the banquet and will not stop, whatever it costs Des. The scandal ends Des's career, and he asks for a remote desert parish. Years later Tom visits him there; Des, dying, tells him the ordeal was his salvation and shows him their graves.
inclusion: Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne adapted Dunne's novel, and the film has a real feel for the Irish Catholic Los Angeles of the 1940s: Cyril Cusack's cardinal, the banquets and building drives, the brothers' shared past. De Niro plays Des with almost total restraint; William F. Buckley thought him miscast, and Duvall is the livelier of the two. Vincent Canby praised it highly, while Roger Ebert thought it never finished its story. The Bishops' Conference of England and Wales calls it one of the best portrayals of a diocesan priest torn between administration and pastoral work. Its subject is a priest who loses the world and finds his vocation, and that is told seriously, if obliquely, inside a hard-edged crime story.
themes: The Catholic subject is vocation corrupted by worldliness and recovered through humiliation. Des is not a bad priest in the obvious sense; he is an administrator who has made the Church's prestige and buildings his work, and he covers scandal in its name. His fall sends him to a poor desert parish, and the frame shows him at peace there, dying, telling his brother that what destroyed his career saved him. The archdiocese is shown as powerful and compromised, with money and political ties, but the Church itself is not shown as false; its ritual is filmed with care, and the story belongs to a priest's repentance.
advisories:
A murdered young woman's mutilated body, cut in two, and an explicit investigation of the crime.

Prostitution, a pornographic film, a priest who dies in a brothel, and frank sexual talk.

Strong language and some violence.

Adults only (R in the US; 15 in the UK).

The archdiocese is shown as worldly; some Los Angeles priests refused the production access to their churches.

grey.question: The film's arc is a priest's repentance: an ambitious monsignor loses his career in a scandal and finds his vocation in a poor desert parish. But it is told through a sordid murder case, with a mutilated body, a stag film, a priest who dies in a brothel and much crude talk, and it shows an archdiocese run on money and connections. Viewers should weigh whether the repentance at its centre justifies the material; it is strictly for adults.

title: A Day in the Life
decision: GREY: Catholic-centred and established by the Cinemateca Portuguesa's programme note (Manuel Cintra Ferreira, quoting Comencini, Palmieri and Aristarco) and the Italian and English encyclopaedia entries: enclosed nuns shelter wounded partisans, one nun is drawn to leave the cloister with them, the Germans shoot the nuns in reprisal, and the film ends refusing vengeance. Its treatment of the cloister and of the nun's temptation, and the political frame of Church and Left reconciled, are not independently assessed in any source I found, and no contemporary Catholic rating was found. Reservation, not PUBLISH, until the dialogue is checked.
summary: Blasetti's post-war drama about a community of enclosed nuns who shelter wounded partisans, are tempted and divided by their presence, and are shot by the Germans for it.
synopsis: Late in the war, a band of partisans hunted by the Germans takes refuge in a convent of enclosed nuns, who regard the presence of men in the enclosure as a sacrilegious violation. They try to keep apart but must nurse a badly wounded man, and the mother superior recognises in him the man who years earlier killed her husband. Allied bombing traps everyone together in the cellars, where the men and the nuns begin to understand one another, and one young nun wants to leave with the partisans. When they have gone, the Germans discover what the nuns have done and shoot them in reprisal. The partisans return with the Allies and want revenge on the prisoners, but the dead nuns seem to ask for none. The one surviving nun, out of her mind, keeps repeating that none of us knows what we do.
inclusion: Blasetti, best known for historical spectacles under Fascism, made this in 1946 with a writing team that included Cesare Zavattini and Diego Fabbri; it competed at the first Cannes festival and won Nastri d'argento for direction and photography. Contemporary critics were divided. Guido Aristarco praised an intensely dramatic human story free of rhetoric; Luigi Comencini complained that it sacrificed the nuns as characters; Eugenio Palmieri called it a star vehicle rather than neorealism. Manuel Cintra Ferreira, introducing it at the Cinemateca Portuguesa, calls it melodrama rather than neorealism and singles out the ending, a single fixed shot in which the shooting of the nuns is heard while a German officer walks away, as one of the best things Blasetti did. It is a rare film that takes the enclosed life as its subject.
themes: The film sets the enclosure, prayer and the vow of separation from the world against the corporal works of mercy. The nuns break their seclusion to nurse the wounded, the mother superior must care for her husband's killer, and the community pays with their lives. The ending turns away from revenge, and the surviving nun's refrain echoes Christ's prayer for those who 'know not what they do'. Against this, the cellar scenes show the nuns drawn towards the men and their cause, and one sister wanting to abandon her vows; the sources do not say how the film resolves her temptation. The film also offers the Church and the Resistance as reconciled in one national suffering.
history: Enclosed communities in German-occupied Italy in 1943-45 sheltered Jews, escaped prisoners and partisans, and several religious houses suffered reprisals. The film's convent and its story are fictional, a more dramatic variation on Vittorio De Sica's 1942 comedy Un garibaldino al convento.
advisories:
The shooting of a community of nuns (heard, then their bodies shown); war violence and bombing.

A nun is tempted to leave the cloister with the partisans.

Suitable for teenagers and adults.

The film presents the nuns' breach of enclosure for charity as heroic; its handling of the nun's temptation is not established.

grey.question: This is a film about enclosed nuns who give their lives for charity, and it ends by refusing revenge. But the cellar scenes, where the nuns are drawn towards the partisans and one sister wants to abandon her vows, have not been assessed by any source we found, and it is not clear how the film judges her. Its political frame, Church and Resistance united, also deserves a reader's attention. A check of the dialogue would settle whether the cloister is honoured or quietly questioned.

title: A Missionary
decision: GREY: Identity is secure (French visa 16734; Wikipedia citing Crisp's critical filmography; cinefiches). Content is known only in outline: a young priest's disillusion at a West African mission, from a script credited to a priest, Father Bernier (an interested source). No contemporary review or Catholic rating has been opened. Unverified; a Radio-Cinéma or Centrale Catholique notice, or the Credic study in Mission et Cinéma, would settle it.
summary: Maurice Cloche's colour drama, written with a missionary priest and shot in West Africa, follows a young missionary whose dreams of heroism give way to hard daily work.
synopsis: Père Jean Maurel (Yves Massard), a young priest, arrives at a mission in French Guinea expecting a heroic destiny. What he finds is routine: thankless daily work, slow results and the difficulty of building a real relationship with the people he has come to serve. He works under an older missionary, Père Gauthier, played by Charles Vanel, alongside a lay brother, Brother Timothée (Albert Préjean), and another priest, Père Duval (Jacques Berthier). The film follows his disillusion and his effort to understand the place; the sources opened do not describe how the story resolves. It was shot on location in Guinea and Cameroon, in Eastmancolor, with photography by Claude Renoir.
inclusion: Cloche made Monsieur Vincent (1947), and in Aristide Leucate's phrase was saddled with an absurd reputation as the official Catholic director; this is one of the films that earned it. The screenplay is credited to a priest, Father Bernier, so the film comes from inside the missionary world. Its subject is unusual for a mission film: not martyrdom or adventure but a young priest's disappointment at how small and slow the work is. Claude Renoir's colour location photography is a draw, and Vanel and Préjean head a strong supporting cast. A commenter on the French reference site cinefiches calls it a beautiful film for a religious audience, now hard to find. No critical review has been located.
themes: The film concerns the missionary vocation as it is lived rather than imagined: the priest's romantic idea of heroism has to give way to patience, obedience to his superior and daily service. The relation between the mission and the African population is the other subject, and summaries speak of his struggle to build a harmonious relationship with the people. How the film presents the sacraments, catechesis and conversions, and how it treats colonial rule and local religion, is not documented in the sources opened.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable is reported; content not fully documented.

Probably suitable for older children and up.

A colonial-era mission film; its picture of African customs and religion has not been checked.

title: Miracle of the White Suit
decision: GREY: Identity (Wikipedia citing Bentley and Carlos Aguilar's Guía del cine español; CEC medal) and plot (Santiago Aguilar's account; Decine21) are established. No contemporary Catholic rating or detailed assessment of the treatment of the First Communion has been found. Unverified.
summary: Rafael Gil's melodrama of a poor Castilian boy who will not make his First Communion without the white suit his dying mother promised him.
synopsis: In a village in Castile, Polonio tries on the white suit he will wear for his First Communion, and his poor friend Marcos looks on with envy. Marcos's mother promised him such a suit as she was dying, and he will not make his Communion without one. His campaign to get it takes him down a crooked road: he lies to his father, betrays his schoolmaster's trust, runs away to Madrid and even wishes for the death of the richest woman in the village. Betrayed by his brother, he takes clandestine work on the slag heap of a foundry and loses an arm in an accident. Only then does the press take up his story, and public sympathy gets him his suit.
inclusion: Rafael Gil and the producer-writer Vicente Escrivá were the leading makers of Catholic films in 1950s Spain, and this co-production with Italy's Lux Film is typical of their work: a child, a sacrament and a good deal of pathos. Cecilio Paniagua's black-and-white photography won the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos medal, and the Basque composer Jesús Guridi wrote the score. Decine21, a present-day Spanish review site, gives it 4/10 and calls it a social drama with a child's sensibility. Santiago Aguilar's retelling suggests the climax is staged as a spectacle of public compassion. It is little seen today.
themes: The sacrament is both the occasion and the question. The film turns on a boy who makes his First Communion conditional on a fine suit, and on what that desire leads him to: lies, betrayal, an evil wish against a neighbour. Whether the film presents this as vanity to be corrected, or as a poor child's right finally honoured, is not clear from the sources. The promise to his dying mother gives the wish a filial piety, and the loss of his arm a sacrificial colour. How the Communion itself is staged, and what part the parish priest plays, is not documented.
advisories:
A child is badly injured in an industrial accident and loses an arm.

A dying mother; poverty; a child's lies and dishonesty.

For older children with an adult.

The story ties a child's First Communion to getting a costly suit; it is worth discussing what the sacrament is for.

grey.question: A poor village boy refuses to make his First Communion without the white suit his dying mother promised him, and lies, betrays trust and finally loses an arm in a foundry before public sympathy gets him the suit. The film comes from Spain's leading Catholic film team and is plainly Catholic in intention. But no contemporary Catholic rating or detailed review has been found, so it is unknown whether it treats the boy's fixation as vanity corrected by grace or makes the suit, rather than the sacrament, the reward.
